Frasers closes in on Harvey Nichols rescue deal
sub_title: Frasers Group is reportedly finalising a rescue deal for Harvey Nichols that could be announced as early as Thursday, with commitments covering jobs, suppliers and the luxury retailer’s London head office under discussion.
article_content: Frasers Group is reportedly finalising a rescue deal for Harvey Nichols that could be announced as early as Thursday, with commitments covering jobs, suppliers and the luxury retailer’s London head office under discussion. According to Sky News, the owner of Sports Direct, Flannels and House of Fraser has spent several weeks in negotiations with FTI Consulting, Harvey Nichols’ adviser and expected administrator. The deal could be completed through a pre-pack administration, with Frasers buying Harvey Nichols’ business and assets after the retailer briefly enters administration. No agreement, however, has been confirmed so far, and NEXT remains a rival bidder. Frasers is understood to be considering a 12-month commitment to keep Harvey Nichols’ London head office, alongside wider commitments to protect jobs. It is unclear whether any employment guarantee would cover all of the retailer’s roughly 1,200 UK employees. The group is also reportedly willing to clear unpaid sums due to Harvey Nichols’ brand partners and suppliers. Those commitments are central to negotiations after some luxury labels raised concerns about Frasers joining the sale process. One source told Sky News that Frasers was prepared to acquire all Harvey Nichols stores except potentially its Dublin store, although discussions over the estate have continued. Its seven-store UK and Ireland network comprises the Knightsbridge flagship, large-format locations in Edinburgh, Birmingham, Leeds and Manchester, plus smaller stores in Bristol and Dublin. Keeping almost the entire estate could preserve more of the physical network than some earlier scenarios involving an acquisition by NEXT. When the retailer entered the process in July , it was understood to be weighing up options including keeping the regional stores open, or only acquiring the Harvey Nichols brand and intellectual property. Frasers and NEXT remained the leading contenders after a late-July bid deadline . Gordon Brothers also submitted an offer , while Dubai-based Chalhoub Group and India’s Reliance Retail examined possible bids. The talks follow Harvey Nichols’ warning that it could collapse without a rescue deal . The accounts for the year ending 29 March 2025, filed on 7 August, used a non-going-concern basis, reflecting directors’ conclusion that the business was unlikely to continue trading normally over the following 12 months. The department store has posted losses in each of the past five years. The retailer’s latest accounts highlighted its financial difficulties. For the full group revenue fell £184.8 million from £204.8 million in the year to the end of March 2025, while losses before tax widened to £49 million from £34 million. Its London store saw sales drop from £78 million to just under £69.5 million in the same period. The purchase price would be separate from the £50 million to £60 million that prospective buyers were asked to provide in order to fund refurbishment of its Edinburgh store, international expansion, digital development and management’s wider turnaround plan. Mike Ashley, Sports Direct founder and a major Frasers shareholder, has previously described reviving Harvey Nichols as a “huge challenge” . Speaking to the Financial Times last week, he said: “If it was a little bit tough before, it is in a death spiral now.” Ashley estimated that Harvey Nichols would sell for less than £40 million, excluding future investment. A completed Frasers transaction would end 35 years of ownership by Sir Dickson Poon’s family, which appointed FTI Consulting to oversee the sale in June.

article_title: The Interview: Founder Aimee Smale on building Odd Muse, one timeless piece at a time
sub_title: At just 22, Aimee Smale launched her clothing brand, Odd Muse, from her bedroom during the Covid-19 pandemic. What began as a personal project has since
article_content: At just 22, Aimee Smale launched her clothing brand, Odd Muse, from her bedroom during the Covid-19 pandemic. What began as a personal project has since grown into a significant fashion business, becoming a $30 million brand with a one-million-strong Instagram following and retail spaces in London and New York. Smale’s rapid rise as a young founder saw her named under the Forbes 30 Under 30 list in 2023, but she says the origins of Odd Muse can be traced back to a simple frustration with the fashion industry. Speaking to TheIndustry.beauty, Smale explains that she felt there was a gap between trend-led fashion and true investment dressing. "Everything was either disposable or completely inaccessible. I felt all that was being offered to younger women was the throw away fashion culture, we were being spoken to like we just needed an outfit for the weekend, no one was designing capsule pieces at a mid luxury price point," she says. This gap became the foundation for Odd Muse: creating elevated, timeless pieces at a more accessible price point. Smale believes the brand’s early growth came from addressing that genuine need in the market. "I wanted to create a brand that felt elevated, intentional and timeless, but still wearable and relevant to everyday life," she adds. With limited resources at launch, Smale says her own belief in the idea and her story as a founder became a big part of Odd Muse’s identity. "From the very beginning, I knew I had no marketing budget or real experience, but I had my story. I was a 22-year-old who genuinely believed I was onto something. I was willing to leave my job and invest everything I had into building it. That level of conviction naturally became part of the brand’s voice," she reveals. Since launch, Odd Muse has focused on creating wardrobe staples intended to last beyond a single season, from structured tailoring to versatile everyday pieces. "It’s a more considered way of dressing and buying. Also, from a brand perspective, it builds trust. When customers invest in Odd Muse, they know it won’t feel irrelevant in three months and that’s incredibly powerful," notes Smale. Maintaining relevance while staying true to the brand’s core identity remains a key consideration. Rather than constantly reinventing, Smale says the business has focused on carefully expanding into new categories. "One thing about Odd Muse is, we’re still so new to this! For example, we only just launched Knitwear in year four. I think bringing what our customers love about the brand into new categories and really taking our time category by category is one strategy," she says. This measured approach has allowed the brand to evolve while maintaining consistency. "Our customer is slowly on this journey as we evolve into a legacy brand, I think that’s how we continue to keep it fresh and exciting. We take our time with everything we do, we don’t try and do it all at once and our customer comes with us," shares Smale. "Meanwhile, our core silhouettes stay consistent. Some styles that we have been running for the last three to four years continue to be 50% of our whole business. That’s what we’re trying to achieve when we’re designing, something that can be relevant and continue to sell. It just proves our mission." Beyond product, Smale credits community-building and strong storytelling as key parts of Odd Muse’s development. Remaining self-funded has also influenced how the company operates. "We treat our audience like a community, not just customers. That means consistency, transparency, and bringing them into the journey - whether that’s product development, behind-the-scenes or brand decisions. It’s not just about selling; it’s about building a world people want to be part of," she explains. "I think the founder strategy I fell into helps. For years, not a lot of customers have been able to put a name to a face when it comes to established fashion brands. I’ll always proudly be 'that odd muse girl'." From its beginnings online, Odd Muse has expanded into physical retail, with stores designed to strengthen the connection between customers and the brand. While digital remains a key driver of global growth, Smale says stores provide an opportunity for customers to experience the product in person. "Our physical spaces allow customers to fully understand the product: fit, fabric, quality and that deepens trust. But also, an invite to experience the Odd Muse universe IRL," she highlights. "The two channels really complement each other: digital drives discovery and retail builds connection." The brand opened its Covent Garden store in 2023 following a successful pop-up, before expanding with a New Bond Street location in London. Smale says the two spaces serve different purposes: Covent Garden is more high-energy and community-focused, while New Bond Street reflects the brand’s ambitions in the luxury market. "New Bond Street is a three-storey townhouse on London’s most prestigious shopping street, inviting our community off Oxford Street and onto a luxurious street they may not have previously been able to shop on regularly," adds Smale. The brand has also expanded internationally with its Mercer Street store in Soho, New York, which Smale describes as an important milestone for Odd Muse’s US growth. "This was a huge step change for the brand, it heightened our credibility, and was huge for US growth. I’ve never seen a UK self-funded brand take a step like that before. I still pinch myself!," Smale reveals. Looking ahead, she says future retail expansion will be approached carefully, with a focus on locations where there is already a strong customer base. "For us, retail isn’t about opening as many stores as possible, it’s about opening the right spaces that genuinely add to the brand," she says. Reflecting on her journey as a young female entrepreneur, Smale says some of her biggest lessons have centred around trusting her instincts, developing strong leadership skills and building resilience. "My biggest learnings are probably to trust your instinct early and not wait for permission. Also, building the right team is everything. As you scale, your role changes completely - it becomes less about doing and more about leading," she notes. "And resilience. There’s always another challenge, but that’s part of building something meaningful. I always credit myself for how many times over the years where I have just got back up again. My failures have been my biggest lessons." For aspiring founders, Smale’s advice is to begin before everything feels perfect. "Start before you feel ready. You don’t need everything figured out - you just need a clear idea and the willingness to learn quickly," she suggests. "Also, focus on building something with depth. It’s easy to start a brand, but much harder to build one that lasts." As Odd Muse continues to grow, Smale’s ambition remains focused on creating a globally recognised fashion brand built around longevity. "We want to continue expanding internationally, strengthen our core collections, and deepen the brand experience across every touchpoint - online, offline, and community," she concludes. "Ultimately, it’s about longevity. I want Odd Muse to be a brand that people come back to for years."

article_title: The Interview: The Materialist's co-founder Liv Khan on why deadstock fabric is a sourcing opportunity, not a compromise
sub_title: The Materialist is building a business around turning a structural problem across fashion manufacturing – surplus fabric – into a scalable sourcing channel for brands at every level of the market.
article_content: The Materialist is building a business around turning a structural problem across fashion manufacturing – surplus fabric – into a scalable sourcing channel for brands at every level of the market. Liv Khan, who co-founded The Materialist together with Lavinia Santovetti in 2024, says the platform now holds over 10,000 fabric varieties in its showroom, with fabric rolls available at various quantities, from 30 to 3,000 metre lengths. The Materialist's business proposition is simple, yet pioneering. The platform connects fashion houses, designers, students and "other visionaries" with high-quality fabrics that have gone un-used in a manufacturing process. A staggering 25% of fabrics that are produced end up being unused, so there is no shortage of stock. Most importantly, the platform isn't just inspiring a more circular textiles ecosystem – it's scaling it. The commercial model of the business is built around repeat supply rather than one-off collaborations, with core fabrics, such as plain black wools and white cotton poplin, forming a core part of the offer alongside seasonal and luxury pieces. Recent pop-ups with LVMH-backed Nona Source and Vivienne Westwood have raised its profile, but the brand has its sights set on far more. In this interview, Liv addresses misconceptions around deadstock quality and scale, explains why fashion has historically handled surplus differently from other industries, and sets out what it takes for brands to move deadstock from capsule experiment to embedded sourcing strategy. Surplus fabric, new and unused material the industry calls deadstock, is a problem baked into the way fashion manufacturing works, with at least 25% of all fabric produced ending up unused. The causes are largely structural. Mills and brands routinely overestimate what they need, and minor but unavoidable production variations, such asa shade inconsistencies, slight weaving or dyeing defects, mean large volumes are rejected before a single garment is cut. Minimum order quantities compound the issue further: brands are locked into buying more than they require, and when external shocks like Brexit or Covid cause cancelled or reduced orders, that excess only grows. It varies. More brands are making genuine efforts to work through their own inventory, but doing so properly requires resources – stock needs to be catalogued, stored, and managed, which many brands don't have the capacity for. Beyond that, the most common routes are selling to jobbers at a low per–metre price, donating to students or educational institutions, or simply doing nothing – leaving stock to sit in warehouses for seasons, sometimes years. It's a problem that touches every level of the industry, from small independent labels to large high street retailers. What's been missing is a reliable, efficient way for brands to actually unlock the value sitting in their inventory – and to ensure it doesn't ultimately end up as waste. That's exactly what we provide. The biggest misconception is around quantity. Many designers and buyers assume deadstock means offcuts and end–of–roll remnants –a few metres of this, a few metres of that. In reality, we hold over 10,000 varieties in our showroom alone, many with more than 300 metres available and some with quantities as high as 3,000 metres - it's a genuine, scalable resource. The other persistent myth is around quality. Deadstock carries an unwarranted reputation for being defective or second–rate. Our fabrics are premium, luxury, and brand new – they simply weren't used by the original buyer. That's it. There's no hidden reason they're available. Both of these perceptions have begun to shift over the last couple of years as deadstock has moved further into the mainstream conversation around sustainable sourcing, but they still come up regularly – which is why education remains such an important part of what we do. The fundamental difference is how other industries treat surplus materials as an asset to be recovered, whereas fashion has historically treated it as a problem to be hidden or disposed of. In automotive, surplus components are rigorously tracked, returned to suppliers, repurposed across model lines, or fed back into manufacturing. Waste has a clear cost attached to it, and there are established systems for managing it. Interior design works similarly – surplus fabric and materials are catalogued, held as samples, or sold on through well–established trade channels. There's no stigma attached to it; it's just inventory management. Fashion, by contrast, has long had a cultural resistance to transparency around surplus. Admitting to excess stock – particularly in luxury – has been seen as a brand risk, which is partly why so much has historically been destroyed rather than redistributed. The supply chain is also far more fragmented, with fabric often held at both mill and brand level, with little visibility across either. What's changing is that sustainability pressure and cost pressure are converging. Brands that once wouldn't acknowledge their deadstock publicly are now actively looking for solutions, which is exactly where we operate. The infrastructure for managing surplus fabric properly is finally starting to catch up with the scale of the problem. Our range is broad enough that we're not really beholden to trends in the way a conventional fabric supplier might be. We carry everything from tailoring wools, cotton shirting, silks, lace and organza through to jerseys, technical fabrics, tulles, satins and faux furs: there's genuine depth across categories. What we do see is a natural seasonality in how clients come to us. Designers tend to arrive with a specific collection in mind, and we work with them across multiple departments within a brand – womenswear, menswear, kidswear, accessories – which means we need to hold a wide and varied inventory at any given time. A core part of our offer is continuity fabrics: plain black wools, white cotton poplin, and other wardrobe staples that never really go out of demand and can be worked into collections season after season. Alongside those, we regularly receive more special or seasonal pieces – bridal satins, for instance – and when something exceptional comes in, we make sure our network knows about it. There's always something new arriving, which keeps the offer fresh without it ever being trend–dependent. Supply is strong and constantly moving. We're receiving new stock all the time, which is necessary because good deadstock sells quickly – clients who know the market move fast when they see something they want. Quantities vary enormously, which is part of what makes us different from the offcuts–and–remants perception we touched on earlier. We hold anywhere from 30 metres up to 3,000 metres on a single article, which means we can genuinely service brands at scale, not just independent designers looking for a few metres to sample with. It really depends on the client and where they are in their process. Some arrive with a very specific brief – a swatch they need to match, a particular weight or composition – and we work to find the closest possible option from what we hold. But the most exciting and, we'd argue, most impactful way of working is when a whole design team comes in at the very beginning of the design process and uses our inventory as a starting point for their collection. Rather than deadstock being a last–minute substitute or a sustainability add–on, it becomes the foundation – collections are built around what's available, which is how it should work. When clients engage with us that way, there's far more scope to embed deadstock meaningfully into the core of the brand's sourcing strategy. It also tells us something about their intentions – these are the brands making a genuine, considered commitment to more sustainable sourcing, rather than ticking a box. That's the kind of relationship we find most rewarding, and frankly, it produces better results for everyone. It was a brilliant collaboration and Nona Source are a fantastic partner – they're doing important work in proving that deadstock and luxury are not mutually exclusive, which is a message the industry still needs to hear. Our approaches are closely aligned in many ways, but where we differ is in the breadth of what we offer. We work with brands holistically – clients can come to us to source deadstock fabric, but they can also use us to sell their own excess inventory, or participate in our donation programmes supporting emerging designers and students. It's a full circle solution rather than purely a sourcing platform, which means brands can address both sides of the problem: what they need to buy and what they need to clear. The Vivienne Westwood pop–up was a real highlight for us, and there's plenty more in the pipeline. We have a whole wishlist of brands we're hoping to work with over the next year – household names that we believe will genuinely help bring deadstock into the mainstream conversation. Beyond fashion, we're also increasingly working with theatre, film and TV, which is a really exciting space for us, as well as expanding into the interiors world. Both industries have a huge appetite for quality fabric and a real appreciation for what deadstock can offer. We don't want to give too much away just yet, but watch this space! Experimentation is easy; integration is the hard part. A brand can dip into deadstock for a capsule collection, generate some great press around it, and then quietly go back to their usual supply chain. Scaling it requires a genuine shift in how a brand approaches the design and sourcing process. The brands that make it work at scale are the ones that stop treating deadstock as a constraint and start treating it as a creative starting point – which brings us back to how we prefer to work with clients. When design teams come to us at the beginning of the process rather than the end, deadstock stops being a compromise and becomes a genuine foundation. There are also practical requirements: you need a reliable supply partner who can offer consistency and volume, not just one–off pieces. That's a big part of what we've built – continuity fabrics that can be reordered, and enough depth of stock across categories that brands can plan around us with confidence rather than treating us as a back up option. Ultimately, it comes down to intention. The brands that scale deadstock successfully are the ones where sustainability is embedded in the business, not bolted on for marketing purposes. You can usually tell the difference quite quickly. It varies by brand, and often comes down to individuals rather than departments. That said, design teams tend to be the earliest adopters – there's a natural creative excitement around working with something exclusive and designers really appreciate our quality. Interestingly though, once finance, production and buying teams understand what we offer, they're often just as enthusiastic – sometimes more so. Our fabric is competitively priced and available immediately, which solves real problems for those teams around budget, lead times and speed to market. The biggest shift is moving deadstock from an afterthought to a starting point. For too long it's been treated as a compromise – something you turn to when a preferred fabric isn't available, or when a brand needs a sustainability marketing story. That thinking has to change. The industry also needs to let go of the idea that working with what already exists is a creative limitation. The most exciting work we see comes from designers who treat constraint as a creative tool, not an obstacle. And practically, brands need to build sourcing timelines that allow deadstock to be genuinely considered from the beginning – not approached at the last minute when decisions have already been made. Treat fabric that already exists as the first option, not the last resort. The last few years have been about foundations – getting a real understanding of the industry and how it works; building our product, and establishing strong supplier relationships and partnerships. We feel confident those foundations are solid, and now we're ready to scale. The ambition is to become the number one destination for sustainable fabric sourcing – not just within fashion, but across industries. We're growing our supplier base, expanding our network, and building out some genuinely exciting new features on our platform that will make it far simpler for brands to find exactly what they need without having to manually browse thousands of products. A lot of what we're developing uses AI to automate processes that have remained stubbornly analogue for decades – sourcing fabric is still an incredibly time–consuming, human–intensive process, and we want to change that. There's a lot coming!

article_title: Rains names new CEO as co-founder steps back after completing brand transformation
sub_title: The former Conran Shop executive returns to the top job at Rains after helping reshape its sales operation, with Daniel Brix Hesselager shifting focus following an 18-month transformation programme.
article_content: Danish outerwear and lifestyle brand Rains has named Tom Bettinson as its new Group CEO, succeeding co-founder Daniel Brix Hesselager, who held the position for the last 18 months and led a large-scale transformation of the business. Bettinson takes over as CEO after serving as Chief Sales Officer since October 2025, with responsibility for the company’s sales channels. Hesselager will be moving into a Business Development role. Bettinson's appointment follows an 18-month business transformation led by Hesselager, who became CEO in early 2025. Under Hesselager, Rains transformed its product assortment, logistics, organisational structure, store concepts, customer experience and go-to-market strategies. "1.5 years ago, I stepped into the CEO role to lead a fundamental transformation of our concept and organisation. It was an extensive undertaking that required swift decision-making. Today, the foundation is in place, and the time is right to pass the baton," Hesselager said. Rains has also expanded its product universe, shifting to a broader consumer-oriented business model. Once primarily known for outerwear and bags, the company now offers a broad lifestyle portfolio that includes ready-to-wear, footwear, skiwear, activewear and home décor. Its product calendar has also moved from two principal seasons to four seasons and 12 annual deliveries. Monthly product drops are intended to keep customers engaged year-round and support the expanded assortment. “We have launched a series of strategic initiatives that will shape Rains for years to come. The priority now is ensuring excellence in execution and driving commercial success across all areas of the business. Tom is the right person to lead that next phase,” Hesselager added. Retail expansion has also been part of the plan. In May 2025, Rains opened its first Scottish store in Glasgow , adding a 1,076 sq ft unit on Ingram Street to its UK and Ireland footprint. Rain's new CEO, Bettinson, first joined the company in 2017 to establish its UK organisation and showroom. That operation later became the model for the brand’s international market integration strategy. Under his leadership, the UK wholesale business recorded seven consecutive years of growth and was Rains’ largest wholesale market worldwide between 2021 and 2023. He also supported the company’s early retail expansion by establishing three profitable London stores. Bettinson subsequently left Rains to become Head of Commercial at British design and interiors retailer The Conran Shop. Since returning as Chief Sales Officer in October 2025, he has helped restructure the sales organisation and advance growth plans in established markets and the Asia-Pacific region. “Rains has undergone a remarkable evolution in recent years. The company stands on a strong foundation, with a distinct brand identity, an expanded product universe, and an ambitious global strategy,” Bettinson said. “I am proud to have the opportunity to lead the next chapter and continue the growth journey that Daniel and the wider organization have set in motion.”

article_title: Peter Alexander to exit UK market after closing all three stores
sub_title: Australian sleepwear and lifestyle brand Peter Alexander is exiting the UK market, with its there stores having now closed, while its dedicated e-commerce website to shut down in the coming weeks.
article_content: Australian sleepwear and lifestyle brand Peter Alexander is exiting the UK market, with its three stores having now closed, while its dedicated e-commerce website is due to shut down in the coming weeks. The brand has now closed its stores at Bluewater in Kent, Westfield Stratford City and Westfield London in White City, although customers can still order pyjamas through its Australian website, which will offer shipping to the UK. In a trading update published by parent company Premier Investments, the company noted "sustained difficult trading conditions" and the "continued negative outlook for the United Kingdom economy" as reasons for the UK exit of its Peter Alexander brand. The parent company highlighted that it was now actively exploring international wholesale opportunities for the sleepwear brand, and was looking to expand its store estate in Australia and New Zealand with five new stores planned for in 2027, including a new flagship in Sydney. Peter Alexander entered the UK market in 2024 Peter Alexander entered the UK online in October 2024 before opening its three stores in November. At the time, the brand operated about 135 locations across Australia and New Zealand. The stores carried colourful sleepwear alongside candles, slippers, gift products and accessories for dogs. Around 20% of the wider assortment was based on licensing partnerships, with UK ranges featuring properties including Wicked, Winnie the Pooh and Paddington Bear. In an interview with TheIndustry.fashion shortly after the launch , founder and Creative Director Peter Alexander said the company intended to spend its first year learning about British demand before committing to further expansion. “It’s going to take a good 12 months to figure out what the UK is attracted to, what fabrics, what prints, whether they need separate designs, I’m going to learn a lot. I’m not coming here knowing everything, I have to learn,” he said. Alexander regarded service and sensory presentation as central to the physical format. “A store should not be a place where you just go, buy one thing and walk out,” he told TheIndustry.fashion in 2024. He also shared that the business was considering opening another 10 stores the following year, but stressed that none had been approved at the time. At that point in time, the UK had been identified as the brand's strongest potential market outside Australia and New Zealand. Speaking on the decision to now shut down the brand's UK presence, the Chairman of the brand's parent company, Solomon Lew, noted that Peter Alexander was “one of Australia’s and New Zealand’s most loved brands" and that "the decision to close our UK stores allows us to concentrate our investment where the brand is performing strongly." He added: “Our entry to the UK market was phased to allow us to test market response. Premier has strict store profitability and return hurdles and we allocate capital prudently on behalf of our shareholders. We have decided to channel our growth capital for Peter Alexander into our Australia and New Zealand markets, online and potentially capital-light wholesale which we continue to explore with global partners.

How I started in fashion: AKYN founder and Creative Director Amy Powney
sub_title: Powney speaks to TheIndustry.fashion about the respect she has for every role within the fashion industry, how the natural world continues to shape her creative process, and what it takes to build a fashion label with environmental responsibility at its core.
article_content: Amy Powney is one of British fashion's leading voices on sustainability. After nearly two decades at Mother of Pearl, where she has helped position the brand around conscious design and responsible production, she is now bringing that same philosophy to AKYN, the purpose-led fashion label she founded in 2025. Powney's route into fashion was not a conventional one. She spent part of her childhood living off-grid in a caravan in rural Lancashire, an upbringing she now recognises as inseparable from both her passion for fashion and the values that underpin her work today. Growing up so closely connected to the land instilled an awareness of the relationship between people and the natural world. That perspective has shaped her approach to materials, manufacturing and supply chains throughout her career. The connection between her childhood and her work is also explored in the 2023 documentary Fashion Reimagined, which follows her mission to create Mother of Pearl's first fully traceable, sustainably sourced fashion collection. Powney stepped down from Mother of Pearl in December 2024 and launched AKYN the following year . Building a new business allowed her to place traceability and environmental standards within its operating model from the outset. Her long-term ambition now is to develop AKYN into a regenerative business that supports workers, improves soil health and protects water quality. She also wants its methods to provide a practical blueprint that other fashion companies can follow. Powney speaks to TheIndustry.fashion about the respect she has for every role within the fashion industry, how the natural world continues to shape her creative process, and what it takes to build a fashion label with environmental responsibility at its core. I had a rather unique childhood as I grew up on off grid, in a caravan for some of my childhood in Lancashire. My father sunk a well where we got our water and we had no electricity for a while until he later got a small wind turbine. We did not have much and so me and my sister used our creativity to play. Art was my favourite subject in and out of school and I always knew creativity as a job would be my happy place. As a teenager I naturally rebelled my farm-working parents with off grid life. I wanted to conform, to fit it. At the time the Spice Girls were my inspiration and so I dreamed of tracksuits and suits with wonder bras and ‘fitting in’. My creativity took a turn towards textiles at school, and I became fascinated by fashion and subculture, and the status an outfit could bring. What I now realise is that everything has come full circle, with my upbringing and my passion for fashion coming together. My upbringing was the grounding in my understanding of how we give and take from the earth. That has since informed everything I have tried to do within my career, and why I strive to create without costing the planet. After graduating from university I joined Mother of Pearl (MOP) where I spent the first 20 years of my career. I really started from the bottom, from sweeping the studio floor to eventually working my way up to Creative Director. That journey immersed me in every part of the business almost immediately, not just design. I wasn't shielded from the boring or difficult bits, and looking back, that's exactly what gave me the grounding to eventually launch my own label AKYN. There are many, firstly that running a small scale business is hard, and that every single decision counts. I have a genuine respect for each job in the building, because I've done most of them and I've also learned that small teams have the power to move fast and be flexible. When I won the Vogue Fashion Fund while at MOP, I used the money to produce the brand's first fully sustainable collection, the subject of the documentary 'Fashion Reimagined'. This was the start of something for me. How slowly but surely, one step at a time, I reimagined what I was creating to take into account the people who make it, the way it is made and how this affects the planet we live on. I discovered which processes worked most in harmony with those things and which ones nurtured and didn’t take too much. At my new label AKYN I have taken that even further with the long term ambition to be a fully regenerative business. My collections are now my love letters to the planet and to the women that buy them and make them. It is my way of telling them we can and should do better, while making them feel good along the way. With AKYN it has been the freedom to build something from the ground up with transparency and ethics at its heart from day one, rather than retrofitting sustainability onto an existing system. There's something really energising about designing the whole model — not just the clothes. With every single business decision I make, I question how can I do this better? Is this right for the people, the planet? If it isn’t, we simply don’t do it. One of my favourite quotes is ‘I always wondered why someone didn’t do something about that, then I realised I was someone.’ This is how I now see my career and the advice I would love to give to my younger self. To become a conscious designer but to also be brave and bold as an industry leader, to support and nurture change. I would also want to tell my younger self to celebrate my background and not wait for permission to care about the things I care about. When I started, sustainability wasn't really part of the industry conversation, and I sometimes felt like I had to justify caring about it, or where I came from. I'd tell my younger self to trust that instinct sooner and louder and that being a working class northerner absolutely could have a place in the industry and I should have felt that loud and proud. I am always learning and AKYN is a work in progress, not perfection. We’re only a year old, though it feels longer with all the amazing support we have received. My ambition is for us to be the most responsible and traceable brand. What if you could create a collection which could leave no trace on the planet and could actually improve it, supporting local workers, regenerating the soil, and improving water quality? I want to provide a regenerative blueprint for other brands, to show that it can be done! That would be the ultimate success for me. There have been too many incredible people to mention but I am particularly drawn to women who refuse to accept the status quo. Who fight to challenge and change systems and who are willing to be the difficult voice in the room when it isn’t fashionable to be so. There are so many incredibly intelligent, passionate and strong women in this industry who are striving for a better system and I’m so grateful to my amazing advisory board who agreed to advise my journey, they are forever my inspiration and a source of trust and wisdom. As Anne Klein said "clothes won’t change the world but the women that wear them can". I like to see this quote as a powerful reminder that all of us that work in this industry have the power to change something within our work for the better, no matter how big or small.

Gap launches new denim campaign starring Malcom Todd and Inde Navarrette
sub_title: Gap has launched a new campaign for autumn under the title of ‘Denim on Your Own’, fronted by American musician Malcolm Todd and actress Inde Navarrette.
article_content: Gap has launched a new campaign for autumn under the title of ‘Denim on Your Own’, fronted by American musician Malcolm Todd and actress Inde Navarrette. Bringing together two rising talents from different creative worlds, the video is set to Malcolm Todd's original rendition of Robyn's anthem ‘Dancing On My Own’, created specifically for this new campaign. Mark Breitbard, President and CEO of Gap brand, said: “Gap has always been at the intersection of music, style, and culture - partnering with artists who bring a unique point of view and inspire people to express themselves. “From our heritage of iconic creative collaborations to championing today’s emerging voices, we continue to evolve how we show up in culture - building our own cultural currency through authentic partnerships, original storytelling and a clear point of view.” Fabiola Torres, Chief Marketing Officer of Gap brand, added: “For this campaign, we didn’t simply ask Malcolm to cover ‘Dancing On My Own’; we asked him to reinterpret the song through his own perspective. “That same spirit of making something your own defines Gap denim - a collection designed for people to find the fits and styles that feel uniquely theirs. It’s how Gap has connected with culture for generations, and how we continue to inspire originality today.” The campaign follows Todd and Navarrette through white boxed-out spaces, some with mirrors like a big changing room. Key denim styles include the ‘Mid-Rise Straight Taper Jeans’, as seen on Navarrette, and the worn-look ‘90s Loose Jeans’ (with a ripped knee), as sported by Todd. Oversized styles feature strongly, such as a boxy denim shirt worn by Todd. There’s also brown denim and duck cloth pieces, including a mini-skirt and matching jacket, as seen on Navarrette. Todd has become known for his catchy and playful approach to songwriting and production, with multiple songs having reached platinum status. His latest album, ‘Do That Again’, out via Columbia Records, debuted in the top five of the Billboard charts, and he is now preparing for his instantly sold-out 38-date North American tour, kicking off on 2 September. Commenting on the new campaign, Todd said: “To be part of a Gap campaign on such a big set, surrounded by so much creativity, and still feel like I could just be myself was really meaningful.” Navarrette is described as “one of Hollywood's most exciting rising talents”, fresh off the breakout success of ‘Obsession’, the critically acclaimed box office “phenomenon”. She said: “From the moment we started filming the Gap campaign, it felt like we were able to bring our own energy and personalities to the campaign. There was so much freedom to move, experiment and express ourselves.”

Tesco to relaunch dedicated F&F clothing website
sub_title: Tesco is gearing up to relaunch a dedicated F&F website in September, following the success it has had since it first relaunched F&F on Tesco.com in May 2025 with over 2,000 products.
article_content: Tesco is gearing up to relaunch a dedicated F&F website in September, following the success it has had since it first relaunched F&F on Tesco.com in May 2025 with over 2,000 products. The new website has been designed to make it easier than ever for customers to shop the latest F&F ranges, with a refreshed look and feel, enhanced functionality and a range of modern features aimed at improving the online customer journey. A Tesco spokesperson told TheIndustry.fashion: “F&F has become a go-to destination for stylish, affordable fashion that keeps pace with customers’ ever-changing needs. As our range continues to grow and inspire customers, we want the online experience to reflect that excitement. “The new F&F website will offer a more modern, intuitive and inspiring way to shop, making it easier than ever for Tesco customers to discover our latest collections and find the styles they love.” The relaunch marks a significant step forward for the F&F brand as Tesco continues to evolve its fashion offer to meet changing customer expectations and growing demand for accessible, affordable style. The initial online relaunch on the retailer’s main website (and its Clubcard app) followed Tesco’s decision to close its dedicated non-food website, Tesco Direct, in 2018. As a result, F&F primarily remained an in-store proposition, while its clothing was also available via Next (until January 2024). In April, Tesco reported stronger-than-expected adjusted operating profits of £3.15 billion for the year to 28 February, up slightly from £3.13 billion a year earlier. F&F clothing sales rose by 5.1% to exceed £1.2 billion, driven by strong demand in womenswear and standout performances from the F&F Active and F&F Edit ranges.

article_title: American Vintage heads east for 11th London store
sub_title: American Vintage has opened a 963 sq ft flagship store at 54 Redchurch Street in East London, marking its 12th UK store and 11th in the capital.
article_content: American Vintage has opened a 963 sq ft flagship store at 54 Redchurch Street in East London, marking its 12th UK store and 11th in the capital. It’s also the French fashion retailer’s second store in East London, adding to its existing location at 16 Horner Square in Spitalfields. Other stores are located at 105 King’s Road in Chelsea, 21 Floral Street in Covent Garden and 15 Hampstead High Street in North London, among others. The only American Vintage store in the UK outside the capital is at 62 King Street in Manchester, which opened last year. Spanning two floors and now showcasing American Vintage’s AW26 women’s, men’s and kids’ ranges of T-shirts, knitwear, joggers and denim, the new Redchurch Street space has been “conceived as a fluid journey, encouraging exploration and curiosity”. The layout breaks traditional codes, with menswear not confined to a single level, “allowing for a more flexible and intuitive customer experience”. Particular attention has been given to guiding visitors throughout the space. Light installations, including a distinctive light box, subtly lead customers upstairs, while a brightly lit staircase enhances visibility and flow. Contemporary elements contrast with the building’s original architecture, preserving the charm of its brick façade while integrating the American Vintage DNA without imposing it. Colour plays a central role in the concept. A pale yellow, first introduced by the brand in Barcelona, defines the exterior and part of the interior identity. The bold colour choice allows the store to stand out on the street while highlighting the product, particularly a curated selection of T-shirts echoing the same tones. Inspired by his trips to the US, Michael Azoulay founded American Vintage in Marseille, in the south of France, in 2005, originally with T-shirts before expanding the product lines. The brand is best known for its natural tones and monochrome pieces, as well as bold colours.

article_title: Mary Portas and Superdry's Julian Dunkerton join TheIndustry.fashion Fashion [Un]Bound Summit line-up
sub_title: The retail leaders will join senior executives from H&M, Topshop, Aligne and Toast at the one-day event in London this October.
article_content: Globally renowned retail expert Mary Portas and Superdry founder and CEO Julian Dunkerton have joined the speaker line-up for TheIndustry.fashion Fashion [Un]Bound Summit on 15 October 2026. The one-day event at The Forum, Leadenhall, will bring together about 200 fashion-industry leaders for interviews, presentations and panel discussions focused on changes in retail. Portas, the author, activist and founder of Portas Consultancy, will take part in a keynote interview with TheIndustry.fashion Co-founder Lauretta Roberts. The session will examine her approach to turning physical stores into places for human connection and building loyalty beyond individual transactions. She will also discuss how large and small brands can create consistent experiences across retail channels and develop a clear voice grounded in purpose. Portas has worked with British retailers including Harvey Nichols, John Lewis and Topshop during a career spanning more than 40 years. She is also known for presenting the BBC series Mary Queen of Shops and for her long-running advocacy for the British high street. Her consultancy works with businesses across fashion, beauty and lifestyle, with a focus on translating brand strategy into customer experience and company behaviour. Portas’s work on physical retail includes the government-commissioned Portas Review, published in December 2011. The review proposed measures covering town-centre management, business rates, vacant properties and local markets, while arguing that high streets should function as social and commercial centres. Julian Dunkerton CEO and Founder of Superdry Dunkerton’s appearance comes as Superdry continues its restructuring and repositioning. For the year ended 26 April 2025, the business posted a statutory profit after tax of £50.5 million, reversing a £67.7 million loss in the previous year. In November 2025, Dunkerton presented the Superdry & Co strategy at its Oxford Street flagship. The approach combines a revised mainline identity with the return of Bench and an offer spanning vintage and upcycled clothing. The Forum, Leadenhall: a brand new, state of the art event venue Additional confirmed speakers include some Of H&M UK and Ireland Managing Director Karen O’Rourke, Topshop and Topman Global Chief Marketing Officer Moses Rashid, Aligne CEO Ginny Seymour, Albaray CEO Paula Stewart and Toast CEO Suzie de Rohan Willner. See the full speaker line-up here . The summit programme will cover AI and new retail technologies, connected stores, circular business models, workforce development and creativity as a driver of demand. Tickets are on sale now, priced at £225 plus VAT, and are open to senior executives from fashion brands and retailers. Lunch, refreshments and a drinks reception are all included in the cost of each ticket. The event is staged at The Forum, Leadenhall, a brand new state-of-the-art event venue in the City of London, which will allow for an elevated and engaging experience for speakers and delegates alike. Industry suppliers can take part in the event through our flexible sponsorship packages. For more information, please contact partnerships@theindustry.fashion . TheIndustry.fashion Fashion [Un]Bound Summit is staged in proud partnership with global logistics expert Bleckmann, with StoryStream AI and Aptos sponsoring the programme.

article_title: Fashionphile opens first physical UK space with London pop-up
sub_title: Fashionphile, the US-founded luxury resale platform that acquired Luxe Collective in October 2025, has opened a pop-up in London’s Vauxhall.
article_content: Fashionphile, the US-founded luxury resale platform that acquired Luxe Collective in October 2025 - marking its entry into the UK luxury resale market - has opened a pop-up at China Works, 100 Black Prince Road in London’s Vauxhall. The move marks Fashionphile’s transition from a digital-first model to physical retail in the UK, offering customers the opportunity to shop its edit of authenticated luxury pieces in person, as it does with its established US retail model. The Vauxhall pop-up will showcase an edit of iconic pieces from Chanel, Hermès, Louis Vuitton and Gucci, including rare colourways, limited-edition designs, sought-after classics and hard-to-find vintage pieces. Appointments can be booked on the Fashionphile website . Created for established collectors and first-time resale shoppers alike, the space allows visitors to view pieces up close and appreciate their craftsmanship and condition, as well as receive support from Fashionphile’s UK team, which includes Luxe Collective co-founder Ben Gallagher, who is now Head of UK Brand & Growth. Gallagher said: “Opening the Fashionphile London pop-up is a major moment for us. We have established Fashionphile in the UK online, but there is nothing like seeing a piece in person, especially where craftsmanship and condition matter so much. “This is the first big step in bringing a physical retail experience we have developed across the US to the UK, and we are excited to grow from here.” Fashionphile’s US retail portfolio includes flagships, salons, stores and pop-ups. Depending on the location, these sites combine shopping with services such as selling, returns, order collection and drop-off. The company has not confirmed how long its London pop-up will operate. Its current offer focuses on in-person shopping and collection, while the wider UK business is being developed around online retail, authentication and direct purchasing from sellers. Luxe Collective was founded by brothers Ben and Joe Gallagher in 2018 from their parents’ bedroom on Merseyside. They sourced pre-owned designer items from the likes of eBay and Depop, then refurbished them and sold them via social media channels - building a following of millions. That led to an appearance on Dragon’s Den , which secured a £100,000 investment from entrepreneur Steven Bartlett, who took a 3% stake in the business. However, a devastating warehouse burglary in July 2024 saw around £500,000 worth of stock stolen . The company struggled to recover and subsequently closed down operations . Fashionphile, which was founded in 1999, came knocking soon after to launch Fashionphile UK, with B en and Joe Gallagher joining the new company and now leading its UK charge .

article_title: Pandora appoints new CFO to succeed long-serving finance chief Anders Boyer
sub_title: Pandora has appointed Paulo Garcia as its new Chief Financial Officer, succeeding Anders Boyer, who will retire after more than 14 years at the jewellery
article_content: Pandora has appointed Paulo Garcia as its new Chief Financial Officer, succeeding Anders Boyer, who will retire after more than 14 years at the jewellery giant. Garcia will join Pandora on 1 October and assume his new role on 1 December, with Boyer remaining until 31 March to support the transition, according to WWD. He brings extensive experience from Walmart Mexico and Central America, where he has served as Chief Financial Officer for more than five years. Chair Peter Ruzicka said the appointment follows "robust succession planning" alongside Chief Executive Officer Berta de Pablos-Barbier. De Pablos-Barbier described Garcia as "the ideal candidate to further strengthen and build on Pandora's financial performance" thanks to "an excellent track record and deep financial expertise from senior roles in the consumer goods industry". Prior to his role at Walmart, Garcia was CFO for Europe and Indonesia at Ahold Delhaize. He began his career at Unilever, where he spent more than two decades in senior finance roles, culminating in his appointment as CFO for Europe. Commenting on his new appointment, Garcia said he looked forward to unlocking "the next phase of growth" for a company he described as having "an attractive and unique business model with industry-leading margins and very high cash generation". He joins Pandora following a series of leadership changes over the past year. Chief Executive Officer Alexander Lacik retired in March, with Chief Marketing Officer Berta de Pablos-Barbier succeeding him . The company also named David Boynton, former Chief Executive Officer at The Body Shop, as Managing Director for Northern Europe , after spending nine months as Interim General Manager for Pandora’s Central Eastern Europe team. Most recently, Pandora appointed André Branch as President of North America. Branch brings more than 25 years of experience across global consumer, beauty and lifestyle brands, joining the company from his position as CEO of R.E.M. Beauty. As President of North America, Branch is leading Pandora's next phase of growth across the region, reinforcing North America as a key strategic growth engine for the business.

H&M's latest designer collaboration with WARDROBE.NYC has arrived
sub_title: H&M has today launched its highly anticipated collaboration collection with New York-based “luxury essentials” label WARDROBE.NYC.
article_content: H&M has today launched its highly anticipated collaboration collection with New York-based “luxury essentials” label WARDROBE.NYC. Founded by editor and stylist Christine Centenera and Australian designer Josh Goot, best known for his minimalist silhouettes, the new H&M x WARDROBE.NYC collection “translates the duo’s defining vision, distilling a pioneering decade into a single, definitive wardrobe”. The collaboration “draws on the WARDROBE.NYC archives” to present “a tight edit of archetypal urban style” , with a black mini-skirt, a long figure-hugging dress, a 90s-inspired oversized and padded cropped bomber jacket with accentuated shoulders, an oversized double-breasted overcoat, and voluminous black trousers that hit the floor. Ann-Sofie Johansson, Creative Advisor and Head of Design Womenswear at H&M, said: “The way every shape is so well considered - you can really feel how it will be to wear one of these garments just by looking at it. These are pieces that will be in your wardrobe for a long time.” Goot commented: “We wanted to create a capsule for H&M that was true to the wardrobe concept: a timeless and honest statement that was both essential and of the moment. This approach comes from our personal philosophy of dress – this approach has always been a vital part of WARDROBE.NYC, and you can feel it in the H&M collaboration.” Centenera added: “What we wanted, above all, was for all these pieces to become staples. You’re building the base of a wardrobe and mixing it back in – with things you already own and with pieces from the collection itself. That versatility was always the goal.” H&M will return to London Fashion Week on 17 September 2026 , partnering with photographer Nick Knight and digital fashion platform SHOWstudio “to reconsider how a runway show can work”.

article_title: Oxfam branches into fashion rental with 14-day online pilot
sub_title: The charity is testing whether distinctive donated garments can generate income through repeated hires, supported by rental and fulfilment specialist ACS.
article_content: Oxfam has launched an online clothing rental pilot, offering distinctive donated garments to rent from £22 for 14 days. The charity describes the initiative as the first rental service launched by a national UK charity. It began the pilot on 3 August, ahead of its annual Second-Hand September campaign. The Oxfam Rental platform offers hundreds of garments selected from donated stock, including vintage finds and directional designer pieces considered less suited to its standard shop rails. The womenswear launch range features a Balenciaga dress with blue-and-white spots, a tailored yellow jacket by Stella McCartney and a strapless black Dolce & Gabbana dress. Oxfam will use the pilot to test demand for hiring second-hand fashion, focusing on customers seeking event clothing without committing to a purchase. Each item is cleaned, pressed and prepared before dispatch, then returned for another customer to hire. Oxfam said the model could extend garments’ useful lives while generating income for its humanitarian and charitable work. Julie Tyrell, Head of E-Commerce & Retail Sustainability at Oxfam, said: “We see pieces come through our shops that you simply won't find anywhere else - and until now, the only way to own one was to buy it outright. Rental means people can access that wardrobe for the moment they actually need it and then not let it just sit in a cupboard afterwards "This is another interesting option which gives people access to pieces that are genuinely different, without adding to that wear-once cycle. If our pilot shows people want to rent rather than buy for a single occasion, that's a real shift in how clothes get used, not just where they come from." Customers can choose their rental dates online, with delivery and prepaid return shipping included in the price. Oxfam says orders need to be submitted at least 48 hours before the hire period begins, although it recommends arranging delivery four days before an event. The service currently covers UK Mainland addresses, excluding Northern Ireland and the Channel Islands. Garments cannot be collected from or returned to Oxfam shops because the online operation is managed separately. Fashion rental and fulfilment company ACS is supplying the operational infrastructure, including garment preparation, dispatch and returns. According to Oxfam’s service information, womenswear items are hand-checked and ozone-cleaned ahead of each rental. Menswear is supplied through a partnership with ACS and includes suits, tuxedos and other occasionwear. Measurements are provided online, while product pages for vintage womenswear without standard labels include garment dimensions. Customers do not need to dry-clean items before returning them. Late returns carry a £10 daily charge, while optional insurance covers accidental damage beyond expected wear. The platform does not currently allow renters to buy hired garments. Anthony Burns, Chief Operating Officer at ACS, said the partnership would help extend the life of clothing while supporting Oxfam’s fundraising. "We are incredibly proud to partner with Oxfam on an initiative that demonstrates the power of circular innovation to deliver both environmental and social value. ACS and Oxfam share a commitment to creating a more sustainable future for fashion, while ensuring positive outcomes for communities. “By providing the operational infrastructure behind Oxfam's online rental proposition, we are helping to extend the life of garments, increase access to more sustainable fashion choices, and support the generation of vital funding for Oxfam's important work around the world. This partnership is a strong example of what can be achieved when organisations come together with a shared purpose and a commitment to driving meaningful change," Burns said, The pilot adds rental to the charity’s existing shop (the charity operates 500 stores nationwide) and e-commerce operations as it prepares for Second-Hand September, its campaign encouraging consumers to choose pre-owned fashion.

article_title: Capri Holdings lowers outlook as Michael Kors weighs on growth
sub_title: Capri Holdings reported a 3.5% decline in first quarter revenue to $769 million for the period ended 27 June 2026, with weaker performance from Michael Kors offsetting growth at Jimmy Choo.
article_content: Capri Holdings reported a 3.5% decline in first quarter revenue to $769 million for the period ended 27 June 2026, with weaker performance from Michael Kors offsetting growth at Jimmy Choo. Michael Kors revenue fell 7.1% year-on-year to $590 million. On a constant currency basis, revenue declined 7.6%. The company noted that approximately $10 million of revenue was attributable to wholesale shipments occurring earlier than anticipated. Jimmy Choo delivered stronger results, with revenue rising 10.5% year over year to $179 million. On a constant currency basis, Jimmy Choo revenue increased 9.3%. Capri Holdings reported gross profit of $500 million, with a gross margin of 65.0%, compared with gross profit of $502 million and a gross margin of 63.0% in the prior-year period. The 200 basis point improvement in gross margin was primarily attributed to higher full-price sell-throughs and lower tariff rates compared with the first quarter of fiscal 2026. Looking ahead, Capri Holdings cautioned that results could vary materially from current expectations due to external factors, including changes in global economic conditions, additional tariff increases, inflationary pressures, shifts in consumer confidence and foreign currency fluctuations. The company now expects FY27 revenue of approximately $3.4 billion. The revised outlook reflects an estimated $50 million impact from lower-than-expected second-quarter revenue at Michael Kors due to inventory delays, a $50 million impact from softer EMEA trends related to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, and a $35 million impact from foreign currency headwinds compared with previous expectations. Chairman and CEO John D. Idol said: "Looking beyond fiscal 2027 the opportunity for Michael Kors and Jimmy Choo remains significant. "As our strategic initiatives continue to gain momentum, Capri Holdings is well positioned to drive sustainable growth, enhance profitability and create meaningful long-term value for our shareholders."

article_title: About Us
Nobody’s Child accelerates UK retail expansion with new Bath boutique
sub_title: Womenswear retailer Nobody’s Child is opening a new store at SouthGate Shopping Centre in Bath on 8 August 2026.
article_content: Womenswear brand Nobody’s Child is opening a new store at SouthGate Shopping Centre in Bath on 8 August 2026. The 1,500 sq ft space is the brand’s eleventh standalone UK boutique and fourth opening of 2026, having opened a new store in Cambridge last month, as well as stores in Harrogate in April and at Bluewater Shopping Centre in Kent in March. As with other Nobody’s Child stores, the new Bath boutique features reclaimed and vintage furniture and fittings, carefully curated by the brand’s in-house team. Jody Plows, CEO of Nobody’s Child, said: “Bath has always felt like a natural home for Nobody's Child. It's a city that values craftsmanship, creativity and considered style, qualities that feel closely aligned with our own approach to design. “We’re thrilled to open our doors here and welcome customers into the space to explore the collections up close, feel the quality of each piece and find styles made to be worn and loved season after season.” Camilla Holdsworth, Senior Retail Leasing Manager at SouthGate Shopping Centre owner British Land, added: “The arrival of Nobody's Child at SouthGate is a fantastic addition to our fashion offering and reflects Bath's growing appeal to brands looking to extend their reach beyond London. “With an affluent catchment, strong commuter links to the capital and a thriving visitor economy, we’re offering retailers access to a highly engaged customer base. “Our leasing strategy is focused on creating a balanced mix of national names and growing brands that keeps the destination evolving. Nobody's Child is a great example of what we're bringing to SouthGate to ensure the destination continues to evolve in line with customer demand.” To celebrate the opening, Nobody’s Child will host a special in-store launch event on 8 August, with gifts from two independent Bath businesses. Customers who make a purchase on the day will receive a complimentary cookie dough brownie from The Good Day Cafe, while the first 50 customers to spend £50 or more will also receive a complimentary mini bunch of flowers from Nice Bunch, while stocks last. Nobody's Child also recently strengthened its senior team with two new appointments spanning merchandising and retail, as the brand continues to grow. The brand appointed Jennie Clarke as Head of Merchandising and Amy Boswell, previously Executive Assistant to Nobody's Child CEO Jody Plows, as Interim Head of Retail. Clarke previously spent 13 years at Phase Eight, most recently in the role of Head of Merchandising. Prior to that, she had stints at both Reiss and Hobbs.

Fabletics launches second collaboration collection with Keke Palmer
sub_title: California-based activewear brand Fabletics has launched a second collaboration collection with actress, singer and TV personality Keke Palmer.
article_content: California-based activewear brand Fabletics has launched a second collaboration collection with actress, singer and TV personality Keke Palmer. Building on the success of the debut collaboration earlier this year, the 27-piece second Fabletics x Keke Palmer collection “brings Keke's playful perspective to elevated everyday style”, blending fashion and function through bold prints, on-trend silhouettes and fresh takes on everyday dressing. The collection features a mix of activewear and lifestyle pieces, including the ‘Cropped Trench Jacket’, ‘Easy-Twill Oversized Blazer’ and ‘Pleated Bermuda Shorts’. There are also versatile new bottoms, including the ‘Pull-On Barrel Pant’, the ‘On-the-Go Classic Mini Skirt’ and Fabletics' signature ‘Define PowerHold High-Waisted Leggings’ in bold new prints. Kate Williams, Vice President of Women's Design at Fabletics, said: “There's an undeniable relatability to how Keke moves through life, juggling work, wellness, motherhood and everything in between, just like so many women today. “This second collection was designed with them in mind, creating easy wardrobe staples that feel current, work as hard as they do and make it effortless to look put together.” Palmer added: “This collection is a true reflection of who I am and how I live my life. Between my career, being a mom and making time for my wellness routine, I'm always looking for pieces that let me do it all without sacrificing style or comfort, and Fabletics helps me do exactly that. “With this collection, I hope women who are constantly on the go, just like I am, feel confident knowing they can look good, feel good and take on whatever the day brings.” The Fabletics x Keke Palmer collection is available online in sizes ranging from XXS to 4X, with prices ranging from £12 to £202.
