Alo launches ‘pre-fall’ campaign starring Bella Hadid
sub_title: Los Angeles-based premium “studio-to-streetwear” brand Alo has today launched its latest campaign for ‘pre-fall’, starring American model and entrepreneur Bella Hadid.
article_content: Los Angeles-based premium “studio-to-streetwear” brand Alo has today launched its latest campaign for ‘pre-fall’, starring American model and entrepreneur Bella Hadid. Shot in Los Angeles by acclaimed fashion photographers Mert & Marcus and styled by fashion stylist Mimi Cuttrell, the campaign blends intimate portraiture with cinematic storytelling “to bring Alo’s vision of wellness to life”. Against the backdrop of the city that shaped both Alo and LA-born Hadid, each image captures a refined sense of ease through striking compositions, natural light, and understated styling - “offering an intimate look at Hadid in moments of strength and stillness”. Hadid wears a number of signature Alo performance essentials in the campaign, including the ‘Airbrush Better Together Bra’, the ‘Full Stride Micro Short’, the ‘Trail Sneaker’, the ‘High-Waist 7/8 Rebel Legging’, and the ‘Softsculpt Precision Tank’. Summer Nacewicz, EVP of Marketing & Creative at Alo, said: “Bella has been part of our community for years, and she represents the ultimate Alo girl who moves seamlessly between the worlds of fashion, wellness, and culture while remaining deeply connected to herself through it all. “Together, we've created a campaign that captures the spirit of Alo through Bella's personal approach to wellness, set in the city that shaped us.” Hadid added: “As I've got older, I've realised how important it is to create space for myself. Whether that's slowing down, moving my body, or just taking a moment to reconnect, those little rituals have become such a big part of how I take care of myself. “To me, that's what wellness is all about, and it's always been something I associate with Alo. That's why this partnership felt so authentic – it reflects a part of my everyday life that's been there for years.” Alo's parent company, Color Image Apparel, confirmed the sale of its wholesale T-shirt business Bella+Canvas in May, although a purchase price was not disclosed. That led analysts, M&A advisors, and investors to suggest that it could set up Alo Yoga for an IPO or sale . Co-founders Danny Harris and Marco DeGeorge, who each own 50% of Color Image Apparel, started the business in 1992 as a screen-printing and wholesale T-shirt operation. Alo Yoga was launched in 2007 in Los Angeles and has since grown into the more visible half of the parent company’s portfolio. Forbes reported in April 2025 that the parent company had revenue estimated at nearly $2 billion, with Alo's sales having roughly doubled over the prior two years and grown tenfold since 2020. Today, Alo operates more than 150 global stores, nine of which are located in the UK, with a product range spanning activewear, skincare, footwear and beauty. In June, Alo announced that it was further expanding its UK footprint with the opening of a tenth “sanctuary” in Edinburgh, located at 16-17 Multrees Walk, in November 2026, marking its first physical presence in Scotland.

article_title: Levi’s joins fashion line-up at Cribbs Mall as Moss upsizes
sub_title: Levi’s has become the latest brand to join the line-up at Cribbs Mall, having signed a five-year lease for the 2,265 sq ft former Moss unit.
article_content: Levi’s has become the latest brand to join the line-up at Cribbs Mall, having signed a five-year lease for the 2,265 sq ft former Moss unit. Meanwhile, Moss is upsizing to a 4,124 sq ft store on a 15-year lease at the shopping centre on the outskirts of Bristol. Levi’s follows recent arrivals including Rodd & Gunn, AllSaints and Animal, as brands continue to invest in Cribbs and its growing shopper audience. Moss has been a longstanding part of the Cribbs retail line-up, and its decision to relocate to a larger unit affirms the success it is having at the popular retail destination. The move will provide Moss with an enhanced trading environment, allowing it to showcase a wider range of products, including suits, formalwear, casualwear and accessories, while “delivering an enhanced shopping experience for Cribbs’ shoppers”. Cribbs Mall is owned by M&G Real Estate, with Sovereign Centros by CBRE appointed as operating partner to provide full asset management services. Katie Searle, Director of Asset Management at Sovereign Centros by CBRE, said: “We're delighted to welcome Levi’s to Cribbs. Securing another internationally recognised fashion brand further strengthens our retail mix and demonstrates the continued appeal of the centre to both new and existing occupiers. "At the same time, Moss's decision to relocate to a larger unit reflects the confidence that established brands continue to have in the centre. We are pleased to support the brand's growth by providing a space that enables it to enhance its offer and create an even better experience for our shoppers. “These latest deals highlight the momentum we are seeing in 2026 across the centre, closely following major upgrades from existing occupiers like Skechers and Crew Clothing.”

article_title: Make it British Live! to return with The London Textile Fair in 2027
sub_title: Make it British Live! will return on 12–13 January 2027 as a dedicated hall within The London Textile Fair, bringing British manufacturers and textile
article_content: Make it British Live! will return on 12–13 January 2027 as a dedicated hall within The London Textile Fair, bringing British manufacturers and textile suppliers together at London’s Business Design Centre. The trade show, founded by Make it British founder Kate Hills (main image), is returning after its planned 2020 edition was cancelled because of the pandemic. The collaboration will give brands, designers and buyers access to materials and UK production services during a single visit. The Make it British Live! hall will feature British manufacturers covering garments, knitwear, swimwear, lingerie and home textiles. Fabric printers, sample makers, pattern cutters and accessory manufacturers will also exhibit alongside the textile mills already represented at The London Textile Fair. Organisers said the combined January event will be the only UK trade show bringing fabric suppliers and manufacturers together in this format. Hills launched the show as Meet the Manufacturer in 2014, before renaming it Make it British Live! in 2018. Those five earlier editions drew more than 18,000 visitors, and the latest completed event was held at the Business Design Centre in 2019. “The London Textile Fair was the obvious choice for a collaboration with Make it British Live!” Hills said. “It is the biggest textile event in the UK and many of the mills that exhibited with us in the past already show there, and a large part of our audience is already walking through its doors to source fabrics, so it makes sense to offer them the option to be able to find local manufacturers in the same place.” She said renewed political attention on reindustrialisation made it important to bring different parts of the domestic supply chain into one venue. The London Textile Fair was established by John Kelley in 2007 and runs twice a year at the Business Design Centre in Islington. Around 350 exhibitors attend each edition, while the fair says it attracts approximately 5,000 professional visitors from high-street retailers, designer brands and independent businesses. John and Fergus Kelley, organisers of The London Textile Fair, said the partnership aligned with the event’s work connecting fashion businesses with suppliers from Britain and overseas. The show’s revival follows calls for more dependable demand for domestic manufacturers. A 2026 Fashion Roundtable report identified longer contracts, clearer demand forecasts, accessible contract sizes and improved payment terms as ways to support investment and skills. Hills also backed a recent industry call for British-made requirements in public textile contracts , starting with NHS and defence uniforms. The campaign said procurement rules should depend on where products are manufactured, not on where the winning supplier is registered. British manufacturers can register their interest in exhibiting through Make it British , while brands, designers and buyers can register to attend through The London Textile Fair .

article_title: Harrods returns to profit ahead of new COO arrival and further store investment
sub_title: Harrods’ latest accounts reportedly show a move back into profit after the previous year was weighed down by compensation and associated costs linked to compensating historic abuse victims of former owner Mohamed Al-Fayed.
article_content: Harrods’ latest accounts reportedly show a return to profit after the previous year was weighed down by compensation and associated costs linked to historic abuse suffered by victims of former owner Mohamed Al-Fayed. The financial results, which have reportedly been filed at Companies House but are not publicly available yet, come as the Knightsbridge luxury department store carries on with its womenswear redevelopment and looks to bring end-to-end operations under a new Chief Operating Officer role in September, According to Sky News, Harrods made a pre-tax profit of £84.9 million over the 52 weeks ended 31 January 2026. It also reported a turnover of £1.08 billion, representing a 1.2% year-on-year increase. The results show a marked increase compared with the £36.5 million pre-tax loss recorded in Harrods' financial results for the year ending 1 February 2025 . That year, turnover reached £1 billion, while operating profit fell from £213.9 million to £177.7 million. The department store noted that this prior financial performance reflected the department store's investment in employee salaries and higher distribution costs, alongside a transformation in its enterprise resource planning (ERP) system and the financial impact of the historical abuse victim redress programme. Managing Director Michael Ward said at the time that trading conditions across luxury remained challenging, but maintained that Harrods would continue investing in its customer offer and Knightsbridge store. "Our results demonstrate the resilience of our strategy of commitment to exceptional customer offerings and ongoing investment in this period across our Knightsbridge store including the continued redevelopment of our womenswear spaces and renovation of The Georgian restaurant," Ward previously said. "The current domestic and global economic environment means that current trading conditions in the luxury sector remain challenging. However, we remain confident in the strength of the business, and the resilience of the luxury sector, and that we will continue to drive progress towards longer-term growth and performance objectives." Harrods' previous accounts also showed that the department store had set aside £62.5 million for compensation and related costs involving survivors of historic abuse tied to Al-Fayed. That provision was not repeated in its most recent filing, although extra costs beyond the original amount were still recorded. The Harrods Redress Scheme was launched on 31 March 2025 and stopped accepting new applications on 31 March 2026. So far, it has compensated roughly 100 women who have come forward to make redress claims, while hundreds more are still seeking to reach settlements with the luxury retailer. The return to profit follows a wider restructuring of Harrods’ senior management . Chief Information Officer Andreas Efstathiou will become Chief Operating Officer in September, bringing its supply chain operations, facilities management, engineering and security function under one executive role. The structure also names Mark Blundell as Chief Retail Officer and Sarah Myler as Chief Brand & Reputation Officer. Geoff Weaver came into the business as Chief Financial Officer in 2025. Harrods has continued investing in its flagship during the period. In June, it opened its first International Designer Room within its first-floor womenswear redevelopment , with three interconnected rooms planned as part of the retailer’s broader Womenswear Masterplan.

article_title: Fenwick returns to sales growth as operating loss falls 40%
sub_title: Fenwick has cut its operating loss by 40% to £23.4 million for FY2025, with sales growth and a firmer gross margin supporting the first year of its three-year transformation strategy.
article_content: Fenwick has cut its operating loss by 40% to £23.4 million for FY25, with sales growth and a firmer gross margin supporting the first year of its three-year transformation strategy. After the first year of its three-year plan, Fenwick is closer to its target of sustainable profitability. Sales advanced across its eight stores and online operation, while margin edged higher despite pressure on the UK high street in the final quarter. Fenwick is directing further investment towards its Kingston and Brent Cross stores, following strong returns from Newcastle. Fenwick, the UK’s largest family-owned department store group, reduced its operating loss from £39.1 million to £23.4 million in the 52 weeks ended 30 January 2026. Gross sales increased by £7 million to £287.4 million, compared with a restated 52-week figure of £280.4 million in FY24. Like-for-like gross sales rose 2.5% across the retailer’s stores and online business. Turnover advanced from £177 million to £179.2 million, while gross profit margin edged up from 44.2% to 44.4%. Fenwick said the margin performance was maintained despite pressure across the UK high street during the final quarter. The retailer ended the year with a debt-free balance sheet and cash reserves of £63.4 million. Sian Westerman, Chair of Fenwick, said: “These results demonstrate that our strategy is delivering. Achieving a 40% reduction in operating loss in what remains a challenging retail environment is a significant milestone. "Fenwick is now in a stronger position than it has been for many years, and I am confident our three-year strategy will return the business to sustainable profitability.” Fenwick completed its migration to Shopify during the year, establishing a single customer interface across its stores and ecommerce operation. It also introduced data tools intended to improve customer insight and business reporting. The group also unified its customer relationship management database and launched MyFenwick Loyalty in September 2025, which has already recruited more than 350,000 members. Mia Fenwick, Executive Deputy Chair, said: “The first year of our three-year plan has delivered strong progress and demonstrates that our strategy is gaining real momentum. We have built stronger foundations for the business, invested in the customer experience and continued to evolve Fenwick as a truly omnichannel retailer." She added that the department store's loyalty system had been embraced by customers and that the integration of physical and digital channels was creating a more consistent customer experience. She also confirmed that further improvements are planned for Kingston and Brent Cross, while the Newcastle flagship continues to generate strong returns. Recent store activity has included selected activations across all eight Fenwick locations and a 500 sq ft Wax London concession at Kingston .

article_title: Backlash’s Katie Peake on why experiential retail matters to fashion now more than ever
sub_title: In an increasingly digital-first world, physical activations remain one of the most engaging ways for fashion brands to emotionally connect with customers, says Katie Peake, Co-Founder of brand experience agency Backlash.
article_content: In an increasingly digital-first world, physical activations remain one of the most engaging ways for fashion brands to emotionally connect with customers, says Katie Peake, Co-Founder of brand experience agency Backlash. Having worked in experiential advertising for the last 15 years, she has seen first-hand how the popularity of pop-ups has exploded. As customer expectations keep rising, Peake says the real challenge today is pushing the creative boundaries of what a pop-up can look like, and finding the many different ways it can deliver value for the brand. In this interview with TheIndustry.fashion, she reflects on why physical activations continue to be the most powerful form of capturing consumers’ hearts and minds, how Backlash’s creative-first approach sets the agency apart from competitors, and how experiential retail can solve real business problems while also sparking entirely new ways of connecting with customers. Since Peake launched Backlash in 2017, pop-ups have become such a fixture of fashion and beauty marketing that consumers now almost expect them. And there are good reasons for this. “Experiential is one of the only forms of marketing that actually can speak to people one-to-one,” explains Peake. For her, the format’s value lies in its ability to strengthen customer community and loyalty. Unlike a digital ad, which a consumer might engage with for a second or two, visiting an in-person destination demands dedicated attention from its audience and allows for a much more memorable interaction. Especially as, on average, a customer spends between five and 45 minutes inside a pop-up. “That's a really long time to have your target audience inside a physical advert, and I think that's what makes pop-ups so successful,” Peake adds. Backlash x Sunglass Hut's Covent Garden pop-up Personalisation and community building can be particularly impactful ways of ensuring a successful pop-up, since consumers are looking for experiences that are otherwise unavailable in a brand's existing physical retail or e-commerce spaces. In Peake’s experience, personalisation opportunities that work particularly well are product customisation services, or offering limited-edition merchandise that's not available anywhere else. Digital media, meanwhile, remains key to community building. It doesn't just help followers find the pop-up – it lets visitors share their experiences, strengthening community bonds both online and in-store. But experiential retail can go far beyond simply selling products. It can also help change the perception of a brand. One of Backlash's earlier projects, for example, saw it launch a denim laundrette pop-up with retailer NEXT. This addressed a difficult challenge: attracting younger shoppers to the retailer's jeans offering. By creating a pop-up space that was clearly meant to engage a younger audience, NEXT finally attracted its target customer. Visitors received one-to-one jeans consultations and could even exchange an old pair of jeans for a new one, with the activation exceeding its target-audience KPIs and follow-up survey benchmarks. Years of delivering brand activations have given Backlash a clear understanding of how the right combination of creative, design and execution drives impact. The agency has managed activations where visitors arrived at sunrise and queued for hours just to get a glimpse of the space. Today, the challenge isn't getting people through the door, Peake explains. It's making sure their experience stands out in an increasingly crowded market. For Backlash, that differentiation comes down to one thing: consistently creating a sense of wonder. Peake has worked in experiential marketing for more than 15 years, having started in traditional advertising across television, print and campaign production. Her move into physical experiences began when advertising agencies received briefs that did not fit their existing media departments. “I found this way more interesting than TV and print because I actually found thinking in a 3D world easier,” she shared. “It’s not an advert that you see on TV. It’s an advert that’s there for a few days, and people get to walk through.” Peake later became a Creative Director at 26, working on experiential projects for Coca-Cola and Nestlé. Together with her colleague Aarron Taylor, she built an experiential creative department from the ground up, later using this experience to launch Backlash in 2017. Following the launch, the pair quickly built strong relationships with both fashion and beauty brands, expanding its client base through word of mouth. Debenhams was among its first clients, with the retailer commissioning Backlash to deliver an entire wedding show. Despite a tight budget, Backlash delivered – and the project set the foundations for how the company still approaches work today. Central to Backlash’s value proposition is its identity as a creative-owned agency, with its co-founders infusing every project with a shared commitment to original thinking, innovation and thoughtful design. “We’re focused on creativity and we’re focused on the product that we create being high quality, standing out and being something we’re proud of,” Peake shares. This is also where the agency gets its name from: Backlash reflects the team's drive to do things differently from how other agencies might approach a project. Backlash x Marc Jacob's ' The Big Silver Box ' pop-up The creative-first ethos runs through every step of a Backlash project, starting with a thorough examination of the brief, intended audience and business problem before a visual concept is proposed. “We really pull apart briefs, and we really try and understand the brand before we come up with ideas,” Peake explains. “So we take quite a bit of time on that creative part, which sets us apart.” The creative team may spend around a week developing the initial direction, working closely with the client to ensure the concept is fully formed before the implementation begins. “A pop-up is really exciting because you can make it whatever shape, structure or materials you want,” shares Peake. “So the rulebook can almost go out of the window, as long as you're making sure it’s still got the look and feel of your brand.” By spending more time on the creative ideation, Backlash ensures that the activation not only brings a fresh perspective but also helps the brand stay ahead of the competition by creating a genuinely unique experience. With so many possibilities and unbridled creative freedom, it becomes even more important for the brief to be clearly defined. Peake’s top tip for any fashion brand eager to explore launching an activation would be to focus on just one objective – be that changing brand perception or driving awareness, and work from there. “It’s about focusing on the number one thing that you want to achieve as a brand, not the eight things,” Peake said. “Don’t overthink it. Speak to people who are experts in that field, and we can overthink it for you.” That philosophy shapes every aspect of how Backlash approaches the work. Rather than asking brands to juggle multiple suppliers and moving parts, the agency simplifies the process by bringing creative, design and project management together under one roof. Specialist construction partners are managed on clients' behalf, while Backlash oversees every stage of delivery. Its full-service offering spans location sourcing, staffing, health and safety, visual merchandising, retail systems and installation, giving brands a single point of contact and a seamless route from concept to completion. By accommodating both regional and global approvals, concepts can be adapted quickly, ensuring the final experience reflects the brand intentions in the best possible way. That’s once again where Backlash’s agile, collaborative approach with clients stands out. The agency’s track record speaks for itself. It has already produced a number of standout case studies, one of the most successful being the Marc Jacobs activation, "The Big Silver Box". What defined this activation was that “it was completely different to anything that they had in their UK stores,” according to Peake. “It was specifically launching a collaboration with Kim Kardashian and in that pop-up were items that you couldn't get anywhere else. “So it was not only visually really different to what the brand was doing in its flagship, but it also gave shoppers a reason to go there because it was the only place that you can get a very limited edition item.” The month-long installation was not only successful in achieving Marc Jacobs’ objectives, and it also won Best UK Pop-Up at the VM & Display Awards, with parts of its internal fit-out later reused in a flagship store. Backlash x Marc Jacob's 'The Big Silver Box' pop-up Of course, success can be measured in different ways. As budgets grow, brands are understandably looking for ways to measure marketing impact more comprehensively. As Peake outlines, success metrics need to correspond to the brand's key objectives — and that means looking beyond hard numbers alone. That's not to say numbers don't matter: data points like footfall, sales, social reach and customer feedback can all be collected and tracked. But they only tell part of the larger success story. The harder thing to capture is the long-term impression a campaign leaves on a customer's mind. Take one of Backlash's more recent pop-ups, with global retail chain Sunglass Hut. Visitors could browse a small selection of best-selling sunglasses in person, then scan a QR code to access the brand's full range via its e-commerce store. Each visitor also received a small gift — a very useful lens wipe that I still carry around in my purse — that doubled as a voucher for future use. It's a great example of how a pop-up can pique someone's interest and create a memorable experience while also building in long-term value. A visitor might not buy a new pair of sunglasses that day, but they walk away inspired, carrying a call to action they can act on later. While it is hard to quantify the exact impact of the pop-up on future sales, it is undeniable that an impression has been made that will influence consumers’ future decisions. Consumers will continue to expect more from the pop-ups they visit, which makes it ever-more important for brands to push the creative envelope. For Peake, fashion shows demonstrate how visually stunning sets and storytelling can generate impact far beyond immediately measurable data points. The same principle can be adapted to physical spaces, as they can become a brand’s creative microcosm, instead of another retail outlet. article_title: Shein IPO pitched below $30bn following sales slump
sub_title: For its planned Hong Kong IPO, online fast-fashion group Shein is presenting prospective investors with a valuation in the mid-to-high $20 billion range, according to the Financial Times.
article_content: For its planned Hong Kong IPO, online fast-fashion group Shein is presenting prospective investors with a valuation in the mid-to-high $20 billion range, according to the Financial Times. The latest range is another reduction in expectations for the Singapore-headquartered company, which was valued at $98.2 billion in a 2022 funding round and about $66 billion in 2023. According to Reuters, Shein was still seeking a valuation ranging from $30 billion to $40 billion as recently as last week. The float could reportedly launch as early as next week, although its final valuation and timing remain subject to investor demand. Shein secured approval from Chinese regulators to pursue the Hong Kong listing in July, after earlier attempts to float in New York and London . Shein’s listing documents showed that revenue increased 8% to $41.8 billion (£31 billion) in 2025, while net profit fell 38.7% from $3.37 billion (£2.49 billion) to $2.06 billion (£1.52 billion). Performance weakened further during the first quarter of 2026. For the three months ending in March, the group reported a $99 million (£74 million) net loss , compared with a $395 million (£296 million) profit a year earlier, while revenue edged 1.1% higher to $9.05 billion (£6.78 billion). The loss included a $328 million (£246 million) accounting charge linked to special investor shares, so the reported figure did not reflect trading alone. However, US revenue fell from $2.38 billion (£1.76 billion) to $2.04 billion (£1.51 billion) as changes to import rules affected Shein’s direct-to-consumer model. In May last year, the US removed a so-called “de minimis” tariff exemption on small packages, which Shein had previously used to ship garments from China directly to customers. Shein said: “Since May 2025, the removal of the US de minimis exemption has had an adverse impact on our sales in the US and the overall growth of our net revenues.” It said it had “since observed signs of normalisation in consumer purchasing behaviour and sales trends in the US”. Earlier this month, the EU also made the same move by imposing a three euro (£2.56) duty on small parcels imported from outside the trading bloc. The group added that the EU’s removal of the small parcel exemption may also have a “material adverse effect on our business, financial condition and results of operations”. Given that Shein made around a third of sales from Europe last year, it said the impact on the group could be larger than that from the US hit. “Although it remains too early to fully assess, it is possible that trends in the EU could be generally in line with or exceed the impact observed in the US after the removal of the US de minimis exemption,” Shein cautioned. The group said it was looking at raising prices across the US and Europe to offset the sales impact. Higher prices could weaken one of its central competitive advantages as investors assess the durability of its growth and margins. The UK is also looking to close the small parcels loophole, but not for some years. Former Chancellor Rachel Reeves confirmed plans in the 2025 autumn budget to follow in the footsteps of the US and Europe and review the customs loophole, saying she wants to “support a level playing field in retail”. But the proposed reforms are not expected to be in place until 2029, which has prompted calls from high street retailers to bring this forward. The IPO has also faced scrutiny over Shein’s supply chain and sourcing practices , including working conditions at supplier factories. A valuation below $30 billion would leave the business worth less than one-third of its 2022 funding-round level as it makes its third attempt to enter public markets.

article_title: Boden accelerates US retail expansion with third store in Alabama
sub_title: British clothing brand Boden is set to open a new 2,000 sq ft store at The Summit in Birmingham, Alabama, this autumn, as its US retail expansion gathers pace.
article_content: British clothing brand Boden is set to open a new 2,000 sq ft store at The Summit in Birmingham, Alabama, this autumn, as its US retail expansion gathers pace. It will mark the brand’s third store in the US, following the opening of a new 1,700 sq ft store at Hill Center Green Hills in Nashville, Tennessee, last month , and its first store in Atlanta, Georgia, which opened in November 2025. Boden identified Birmingham as a strong opportunity for growth, supported by existing customer demand in the region and insights from recent US customer focus groups. Participants highlighted a strong affinity with the brand’s “optimistic, colour-rich aesthetic” and expressed enthusiasm for experiencing Boden in a physical retail environment. The new Birmingham store will place Boden at the heart of one of the Southeast’s premier retail destinations, alongside a mix of premium and contemporary retailers including Tory Burch, BOSS and Madewell. Since launching online in the US in 2002, Boden has built a loyal customer base nationwide. The addition of stores in Nashville and Birmingham reflects the next phase of the brand’s strategy to complement its strong digital business with carefully selected physical retail locations in key US markets.

article_title: Harvey Nichols warns risk of collapse as Frasers closes in on rescue deal
sub_title: Harvey Nichols has warned it could collapse without a rescue deal, with Frasers Group reportedly leading the race to buy the loss-making luxury department store.
article_content: Harvey Nichols has warned it could collapse without a rescue deal, with Frasers Group reportedly leading the race to buy the loss-making luxury department store. Accounts filed at Companies House on 7 August for the year ended 29 March 2025 were drawn on a "non-going-concern basis", meaning the Harvey Nichols Directors have concluded that the department store is unlikely to continue trading as a normal, functioning business within the next 12 months. Reportedly Frasers could complete a takeover through a pre-pack administration, which would see Harvey Nichols briefly enter administration before its business and assets were sold to the retail group. No agreement has been confirmed so far. NEXT has also competed for the business, although sources close to the process indicated that Frasers was leading and unlikely to be overtaken by a rival offer. The uncertainty threatens about 1,200 UK jobs and Harvey Nichols’ seven stores in the UK and Ireland. Its estate includes the Knightsbridge flagship, four large regional locations and smaller-format stores in Bristol and Dublin. The department store has now logged five straight years of losses. The full group revenue fell £184.8 million from £204.8 million in the year to the end of March 2025, while losses before tax widened to £49 million from £34 million. Its London store saw sales drop from £78 million to just under £69.5 million in the same period. Mike Ashley, the founder of Sports Direct and a major Frasers shareholder, called reviving the retailer a “huge challenge” . Speaking to the Financial Times, Ashley said: “If it was a little bit tough before, it is in a death spiral now”. Ashley added that he thinks Harvey Nichols will sell for less than £40 million. That figure would not include the cash needed to support its recovery, with prospective buyers previously told to make between £50 million and £60 million available over the medium term. The funding ask covers refurbishment of the Edinburgh store, international expansion , digital development and management’s broader business plan. Sir Dickson Poon’s family brought in FTI Consulting in June to handle a possible sale after 35 years of ownership. Gordon Brothers joined the auction, while Dubai-based Chalhoub Group and India’s Reliance Retail also examined potential offers. Frasers, owner of Flannels and House of Fraser , joined the Harvey Nichols process in July . Some luxury suppliers raised concerns about its involvement, while Harvey Nichols said letting the group in would help maintain a competitive process. Ashley told the FT that Frasers could bid more than NEXT because Harvey Nichols fits its existing portfolio. However, he indicated that neither bidder would be deeply disappointed if it lost the auction, given the expected cost of the turnaround. Chief Executive Julia Goddard, who joined in June 2024, has overseen investment in the Knightsbridge flagship. Recent work includes a fourth-floor wellness destination and a redesigned ground floor for jewellery, lifestyle products and flexible brand spaces. Meanwhile, the retailer recently strengthened its senior leadership team with the appointment of Shaun Donnelly to Buying Director for Non Apparel & Menswear. Sir Dickson Poon's Dickson Concepts International bought Harvey Nichols from Burton Group in 1991 for £53 million. The company listed on the London Stock Exchange in 1996 before being taken private again six years later. Sir Dickson is no longer actively involved in running the group, having stepped down from the Harvey Nichols board and his other European directorships. In June last year, TheIndustry.fashion took an in-depth look at Harvey Nichols' transformation plans , featuring exclusive commentary on the challenges it faces and expert insights into how it might successfully navigate its transformation.

article_title: Zalando’s former sports merchandising lead joins Puma
sub_title: Puma has made another senior leadership appointment, with Zalando's former Head of Merchandising Sports, Carlo Alberto Cingolani, joining the sports footwear company as its new Global Director for Commercial Go-To-Market.
article_content: Puma has made another senior leadership appointment, naming Carlo Alberto Cingolani, Zalando's former Head of Merchandising Sports, as its new Global Director for Commercial Go-To-Market. Cingolani announced the move on LinkedIn last week, noting that he looked back at his almost 12-year tenure at Zalando with "immense gratitude". He joined the Berlin-based online marketplace in 2015 as its Kids & Accessories Private Label Merchandiser, rising through the ranks to become Head of Merchandising Sports. He previously spent three years in the merchandising department at the major multinational footwear and fashion accessories manufacturer and retailer Bata Group. "Stepping into the Puma HQ, the energy and vibrant atmosphere have been palpable from day one, making me feel extremely welcome right off the bat," he added. "I’m thrilled to join such an iconic brand and look forward to collaborating with a fantastic team to deliver the absolute best value PUMA has to offer to our customers worldwide." The appointment comes as Puma continues its strategic transformation under CEO Arthur Hoeld. The company has described 2026 as a transition year as it works to restore growth through cost efficiencies, inventory reductions and improvements to its distribution model, while investing in its digital infrastructure and direct-to-consumer channels. Puma reported a 9.4% organic fall in second-quarter revenue to €1.69 billion (£1.45 billion), a steeper decline than its 1% currency-adjusted fall in Q1, as its distribution clean-up and move away from heavy promotions continued to weigh on sales. Yet the brand also showed progress on controlling costs and margins, with its EBIT loss narrowing. Since the beginning of the year, Puma has been in a recruitment drive, with Hamlin becoming the sixth hire for the company over the last few months. Notably the majority of the new hires have backgrounds with the sportswear brand's biggest rivals, mainly Adidas and Nike, highlighting Puma's ambitions to establish itself as a top-three global sportswear brand. In May, the sportswear brand appointed a new Managing Director for Europe , a new Chief Financial Officer , a new lead for its Sportstyle business unit. It also hired a new Senior Vice President of Creative Direction and a new Vice President of Global Wholesale .

Armani’s 15% stake sale could be delayed amid weak luxury market conditions
sub_title: Armani Group’s planned sale of an initial 15% stake could be delayed beyond March 2027 as weak luxury-market conditions slow preparations for the ownership transition.
article_content: Armani Group’s planned sale of an initial 15% stake could be delayed beyond March 2027 as weak luxury market conditions slow preparations for the ownership transition. Company sources cited by Italian newspaper Corriere della Sera said negotiations could take time because of the difficult trading environment, according to a report by Reuters. The March deadline comes from the will of Giorgio Armani, the Italian designer who died aged 91 in September 2025 . The document requires his heirs to sell an initial 15% holding within 18 months of his death. A delay would extend the first stage of the succession process at the privately held Italian fashion group, which Armani co-founded with Sergio Galeotti in 1975. Armani remained its major shareholder and retained creative and managerial control until his death. The will gives priority to LVMH as a potential buyer, alongside L’Oréal and EssilorLuxottica, which already have commercial relationships with Armani. The group has considered dividing the stake equally , which would give each company a 5% holding. Such a structure would keep all of the preferred parties involved during the initial phase. Until 2050, L’Oréal holds the licence covering Armani fragrances , skincare and makeup, while EssilorLuxottica manages the fashion house’s eyewear business. The minority stake process is separate from L’Oréal’s reported examination of a possible acquisition of the Armani Beauty business. Under the wider succession plan, Armani’s heirs are instructed to sell a further 30% to 54.9% stake within three to five years, effectively transferring control of the company. An initial public offering is available as an alternative route for that later stage. The possible delay follows a year in which Armani’s 2025 annual sales declined by 2.8% to €2.192 billion , although consolidated EBITDA increased by 3.2% to €152.7 million. The group attributes the results to the company's focus on stability and managerial solidity during a year marked by both geopolitical turmoil and wider structural challenges across the sector. In 2025, the group's direct retail channels reported 2% growth at constant exchange rates, while indirect channels recorded a 7% decline, which the company attributed to a fall in wholesale orders and the "justifiable caution" of distribution partners given current market conditions. The group highlighted that the decline in indirect sales further aligned with its strategy of "cautiously declining and consolidating its wholesale orders" to focus on selectivity and distribution quality. Full-price and high-end channels performed more strongly, with double-digit growth at Giorgio Armani boutiques and the Armani Privé line. Giuseppe Marsocci, CEO and Managing Director of Armani Group, said at the time of the result publication: “We are facing a possible structural change in the approach to luxury and fashion, by current and potential consumers, which must be taken into account.” Marsocci has reportedly been preparing a five-year business plan before advisers are appointed to oversee the potential stake sale. The latest report suggests the timetable may depend on those preparations and a recovery in luxury dealmaking. Since Armani's passing, the brand has embarked on a new chapter, marked by its spring/summer 2026 haute couture show in January , which focused on demonstrating continuity for the brand, honouring a legacy built on discipline, precision, and enduring style. Last September, TheIndustry.fashion explored how the designer became a global icon , with a name recognised well beyond the industry itself.

article_title: Daniel Kearns reunites with David Beckham to lead BOSS BY BECKHAM design
sub_title: Hugo Boss has appointed Daniel Kearns as Head of Design for BOSS BY BECKHAM, reuniting the menswear designer with David Beckham after their earlier collaboration at Kent & Curwen.
article_content: Hugo Boss has appointed Daniel Kearns as Head of Design for BOSS BY BECKHAM, reuniting the menswear designer with David Beckham after their earlier collaboration at Kent & Curwen. Based in London, Kearns will oversee collection creation and design, alongside merchandising and branding, from initial concept through to execution. He will work closely with Beckham, with his first collection scheduled for AW27. The appointment gives BOSS BY BECKHAM dedicated creative leadership as Hugo Boss develops its multi-year partnership with the former England footballer. The multi-year Beckham collaboration was announced in May 2024 and covers capsule and seasonal collections spanning formal and casual menswear. David Beckham with Boss CEO Daniel Grieder Daniel Kearns Beckham said Kearns’s arrival marked the next phase of his work with BOSS, supported by a dedicated team in London. “Having known Daniel for some time, I’ve seen firsthand how his attention to detail and talent will be a great fit as we develop each collection,” Beckham said. Beckham’s relationship with BOSS has expanded from ambassadorial and modelling work into product design. He appeared in the brand’s AW24 campaign and subsequently fronted BOSS ONE Bodywear before launching his first co-designed SS25 collection in April 2025. That collection combined tailoring and elevated casualwear, including knitwear, outerwear, denim and accessories. It also introduced an exclusive signature cut for its tailored pieces. Kearns previously led creative direction at British heritage menswear brand Kent & Curwen, while Beckham was involved in its relaunch. Beckham joined the business in 2015 and participated in product design, store design and campaigns before ending his involvement in 2020 . Kearns and Beckham during their time at Kent & Curwen The pair’s work at Kent & Curwen included collections influenced by Peaky Blinders and The Stone Roses. Kearns later returned to the brand as Chief Creative Officer, also holding the same position at Cerruti 1881. His wider menswear experience includes positions at Alexander McQueen, John Galliano, Yves Saint Laurent and Gucci, with a background spanning tailoring and contemporary luxury menswear. Kearns said: “I have known David for many years and always admired his approach to design, style and curation. I am very much looking forward to working with him and the team at BOSS to bring the joint vision and David’s personal style to life.” The appointment comes as Hugo Boss is subject to a takeover bid from British retail group Frasers. Frasers has been amassing shares in the German giant and currently owns nearly 38% of its shares. It has tabled a €38-a-share takeover offer which has been cleared by regulators in Germany, making the offer “unconditional”. The Boss board, however, has urged shareholders to reject the deal.

article_title: Frasers Plus East Midlands sees ‘strong’ growth after fashion store expansion
sub_title: Frasers Plus Designer Outlet East Midlands has reported sales increases of up to 42% following store expansions by Barbour,  Levi’s and Skechers.
article_content: Tenant stores at Frasers Plus Designer Outlet East Midlands have reported sales and footfall growth, following store expansions by Barbour, Levi's and Skechers that allowed the brands to increase product ranges and refresh their store environments. Levi's performance stood out in particular. After a 68% store expansion in July 2025, which increased the floorspace to 3,485 sq ft, the denim retailer saw a 42% year-on-year increase in sales and a 28% jump in footfall. The larger layout allowed Levi’s to carry a broader and deeper product offer, while introducing larger changing rooms and creating a more open shopping environment. British lifestyle brand Barbour meanwhile grew its footprint by 51% to 3,101 sq ft in March 2026. Sales then rose 23%, as the bigger format gave it room to broaden its product offer. Skechers also enlarged its store by 76% in December 2025 and has since reported a 15% sales uplift. Kurt Geiger completed a full refit in March 2026, although no sales or footfall figures were disclosed for the refurbished store. Paul Sutton, Centre Manager at Frasers Plus Designer Outlet East Midlands, said : “These results demonstrate the strength of the centre’s trading performance, and the positive impact that larger, better-designed store formats can have on both sales and footfall.” Sutton said customers had responded well to broader ranges and improved layouts, with the performances of Barbour, Le Creuset and Levi’s showing the effect of the changes. The results follow Frasers Group’s acquisition of East Midlands Designer Outlet and York Designer Outlet in April 2026 , extending the retail group’s UK property portfolio. The East Midlands destination spans 170,000 sq ft near the M1 and houses more than 65 designer brands. It attracts approximately 3.5 million visitors annually. Its tenant mix features BOSS, Calvin Klein, Molton Brown and Tommy Hilfiger. In April, Frasers Group said it owned more than one-fifth of the UK outlet market and intended to grow that share. The group also added Swindon Designer Outlet to its portfolio in December 2025 , after a broader run of shopping centre and retail property acquisitions.

Editors' Top Reads: News from John Lewis, Hugo Boss, BRC and more...
sub_title: Here are some of this week’s news and features highlights handpicked by TheIndustry.fashion team.
article_content: Here are some of this week’s news and features highlights handpicked by TheIndustry.fashion team. The enduring appeal of David Beckham is evident in his highly successful tie-up with Hugo Boss. In 2024, the football star turned brand builder signed a multi-year deal to create BOSS BY BECKHAM, covering capsule and seasonal collections spanning formal and casual menswear. He’d been a long-standing ambassador of BOSS before that deal was signed. It has just been revealed that Irish designer Daniel Kearns has been appointed to head up design for the Beckham sub-brand and will be leading a dedicated London design team for it. This seems to suggest it’s selling well, though BOSS's latest numbers for the group as a whole show sales down 9% in its second quarter, however progress is being made on gross margins. Kearns and Beckham know each other well, having collaborated on British heritage brand Kent & Curwen. I’m interested to see how the London team and Kearns’ input shape BOSS by Beckham. They make a promising team. Of course, all of this is happening against a backdrop of Frasers still piling pressure on BOSS with its takeover bid. The €38-per-share bid it has tabled has cleared the German regulatory process, but the BOSS board’s position remains steadfast. They want shareholders to reject the bid. However, Frasers continues to buy shares and now has a stake with around 38%. How long can they be held off? Lauretta Roberts, Co-founder, CEO and Editor-in-Chief. The irony of choosing this as my top read, given I’m someone who only occasionally dips into yoga, isn’t lost on me. I know I should probably be doing more - and perhaps even joining the growing wave of consumers that John Lewis is hoping to attract with its latest investment. This week, the department store announced plans to capitalise on the booming fitness and wellbeing market by relaunching its sports and wellbeing offering. John Lewis boss Peter Ruis described the move as an “important step” in the British retailer’s wider store investment strategy. The business says its revamped sports and wellbeing departments will make it the first UK retailer to bring sportswear, footwear, wearable technology, recovery products, AI-powered fitness solutions and expert services together under one roof. The move is designed to strengthen John Lewis’ position in the increasingly competitive fitness market, helping it challenge established players such as Sports Direct and specialist technology brands. The multimillion-pound investment has already transformed the sports department at its London Oxford Street store, with further redevelopments planned for Liverpool and Cheadle, alongside a new department launching in its Glasgow store. Read more here. Sophie Smith, News Editor & Senior Writer. I had the best time interviewing Katie Peake, co-founder of brand experience agency Backlash. We spoke about how, in an increasingly digital-first world, physical activations remain one of the most engaging ways for fashion brands to emotionally connect with customers. Having worked in experiential advertising for the last 15 years, she has seen first-hand how the popularity of pop-ups has exploded. As customer expectations keep rising, Peake says the real challenge today is pushing the creative boundaries of what a pop-up can look like and finding the many different ways it can deliver value for the brand. In this interview with TheIndustry.fashion , she reflects on why physical activations continue to be the most powerful way of capturing consumers’ hearts and minds, how Backlash’s creative-first approach sets the agency apart from competitors, and how experiential retail can solve real business problems while also sparking entirely new ways of connecting with customers. Camilla Rydzek, Senior News & Features Writer. It seems retailers really can’t win when it comes to the great British weather. For so many years, late starts to warm spring/summer weather meant the big boys on the high street jumped early into Sale to try to offload excess stock. Inevitably, the smaller independents, despite hanging on for as long as they could, had to follow suit. This was especially the case with the increase in online shopping and diminishing exclusivity for the most sought-after brands (even if they’d helped to build them in the first place). But this week’s latest data from the BRC-Sensormatic Footfall Monitor , looking at UK footfall from 5 July to 1 August - when the Sales were certainly in full swing - showed footfall on the high street down 3.8% year-on-year, although that was actually up from a meagre -6.2% in June when the very warm weather first hit. You’d have hoped that early, properly warm weather would get people shopping to refresh their wardrobes, knowing it could be a long, hot summer ahead. However, as Helen Dickinson, Chief Executive of the British Retail Consortium (BRC), said: “The heatwave continued to bear down on retail footfall in July, with high streets worst affected. London was hit particularly hard as soaring temperatures made tube and train travel less attractive, with some commuters and shoppers opting to stay home.” That’s not music to the ears of any bricks-and-mortar retailer. And that’s despite shoppers being much savvier too. After all, why buy something in June which could have 30% off or more in July? Unless you’re going on an early summer holiday, that is. I remember speaking to a couple of retailers several years ago who said the spring/summer season is just one “to get through” as it’s just “too short” in terms of full-price sales. Plus, lighter-weight goods and less pricey T-shirts and shorts, as opposed to autumn/winter investment outerwear pieces that command much bigger ticket prices, don’t really make the real money. We’re not far into August, the weather is still glorious (and could be well into September when autumn/winter stock will be on the rails and shelves), and I’m picking up the odd piece for between 30%-50% off that I was interested in back in May and early June at full price, but couldn’t afford. Some of the more desirable items do sell out in certain sizes, of course, but there’s still a chance you might find said piece online somewhere – even if it’s a return that’s recently made a size available again. I guess what I’m saying is that retail is still very much a tough old game, and the weather – be it too mild in autumn/winter or, these days, too hot in summer – is still the most talked-about thing (apart from business rates!) when it comes to what impacts trade the most. Tom Bottomley, Contributing Editor.

article_title: NEXT expands Cribbs Mall store as retailer's investment spree continues
sub_title: NEXT will relocate and refit its Cribbs Mall store in Bristol, creating a 47,000 sq ft fashion space alongside the region’s first standalone Bath & Body Works location.
article_content: NEXT will relocate and refit its Cribbs Mall store in Bristol, creating a 47,000 sq ft fashion space alongside the region’s first standalone Bath & Body Works location. The larger NEXT store will carry an expanded selection of clothing and accessories, while the retailer has also agreed to lease a separate 1,797 sq ft unit for Bath & Body Works, extending the US personal care brand’s presence in its UK portfolio. Katie Searle, Director of Asset Management at Sovereign Centros from CBRE, said that the existing NEXT location was among the retailer’s best-performing stores in the country, supporting its decision to invest in the larger fashion space and introduce Bath & Body Works to the centre. “These premium stores at Cribbs will act as showrooms, with shoppers of all ages from across the West Country, West Midlands, South West and South Wales travelling to explore the latest styles and trends,” Searle added. The plans form part of a wider programme of store investment at Cribbs, where M&S carried out a complete refit of its 103,000 sq ft unit in December 2024. H&M also selected the centre for a technology-enabled regional flagship, while Boots has modernised its beauty hall to accommodate more than 30 additional premium brands. Cribbs has also signed leases with AllSaints, Levi’s and Rodd & Gunn in recent months, with the centre reporting a 26% increase in domestic tourists over the past year and a 13% growth in Gen Z shoppers . The Cribbs project comes after NEXT’s largest UK store at Bluewater opened in Kent on 30 July 2026. The 132,000 sq ft Bluewater anchor spans two floors and has 83,000 sq ft of trading space, bringing together womenswear, menswear, childrenswear and home. It also has a Costa café and a Bath & Body Works concession with its own entrance. NEXT previously opened stores in Eldon Square, Newcastle, Canterbury and Ripon during 2025, following the relaunch of its Stratford City location in 2024. The investment programme follows NEXT raising its full-year pre-tax profit forecast by £25 million to £1.24 billion. Total full-price sales rose 9.2% year-on-year during the 13 weeks to 1 August 2026, against the retailer’s forecast of 4% growth.
