Frasers eyes Michael Murray as Hugo Boss CEO
sub_title: Frasers Group is reportedly considering appointing its Chief Executive Michael Murray to lead Hugo Boss if its takeover of the German premium fashion company succeeds, according to a report by The Time on Sunday.
article_content: Frasers Group is reportedly considering appointing its Chief Executive Michael Murray to lead Hugo Boss if its takeover of the German premium fashion company succeeds, according to a report by The Times. The proposed appointment would give Frasers direct operational control of Hugo Boss and represent a change from its earlier support for incumbent CEO Daniel Grieder when it originally launched its offer in June. Murray, who has led Frasers since 2022, is the son-in-law of founder and controlling shareholder Mike Ashley. He has overseen the group’s elevation strategy, which has expanded its position in premium retail through Flannels and the Frasers department store business. He joined the Hugo Boss supervisory board in May 2025 for a five-year term. Because of the potential conflict of interest, Murray was left out of the committee reviewing Frasers’ takeover bid and took no part in its talks. The news follows Frasers’ increase in its Hugo Boss holding to 30.28% last week, after it acquired a further 2,549,900 shares in the company. Its direct position now comprises 20,897,361 shares, excluding stock already tendered into the offer. By crossing the 30% ownership threshold, Frasers triggered Germany’s mandatory-bid rules, which are similar to those in the UK. Frasers did not change its €38-per-share offer, however, with the initial acceptance period due to close at midnight Frankfurt time on 27 July. The group had previously declared its original €38 price as final . Frasers had first launched its bid on 10 June, valuing the remaining 73.94% of the Hugo Boss brand at about €1.98 billion. Almost one month later, Hugo Boss’s management and supervisory boards unanimously recommended that shareholders should reject the unsolicited approach, calling it financially "inadequate" . Daniel Grieder, the current Chief Executive Officer of Hugo Boss, said at the time: “Against this backdrop, we firmly believe that the offer price fails to capture the company’s intrinsic value and long-term potential.” Hugo Boss generated revenue of about €4.27 billion in 2025 but entered 2026 amid weaker consumer demand and changes to its product and distribution strategy. Its first-quarter sales for 2026 declined 6% to €905 million, with an EBIT of €35 million . Performance varied across its brands, with BOSS down 3% and HUGO declining 21% in Q1, as the company implemented targeted measures aimed at strengthening long-term brand positioning. Frasers has been building its Hugo Boss position over the last six years. Full ownership would make the fashion house its largest acquisition and expand a portfolio that includes Sports Direct, Flannels, Jack Wills and Gieves & Hawkes. The retail group is also pursuing Australian footwear retailer Accent Group , which has, however, firmly rejected its approach . Last week, Frasers extended that offer until September , with its other terms unchanged.

article_title: Mango on track for €4bn revenue target as first half sales climb
sub_title: Mango increased first-half turnover by 7.2% to €1.852 billion, with growth reaching 10.7% at constant exchange rates as it continued to expand its UK store network.
article_content: Mango increased first-half turnover by 7.2% to €1.852 billion (£1.61 billion), with growth reaching 10.7% at constant exchange rates as it continued to expand its UK store network. Summary of results: Mango’s first half performance keeps it within reach of its €4 billion (£3.48 billion) full-year revenue ambition, although the company did not publish interim EBITDA or net profit. The brand's womenswear offering continued to lead sales during the half-year, followed by menswear, as well as its kids and teen offering. Growth came from both stores and digital trading, with online revenues seeing double-digit growth, generating 32% of total sales. The brand noted that 77% of the company’s total turnover was generated by its international business, which Mango says is a reflection of its "strong global presence and geographic diversification". Spain remained Mango’s largest market and recorded double-digit growth during the half, followed by France, Turkey, Germany and the US. The UK remains one of the brand's strategic markets. The group also highlighted that it had invested nearly €90 million during the period to support expansion, operations, technology and its campus. Toni Ruiz, Chairman and CEO of Mango, said: “We are entering the final stretch of our 4Es 2024–2026 Strategic Plan with a clear ambition to reach €4 billion in revenue this year. Our first half results demonstrate continued positive momentum, with growth ahead of the wider market, further strengthening our position as one of the leading international fashion brands.” Under the Elevate pillar of its strategic plan, the brand had continued to strengthen its differentiated value proposition, centred on original design, quality and an aspirational brand position. Its appointment of Hailey Bieber as the face of its Woman line’s Summer 2026 campaign , as well as its collaborations with British tailoring house Richard James and American label Eckhaus Latta have formed part of its elevation strategy. The results follow a record 2025 financial year, which saw Mango's annual sales increase by 13% to €3.8 billion (£3.31 billion), while EBITDA rose 13% to €722 million (£628 million). Net profit grew 11% to €242 million (£211 million). At the publication of the full-year figures in March, Ruiz said the company had achieved “record growth across our key indicators” after investing in its business model and international expansion. The retailer continued its UK expansion with 10 openings during the half, including stores on Kensington High Street and King’s Road in London, as well as Cheltenham. Mango had previously outlined plans to add 15 UK stores during 2026 and opened its 26th London location at One New Change in May. Mango ended June with more than 2,960 points of sale across over 120 markets after opening 127 stores and renovating another 37. International operations accounted for more than three-quarters of turnover.

article_title: Searches for second-hand bridesmaid dresses up 17% year-on-year
sub_title: Searches for second-hand bridesmaid dresses are up 17% year on year as woman baulk at the cost of performing the honour, figures from resale platform Vinted suggest.
article_content: Searches for second-hand bridesmaid dresses are up 17% year-on-year as woman baulk at the cost of performing the honour, figures from resale platform Vinted suggest. Almost a quarter of women who have been a bridesmaid (24%) have considered turning down the role because of the cost, rising to more than one in three (35%) among women aged 25 to 34, a survey for the online marketplace found. Almost six in 10 women who had already been a bridesmaid (59%) said the role cost more than they expected, while one in three (33%) spent between £250 and £499 at their most recent wedding. More than one in three (36%) paid for their own bridesmaid dress or outfit, rising to almost half (46%) of women aged 25 to 34 - and more than half (52%) of those in London. Among former bridesmaids who have not worn their dress again, the biggest reason was simply not having another occasion to wear it (42%), while one in four (25%) said the dress felt too recognisable from the wedding itself. Nearly two thirds (63%) of women who have been bridesmaids say they would feel comfortable wearing a bridesmaid dress that had already been worn, rising to 70% among women aged 25 to 34. More than one in three (34%) of women who have attended a wedding have already worn a second-hand outfit to the event, with saving money (69%), avoiding buying something they will only wear once (38%) and finding better quality pieces for less (35%) among the biggest reasons. Some 80% of women agreed it was “perfectly acceptable” to resell a bridesmaid dress after the wedding. Formal dressed are listed on Vinted for an average £11, with the most searched-for bridesmaid dress colours being green, pink and blue. Euan Steedman, UK communications lead at Vinted, said: “Being asked to be a bridesmaid is a special moment, but our research shows that the cost of taking part is leaving some women questioning whether they can afford to say yes. “More than one in three women have already worn a second-hand outfit to a wedding, showing that people are increasingly looking for ways to celebrate these important moments without compromising on style or spending more than they need to.” Think BF surveyed 2,000 UK women in July 2026.

article_title: Turquoise to tangerine: 5 colour trends defining 2026
sub_title: After seasons dominated by chocolate brown, burgundy and the ubiquitous butter yellow, fashion seems to have turned up the saturation for 2026. This
article_content: After seasons dominated by chocolate brown, burgundy and the ubiquitous butter yellow, fashion seems to have turned up the saturation for 2026. This summer’s palette looks deliciously zesty with lime, tangerine and lemon yellow cropping up across the catwalks, while turquoise and lavender have also been given a punchier make-over. A post shared by Prada (@prada) Celebrity stylist Deborah Sheridan-Taylor believes the shift has been bubbling away since Michael Rider’s arrival at Celine, saying: “For me [that] may have lit the fuse, but Dario Vitale’s one-and-only collection for Versace really confirmed the mood, reviving the glorious sun-soaked palette of 1980s Miami, with all its saturated turquoise, citrus, coral and purple.” “Fashion never embraces colour in isolation,” she adds, pointing to Christian Dior’s New Look, which emerged in the years following the Second World War. “I think we’re in a similar moment. Wearing bold colour feels joyful, hopeful and defiant.” Turquoise has made a splash as a trending blue for the 2026 summer season. Alisha Boe attends Carolina Herrera's Spring-Summer 2026 collection at Plaza Mayor on September 18, 2025 in Madrid, Spain Credit: MPG/Alamy Live News The vivid blue-green shade has appeared on the runways at Courreges, Christopher Esber and Jacquemus. At Christopher Esber, turquoise appeared on a sheer asymmetric dress, while Courreges incorporated aquatic blues into its spring/summer 2026 collection. Jacquemus, meanwhile, used turquoise for a sheer dress in its Le Palmier collection. A post shared by Alexandra Leclerc 🦋 (@alexandramalenaleclerc) Few colours evoke ‘Euro summer’ quite as immediately as turquoise, but its intensity can make it seem tricky to incorporate into an everyday wardrobe. Sheridan-Taylor recommends pairing it with ecru for a relatively failsafe combination, or introducing a stronger contrast with cherry red, dark chocolate brown, a vivid Kelly green or even tangerine. If a turquoise dress feels intimidating, accessories offer an easier entry point. There are easy colours to wear, and then there’s chartreuse. Sitting somewhere between yellow and green, the acidic shade is unlikely to achieve the universal appeal of navy or ivory – but that awkwardness is precisely why it’s so popular. Lime emerged as one of the notable colours of the spring/summer 2026 collections, appearing at Prada, Versace, Tibi and Erdem. A post shared by ERDEM (@erdem) “Chartreuse and lime are definitely Marmite colours,” says Sheridan-Taylor. Rather than committing to a lime-green dress, she emphasises treating these shades as “punctuation marks, not the whole sentence”. That could mean a skinny scarf, a brightly coloured shoe or sock or a long-sleeved top layered beneath something neutral so only a flash of the cuff is visible. “These are great shades not to shy away from, as they’re full of energy,” she says. Orange has traditionally been treated as an autumn colour, appearing alongside rust, brown and burgundy as soon as September rolls around. But this year it has been reclaimed for summer. From apricot to retina-searing tangerine, orange has become increasingly visible, either worn head-to-toe or used to jolt otherwise classic pieces into the present. Its celebrity endorsement has been equally difficult to miss. Timothee Chalamet made orange central to the press tour for Marty Supreme, culminating in matching custom Chrome Hearts looks with Kylie Jenner at the film’s Los Angeles premiere in December 2025. Timothee Chalamet and Kylie Jenner at the LA premiere for Marty Supreme (Alamy/PA) Chalamet wore an orange leather suit and coordinating boots, while Jenner appeared alongside him in a floor-length orange gown. “Orange isn’t really one colour,” says Sheridan-Taylor, “it covers everything from mandarin, to dusty terracotta, deep Seventies-inspired coral, to burnt Moroccan rust.” For everyday dressing, she recommends popular colour combinations also featuring brown, aubergine, coral, white, turquoise and black And there’s no requirement to wear a traffic-cone-bright dress. An orange shoe, bag or even lipstick can bring the same energy to an otherwise familiar outfit. “We’ve traditionally handed it over to the autumn, but I say we reclaim it for summer, as few colours are as glorious in the heat.” Butter yellow enjoyed an unusually long reign, finally offering a relatively approachable way to wear yellow. But this season its less subtle counter-part has taken centre stage: the brighter, sharper lemon yellow. Olivia Dean wearing a sharp Loewe yellow dress at the 2026 BRIT Awards (Alamy/PA) Is it harder to wear? Perhaps - but Sheridan-Taylor recommends starting with colour combinations that already feel familiar. She notes the purple and gold of the LA Lakers or a strong yellow against brown or blue as combinations we are accustomed to seeing together, even if we have never considered wearing them ourselves. Lavender may sound tame compared with chartreuse and tangerine, but 2026’s take on purple is a long way from sugary pastel dressing. The deep plums and aubergines of winter have lightened into luminous lilacs and mauves for the warmer months, while sheer fabrics, embellishment and unexpected colour combinations can prevent the shade from feeling too traditional. “Purple is a wonderfully creative colour,” says Sheridan-Taylor, who particularly likes blue-toned mauves paired with khaki, beige, warm brown or soft off-white. A post shared by Stella McCartney (@stellamccartney) Those earthier shades can take some of the sweetness out of lavender, while black accessories can have a similar effect. Or consumers may ignore restraint entirely. If so, Sheridan-Taylor suggests clashing purple with cherry red, while make-up provides another way to experiment without investing in an entirely new outfit. “A purple eyeshadow worn with a crisp white cotton summer dress can be just enough mischief for one look,” she says.

article_title: Puma turnaround continues as Q2 losses narrow despite falling sales
sub_title: Puma reported a 9.4% organic fall in second-quarter revenue to €1.69 billion, a steeper decline than its 1% currency-adjusted fall in Q1, as its distribution clean-up and move away from heavy promotions continued to weigh on sales. Yet the brand also showed progress on controlling costs and margins, with its EBIT loss narrowing.
article_content: Puma reported a 9.4% organic fall in second-quarter revenue to €1.69 billion (£1.45 billion), a steeper decline than its 1% currency-adjusted fall in Q1, as its distribution clean-up and move away from heavy promotions continued to weigh on sales. Yet the brand also showed progress on controlling costs and margins, with its EBIT loss narrowing. The results reflect Puma's ongoing strategic transformation plan under CEO Arthur Hoeld. The company had previously described 2026 as a transition year as it works to restore growth through cost efficiencies, inventory reductions and improvements to its distribution model, while investing in its digital infrastructure and direct-to-consumer channels. Puma said it now expects sales to improve sequentially during the second half while it reduces discounting, clears inventory and tightens distribution. Its aim remains a return to growth in 2027 through its reset plan. Revenue for the first half of 2026 declined by 5.2% on a currency-adjusted basis to €3.55 billion (£3.04 billion). The result follows Puma's 1% currency-adjusted sales decline in the first quarter , when revenue reached €1.86 billion (£1.59 billion) and inventory clearance ran slightly ahead of plan. Puma maintained its full-year guidance for a low- to mid-single-digit currency-adjusted sales decline. It also continues to expect an EBIT loss of between €50 million (£42.9 million) and €150 million (£128.6 million), including one-off costs associated with its efficiency programme. Hoeld said that in the second quarter Puma continued to rebuild itself as a brand-led organisation, and that operationally the brand took " significant steps towards a structurally healthier business model" by "reducing inefficiencies, optimising our cost base and improving our organisational setup". “After a solid first quarter and a softer second quarter in line with expectations, we expect sales to improve sequentially in the second half of 2026. This supports our confidence in the full-year trajectory, and we confirm our outlook for the full year," he added. Puma's EBIT loss narrowed to €53.1 million (£45.5 million) in Q2, compared with a loss of €109.1 million (£93.5 million) in the corresponding period of 2025. The improvement came despite weaker revenue and reflected measures intended to reduce costs and improve margins. Performance varied across markets. Sales in Europe, the Middle East and Africa fell 12.9% to €674.1 million (£577.7 million), affected by weak European demand and disruption in the Middle East. North American sales dropped 16.7%, while Latin America declined 13.8%. Asia-Pacific revenue grew 8.6%, supported by demand for low-profile footwear, including the Speedcat family. Footwear, Puma's largest product category, declined 11.7% to €935.6 million (£801.7 million). Growth in running, HYROX training products and low-profile trainers was insufficient to offset wider weakness. Apparel revenue fell 4.3% to €552.1 million (£473.2 million), while accessories declined 12%. The results follow a series of senior appointments under Hoeld, with talent coming from some of the brand's biggest competitors including Adidas, Nike and ASICS. Puma recently named Dusan Hamlin as Vice President of E-Commerce and Dennis Schröder as Managing Director for Europe , alongside Mark Langer as Chief Financial Officer , Laurent Fricker as Head of Sportstyle , James Carnes as Creative Director and Bertrand Blanc as Vice President of Global Wholesale . During the turnaround, Frasers Group took a 5.77% minority stake in Puma in March , building its position largely through derivatives. Puma is a major supplier to Frasers-owned Sports Direct.

article_title: In Conversation: Harvey Nichols, Nadine Merabi, FitFlop and more...
sub_title: Last month, we spoke to founders and business leaders from across the fashion industry about their product strategies, international expansion plans and
article_content: Last month, we spoke to founders and business leaders from across the fashion industry about their product strategies, international expansion plans and how they are differentiating their brands in an increasingly competitive market. “Product is king. Everything we do is tested in a human performance lab. It's clinically engineered, and unlike some others where it's cosmetic, everything for us has a purpose and a reason for being. We try to fuse comfort and aesthetics, because one without the other does not work long term.” -  Gianni Georgiades, CEO of FitFlop Five years after joining FitFlop, CEO Gianni Georgiades has repositioned the independent footwear business from a broad comfort proposition to a science-backed global brand with recognisable design codes. In this interview with TheIndustry.fashion, he discusses the brands transition from a legacy double-density constructions to lighter single-density engineered midsoles, and how this has supported FitFlop’s expansion across sneakers and clogs, while retaining its focus on comfort and performance. "We are doing a series of eight projects this year that we would class as really pushing the boundaries of clothing. I think it's massively important to do projects that are pure moonshot ideas, it's very important to test the limits of what we are capable of." - Nick Tidball, co-founder of Vollebak Product innovation is something that the two brothers and co-founders of experimental clothing company Vollebak know well. The brand is working on eight experimental projects during 2026, with three focused on wearable technology. Its first release this year, the Sonic Jacket, features a prototype design engineered to shift the wearer's cognitive and physiological state through sound. In this interview with TheIndustry.fashion co-founder Nick Tidball discusses Vollebak’s technology projects and distribution plans , including an appearance at Paris Fashion Week to assess wholesale demand. CQP founder Adam Lewenhaupt on trading finance for footwear and following his design dream "We have stayed very true to ourselves and we’ve been very authentic, which clearly shows in our products. I’d like to think we are leaders when it comes to creating products at the intersection of elegance and casual, and that our customers feel that we offer something different in terms of quality and fit." - Adam Lewenhaupt, founder of CQP We also sat down with another footwear pioneer this month, Adam Lewenhaupt, the Founder of Stockholm-based premium footwear brand CQP . Known for its understated, unique and carefully constructed sneakers, the brand has grown slowly and without external financing since Lewenhaupt founded it in 2014. The former investment banker told us all about CQP’s “handmade sneakers without compromise” and his journey so far. "What makes the resale space so rewarding is this constant evolution; heritage and archival pieces are regularly rediscovered, finding passionate new audiences as modern tastes circle back." - Dominic Durante, CEO of Designer Exchange The journey of building and growing businesses was also a theme that we followed in this interview with D esigner Exchange CEO Dominic Durante, who discussed how the pre-loved luxury retailer has been expanding without changing the simple model it established in 2013. All of Designer Exchange's stock comes directly from its customers, and the stores' 'buy, sell and exchange' model remains a strategy that is clearly working. Durante tells us all about it. "Looking back, it was both exciting and incredibly challenging. Those early years taught me resilience, adaptability and the importance of believing in your vision, even before anyone else does." - Nadine Merabi, founder and Creative Director of MERABI Lewenhaupt isn't the only founder who started his career outside of the fashion industry. Merabi founder and Creative Director Nadine Merabi began her fashion business in 2015 with a £250 sewing machine after a career as a competitive hockey player. Selfridges subsequently asked her to develop a full range, helping move the label beyond its early one-off designs. In her interview about starting and scaling MERABI , the designer describes learning every part of the operation herself, from sourcing fabrics to packing orders. The Manchester-headquartered brand is now expanding its offering even more, from its signature occassionwear range now to more every-day styles including denim. With a recently appointed new CEO , the brand is looking ahead towards its next phase of international growth. "Like many people in the fashion industry, my career began at 16 in a shop. It taught me that if you show drive and ambition, you can get noticed and supported into new and exciting roles. I moved from the shop floor into Head Office as an Assistant Buyer and my career developed from there." - Kate Benson, Chief Merchant at Harvey Nichols Another standout interview with a female fashion executive saw TheIndustry.fashion sit down with Harvey Nichols' Chief Merchant Kate Benson , where she traced back how her early retail experience established a customer-led approach that still informs her decisions today. While she started on the shop floor at 16, she now works across more than 300 brands and is overseeing changes to Harvey Nichols’ product strategy and branded spaces. In this interview she reflects on her journey through fashion, the lessons she has learned along the way, the leaders who have inspired her, and her ambitions for the next chapter of her career.

article_title: Editors' Top Reads: News from Primark, Nadine Merabi, Designer Exchange and more...
sub_title: Here are some of this week’s news and features highlights handpicked by TheIndustry.fashion team.
article_content: Here are some of this week’s news and features highlights handpicked by TheIndustry.fashion team. This week I wrote about one of the cheekiest marketing stunts I have seen in quite a long time. Just as SKIMS opened its Regent Street flagship store, Primark placed a mobile billboard just in front to promote its £9 shaping bodysuit as a lower-priced alternative to Kim Kardashian’s widely popular shapewear offering. The slogan on the van showed models wearing the brand's own version of the bodysuit, with the slogan reading: "These Kim's prefer Primark £9 shaping bodysuit". In direct comparison, SKIMS Seamless Sculpt Thong Bodysuit, available in the Regent Street store, currently retails at £84. The move follows Primark's announcement last week that it had lowered prices across hundreds of products as part of a new “Iconic Value” initiative aimed at reinforcing its position as a destination for affordable fashion. While the move strengthens the retailer's value credentials, the reset also put it into closer price competition with online giant Shein , whose cost advantage is coming under regulatory pressure, argued our Editor-in-Chief Lauretta Roberts this week. Camilla Rydzek, Senior News and Features Writer. Congratulations to Fashion Roundtable for reading the mood music of the new Andy Burnham regime and trying to push this to the top of the agenda. The tireless fashion think tank and lobby group, led by Tamara Cincik, has issued an open letter to the Government urging them to implement a British-made-first policy, when it comes to the public procurement of uniforms, beginning with medical and military personnel. The group, which has the backing of business support platform Make it British and a number of other fashion industry signatories, argues that such a policy would support what is left of the UK fashion and textiles manufacturing base, and, hopefully, serve to grow it. The signatories have been at pains to point out, though, that handing over lucrative contracts to companies that are merely registered in the UK is not an acceptable solution. The uniforms must be made in factories here, many of which are in the North, which supports the aims of Burnham's Number 10 initiative. Burnham himself appears to appreciate British-made clothing and is often seen wearing made-in-Manchester Private White VC. The tabloid press jumped on this, criticising a so-called man of the people for wearing £80 t-shirts. But that approach seems to have backfired as the counter-argument that he's wearing durable clothing that supports British industry and jobs and industry is a far stronger one. Better that than he wears something cheap that is made in China. And better still would be his backing of this fine initiative to make uniforms here too. Lauretta Roberts, Co-founder, CEO and Editor-in-Chief. Nadine Merabi's journey from competitive hockey player to fashion founder wasn't conventional, but creativity had always been part of her life. Inspired by her stylish Lebanese father, she developed an early appreciation for the confidence that great design and dressing can inspire. In 2015, she launched her brand with a £250 sewing machine, creating beautifully crafted occasionwear designed to make women feel their best. Her designs quickly caught the attention of Selfridges, leading to a full collection and the rapid growth of the business. Today, the Manchester-based brand offers occasionwear, bridal, jumpsuits and denim, with a flagship store on London's South Molton Street and customers around the world. While Merabi no longer makes each piece by hand, she remains closely involved in every collection as the brand's Creative Director, overseeing both design and production. She shares the story behind her unexpected career path and the insights that have shaped her success . Sophie Smith, News Editor & Senior Writer. Knightsbridge-based ‘buy, sell and exchange’ business Designer Exchange has opened its sixth store today, and its second in Spain, adding a 1,720 sq ft store in Barcelona to its one in Madrid. It comes hot on the heels of its fourth UK store, which opened in Newcastle last month, with the company’s CEO, Dominic Durante, very much a believer in the bricks-and-mortar retail model. Our interview with him makes for an interesting read , as the business, which sells a constantly evolving selection of pre-owned handbags, accessories and ready-to-wear from some of the world's most sought-after fashion houses, including Hermès, Chanel, Louis Vuitton, Prada, Gucci and Miu Miu, pretty much sticks to the same simple strategy as it did when it was established in 2013. It was then that Designer Exchange’s first store opened in Knightsbridge, just around the corner from where its flagship store is today. Unlike traditional consignment platforms, Designer Exchange purchases luxury items directly from customers, offering immediate payment or an enhanced exchange voucher. Every item undergoes a rigorous authentication process before reaching the shop floor, providing confidence for buyers and a simple, transparent experience for sellers. While Designer Exchange does also have a strong online presence, it’s the physical stores that “remain central to the business”. Durante says that’s what differentiates it. What is also interesting is that Designer Exchange is part of CeX (Complete Entertainment Exchange), a global leader in second-hand retail and where many a decent mobile phone gets bought and sold. Durante explains that CeX already had a significant presence in Spain, which gave them access to an “established infrastructure, local market knowledge and operational support”. That made Madrid a very attractive opportunity and reduced many of the challenges associated with entering a new market. Hence, Barcelona was the next “natural step”, with expansion into further European countries now very much the plan. Another one to watch how it grows. Tom Bottomley, Contributor. I found this report particularly interesting because it challenges what luxury has traditionally been associated with. For years, fur and exotic skins have been seen as symbols of exclusivity, but the research suggests that many luxury consumers now place greater value on innovation, sustainability and ethical production. What stood out to me most was that 95% of those surveyed believed the use of fur and wild animal skins made luxury brands appear less prestigious. It highlights how consumer expectations are evolving, particularly as younger generations become more conscious of the environmental and ethical impact of their purchases. As luxury continues to redefine itself, it will be interesting to see whether more brands invest in next-generation materials that balance craftsmanship with sustainability. Catherine Rowe-Kosary, Junior Writer. When it emerged that Harvey Nichols owner – Hong Kong-based billionaire Sir Dickson Poon – was considering offloading the business after 35 years of ownership, I immediately assumed it would end up in either Asian or Middle Eastern hands. Especially given the likely sale price, the geographic spread of its stores and the investment needed to revive its fortunes. However, while there is interest from Asia and the Middle East (from Reliance Retail and Chalhoub Group respectively), we have ended up with a somewhat unexpected list of suitors. High street giant NEXT is acquisitive but it wouldn't have been first on my list of potentially interested parties. However a move for Harvey Nichols would, in one fell swoop, give it a huge foothold in luxury, which is a space it has been circling over the years with limited success. So there's that. Then we have Frasers Group, owner of Frasers, Flannels, Sports Direct and more, which was initially said to have been interested in the regional stores only, but is now talking of a tilt at the entire group. Frasers is ambitous; it's currently piling pressure on the board at Hugo Boss as it seeks to wrest control of the German fashion giant, and this week it was revealed that it has bought a small stake in Burberry. Given past experience, we shouldn't expect that stake to stay small for long. Now, Gordon Brothers, the US-based turnaround specialist, is reported to have thrown its hat its the ring . Gordon Brothers typically buys distressed retail brands with distinct design identities that it can parlay into its asset-light licensing model, which it has successfully done with Laura Ashley and soon will do with Radley. Harvey Nichols doesn't quite fall into that box but the precedent of buying the IP of a beloved department store has been set by fellow American group Authentic Brands, which acquired Barneys New York in 2019. The idea was to use the Barneys name on a range of products, which it does, but we are expecting to see some stores return with reports suggesting a new, smaller format store is set to open in Florida soon, with others in the pipeline. Could Gordon Brothers be thinking of a similar move? Seems likely. I'd be devastated if, like Barneys, the flagship store was closed though. However each potential bidder is being asked to commit £60m investment in the future development of the business, so maybe Sir Dickson won't let that happen. Lauretta Roberts, Co-founder, CEO & Editor-in-Chief.

article_title: THG’s new AI Stylist sees MP Activewear customers 6x more likely to convert
sub_title: THG Ingenuity’s newly upgraded AI Stylist, now live on Google Cloud Marketplace, is transforming the online fashion retail experience by boosting conversion rates, significantly reducing returns, and increasing customer engagement.
article_content: THG Ingenuity’s newly upgraded AI Stylist, now live on Google Cloud Marketplace, is transforming the online fashion retail experience by boosting conversion rates, significantly reducing returns and increasing customer engagement. THG-owned MP Activewear, the apparel offering born out of sports nutrition brand Myprotein in 2025, is already reaping the benefits of AI Stylist’s enhanced capabilities, as comparisons against site-average activewear shoppers revealed UK customers were nearly six times more likely to convert, spent 6.3 times longer on site and had a 2.5% higher average order value. Built in collaboration with Google Cloud and on Gemini’s Enterprise Agent Platform, the virtual try-on solution empowers customers to upload personal photos and visualise how clothing items on product pages would appear on them before making a purchase. Neil Mistry, CEO of THG Nutrition, said: “Myprotein Activewear is a core and fast-growing part of the Myprotein brand, and it's essential we keep improving how customers experience the range online. “The AI Stylist brings our products to life in a more engaging way, helping customers find the right fit and style with far greater confidence and, ultimately, buy with the certainty that it's right for them.” Jo Drake, Chief Technology Officer at THG Ingenuity, added: “The AI Stylist represents a step forward in how consumers interact with fashion online. Our collaboration with Google Cloud allows us to bring a truly scalable and transformative virtual try-on experience to brands globally. “This not only elevates the customer journey but also directly contributes to improved business performance through enhanced confidence and reduced operational costs.” The MP Activewear results highlight the AI Stylist's capacity to drive tangible return on investment (ROI) for fashion brands by “optimising the purchasing funnel” and improving overall customer satisfaction. In April, MP Activewear made its high street debut in seven Footasylum stores across the UK, including its flagship on London’s Oxford Street, in Manchester Arndale, White Rose in Leeds and Silverburn in Glasgow. The collection includes hoodies, jackets, leggings, shorts and sports bras, targeting Footasylum’s core audience of 16–24-year-old women. MP Activewear is a fast-growing and higher-margin element of the THG Nutrition business, with “annualised run-rate sales” fast approaching £100 million. Approximately 15% of THG Nutrition’s customers purchased activewear between January and March 2026, with average order values on orders including activewear around 31% higher. The launch in Footasylum stores followed the online launch, on 8 April, of an 11-piece Myprotein training collection - for men and women - in collaboration with heritage US sportswear giant Champion. That marked Myprotein’s most high-profile activewear partnership to date, building on partnerships with Decathlon, Frasers Group and Everlast. Activewear now represents approximately 12% of Myprotein’s online sales, up from around 8% in FY24, “demonstrating clear traction as the business diversifies its revenue streams”.

article_title: In Review, July 2026: Headline highlights from SKIMS, M&S, Sports Direct and more...
sub_title: Store expansion continued across the UK and Europe, while warm weather shifted spending online, promotions held down prices and major fashion events brought buyers and new collections to London and Paris.
article_content: As July draws to a close, TheIndustry.fashion reflects on a month marked by sustained store investment and exciting new openings, as well as inflation and stronger online demand. The British high street has seen some great additions this month, from SKIMS opening its first standalone UK flagship, to Frasers Group introducing its combined Sports Direct and Everlast Gyms+ format outside the UK for the first time. Retailers have also invested in refurbishments with Marks & Spencer unveiling its Oxford Street Pantheon transformation. Across the sector, warm weather produced mixed results. While retail sales and clothing spending improved, supported by summer promotions, record temperatures reduced store visits and pushed a greater share of non-food purchases online. We have also seen a lot of interesting data stories this month, from the World Cup and summer racing calendar generating increased demand for football products and occasionwear. Meanwhile a host of events, from the Scoop fashion show trade show to Paris Haute Couture Week gave us the best of fashion this month. We also heard from top industry voices including FitFlop CEO Gianni Georgiades, and Harvey Nichols' Chief Merchant Kate Benson. British spectacle maker Cubitts has opened its first Manchester store , marking the brand's long-awaited arrival in the city after almost a decade of searching for the right location. Oliver Bonas is set to open stores in retail parks for the first time , with new locations at Glasgow Fort in September and Teesside Park later this year. Tod's launches Harrods pop-up for Red Dot sneakers Tod's, the Italian luxury footwear brand, has opened a dedicated pop-up at Harrods centred on its Red Dot men's sneaker collection. The temporary retail space features a selection of Red Dot sneaker styles for men, combining the brand's traditional hand craftsmanship with its focus on product innovation. Meadowhall strengthens fashion line-up with Mint Velvet, Belstaff and Michael Kors deals Meadowhall has added new stores from Mint Velvet and Belstaff , as well as a major refurbishment of Michael Kors' existing flagship. The three deals are part of the shopping centre's push to grow The Avenue with aspirational fashion brands and upgraded retail concepts. Frasers Group opens ‘landmark’ Sports Direct and Everlast Gyms+ flagship in Dublin Frasers Group opened an 85,000 sq ft Sports Direct and Everlast Gyms+ flagship at the former Debenhams site on Dublin's Henry Street. The four-storey location represents an €80 million city-centre investment, created 75 roles and introduced HOKA to Sports Direct stores. SKIMS opens first UK flagship on London’s Regent Street SKIMS has launched its first standalone UK flagship at 245-247 Regent Street, as the shapewear and lifestyle brand expands internationally. The 12,000 sq ft store is based in the former Ted Baker site and follows the 10-year lease agreed with The Crown Estate. Zara’s sister brand Lefties confirms late August opening for first UK store Inditex's budget fashion and lifestyle label Lefties has confirmed that its first UK store will open in Liverpool ONE in late August. The rollout will then move on to Lakeside in early October and Gateshead's Metrocentre in November. Nobody’s Child continues UK retail expansion with new store in Cambridge Nobody's Child prepared to open a 1,000 sq ft store at 3 Grand Arcade in Cambridge, taking its standalone UK estate to 10 boutiques. The Cambridge opening is its third of 2026, following launches at Bluewater Shopping Centre and in Harrogate. M&S relocates Weymouth store with fashion at the fore Marks & Spencer relocated its Weymouth store to Gateway Retail Park , creating more than 70 jobs and giving fashion a prominent role. The new location carries Per Una, Goodmove and Rosie Lingerie, alongside expanded denim and specialist bra selections. Sprayground lands in London with 10-day pop-up New York bag and luggage label Sprayground has opened a 10-day pop-up at the Future Stores space at 95 Oxford Street. Called Sprayground's Soho Playground, the residency ran until 26 July and featured an appearance from founder David Ben-David. Lululemon brings padel pop-up to Manchester’s Trafford Centre As part of the expanded store opening, Lululemon put on a two-week padel pop-up at Manchester's Trafford Centre . The bookable court was open until 23 July and reflected the sport's rising popularity. Wax London expands Fenwick partnership with new Kingston concession Wax London expanded its Fenwick partnership with a 500 sq ft concession in the department store's Kingston upon Thames branch. The new space followed its Newcastle concession and features custom rails, tinted acrylic surfaces and a vintage oak haberdashery counter. Marks & Spencer completes Pantheon flagship transformation and begins format test Marks & Spencer completed the renewal of its nearly 100,000 sq ft Pantheon flagship at 173 Oxford Street . The four-floor store brings Food, Fashion, Home and Beauty together and will test merchandising and customer-service approaches before successful features are rolled out elsewhere. Belstaff gears to open store at Caledonia Park British heritage brand Belstaff has signed for a 2,500 sq ft store at Caledonia Park Designer Outlet in Gretna, Scotland. The planned location will sit beside Crew Clothing and Moss and stock menswear and womenswear spanning outerwear, essentials and accessories. NEXT's 132,000 sq ft Bluewater anchor store to open this month NEXT is due to open a 132,000 sq ft anchor at Bluewater on 30 July, tripling its presence at the Kent shopping centre. The former House of Fraser unit will give Bluewater its first new anchor store since the destination launched in 1999. Damson Madder opens first permanent retail space at Selfridges London fashion label Damson Madder has opened its first permanent retail space at Selfridges' Oxford Street flagship on 6 July. Set within the Contemporary Studio on the third floor, it is the brand's largest physical presence and follows its Selfridges launch in 2024. New Look’s largest concept store to open at Metrocentre New Look has opened its largest concept store at Metrocentre on 9 July, taking 11,000 sq ft in the destination's Red Mall. The digitally enhanced format brings Click & Collect, self-service returns, digital browsing, refreshed fitting rooms and expanded product ranges. ’47 heads back to London’s Soho for new pop-up US cap brand ’47 opened a three-month pop-up at 13 Newburgh Street , returning to physical retail in London's Soho. The temporary store followed its 2023 Air Street unit and coincided with the launch of dedicated UK and EU e-commerce platforms. Garage continues UK retail expansion with new store at Lakeside Canadian activewear, athleisure and denim brand Garage has signed for a 4,221 sq ft store at Lakeside Shopping Centre in Essex. The latest UK location comes after openings on London's Oxford Street and at Bluewater, extending a business with 231 North American stores. Brook Taverner’s retail expansion gathers pace with new Guildford store British menswear retailer Brook Taverner opened its 17th UK store at 76 High Street in Guildford, Surrey. The retail expansion will continue with Ambleside and St Andrews locations, as the company targets an estate of up to 30 stores within five years. Clarks plans up to 20 new European stores as expansion gathers pace Clarks has opened at Santangelo Outlet Village in Italy as it plans between 15 and 20 new European stores this year. The continental expansion follows recent openings across Italy and Spain, with further locations planned in France, Belgium and the UK. Byan set to open first flagship store in London Spanish womenswear brand Byan prepared to open its first London flagship on Chelsea's King's Road in October. The permanent store follows the brand's three-month Covent Garden pop-up, which opened in November 2025 and was its first physical presence in the capital. In Pictures: Selfridges unveils FIFA 1904 World Cup pop-up featuring first-ever licensed fashion collection Selfridges opened a pop-up presenting the first official FIFA-licensed fashion collection, designed by Maison Kitsuné Creative Director Marcus Clayton. The FIFA 1904 collection was developed with VFILES and takes its name from the year in which football's international governing body was established. July's indicators pointed to softer price growth and improved spending, although physical footfall remained under pressure as hot weather moved more purchases online. UK retailers keep prices low as shop price inflation eases According to the British Retail Consortium, UK shop price inflation eased to 0.9% in July from 1.2% in June. The Shop Price Monitor found non-food inflation slipping to 0.2% as retailers stepped up promotional activity across clothing, footwear and food. Clothing prices fall 0.5% in June as retail competition holds down prices The Office for National Statistics said clothing and footwear prices dropped 0.5% in June after rising 0.2% in May . The latest inflation figures showed the Consumer Prices Index at 2.6%, while retailers still faced employment, packaging and energy costs. Heatwave and online shopping rebound delivers boost to June retail spending UK retail sales rose in June as hot weather supported demand for clothing and air-conditioning products, while summer discounting encouraged spending. Office for National Statistics figures also showed online shopping rebounding to its highest level in five years. This was reinforced by Barclays' Consumer Spend report which saw UK consumer card spending rose 1.9% year on year in June , improving on May's 0.8% growth but still below CPIH inflation. UK retail footfall falls 3.4% in June as heatwave keeps shoppers inside According to BRC and Sensormatic data, UK retail footfall dropped 3.4% year on year in June as record temperatures kept shoppers away from stores. The five-week figures put high streets down 6.2%, shopping centres down 2.5% and retail parks down 0.3%. Holiday demand set to drive summer retail spending KPMG UK found that 63% of consumers had booked or intended to book a summer holiday , with 75% of travellers planning purchases before departure. The Consumer Pulse survey showed 42% expected to buy clothing and 25% planned to purchase footwear. Consumer confidence sees six-point ‘Burnham bounce’ Consumer confidence increased by six points in July , its largest monthly improvement since November 2023, according to GfK. The headline confidence measure nevertheless remained negative at minus 17, despite heatwaves, football success and a change of Prime Minister supporting sentiment. Price beats ethics at the checkout for majority of Brits Although 68% of British consumers said ethical production mattered, the most common behaviour during their latest purchase was choosing according to price or quality alone. Research from Zero100 tested willingness to pay more for ethical options across clothing and other consumer categories. Summer racing events drive occasionwear demand, new data shows Data from Debenhams Group shows Britain's summer racing calendar boosted searches and sales in race-day fashion categories. The occasionwear findings covered Debenhams, Karen Millen and PrettyLittleThing, with demand spanning dresses, fascinators and statement accessories around major racing events. TikTok drives £10 billion boost to UK economy as fashion brands benefit TikTok-driven economic activity generated at least £10 billion in gross value added for the UK economy in 2025 and supported an estimated 153,000 jobs. The TikTok-commissioned research looked at the platform's influence on consumer spending, employment and business growth, including fashion brands. Debenhams Group sees demand in ‘football fashion’ surge as World Cup fever strikes Boohoo saw football-related product sales jump 1,827% between May and June , while searches rose 600% during the World Cup. The Debenhams Group data also recorded a 481% increase in official football shirt sales at Debenhams over the same period. Premier League shirt prices soar as fans hit by fresh cost hikes Eight Premier League clubs increased replica shirt prices , leaving supporters facing adult prices of up to £90. The club pricing review found Tottenham's adult first-team shirt had risen by £5 to £90, while a shirt for a young child cost £70. The Interview: Designer Exchange CEO on keeping the ‘buy, sell and exchange’ strategy simple and opening more stores
sub_title: Last month saw Designer Exchange open its latest store at 141 Grainger Street in Newcastle. The store features a curated selection of handbags, accessories and ready-to-wear from brands including Prada, Gucci, Louis Vuitton and Miu Miu.
article_content: Last month, Designer Exchange opened its latest store at 141 Grainger Street in Newcastle. The store features a curated selection of handbags, accessories and ready-to-wear from brands including Prada, Gucci, Louis Vuitton and Miu Miu. The new store forms part of the company's ongoing expansion strategy, joining existing Designer Exchange locations in London's Knightsbridge, Manchester, Birmingham, Cheshire Oaks and Madrid. Another store is set to open in Barcelona on 31 July. All of Designer Exchange's stock comes directly from its customers, and CEO Dominic Durante prefers to keep the company's 'buy, sell and exchange' model simple. It is a strategy that is clearly working. He tells us all about it. Designer Exchange is a business built around buying, selling and exchanging pre-loved luxury. From Hermès handbags and Louis Vuitton trainers to Cartier Love bangles and ready-to-wear, we offer a broad range of authenticated luxury products across different brands, styles and price points. Our headquarters are based at 191 Brompton Road in Knightsbridge, London, which is also home to our flagship store. What really sets us apart is our physical retail presence. We currently operate stores across the UK and Spain, which allows customers to see, touch and try on products before they buy. In a category such as pre-loved luxury, that level of trust and reassurance is incredibly important. We've also always believed in offering customers instant payment. Rather than operating on a consignment model, we buy items outright, taking on the risk ourselves and providing sellers with immediate cash or a higher value exchange voucher. Designer Exchange was established in 2013, with our first store opening in Knightsbridge, just around the corner from where our flagship store is today. As the business has evolved, we've opened stores in a number of locations across the UK, with some coming and going as we've refined our strategy. Previous locations have included Leeds, Kensington, Chelsea and Ashford. Today, we operate stores in Knightsbridge, Birmingham, Manchester, Cheshire Oaks, Newcastle and Madrid. We're also excited to be opening our second Spanish store in Barcelona this month, with further expansion plans in the pipeline. All of our stock comes directly from our customers. We purchase items outright from individuals within our community who are looking to sell their luxury pieces. That means our inventory is constantly evolving and gives us the opportunity to offer customers a broad mix of brands, styles and price points. Our model is simple: buy, sell and exchange. Customers can either visit one of our stores or sell to us online. Once we receive an item, our team carries out quality checks and authentication before making an offer. Once purchased, items are photographed, listed online and distributed across our stores ready for resale. The business has changed considerably since we launched in 2013. We've expanded into new cities, entered international markets and undergone two rebrands as the business has matured. Stores have come and gone over the years as we've adapted our approach, but some things have remained constant such as the buy, sell and exchange model and always offering instant payment. We’ve also always believed in the importance of physical retail. Looking back, those principles have served us well and continue to underpin the way we approach growth today. We're excited about the opportunities ahead. Our focus remains on continuing to expand the business while staying true to the model that has helped us grow over the last 13 years. We're encouraged by the response we've seen in Spain and continue to see opportunities, both within our existing markets and further afield as we bring the Designer Exchange proposition to new customers. There are a number of independent omnichannel retailers operating within our space and the big marketplaces like Vinted and eBay compete in terms of the sheer volume of luxury products available. In contrast to traditional models, we acquire inventory directly to provide sellers with immediate liquidity. For consumers, we offer a seamless bricks-and-mortar shopping experience heavily anchored by our 'Double Lock Guarantee', a strict authentication process that ensures absolute product integrity. We've always tried to maintain the luxury experience without creating an environment that feels intimidating or exclusive. Equally, we don't just focus on the biggest brands or the highest value products. Whether someone is looking for an item at £50 or £50,000, we want them to feel welcome and to have confidence that they'll find something that suits both their style and budget. Yes, although our physical stores remain central to the business and are what really differentiates us. In pre-loved luxury, customers often want to inspect an item and understand its condition before making a purchase. Having stores gives people that confidence and helps build trust in the buying experience. Absolutely. While we don't rely solely on social media, it has played an important role in driving awareness, building trust and showcasing the breadth of our offering. Instagram remains our strongest platform and aligns closely with our audience, while TikTok allows us to showcase more of our culture and the people behind the business. Employee generated content and store-led content continue to perform particularly well for us, as customers increasingly want to engage with the people and personalities behind the brand. Yes, Cheshire Oaks is currently our only outlet location. It was a natural fit for us as it's the largest designer outlet in the UK, with over 140 stores and a strong mix of luxury and premium brands. Importantly, it offers customers a full-day destination rather than simply a shopping trip, which helps drive significant footfall and attracts visitors from across the country. Opening in Madrid wasn’t initially our preferred option. We originally felt that cities such as Paris or Milan might be stronger choices given their global reputation in luxury fashion. However, our sister company, CeX, already had a significant presence in Spain, which gave us access to established infrastructure, local market knowledge and operational support. That made Madrid a very attractive opportunity and reduced many of the challenges associated with entering a new market. Looking back, it has proven to be an excellent decision. The Madrid store has been a real success for us, validating both the market opportunity and our approach. As a result, we’re excited to continue our expansion in Spain with the opening of our second store in Barcelona this month. Spain has become an important growth market for Designer Exchange and we’re very encouraged by the response we’ve seen from customers there. Beyond Spain, further expansion into other European countries is something we’re excited about in the not-too-distant future as we continue to grow the brand and bring our offering to new markets. It might sound like a cliché, but we genuinely believe luxury should be accessible to everyone. One of our key brand messages is making luxury accessible to all, so we aim to offer something for every style and every budget. That's something that's been important to us since the beginning and continues to shape the way we approach the business. Yes, both buyers and sellers benefit from the model. For buyers, we use our internal data and market insights to price competitively and ensure products are positioned to sell within a reasonable timeframe. For sellers, immediate payment removes much of the hassle and uncertainty associated with selling luxury goods privately. Those choosing an exchange voucher receive even greater value, allowing them to trade into something else within our inventory. We don't want to say too much at this stage, but we can confirm that, as well as Barcelona, we plan to open a store in Glasgow this year. Beyond that, watch this space. Louis Vuitton consistently stands out as our ultimate powerhouse brand, dominating both total sales value and overall volume. While it leads the charge, our broader top tier for handbags remains a star-studded lineup of legacy houses, rounded out by Gucci, Chanel, Mulberry and Christian Dior. In terms of shifting trends, we are seeing immense demand for vintage Louis Vuitton ‘Monogram’ pieces. We’ve also witnessed a fascinating spike in the secondary market value of Chloé ‘Paddington’ bags, sparked by Chloé reintroducing the iconic style on their recent runways. It’s a perfect example of how quickly first-hand retail shifts inject new energy and value into the resale market. What makes the resale space so rewarding is this constant evolution; heritage and archival pieces are regularly rediscovered, finding passionate new audiences as modern tastes circle back. Newcastle was a natural choice for us. It’s a city with an incredible energy, a rich cultural identity, and a community that genuinely loves and understands style. North East shoppers have a fantastic eye for fashion, but they are also incredibly smart consumers and, let’s be honest, Geordies love a bargain! We wanted to bring the physical experience of Designer Exchange right into the centre of the ‘Toon’, introducing brands to the city that can be hard to find physically, from Chanel and Hermès to Louis Vuitton, Prada and Miu Miu. But we aren't stuffy or exclusive. We are warm, welcoming, and open to everyone, offering authentic, high quality luxury goods at affordable prices. It’s about making premium fashion accessible, letting people touch and feel the pieces, and giving such unique items a ‘well deserved’ second home. An elevated yet completely down to earth experience. We want to demystify luxury. Whether you have £70 to spend on a sleek pair of sunglasses or a fun accessory, or you’ve saved up £15,000 for a ‘holygrail’ Hermès piece, there is absolutely something here for you. We cater to every single taste, style and budget. Whether you are a seasoned collector looking to sell a piece to fund your next purchase, or someone buying their very first designer handbag to celebrate a milestone, our team is there to guide you. When you walk through our doors, expect a welcoming space with an ever-changing inventory, and a passionate team that loves fashion just as much as our customers do. Pre-loved luxury is no longer an alternative, it's the first choice. Shopping secondhand is now a badge of honour that proves you’re a smart, stylish and a sustainable consumer. However, with the market booming online, buyers are constantly dodging counterfeits and scammers. That’s where we come in. Our bricks-and-mortar stores are built on absolute trust. Our expert authenticators meticulously vet every single piece before it hits the floor, so you get the thrill of finding a unique gem with none of the anxiety. We’re proving that you can offer affordable, circular fashion without ever sacrificing the premium boutique experience.
