London Fashion Week to champion royal favourites and British icons from McQueen to Mulberry and M&S
sub_title: From royal-approved designers to high-street heroes, here’s what to expect from London Fashion Week spring/summer 2027.
article_content: Kicking off on 17 September and running through to 21 September, London Fashion Week is doubling down on British labels, with icons including McQueen and Mulberry returning to the city, while high-street stalwart Marks & Spencer prepares for its Fashion Week show as it celebrates 100 years of fashion. Alongside the runways, the British Fashion Council (BFC) is also launching ‘Fashion Britain’, a nationwide initiative designed to take British fashion beyond the capital for the first time , while sustainability requirements introduced earlier this year remain firmly in place. So, from royal-approved designers to high-street heroes, here’s what to expect from London Fashion Week. McQueen comes home The biggest talking point this season is undoubtedly McQueen’s return to London for the first time in 25 years. Although the house has become synonymous with Paris Fashion Week since moving its womenswear show there in 2001, Dublin-born Creative Director Seán McGirr will present his first London runway show since taking the helm in December 2023, bringing one of Britain’s most influential fashion houses back to the city where it was founded by Lee Alexander McQueen. Kylie Jenner in custom McQueen at the Vanity Fair Oscar’s Party in March (Alamy/PA) the David Geffen Galleries at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA) at 5905 Wilshire Blvd on March 15, 2026 in Museum Row, Miracle Mile, Los Angeles, California, United States. (Photo by Xavier Collin/Image Press Agency) “London has always been at the heart of McQueen,” McGirr told the BFC. “There’s a uniquely visceral energy to the city that runs throughout the house’s history and continues to inspire everything we do today.” The return is one Laura Weir has been working towards since becoming chief executive of the BFC. “One of my earliest ambitions as CEO of the British Fashion Council has been to see Alexander McQueen return home to London Fashion Week,” she said. “Few have shaped the global fashion landscape with the same force, imagination and cultural impact […] McQueen’s return is a statement of confidence in British creativity at its most fearless and distinctive.” McQueen will show at 20:00 on Sunday 20 September. A new chapter for Mulberry McQueen isn’t the only British favourite returning to the London schedule. Heritage leather goods brand Mulberry will unveil its first collection under Christopher Kane after the Scottish designer was appointed Creative Director earlier this year. A post shared by London Fashion Week (@londonfashionweek) The appointment marked Kane’s return to fashion after his namesake label entered administration in 2023, making his London Fashion Week comeback one of the season’s most anticipated debuts. “It is an honour to return to London Fashion Week with Mulberry,” Kane said. “It’s an exciting time, and I look forward to sharing SS27 with everyone.” The show, taking place on Sunday 20 September, also signals a renewed confidence for Mulberry as it continues its “Back to the Mulberry Spirit” strategy centred on British craftsmanship. Marks & Spencer joins the runway Perhaps the season’s biggest surprise comes from the British high street. To celebrate 100 years of fashion, Marks & Spencer will stage a London Fashion Week show on Friday, 18 September. A post shared by M&S (@marksandspencer) Rather than presenting a traditional catwalk collection, the retailer will adopt a “see now, buy now” format, meaning shoppers will be able to purchase pieces almost immediately after they appear on the runway. For the BFC, it’s another sign that London Fashion Week is becoming increasingly consumer-facing. Weir described the show as “a significant moment”, adding that it demonstrates “how heritage, innovation and accessibility can come together to connect exceptional British design with consumers in new and relevant ways.” London stalwarts and royal favourites Beyond the headline-making returns, many of London’s biggest names remain fixtures on the schedule. Royal-approved Tolu Coker, Patrick McDowell, Emilia Wickstead, Richard Quinn and Edeline Lee – frequently worn by the Princess of Wales – will all show, continuing London’s tradition of mixing established designers with newer voices to shape the future of British fashion. The Princess of Wales wearing Emilia Wickstead during the Wimbledon Men’s Singles Final in July (Andrew Matthews/PA) Burberry will once again close the week on Monday evening, while Erdem, Simone Rocha, Ahluwalia and Di Petsa all return with new collections. Paul Costelloe, the longest-serving design house on the London Fashion Week schedule, will once again open proceedings, alongside Harris Reed, Ashish and H&M on Thursday evening. Fashion beyond the capital While London remains the focus, the BFC is looking further afield. Launching alongside Fashion Week is ‘Fashion Britain’ , an initiative designed to decentralise fashion in the UK and create opportunities for investment and cultural participation throughout the UK. A post shared by British Fashion Council (@britishfashioncouncil) The programme will bring together designers, retailers, cultural institutions and educators through events in London, Liverpool, Manchester, Newcastle, Bristol and Edinburgh, with the aim of strengthening regional creative industries and opening up opportunities beyond the capital, occurring concurrently to Fashion Week. “British fashion is one of our greatest cultural exports, yet for too long participation has been concentrated in too few places,” said Weir. “Fashion Britain represents a fundamental shift in how we think about our role as the British Fashion Council.” Sustainability remains a priority Away from the front rows, sustainability continues to be a fundamental concern for London Fashion Week. This will be the second September season to operate under the BFC’s Sustainability Requirements, developed in partnership with Copenhagen Fashion Week. King Charles III and Stella McCartney on the front row of sustainable luxury designer Tolu Coker’s AW26/7 London Fashion Week show in February (Richard Pohle/The Times/PA) Initially introduced for the NEWGEN cohort, the framework requires participating designers to meet a series of minimum environmental and social standards In order to remain on the official London Fashion Week schedule, applicants must provide responses to 18 minimum sustainability requirements, with designers required to demonstrate how they meet key environmental, social and governance considerations.

article_title: Primark Menswear Director departs to join NEXT
sub_title: The former Primark director returns to Next after more than 12 years with the value fashion retailer, taking over from a product chief who joined in 2001.
article_content: NEXT has appointed Steve Coates as its new Menswear Product Director, returning him to the retailer where he began his buying career. Coates, who is joining the retailer from Primark, will be taking over from Giles Vinning, who will reportedly be departing NEXT after almost 25 years. Primark has confirmed that Coates has left his role, but NEXT has not yet made a public statement announcing the appointment or the exit of Giles Vinning. Coates spent more than 12 years at Primark, joining the Dublin-headquartered retailer in August 2014 as Head of Buying for Menswear. He became its Menswear Director in June 2023. Before moving to Primark, Coates worked at George at Asda, serving as Buying Director between 2013 and 2014. He began his career at NEXT as a Senior Buyer in 1997. Coates succeeds Vinning, who has been with NEXT for the last 25 years. He first joined the retailer in 2001 as a menswear casual shirt buyer, becoming Menswear Buying Manager in 2007 before taking on the role of Menswear Product Director in 2018. Prior to joining NEXT, Vinning has held positions at George at Asda, Reiss and Paul Smith. His departure ends a tenure that spanned NEXT's shift from a predominantly store-based chain to an international online platform selling its own products and third-party labels. The appointment comes just a few days after ASOS named Jon Bennett to the role of Menswear Product Director for ASOS Design. Bennett joined ASOS from NEXT, where he had served as Managing Director of NEXT Wholly Owned Brands since January 2025. He previously spent almost four years as Primark's Trading Director for Menswear. In its latest trading update, NEXT reported full-price sales growth of 9.2% for the 13 weeks to 1 August 2026, compared with its forecast of 4%. Sales exceeded the retailer's forecast by £70 million, comprising £19 million from the UK and £51 million from overseas markets. International online sales rose 36.9%, while total UK sales increased 2.8%. NEXT attributed the result to warmer UK weather, returning demand in the Middle East and Northern Europe, and higher spending on profitable marketing. The retailer further raised its full-year pre-tax profit guidance, adding £25 million to reach £1,243 million, representing annual growth of 7.3%.

article_title: How I started in fashion: Nadine Merabi, founder of MERABI
sub_title: Nadine Merabi is a competitive hockey player turned fashion creative director. Her early career as a sportsperson may not have been the obvious place for a fashion founder to start out, but Merabi had always been surrounded by creativity and had always appreciated the impact of colour, design and style.
article_content: Nadine Merabi is a competitive hockey player turned fashion creative director. Her early career as a sportsperson may not have been the obvious place for a fashion founder to start out, but Merabi had always been surrounded by creativity and had always appreciated the impact of colour, design and style. Her inspiration came from her stylish Lebanese father and, from him, she learned about the power of a good outfit. So, in 2015, she set to work on her £250 sewing machine to create clothing that made women feel their absolute best. Merabi began producing carefully crafted, one-off pieces of occasionwear for women, and it wasn't long before she caught the attention of Selfridges, who asked her to create a full range. The brand took off from there and has gone on to dress some of the most high-profile women in the fields of entertainment, fashion and, of course, sport. But the brand isn't just about dressing celebrities. Merabi has always been committed to creating the best quality clothing she can at an accessible price point. Today, the brand's range takes in occasion dresses, bridal wear, jumpsuits and new line of denim . While Merabi herself no longer makes the clothes, she does design them and is heavily involved in production. While the business is headquartered in Manchester, the brand has a store on London's South Molton Street and is available globally via its website . She talks us through her unexpected career path and the lessons she has learned along the way. Have you always had an interest in fashion? Why does it appeal to you and why did you want to work within it? I've always been drawn to fashion because of how it makes people feel. For me, clothing has never just been about what you wear, it's about confidence, self-expression and celebrating life's moments. Growing up, I was surrounded by creativity. My father had a great eye for style, and watching him sparked my own love of colour, texture and design from a young age. That curiosity eventually became a passion, and I realised I wanted to create pieces that made women feel their absolute best. Fashion gave me the opportunity to combine creativity with purpose. Every MERABI piece is designed to empower women to celebrate themselves, whether that's for a wedding, a milestone or simply a moment where they want to feel incredible. Tell us about your first job in fashion. What drew you to the role? What this experience was like? My first job in fashion was starting NADINE MERABI. Before that, I was a competitive hockey player, so fashion wasn't the obvious career path for me. But I'd always had a creative side and a fascination with how clothing could transform the way women felt. I recognised a gap in the market for modern, statement occasionwear that combined glamour with confidence, and I decided to take the leap and create it myself. In the early days, I was doing everything, from sketching designs and sourcing fabrics to packing orders and speaking directly to customers. There wasn't a roadmap; I learned every aspect of the business by doing it. Looking back, it was both exciting and incredibly challenging. Those early years taught me resilience, adaptability and the importance of believing in your vision, even before anyone else does. What were the most valuable skills or lessons you gained from that first experience? One of the biggest lessons I learned was that success comes from understanding every part of the business, not just the creative side. I also realised the importance of listening. Whether that's listening to your customers, your team or your suppliers, some of the best decisions come from staying curious and being open to learning. I've carried that mindset throughout my career. Even today, we're constantly speaking to our community and evolving the brand based on their feedback. Tell us about your current role. How did you get here and what do you most enjoy about it? As the Founder and Creative Director of NADINE MERABI, my role is incredibly varied, and that's one of the things I love most. Creatively, I work closely with our design team to shape every collection, ensuring each piece reflects the confidence, craftsmanship and timeless glamour that define MERABI. Alongside the creative direction, I'm also deeply involved in the wider business, from long-term strategy and product development to mentoring our team and staying closely connected to our community. Over the past decade, the brand has evolved significantly, but our purpose has remained the same: to create beautiful pieces that empower women to feel their most confident. The most rewarding part of my role is seeing women wearing MERABI during some of the biggest moments of their lives. Whether it's a wedding, a milestone celebration or simply a day where they want to feel their absolute best, knowing we've played a small part in those memories is incredibly special. If you could go back and give your younger self one piece of advice at the very start of your career, what would it be - and why? Trust yourself sooner. When you're starting out, it's easy to compare yourself to others or feel like you need all the answers before taking the next step. The reality is that building a business is a constant learning process. Some of our biggest lessons have come from the moments that didn't go to plan. Every challenge has helped shape the business we are today. You don't need perfect timing or permission. You just need the courage to start. What does the next chapter of your own career look like and how are you hoping to grow from here? The next chapter is about continuing to evolve MERABI while staying true to the values we've built the brand on. We're expanding into more versatile day-to-night dressing, growing internationally and continuing to invest in our community by listening even more closely to what women want from us. Personally, I want to keep growing as a leader. Building a business teaches you something new every day, and I'm passionate about creating a culture where creativity, collaboration and ambition can thrive. Has there been a person in fashion that you have always admired and why? I've always been inspired by people who have the courage to create something from nothing and stay true to their vision. Closer to home, one of my biggest inspirations has always been my father. He had an incredible sense of style and an appreciation for quality and craftsmanship, and I think that's where my love of fashion first began. Watching how he expressed himself through what he wore taught me that clothing can be a form of confidence and individuality, and that has stayed with me ever since. Beyond that, I'm inspired by entrepreneurs and founders who lead with authenticity, resilience and purpose. Building a business is never a straight line, and I have huge respect for people who continue to evolve while staying true to who they are. That's something I've always tried to bring to MERABI as we've grown.

article_title: IKEA takes on eBay and Vinted with new UK second-hand marketplace
sub_title: Ikea is looking to take on the likes of eBay and Vinted with plans to launch a new marketplace platform for its second-hand furniture and homewares.
article_content: IKEA is looking to take on the likes of eBay and Vinted with plans to launch a new marketplace platform for its second-hand furniture and homewares. The Swedish retail giant hopes the platform will make it “as seamless as possible” for consumers to buy and sell their pre-owned IKEA products. It has not confirmed a launch date but said it would provide more details “in the coming months”. Members of the firm’s membership scheme, IKEA Family, will be able to connect with other customers through the platform. The furniture giant has already launched trials of second-hand marketplace services in other countries, including Spain and Norway. An IKEA spokeswoman said: “At IKEA, we are always looking for new ways to make life at home even better and help our customers discover products they love. “With the launch of IKEA second-hand marketplace in the UK, we’re taking a meaningful step toward creating a destination that simplifies access to pre-owned IKEA furniture. “We’re creating a trusted and vibrant space to make it quick and easy for our IKEA Family members to trade directly with one another.” The move represents a push by IKEA into the second-hand market amid the growing use of eBay, Vinted and Facebook Marketplace by consumers. Other retailers such as John Lewis and Currys also sell pre-loved and refurbished products through their platforms. Vinted, especially, recently reported a jump in annual revenues of 38% to €1.1 billion (£957 million) for 2025, particularly highlighting its "strong" performance in women's and children's clothing. The platform said that beyond its core fashion category it had also expanded into more consumer goods categories, including sports, homeware, electronics and collectibles, welcoming more members as a result. This increase in members has also translated into a 47% increase in gross merchandise value traded on the platform to €10.8 billion (£9.4 billion) over the year. With competition in the resale market intensifying, eBay only last month completed its $1.2 billion (£890 million) acquisition of fashion resale platform Depop, following clearance from the UK Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) earlier this month. The deal, first announced in February, strengthens eBay's position in the fast-growing fashion resale market and expands its reach among Gen Z and Millennial consumers through Depop's community-led marketplace. Resale in fashion and beyond is only gaining more traction with consumers, Vinted's 2025 Impact report revealed. It showed that nine in ten of surveyed UK buyers check the resale platform before buying new items, with 35% saying that they think about the resale value of an item before purchasing something new. Vinted has coined the term "Vinted Math" to describe this shift towards more value-conscious consumer behaviour, with CEO Adam Jay commenting that the findings show that "people are changing not just where they shop, but how they value what they own".

article_title: New York, London, Milan, Paris: What’s coming up this fashion month
sub_title: Fashion month is almost upon us, with designers and models descending on New York, London, Milan and Paris to show their latest collections.
article_content: Fashion month is almost upon us, with designers and models descending on New York, London, Milan and Paris to show their latest collections. Each city has a distinct personality. New York is classy cool; London is the edgy one, with the most experimentation and up-and-coming designers; Milan is all about fabulous glamour; while Paris rounds things out with the biggest, most established names in fashion. But all will bring celeb sightings, new trends and some seriously major fashion moments, as designers jostle for attention when showing their spring/summer 2027 collections. Last September was one of the biggest fashion months to date, with an eye-watering number of blockbuster debut designers (think Jonathan Anderson at Dior and Matthieu Blazy at Chanel). Now, these designers are set to show their third collections, so have settled into the job and really have the opportunity to show their vision for their brand. With the fashion week calendar constantly shifting, here’s what to expect from each of the Big Four fashion cities… New York 10-15 September A post shared by Fashion Week (@fashionweek) New York Fashion Week (NYFW) often shows a solid mix of big-name brands and edgier, independent labels, and this season is no different. Michael Kors, Calvin Klein and Christian Siriano are some of the NYFW mainstays on the schedule, along with exciting names like Collina Strada and Eckhaus Latta. Thom Browne – a NYFW stalwart, who is currently chairman of the Council of Fashion Designers of America – was missing from last season’s schedule (instead, he took his show to San Francisco, where the Super Bowl was taking place) – but he’s now back in his regular closing slot. There are a couple of international transplants – Off-White (the label established by the late Virgil Abloh) normally shows during Paris, and American designer Conner Ives is a familiar face at London Fashion Week, but both are appearing in New York this season. One of the most exciting shows comes on the opening morning, when Russian-born, American designer Henry Zankov will present his debut collection for the Diane von Furstenberg brand – with everyone curious to see how he modernises the wrap dress. Otherwise, fashion fans are keen to see what Wiederhoeft will show this season. The label is known for extravagant gowns with tight corsetry, and has hit the headlines in the past few months for some big fashion moments – including designing the wedding dress worn by Sydney Sweeney’s character Cassie in the third season of HBO show Euphoria, as well as dressing model Gigi Hadid in a hot-pink gown for Taylor Swift’s marriage to Travis Kelce in July. London 17-21 September The King was front row for Tolu Coker’s last London Fashion Week show (Richard Pohle/The Times/PA) There’s plenty of consistency on the London Fashion Week (LFW) schedule – Richard Quinn will bring drama to his regular Saturday night slot, heritage house Burberry will close proceedings on Monday night, Princess of Wales-favoured designers Erdem, Emilia Wickstead and Roksanda are set to return, and popular labels like Ahluwalia and KNWLS will also show. But what’s most exciting about this LFW are the new additions to the schedule. Perhaps the biggest moment of the week will come from Alexander McQueen, as Sean McGirr is bringing the label – which has been showing in Paris since 2001 – back to its hometown of London. Elsewhere, leather-goods brand Mulberry is seeing a revamp thanks to its new creative director, Christopher Kane, who will be presenting his first collection – no doubt putting British craftsmanship in the spotlight. Another big addition to the calendar is Marks & Spencer, as the British high-street brand will be staging its first ever LFW show to celebrate 100 years of fashion – with a ‘see now, buy now’ format meaning that shoppers can buy the clothes on the runway almost immediately. M&S isn’t the only high street addition to this season’s calendar – H&M will be showing on the first night of LFW. Milan 22-28 September A post shared by Camera Nazionale della Moda Italiana (@cameramoda) Italian glamour will hit the runway at Milan Fashion Week (MFW) with familiar names Dolce & Gabbana, Roberto Cavalli, Giorgio Armani and Bottega Veneta all on the schedule this year. There’s been a slight schedule change, with Prada now in the opening slot of MFW – which could mean the label wants to start things with a bang. Meanwhile, Maria Grazia Chiuri and Demna Gvasalia will be showing their sophomore collections for Fendi and Gucci respectively. Notable absences include Boss and Versace – with new creative director Pieter Mulier set to show his first collection next year – but cult brand Marques’ Almeida, which normally shows in London, will be making a guest appearance. There are two highly anticipated moments at MFW. The first comes from Moschino, which will see its debut collection from new designers Loris Messina and Simone Rizzo – the brains behind independent label Sunnei. Secondly is Vogue World, which will touch down in Milan on September 22. After similar events in New York, London, Paris and Los Angeles, Vogue World will be a celebration of Italian fashion – it’s set to take place in the glass-topped shopping arcade Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II, with the theme of “craftsmanship and the human touch” in the age of technology. Paris 28 September - 6 October Zendaya was front row for the last Louis Vuitton Paris Fashion Week show (Alamy/PA) Paris Fashion Week (PFW) is the longest of all four events, with the most shows on the calendar – and this season is no exception. While there are some big names missing – such as Rabanne, with new creative director Olivier Rousteing set to present his debut next year; and Nina Ricci (designer Harris Reed’s replacement is yet to be announced), there’s plenty to keep up with. After taking their shows elsewhere last season, big names Valentino and Maison Margiela will be returning to the Parisian schedule, joining mainstays Saint Laurent, Stella McCartney, Tom Ford, Balenciaga, Schiaparelli, Loewe, Givenchy, Victoria Beckham and Vivienne Westwood, with Louis Vuitton taking the final slot. While creative directors will be making their debuts at Courreges and Carven, the buzziest shows will likely belong to Anderson’s Dior and Blazy’s Chanel.

article_title: The Eric Musgrave Interview: Soulboy Keith McNichol of Richmond Classics, Bournemouth on why he keeps on keeping on
sub_title: Keith McNichol is keeping himself busy planning the 40th anniversary for Richmond Classics, his influential multi-brand store in Bournemouth.
article_content: Keith McNichol is keeping himself busy planning the 40 th anniversary celebrations for Richmond Classics, his influential multi-brand store in Bournemouth. Opened on 1 st April 1988 – yes, he admits the date can be regarded as very appropriate – it continues as one of the very few survivors of a golden era of strong local indies that has been erased by the recent domination of Flannels in the sector. The genial self-confessed fashion fanatic has lost none of his zeal for finding new brands for his loyal customers, some of whom now bring their grandkids in to shop with Richmond Classics. In this candid conversation, McNichol is blunt, however, about the difficulties an independent fashion retailer faces due to significant societal and economic changes, plus huge shifts in relationships between brands and their stockists. McNichol was 30 years old when he opened his business and was able to draw on more than a dozen years’ experience in retailing. He is a retailing lifer. Along with music, fashion is an all-consuming passion which he is now passing on through regular videos on Instagram. Now selling only menswear, his current brands include Android Homme (footwear), Billionaire Boys Club, Gabicci, Moose Knuckles, Only The Blind and Paul & Shark. Some of his stories may bring back memories for our Editor-in-Chief, Lauretta Roberts, who was a regular customer of Richmond Classics as she grew up in Dorset. You’ve been in retailing for a few years now… My two loves for the past 52 years have been music and fashion. Straight from school I had the choice of working for Beales of Bournemouth, established in 1881, or its rival department store Bobby’s, which was founded in 1915. I thought Beales was a bit old-school for me, so I joined Bobby’s. Surprisingly enough, started in the dress fabrics department before graduating to menswear. After three or four years, I rebelled and went to work on the beach. Then I decided I better get a proper job again, so I joined Tailors Fashions, a small company with eight branches locally that traded under names like Discus, Gemini and Ashes. They were very early adopters of middle market brands. I was there for 10 years, troubleshooting, going into various branches, improving their environments and displays – and making them a lot of money in the process. In 1987 the owners decided to close the company and gave me a small amount of money as redundancy or a parting gift. I started helping a friend of mine who had a shop on Richmond Hill in Bournemouth selling American gridiron sportswear and surfwear like Ocean Pacific. I loved the shop because it had a beautiful mezzanine floor. One day I told him I’d like to take the unit from him and he agreed as the American football thing wasn’t working. As it was on Richmond Hill I called it Richmond Classics. The opening party invitation for the original store, which opened in 1988 What were you selling at the start? It was a tiny store, around 1,000 square feet including the little mezzanine upstairs. Early doors, it was all American brands and European labels. I went to Le Sentier district in Paris every other week to buy from their cash and carries. The rue de Nazareth was like their Great Portland Street. I brought stuff back in bin liners. They called me Mr. Richmond. I’d buy it, sell it and go back again and again. My problem was that I was being blocked from getting UK-based brands by my local rival John Anthony. Fashion agents then were lazy and they sold to whoever was first with them, not necessarily who was the best store. Everything changed for me when in 1989 I took out an advertorial in the lads’ mag FHM, which at the time was edited by Mike Soutar, who’s now regularly seen on The Apprentice. I met Mike Soutar recently and he told me I was the first indie to do take out such an ad. We shot my beautiful shop from the mezzanine, aiming down at a table, and I was inundated with calls from agents saying, Do you want to come and see what I’ve got? By then we were selling very curious, expensive Italian and French shirts from labels like La Garage, CPA and Replay at up to £300. After we appeared in FHM people were calling and going, can I buy that shirt? It was the best thing I ever did because little old me and my tiny shop put Bournemouth on the fashion map. An Eric Musgrave profile of Richmond Classics in Sportswear International in 1992 The next big boost, Eric, was when you came to interview me in 1992 for a feature in Sportswear International, the most important magazine in Europe for the jeans and casualwear sector. Your photographer Fred Anderson made the shop look brilliant in the double-page spread and suddenly lots of European brands wanted to talk to me too. You already had a good reputation, which is why I visited you. Although you’ve always retained the Richmond Classics name, you’ve devised a few different concepts over the years… A big inspiration for me was Ray Bacon, who had a brilliant store in Cardiff called Woodies. That shop showed me what was possible. At Richmond Classics we took the adjacent unit and knocked through. We later added a third unit next door. In the early 1990s the French denim brands like Chevignon, Liberto, Aviatic and Chipie were in fashion. I did a deal with Steven Peters, the Chipie agent, to open a Chipie shop. As it wasn’t a franchise I also sold other related brands, like Avirex and Diesel. It gave us another point of difference. I’m not bragging, but the stores looked great. The interior of the former Sussed Out store Subsequently I had nearby branches such as Sussed Out, which was me plagiarising our friend Mr. Shawn Stüssy. I've had The Lounge of Geeks and Freaks – everyone said to me, you can't call people geeks or freaks. I've had The Fashion Pharmacy, which, again, was mental. These were all reinventions to keep people interested, but Richmond Classics has always been the focal point. When I opened The Fashion Pharmacy I was challenged by the Association of the British Pharmaceutical Industry to relinquish the word “pharmacy” as I did not administer medicines. At the time Damian Hirst had just opened his Pharmacy restaurant in Notting Hill and the ABPI challenged him too. Damian lost and I won! After I told them I was giving fashion remedies for fashion illnesses I didn’t hear from them again. I started out with menswear only but added womenswear in the late 1990s when US labels like 7 For All Mankind, Juicy Couture and Ed Hardy were big. We even had a creche in the shop. It all ended around 2017 when Grazia magazine kept telling their readers where they could get cheap high street knock-offs of the hot womenswear brands. Imagery from The Fashion Pharmacy What was the local competition like in the early days and what’s your competition now? My only strong competition at the start was from John Anthony, which had opened in Bournemouth the year before me. (Southwest-based mini chain John Anthony was taken over by Frasers, owner of Flannels, in December 2023 and the fascia disappeared soon after). As for now, I don't think there is competition anymore. We don't have a level playing field, so competition doesn't exist. The only thing we independents can do is to control our own little space. The big boys have got the ball, they won't give it back, and therefore there's no competition. You can't play without a ball. As an example, in February Mainline Menswear (another Frasers company) was already on Sale! We’re still waiting for some deliveries and they're on Sale. Online is competition, I suppose, but I’m not online because we're too weak as an independent and it's too expensive. To put, say, 1,000 garments online, you've got to press them, photograph them, write content about them, and at the end of the season, how much of that stock have we actually sold? And I've paid £20,000 to put it online? I could have saved myself all that money by not being online. Of course we need presence and a platform. On my Richmond Classics site , it looks like we're the best thing ever because we have sold out of everything! Psychologically, customers are like, Oh my God. we need to get there early. Who are your customers? We have people who have been with us for 38 years. They have brought their kids here and now some are bringing their grandkids. As a retailer, you don't realise how much influence you have on people's lives. It's bizarre. We have started doing regular videos on Instagram. One of them has had more than 38,000 views. The comments we get are amazing. People are remembering shopping with us when they were 12 or 14, telling us we made their life great. They lived and breathed what we were doing. We revisit brands too. I’ve just rebooked Evisu, which I sold through the 1990s. Young kids aged 18 have been buying pre-loved Evisu to get an appetite and now they're coming to me. In the shop they look like rabbits caught in the headlights because they can't believe the information, the histories I can share. Such things are priceless. When people come to me, it's for a shopping experience. McNichol outside the current side. His videos draw visitors to the store from far and wide How is Richmond Classics faring after 38 years? To be totally honest, it's very, very hard. Right now, footfall has virtually disappeared. Unfortunately, all independents are in the same boat. We've had to change a lot of strategies. We've had to change a lot of brands because they've gone you-know-where for the quick buck. There's no longevity or loyalty from most brands. With some, there is, but a lot of them go direct-to-consumer. Covid destroyed any friendships as such because they realised they could make more money without using us retailers. New brands coming out are also going DTC. We have to do what we feel is best for our business and for our customers, so we introduce new brands. I go to Pitti Uomo in Florence, I visit the Paris shows. We reinvent. We still have our core and we have the ability to direct customers. We go out, look and find. (Norwegian outerwear brand) UBR is a prime example. I was doing UBR three years ago when no one knew it. I found it in a multi-brand showroom. I put a coat on and loved it. It’s a beautiful product. I didn’t need to know David Beckham or some football manager wore it. That's the strength of what we do. In the first season we sold 30 coats. Another prime example of my belief and energy in seeking out brands was the first time I saw (Swiss brand) On Running footwear at Mark Batista’s Jacket Required trade show five or even six years ago. They were only a tiny stand, the size of a shoe box – no pun intended! They had three very ugly styles that were not aesthetically pleasing to the eye, more special needs than style, to be honest. I bought one style in four colours and for six months I couldn’t give those On Running shoes away. Then the Liverpool scallies adopted them and the rest is history. We no longer work with On as they are now in the likes of JD Sports, but we’ve found a new footwear brand, which has very few accounts and none in the multi-brand sportswear stores. That’s a unique USP these days! People will have to come and see me in Bournemouth to learn what I’m talking about. I used to go to the US looking for stuff too but now the exchange rate and tariffs have killed that. How many people do you employ? The answer is very boring and very simple. Due to our lovely Rachel Reeves (former Chancellor of the Exchequer), I have nowhere near the staff I should have because I can't afford them. We’ve cut our cloth accordingly. I have two floors in my store and every day I have just two staff, including myself. On a Saturday, I have three. In the old days, you needed to double your staff on Saturdays, but Saturdays aren't Saturdays anymore. Wednesday is a Saturday now, or Tuesday is a Saturday now. Because of our beautiful government and our councils, the town centres are drying up because there's no footfall because no one's working in the cities because none of the businesses are in the cities. Everyone’s working from home. Now we have a situation where no one has any necessity to come into the towns. I was talking about this to my MP, Jessica Toale (Labour) recently. I told her that the government should increase the tax on online businesses. It would cost Labour nothing and they could use that money  to entice businesses back into the cities and towns. This in turn would give money to entice staff to come back into town, as they used to five, or six years ago. They could go for something to eat, go for a drink, go window shopping – except there aren’t the windows to look at now. If all that came back, which it could very easily, then we'd be happy, and we’d go back to where we were, to have a weekend when people go out to spend money because on Monday to Friday they're working in a working environment they can't get away from. Does the consumer today have a better time than they had back in 1988? They certainly have more knowledge. Between 1988 and say 2010 they came to us and said, What should I be buying? What's in fashion? You never hear that now because the kids – and their parents for that matter – have got so much information available to them. They don't need us. It's a different world. A post shared by Richmond Classics (@richmondclassics) Tell us about your recent videos. I shied away from social media for a very, very long time because I didn't think it worked. And the people doing it for me weren’t good. Then I met a young guy at the local university who asked to do it. As he didn’t know fashion retail, the first two or three things we did were disastrous, but we worked out how to work together. I am telling the story of Richmond Classics and all my other fascias. As I said, one of them has attracted 38,000 views. People are identifying with it, which is great. But it's also brought customers to me from other cities. I had a customer the other weekend who said he’d seen the videos and had decided to come to Bournemouth to see me. He spent £2,500 on the day, so the proof is in the pudding. What have been the highs and lows of 38 years as an independent? The lowest point was being forced out of my Richmond Hill shops late in 2016. My original landlord from 1988 treated me like a son. When he sold the property the new owner threatened me with a massive dilapidation bill and my lawyer told me to leave. I’ve been at my Westover Road site since spring 2017. Behind the counter at Richmond Classics Before then, in the mid-1990s, I was broken into five times in quick succession. I knew who’d done it – they were walking round in my Henri-Lloyd jackets. When I confronted the ringleader it all kicked off in a very big way and the police arrived, but it didn’t happen after that. That’s all part of retail. Probably my high point was going to Buckingham Palace in 2010 for a reception for fashion industry people, that thanks to you, Eric, including independent retailers. (NB: I was asked by the Home Office for names of indies for some unspecified event.) I ended up chatting to the late queen about Hunter and Barbour as fashion brands. She told me she’d been on a catwalk and laughed. It was quite a high point. Do you still have a passion for it now you’ve just turned 68? I haven’t lost my passion for music or for fashion. I’m the main man behind the revival of the Bournemouth Soul & House Weekender (BSH), which ran for four days over the May Bank Holiday Weekend. Like music, fashion is in my blood and it has been since I was 14 years old. It's all I've ever wanted, it's all I've ever done. I've got friends that play golf, do padel, do this, do that. I don't need to do anything like that because I enjoy what I do. I don't regard it as a job. My son asks me all the time, why are you still doing this, Dad? I say, because I enjoy it. I just got excited about booking Evisu again. When there's no excitement, I'll stop.

article_title: Harvey Nichols shuts website after Frasers takeover
sub_title: Harvey Nichols website has gone offline following its acquisition by the Frasers Group, with a notice reading that it will remain so while the new owners "complete a period of transition". The department store's physical locations remain open.
article_content: Harvey Nichols website has gone offline following its acquisition by Frasers Group, with a notice reading that it will remain so while the new owners "complete a period of transition". The department store's physical locations remain open. "We are pleased to confirm that Harvey Nichols has entered an exciting new chapter with new ownership, supporting its future, under Frasers Group", the website reads. The shutdown of the online store, with no date given for its return, is the first visible customer-facing disruption since the ownership change took place last week. The website notice adds that orders and gift cards purchased before 13 August 2026 remain the responsibility of the former ownership structure and therefore Harvey Nichols itself cannot process refunds for those purchases directly. Customers are asked customers to contact FTI Consulting instead. Orders placed from 13 August onwards, the day Frasers Group completed the acquisition of the business, will be handled under Harvey Nichols’ standard refunds and returns policy, according to the notice. Frasers confirmed last week that it had acquired the business , assuming control of Harvey Nichols’ online business, inventory and international franchise agreements, along with more than 1,000 employees. The transaction covered six UK stores in Knightsbridge, Manchester, Birmingham, Bristol, Leeds and Edinburgh – with all of these expected to continue trading until further notice. The exception is the Harvey Nichols Dublin store, which will cease trading. While Frasers acquired stock and fixtures, the Irish company entered liquidation last week after the High Court heard it had net liabilities of €28.2 million. Frasers acquired the business from FTI Consulting, which was appointed administrator in June after Harvey Nichols faced sustained trading and operational difficulties, which were highlighted in the its latest accounts. For the full group revenue fell £184.8 million from £204.8 million in the year to the end of March 2025, while losses before tax widened to £49 million from £34 million. Its London store saw sales drop from £78 million to just under £69.5 million in the same period. It was the company’s fifth consecutive loss-making year. Michael Murray, Chief Executive Officer of Frasers Group, described the business as having “significant potential” but requiring “meaningful change”. He said the turnaround could involve “tough choices” and a smaller business in the near term as Frasers reviews Harvey Nichols’ store portfolio, cost base, operating model and organisational structure. The acquisition plays into Frasers Group's luxury ambitions , placing Harvey Nichols alongside Flannels within the group’s luxury division and is intended to strengthen the group’s relationships with brands including Gucci, Moncler, Burberry, Prada and Dior. article_title: Poundland owner weighs sale just over a year after £1 takeover
sub_title: Gordon Brothers is reportedly weighing a sale of Poundland, having acquired the UK discount retailer from Pepco Group for £1 just over a year ago.
article_content: Gordon Brothers is reportedly weighing a sale of Poundland, just over a year after it acquired the UK discount retailer from Pepco Group for £1. The US investment firm, which also owns LK Bennett and Radley, could be appointing advisers within days, according to Sky News. Prospective bidders could include turnaround funds, private equity firms, strategic buyers and other industry players. There is no clear reason why Gordon Brothers would be motivated to sell the business now. A Poundland spokesperson told Sky News: “We've made very significant progress over the past year with a recovery plan that's created simpler, better value for customers centred around thousands of items back at our iconic £1 price point.” A trading update from the retailer is due in the coming days. Gordon Brothers acquired Poundland from Pepco Group in June 2025 after a period of weaker trading. The retailer had recorded a £79 million pre-tax loss for the year to September 2024, while revenue fell 2.5% to £1.8 billion. In August 2025, the High Court approved Poundland’s restructuring plan , shortly before the business was expected to run out of money. The agreement provided for as much as £60 million in new funding, a £30 million overdraft facility and reductions to some store rents. Following this, nearly 150 shops shut and about 2,200 jobs were lost. At the end of 2025, Poundland had 651 locations, down from around 800 before the reorganisation, while its workforce had decreased from 14,200 to about 12,000. It now runs roughly 600 stores across the UK and Ireland. Poundland said in January that its large-scale closure programme had finished, with future exits expected to result from routine lease events. The turnaround has focused on simplifying Poundland’s ranges and restoring its discount positioning. Around 60% of grocery products were priced at £1, while the retailer introduced clearer £1, £2 and £3 price points across its UK estate. Poundland has also c ontinued rebuilding its PEP&CO clothing range, now stocked in around 450 stores. About 90% of the range is priced below £10, while adult clothing has returned to in-house design and PEP&CO branding. Underlying like-for-like sales for the retailer in the Christmas quarter dropped 2.9%, while comparable store volumes rose 2%. First-quarter underlying earnings increased by £8.4 million to £17.3 million. In July, the retailer appointed former Superdry and Marks & Spencer executive Shaun Wills as Chief Finance Officer . Gordon Brothers has recently pursued other UK retail opportunities, including an offer for luxury department store Harvey Nichols. In May, Gordon Brothers confirmed its acquisition of the British handbag brand Radley , a deal that has resulted in the immediate redundancy of 42 employees. A few months earlier, in January, the US investment firm had acquired LK Bennett as part of a strategy to transition the business to an asset-light model.

article_title: Tommy Hilfiger launches ‘Always Denim’ campaign starring Romeo Beckham
sub_title: Tommy Hilfiger has today launched a new autumn 2026 campaign under the title ‘Always Denim’, starring Romeo Beckham alongside Dutch fashion model Yasmin Wijnaldum and a “next generation cast of tastemakers”.
article_content: Tommy Hilfiger has today launched a new autumn 2026 campaign under the title ‘Always Denim’, starring Romeo Beckham alongside Dutch fashion model Yasmin Wijnaldum and a “next generation cast of tastemakers”. Shot at The Mark Hotel in New York, including on the rooftop, the mood is one of “downtown escapes and time spent with friends”, with everyone wearing the latest Tommy Hilfiger denim collection featuring a wide range of washes, fits and silhouettes. Romeo Beckham wears the relaxed, 90s-inspired ‘Theo’ baggy jean with a cable-knit sweater before changing into the classic straight-leg ‘Dover’ jean, paired with a tucked-in denim shirt. He also wears a denim jacket with a Tommy Hilfiger flag on the back and a logo T-shirt. Yasmin Wijnaldum highlights the women’s offering in the high-rise ‘Sarah’ jean, known for its clean, flattering shape, alongside the low-rise ‘Daisy’ silhouette with its relaxed proportions. She also sports a burgundy varsity jacket with leather sleeves and ‘Tommy Hilfiger 1985’ on the back. Tommy Hilfiger said: “Denim has always represented the pinnacle of self-expression to me. When I was a teenager growing up in Elmira, I’d drive to New York City to buy jeans, customise them and sell them out of the trunk of my car. “Through every decade, it’s evolved with music, youth culture and changing attitudes, yet never lost that timeless appeal. This campaign celebrates that legacy through a new generation, showing how the classics continue to be reimagined in personal ways.” Romeo Beckham added: “There’s no right or wrong way to wear denim - that’s the whole point. One day I’ll wear it with a leather jacket, the next with a classic white T-shirt. You can take inspiration from rock, prep or vintage, any kind of style. “Tommy’s iconic denim has been around for my entire life, but it always feels current because everyone makes it work in a way that feels natural to them.” Last month saw Romeo Beckham capitalise on his growing exposure, as well as the fame of his parents, David and Victoria, with the launch of his own football-inspired label called Intra . Partnering with Justin Saul, who had previously revived the dormant skateboard clothing brand Elwood Clothing in 2020 by refocusing it on vintage-inspired essentials and streetwear, Intra is a sportswear label built around the intersection of football culture and fashion. The first Intra release, timed with the start of the World Cup, was called ‘The Nations Collection’. It featured three retro-inspired, limited-edition football jackets representing the USA, England and Brazil. The co-founders described this debut collection as “a love letter to a footballing culture that shaped us, cut and finished in the spirit of the eras we grew up worshipping”.

article_title: Frasers lifts Hugo Boss stake to 47.89%, inching closer to majority ownership
sub_title: Frasers Group has increased its stake in Hugo Boss to 47.89% after further shareholder acceptance of its takeover offer, bringing the retail group close to majority ownership of the German fashion brand.
article_content: Frasers Group has increased its stake in Hugo Boss to 47.89% after further shareholder acceptance of its takeover offer, bringing the retail group close to majority ownership of the German luxury fashion brand. Following the end of the additional acceptance period on 13 August 2026, Fraser Group's offer was accepted for 12,157,598 Hugo Boss shares, representing an additional 17.62% of the company’s share capital and voting rights. This marks the latest increase in share purchases by Frasers Group, which has now lifted its stake from 37.58% (as of 30 July) to 47.89% today. This makes Frasers Group Hugo Boss's single largest shareholder, although it does not automatically give Frasers majority ownership of Hugo Boss. "We appreciate Frasers Group’s continued long-term commitment to Hugo Boss and look forward to maintaining a constructive relationship with them," said Hugo Boss Supervisory Board Chairman Stephan Sturm on the latest transaction. He added that the Supervisory Board would continue to support the brand's execution of its Claim 5 Touchdown strategy while remaining "firmly committed to Hugo Boss" established governance framework and acting in the best interests of the company and all its stakeholders". Introduced in December 2025, Claim 5 Touchdown sets Hugo Boss’ direction through 2028, with a focus on brand equity, distribution and operational performance. The company said the plan had supported improved productivity, earnings quality and cash generation during the first half of 2026. Chief Executive Officer Daniel Grieder also said: “We value the trust and support our shareholders have shown throughout the offer period and welcome Frasers Group's support for our long-term strategic direction." He added that the company would remain focused on executing its strategy "with discipline" and and highlighted his trust in the brand's "strong brand", committed team and "sound financial position". "We are well positioned to unlock substantial value creation potential and deliver on our strategic and financial ambitions,” he said. In its latest financial results from 4 August Hugo Boss reported “tangible progress” for the second quarter of 2026, despite earnings before interest and tax (EBIT) falling 28% to €59 million (£50.5 million). Group sales declined by 9% on a currency-adjusted basis to €905 million (£775 million) in the second quarter, versus €1.002 billion (£858 million) in Q2 2025. However, gross margin increased by a strong 200 basis points to 64.9% in Q2, “driven by sourcing efficiencies, improved pricing, and a higher share of full-price sales”. At the time, Grieder said the financial results showed that the strategy "was already translating into tangible benefits" and that the "results confirm that we are in control of what matters". Frasers launched its voluntary public takeover offer on 10 June for all Hugo Boss shares it did not already own. This followed six years in which Frasers had been building its position in Hugo Boss. At launch, the bid valued the outstanding shares at approximately €1.98 billion and Hugo Boss as a whole at around €2.7 billion. The group had declared the €38 offer price final on 25 June . In July, Frasers crossed Germany’s 30% mandatory-offer threshold after buying a further 2,549,900 shares in Hugo Boss. The week after, on 27 July, the European Commission granted merger-control clearance, satisfying the offer’s only completion condition. The bid therefore became legally unconditional on 28 July. Hugo Boss’s Managing Board and Supervisory Board unanimously recommended that shareholders reject the bid in a reasoned statement issued on 25 June. The board described the €38 consideration as financially "inadequate" , arguing that it did not reflect the company’s standalone value or medium-to-long-term potential. Bank of America and Goldman Sachs provided external opinions supporting that assessment. The price represented a 4.8% premium to Hugo Boss’s closing price of €36.26 on 9 June, the final trading day before Frasers announced its offer. It was also 4.3% above the company’s three-month volume-weighted average price before the announcement. Hugo Boss CEO Daniel Grieder commented at the time: “Against this backdrop, we firmly believe that the offer price fails to capture the company’s intrinsic value and long-term potential.” Frasers CEO Michael Murray, who joined the Hugo Boss Supervisory Board in May 2025, was excluded from the committee assessing the offer. Frasers is, however, reportedly considering Murray as a future Hugo Boss CEO if its takeover succeeds.

article_title: Vuori taps former Abercrombie & Fitch exec as new CMO
sub_title: Californian activewear brand Vuori has appointed former CMO of Abercrombie & Fitch as its new Chief Marketing Officer, effective Monday, 5 October.
article_content: Californian activewear brand Vuori has appointed the former CMO of Abercrombie & Fitch Carey Collins Krug as its new Chief Marketing Officer, effective 5 October. In her new role, Krug will lead Vuori's global marketing organisation, overseeing brand, creative, consumer engagement, digital, retail, wholesale and integrated marketing. According to the brand, she will focus on advancing its global marketing strategy and building on the brand’s momentum worldwide. Krug joins Vuori from Abercrombie & Fitch, where she served as Chief Marketing Officer and supported the repositioning of the brand. Vuori credits her leadership with reigniting Abercrombie's positive momentum as "one of the fastest-growing brands in the US", by evolving its brand positioning, influencer marketing and a "disciplined test-and-learn approach to modern marketing". Earlier in her career, Krug served as CMO at David Yurman and spent over five years as Senior Vice President Global Marketing for Polo Ralph Lauren. She also held the position of VP, Global MKT at Donna Karan International for seven years. “Carey brings the kind of brand-building, consumer engagement and cross-functional marketing leadership that will be instrumental as Vuori enters its next chapter of growth,” said Joe Kudla, founder and CEO of Vuori. “Her experience helping global lifestyle brands sharpen their storytelling and build deeper connections with consumers aligns closely with where we’re headed as we continue to scale.” "Vuori has a rare combination of brand clarity, product strength and deep consumer connection," said Krug. "The foundation is already there - a powerful brand and an engaged community. I am thrilled to build upon this momentum and scale globally with intentionality and consistency.” In May this year, Vuori launched its second golf range with a campaign fronted by British actor, brand ambassador and keen golfer, Tom Holland. Only a few months earlier, Vuori had accelerated its move to elite tennis with the launch of the HardKore Short, its most technical performance style to date , fronted by British tennis star and world number 12 Jack Draper. The release also marks the next phase of Vuori’s growing relationship with Draper, who signed a multi-year, "transformative" deal with the California-based brand in 2025 as it made a strategic push into the sport.

article_title: Kurt Geiger to launch free digital learning programme for aspiring fashion creatives
sub_title: Footwear and accessories retailer Kurt Geiger is launching a free digital learning programme called ‘Business by Design Online’ on 1 September. It will
article_content: Footwear and accessories retailer Kurt Geiger is launching a free digital learning programme called ‘Business by Design Online’ on 1 September. It will coincide with the start of the British Fashion Council’s ‘Fashion Britain’ events, running throughout September 2026. Building on the success of the Kurt Geiger Kindness Foundation’s award-winning Business by Design Academy, the Kindness Foundation has developed the new digital programme in response to growing demand beyond London, with the aim to “make fashion knowledge accessible to everyone”. Created by fashion industry professionals, Business by Design Online will offer “an invaluable front-row seat” to the people shaping the world of fashion in an industry that can often feel out of reach to many. Combining bite-sized learning, engaging video content, interactive challenges and real industry case studies, the self-paced programme will explore every stage of the fashion journey, from design and buying to product development, marketing, retail, social media and digital. Learners will also gain exclusive access to live masterclasses and webinars with leading designers, creative directors, celebrity stylists and industry experts, providing unique insight into the careers, creativity and commercial thinking behind today's global fashion industry. Neil Clifford, CEO of Kurt Geiger, said: “As a patron of the British Fashion Council, Kurt Geiger will launch the Business by Design Online course at the British Fashion Council's 'Fashion Britain' events, which are taking place throughout September 2026 across the UK. “Fashion Britain shares the Business by Design Academy's ambition to broaden access to the fashion industry by decentralising opportunity and widening participation, helping to build a more inclusive, diverse and resilient future for British fashion. “The Business by Design education team will also be on hand at each event to answer questions, demonstrate the platform and help young future professionals take their first steps on their digital learning journey.” Laura Weir, CEO of British Fashion Council, added: “Fashion has the power to create opportunity, but for too long, access to our industry has depended on where you live, who you know or whether you can afford to take part. “Through Fashion Britain, we are committed to opening up pathways into fashion across the UK, connecting more people with the knowledge, networks and opportunities they need to build a career in our industry. “Business by Design Online is a brilliant example of that shared ambition in action. By making high-quality, industry-led learning freely available to anyone, anywhere, the Kurt Geiger Kindness Foundation is helping to remove barriers and inspire the next generation of creative talent. “We're proud to support its launch through Fashion Britain and to work alongside partners who share our belief that talent exists everywhere and opportunity should too.”

Marks & Spencer taps Aries to revive historic St Michael label
sub_title: Marks & Spencer is partnering with London luxury streetwear label Aries on a 26-piece collection that reworks its historic St Michael label for contemporary customers.
article_content: Marks & Spencer is partnering with London luxury streetwear label Aries on a 26-piece collection that reworks its historic St Michael label following renewed interest on social media and resale platforms. The M&S x Aries limited-edition capsule, launching on 20 August, will feature womenswear, menswear and accessories, with prices ranging from £10 for socks and £30 for a Spencer Bear T-shirt, to £120 for a silk dress. According to the retailer, Aries has reinterpreted the heritage label's design codes, infusing the new range with its own distinctive visual language to to create a collection that " feels rich in heritage yet unmistakably contemporary". The collection blends the heritage of the St Michael label with modern streetwear, pulling from the label's archive - including its crests, angel motif and the Penny Bazaar imagery and iconic Spencer Bear - alongside Aries' signature codes, including gothic lettering, Ionic columns, Roman coins and the brand's Temple logo. The resulting range combines both tailoring and sportswear pieces, featuring striped shirts, ties, pinstripe tailoring, tracksuits, hoodies, graphic sweatshirts, knitwear, slip dresses and a matching cardigan and brief set. The collaboration also extends to accessories, including a soft green leather handbag (priced at £90) that recreates the shape and appearance of a familiar M&S carrier bag, as well as brooches and hair clips. The retailer said the partnership responds to renewed interest in the St Michael label across social media and resale platforms, where vintage pieces have attracted younger shoppers. A quick search on Vinted reveals over 500 search results for 'Saint Michael', with dresses, shoes, coats and skirts available for sale for around £25. According to Aries founder and Creative Director Sofia Prantera, the collection draws on personal ties that she has with M&S. Prantera, who started the streetwear label out of a love of trash culture, outsider art, graphics and illustration, said that "M&S was part of family life. "Every summer we would visit from Italy, and it was where I bought my lambswool jumpers. Working with the archive brought back a lot of those memories," she said. "Some of my favourite pieces in the collection come from personal references. Spencer Bear was gifted to me by my grandmother when I was a child, so it was fun to reintroduce him in an unexpected way. The collaboration gave us an opportunity to revisit things that felt genuinely familiar and look at them through a different lens. "M&S is a true British institution that has played a role in so many people's lives and memories. To be invited to work with such an iconic brand, and to bring our own perspective to its heritage, has been a real privilege." Maddy Evans, Womenswear Director at M&S, added: "Whilst Aries and M&S come from different corners of the fashion world, both brands have built strong identities through distinctive design codes and a loyal following. "Bringing those worlds together created an opportunity to offer something familiar yet entirely fresh, translating Aries' iconic creative handwriting through the lens of St Michael and making it accessible to a broader audience at a high-street price point." The St Michael label was first introduced across M&S clothing in 1928 by the son of the retailer's co-founder Michael Marks, and it remained one of the retailer's main own-brand labels across clothing, accessories and homewares until it was discontinued in 2000. It briefly returned on two menswear products – a men’s rugby shirt and sweatshirt – in 2021, but the Aries collaboration marks the proper return of the label. The new collaboration will be available through the M&S website and selected stores. The capsule arrives as M&S marks 100 years of fashion in 2026, with the retailer also preparing for its London Fashion Week debut in September , where it will present a shoppable womenswear and menswear collection.

People Moves, July 2026: George at Asda, Gymshark, Temperley London and more...
sub_title: As July draws to a close, TheIndustry.fashion reflects on possibly the busiest month of appoints yet, marked by senior leadership shake-ups across luxury, retail, sportswear and fashion technology.
article_content: As July draws to a close, TheIndustry.fashion reflects on possibly the busiest month of appoints yet, marked by senior leadership shake-ups across the luxury, retail, sportswear and fashion technology sectors. The luxury fashion sector has been particularly active, with Bottega Veneta and Nadine Merabi appointing new CEOs, Chanel naming a new CFO, Manolo Blahnik hiring a new MD of the Americas, Rabanne welcoming a new Creative Director and Tory Burch appointing its first-ever Chief Brand Officer. Across sportswear we have seen new appointments at Gymshark, TALA and Puma, while retail businesses have welcomed both new faces and familiar ones, including Helen Connolly, who returned to George at Asda as CEO. TheIndustry.fashion highlights the most notable appointments, spanning roles from CEOs and commercial leadership to creative directors and finance positions. Luxury womenswear brand Nadine Merabi has appointed former Karen Millen Managing Director Briony Garbett as CEO. Nick Beighton joined as Non-Executive Chair and Hash Ladha became a Non-Executive Director. Adidas' new Chief Financial Officer Birgit Kretschmer joins the brand from fashion retailer C&A, where she also held the role of CFO. Kretschmer brings more than 30 years of experience to the new role, 25 years of which she has spent at Adidas in roles including CFO of adidas International BV and Western Europe. Gymshark promoted Global Supply Chain Director Matt Rogers to Chief Supply Chain Officer after he led sourcing and supply chain operations on an interim basis. Luxury styling entertainment platform DREST has appointed Julien Dulioust as General Manager of Game , where he will oversee product development, drive commercial performance and handle user acquisition. Schuh has appointed Tomas Petersson as its new President , succeeding Colin Temple, who is retiring after 38 years with the footwear retailer. Petersson will join the business at the end of July and work alongside Temple over the coming months to ensure a smooth leadership transition. British knitwear brand John Smedley has hired Stuart Pannell as CFO , Brian Lancaster as COO and Nick Watt as People Director. Bryan Jackson CBE also returned as Senior Independent Director. Luxury footwear brand Manolo Blahnik appointed Kimberly Mimnaugh as Managing Director of the Americas, overseeing regional retail, wholesale, ecommerce and operations from New York. Frasers Group was reportedly considering Michael Murray to lead Hugo Boss if its proposed takeover of the German fashion company succeeded. No appointment had been confirmed. Chanel appointed Hélène de Tissot as CFO , succeeding Philippe Blondiaux. She will join from Pernod Ricard in October, while Blondiaux will remain until year-end to support the transition. Puma named Dusan Hamlin as its new Vice President of E-Commerce, putting him in charge of its global digital commerce strategy. Kate Spade New York appointed Jonathan Saunders as Executive Creative Director , effective 26 August. He will oversee product design and visual identity from the brand’s New York headquarters. London activewear brand TALA confirmed Sally Hughes as permanent CEO after five months in the interim position and appointed former Pai Skincare executive Verity Linnell as CFO. British luxury house Temperley London appointed Morgaine McGee as CEO and Jack Isenberg as Design Director following founder Alice Temperley’s departure. Isenberg’s first collection will be presented in September. JD Sports Fashion appointed Independent Non-Executive Director Darren Shapland as Interim Chair following its annual general meeting. He will serve until a permanent successor to Andrew Higginson is found. The Very Group appointed former Bank of Ireland Chief Marketing Officer Henry Dummer as CEO of Very.ie, the Irish online retail business and flexible payments provider. Marks and Spencer appointed Jane Robson as Fashion, Home & Beauty Director of Sourcing, Quality and Sustainability, effective in August. She will succeed Monique Leeuwenburgh, who retires in October. Kering appointed Romain Spitzer as CEO of Bottega Veneta , effective 1 September. The former LVMH executive will report to Kering CEO Luca de Meo and join its Executive Committee. Designer label Roksanda appointed former Stella McCartney Head of Flou Simon Valer Dacsef as Head of Design, reporting to CEO Patricia Sancho. Calvin Klein and Tommy Hilfiger owner PVH appointed former Sephora Global COO Alexis Rollier as CFO. He will join in September and succeed Interim CFO Melissa Stone. Direct-to-consumer womenswear brand Beyond Nine appointed former AllSaints Global Ecommerce Director Liam Price as its first CEO. Rabanne appointed Olivier Rousteing as Creative Director after his 14-year tenure at Balmain. The house also announced the appointment on Instagram , with his runway debut scheduled for March 2027. American luxury brand Tory Burch appointed Klitos Teklos as its first Chief Brand Officer, tasking him with global marketing, social media and visual merchandising. Gymshark appointed former Boden executive Shaun Perkinson as Chief Technology Officer. He replaced John Douglas, who retired after five years with the activewear company. Liberty promoted Laura Simpson to Chief Marketing Officer alongside her existing position as Managing Director of LBTY, expanding her remit across group brand, marketing and customer strategy. Former Primark CEO Paul Marchant joined George at Asda as an advisor on the fashion and homeware business’s long-term strategy. UK discount retailer Poundland appointed former Superdry and M&S finance executive Shaun Wills as Chief Finance Officer while continuing its post-restructuring turnaround. Asda appointed Helen Connolly as CEO of George . The New Look CEO previously spent more than 15 years with George and will succeed Liz Evans. NEXT appointed former ASOS Head of ESG Jodie Leek to lead brand sales and marketing. Leek brings over 25 years of experience in global sourcing, supply chain management, and environmental, social and governance (ESG), to her new role. Dr. Martens appointed Melanie Richards as an Independent Non-Executive Director from 15 July. She also became Senior Independent Director and Chair of the Nomination Committee.
