sub_title: Here are some of this week’s news and features highlights handpicked by TheIndustry.fashion team.
article_content: Here are some of this week’s news and features highlights handpicked by TheIndustry.fashion team. The Interview: Vollebak co-founder on wearable tech, wholesale ambitions and building clothes for the next century Vollebak, the experimental clothing company founded by twin brothers Steve and Nick Tidball, has built a global following through products made from space-grade materials, fireproof fabrics and biologically engineered textiles. The brand currently sells exclusively online, operates on a 12-18-month development cycle for most products, and counts customers working in robotics, AI, physics, engineering and finance among its customer base. We gained an in-depth insight into the business from Nick, who spoke to TheIndustry.fashion about the brand's origins, its wholesale ambitions, how it continues to push the boundaries of what the future of clothing could look like and where it is heading next. Read the full interview here. Camilla Rydzek, Senior News & Features Writer. Marks & Spencer is making its London Fashion Week runway debut this autumn , unveiling a shoppable womenswear and menswear collection that customers can buy immediately online, in flagship UK stores and across key international markets. This move, which follows on from pitlane fashion show at Silverstone earlier this month, further underscores just how far M&S fashion has come in recent years. Which is to say, a very long way. Fashionability, value for money, construction, fabric and fit have all been pored over and improved. Now the retailer feels confident to show at LFW and will be live-streaming the event to include its customers in the excitement. Not only is this a great move for Marks & Spencer but it's a great thing for London Fashion Week, which had lost some of its sparkle (understandably in some respect given the fall out from Covid). It is most encouraging to see home grown brands support the event and I feel optimistic LFW could be on an upward trajectory again. Both Mulberry and Alexander McQueen are returning too. I hope to see more. I've said it before but a healthy London Fashion Week benefits us all, and it's certainly going to benefit Marks & Spencer. Lauretta Roberts, Co-founder, CEO and Editor-in-Chief. UK retail footfall falls 3.4% in June as heatwave keeps shoppers indoors The Interview: CQP founder Adam Lewenhaupt on trading finance for footwear and following his design dream It was interesting to hear CQP founder Adam Lewenhaupt’s take on design this week , with a focus on being ‘product first’ and preferring to build a few strong and long-term retail partnerships over quantity. It was also almost refreshing to hear how the Stockholm-based premium footwear brand, which was founded in 2014, doesn’t chase influencers or brand ambassadors like so many brands do now. Lewenhaupt says that is partly because of the “sometimes questionable cost/benefit ratio”, but also because he doesn’t really think CQP’s products are well suited for it. He believes their best ambassadors are their customers. With that in mind, they do their best to take “extremely good care of them”. That way they will keep coming back for more. Last month gave them a fresh reason to take another look at CQP, which takes its time to release what it believes to be standout products rather trying to create volume through far too many styles. To coincide with the start of the World Cup, CPQ launched its new ‘Stillo’ sneaker, though Lewenhaupt admits that was more coincidental timing than planned! It’s an ultra sleek trainer inspired by the first pair of football boots he got in the late 1980s, before synthetic materials took over and when stitching and other details contributed to the actual performance of a shoe. So far, he says that those customers who have bought the Stillo “absolutely love it”. Handmade in Portugal from Italian leathers and suedes, it’s easy to see why it could prove to be much more than a World Cup winner. I look forward to seeing more from CQP. Tom Bottomley, Contributor.

article_title: Belstaff gears to open store at Caledonia Park
sub_title: Heritage British brand Belstaff, which was acquired by Castore in August 2025, has signed for a 2,500 sq ft store at Caledonia Park Designer Outlet in Gretna, Scotland.
article_content: Heritage British brand Belstaff, which was acquired by Castore in August 2025, has signed for a 2,500 sq ft store at Caledonia Park Designer Outlet in Gretna, Scotland. Set to open “in the coming months”, the new store will be located next to Crew Clothing and Moss and will sell a selection of menswear and womenswear across outerwear, essentials and accessories. Alex Luker, Senior Asset Manager at Caledonia Park owner Railpen, said: “Belstaff is a legendary British brand and securing it is a significant endorsement for Caledonia Park. It will elevate the line-up for menswear and womenswear, and it will attract a broad and engaged customer base from far and wide. “As we continue to invest in the long-term success of the destination, attracting brands of this calibre is central to our vision for Caledonia Park, enabling us to assert our position as a leading outlet location within Scotland and the wider UK.” Caledonia Park is already home to several premium retailers, including Calvin Klein, Tommy Hilfiger, Polo Ralph Lauren and Kate Spade New York. The Belstaff signing follows the recent news that Superdry & Co opened its first and only UK outlet store at Caledonia Park, boasting a 4,500 sq ft unit. In April, Belstaff drafted in England cricket legend and TV personality Freddie Flintoff as the face of its ‘Icons’ campaign. One month later, the brand's Chief Executive Officer, Kerry Byrne, announced that she was stepping down from the role. Belstaff was acquired by British premium sportswear brand Castore in August last year.

article_title: NEXT expands Cribbs Mall store as retailer's investment spree continues
sub_title: NEXT will relocate and refit its Cribbs Mall store in Bristol, creating a 47,000 sq ft fashion space alongside the region’s first standalone Bath & Body Works location.
article_content: NEXT will relocate and refit its Cribbs Mall store in Bristol, creating a 47,000 sq ft fashion space alongside the region’s first standalone Bath & Body Works location. The larger NEXT store will carry an expanded selection of clothing and accessories, while the retailer has also agreed to lease a separate 1,797 sq ft unit for Bath & Body Works, extending the US personal care brand’s presence in its UK portfolio. Katie Searle, Director of Asset Management at Sovereign Centros from CBRE, said that the existing NEXT location was among the retailer’s best-performing stores in the country, supporting its decision to invest in the larger fashion space and introduce Bath & Body Works to the centre. “These premium stores at Cribbs will act as showrooms, with shoppers of all ages from across the West Country, West Midlands, South West and South Wales travelling to explore the latest styles and trends,” Searle added. The plans form part of a wider programme of store investment at Cribbs, where M&S carried out a complete refit of its 103,000 sq ft unit in December 2024. H&M also selected the centre for a technology-enabled regional flagship, while Boots has modernised its beauty hall to accommodate more than 30 additional premium brands. Cribbs has also signed leases with AllSaints, Levi’s and Rodd & Gunn in recent months, with the centre reporting a 26% increase in domestic tourists over the past year and a 13% growth in Gen Z shoppers . The Cribbs project comes after NEXT’s largest UK store at Bluewater opened in Kent on 30 July 2026. The 132,000 sq ft Bluewater anchor spans two floors and has 83,000 sq ft of trading space, bringing together womenswear, menswear, childrenswear and home. It also has a Costa café and a Bath & Body Works concession with its own entrance. NEXT previously opened stores in Eldon Square, Newcastle, Canterbury and Ripon during 2025, following the relaunch of its Stratford City location in 2024. The investment programme follows NEXT raising its full-year pre-tax profit forecast by £25 million to £1.24 billion. Total full-price sales rose 9.2% year-on-year during the 13 weeks to 1 August 2026, against the retailer’s forecast of 4% growth.

article_title: Daniel Kearns reunites with David Beckham to lead BOSS BY BECKHAM design
sub_title: Hugo Boss has appointed Daniel Kearns as Head of Design for BOSS BY BECKHAM, reuniting the menswear designer with David Beckham after their earlier collaboration at Kent & Curwen.
article_content: Hugo Boss has appointed Daniel Kearns as Head of Design for BOSS BY BECKHAM, reuniting the menswear designer with David Beckham after their earlier collaboration at Kent & Curwen. Based in London, Kearns will oversee collection creation and design, alongside merchandising and branding, from initial concept through to execution. He will work closely with Beckham, with his first collection scheduled for AW27. The appointment gives BOSS BY BECKHAM dedicated creative leadership as Hugo Boss develops its multi-year partnership with the former England footballer. The multi-year Beckham collaboration was announced in May 2024 and covers capsule and seasonal collections spanning formal and casual menswear. David Beckham with Boss CEO Daniel Grieder Daniel Kearns Beckham said Kearns’s arrival marked the next phase of his work with BOSS, supported by a dedicated team in London. “Having known Daniel for some time, I’ve seen firsthand how his attention to detail and talent will be a great fit as we develop each collection,” Beckham said. Beckham’s relationship with BOSS has expanded from ambassadorial and modelling work into product design. He appeared in the brand’s AW24 campaign and subsequently fronted BOSS ONE Bodywear before launching his first co-designed SS25 collection in April 2025. That collection combined tailoring and elevated casualwear, including knitwear, outerwear, denim and accessories. It also introduced an exclusive signature cut for its tailored pieces. Kearns previously led creative direction at British heritage menswear brand Kent & Curwen, while Beckham was involved in its relaunch. Beckham joined the business in 2015 and participated in product design, store design and campaigns before ending his involvement in 2020 . Kearns and Beckham during their time at Kent & Curwen The pair’s work at Kent & Curwen included collections influenced by Peaky Blinders and The Stone Roses. Kearns later returned to the brand as Chief Creative Officer, also holding the same position at Cerruti 1881. His wider menswear experience includes positions at Alexander McQueen, John Galliano, Yves Saint Laurent and Gucci, with a background spanning tailoring and contemporary luxury menswear. Kearns said: “I have known David for many years and always admired his approach to design, style and curation. I am very much looking forward to working with him and the team at BOSS to bring the joint vision and David’s personal style to life.” The appointment comes as Hugo Boss is subject to a takeover bid from British retail group Frasers. Frasers has been amassing shares in the German giant and currently owns nearly 38% of its shares. It has tabled a €38-a-share takeover offer which has been cleared by regulators in Germany, making the offer “unconditional”. The Boss board, however, has urged shareholders to reject the deal.

article_title: Editors' Top Reads: News from John Lewis, Hugo Boss, BRC and more...
sub_title: Here are some of this week’s news and features highlights handpicked by TheIndustry.fashion team.
article_content: Here are some of this week’s news and features highlights handpicked by TheIndustry.fashion team. The enduring appeal of David Beckham is evident in his highly successful tie-up with Hugo Boss. In 2024, the football star turned brand builder signed a multi-year deal to create BOSS BY BECKHAM, covering capsule and seasonal collections spanning formal and casual menswear. He’d been a long-standing ambassador of BOSS before that deal was signed. It has just been revealed that Irish designer Daniel Kearns has been appointed to head up design for the Beckham sub-brand and will be leading a dedicated London design team for it. This seems to suggest it’s selling well, though BOSS's latest numbers for the group as a whole show sales down 9% in its second quarter, however progress is being made on gross margins. Kearns and Beckham know each other well, having collaborated on British heritage brand Kent & Curwen. I’m interested to see how the London team and Kearns’ input shape BOSS by Beckham. They make a promising team. Of course, all of this is happening against a backdrop of Frasers still piling pressure on BOSS with its takeover bid. The €38-per-share bid it has tabled has cleared the German regulatory process, but the BOSS board’s position remains steadfast. They want shareholders to reject the bid. However, Frasers continues to buy shares and now has a stake with around 38%. How long can they be held off? Lauretta Roberts, Co-founder, CEO and Editor-in-Chief. The irony of choosing this as my top read, given I’m someone who only occasionally dips into yoga, isn’t lost on me. I know I should probably be doing more - and perhaps even joining the growing wave of consumers that John Lewis is hoping to attract with its latest investment. This week, the department store announced plans to capitalise on the booming fitness and wellbeing market by relaunching its sports and wellbeing offering. John Lewis boss Peter Ruis described the move as an “important step” in the British retailer’s wider store investment strategy. The business says its revamped sports and wellbeing departments will make it the first UK retailer to bring sportswear, footwear, wearable technology, recovery products, AI-powered fitness solutions and expert services together under one roof. The move is designed to strengthen John Lewis’ position in the increasingly competitive fitness market, helping it challenge established players such as Sports Direct and specialist technology brands. The multimillion-pound investment has already transformed the sports department at its London Oxford Street store, with further redevelopments planned for Liverpool and Cheadle, alongside a new department launching in its Glasgow store. Read more here. Sophie Smith, News Editor & Senior Writer. I had the best time interviewing Katie Peake, co-founder of brand experience agency Backlash. We spoke about how, in an increasingly digital-first world, physical activations remain one of the most engaging ways for fashion brands to emotionally connect with customers. Having worked in experiential advertising for the last 15 years, she has seen first-hand how the popularity of pop-ups has exploded. As customer expectations keep rising, Peake says the real challenge today is pushing the creative boundaries of what a pop-up can look like and finding the many different ways it can deliver value for the brand. In this interview with TheIndustry.fashion , she reflects on why physical activations continue to be the most powerful way of capturing consumers’ hearts and minds, how Backlash’s creative-first approach sets the agency apart from competitors, and how experiential retail can solve real business problems while also sparking entirely new ways of connecting with customers. Camilla Rydzek, Senior News & Features Writer. It seems retailers really can’t win when it comes to the great British weather. For so many years, late starts to warm spring/summer weather meant the big boys on the high street jumped early into Sale to try to offload excess stock. Inevitably, the smaller independents, despite hanging on for as long as they could, had to follow suit. This was especially the case with the increase in online shopping and diminishing exclusivity for the most sought-after brands (even if they’d helped to build them in the first place). But this week’s latest data from the BRC-Sensormatic Footfall Monitor , looking at UK footfall from 5 July to 1 August - when the Sales were certainly in full swing - showed footfall on the high street down 3.8% year-on-year, although that was actually up from a meagre -6.2% in June when the very warm weather first hit. You’d have hoped that early, properly warm weather would get people shopping to refresh their wardrobes, knowing it could be a long, hot summer ahead. However, as Helen Dickinson, Chief Executive of the British Retail Consortium (BRC), said: “The heatwave continued to bear down on retail footfall in July, with high streets worst affected. London was hit particularly hard as soaring temperatures made tube and train travel less attractive, with some commuters and shoppers opting to stay home.” That’s not music to the ears of any bricks-and-mortar retailer. And that’s despite shoppers being much savvier too. After all, why buy something in June which could have 30% off or more in July? Unless you’re going on an early summer holiday, that is. I remember speaking to a couple of retailers several years ago who said the spring/summer season is just one “to get through” as it’s just “too short” in terms of full-price sales. Plus, lighter-weight goods and less pricey T-shirts and shorts, as opposed to autumn/winter investment outerwear pieces that command much bigger ticket prices, don’t really make the real money. We’re not far into August, the weather is still glorious (and could be well into September when autumn/winter stock will be on the rails and shelves), and I’m picking up the odd piece for between 30%-50% off that I was interested in back in May and early June at full price, but couldn’t afford. Some of the more desirable items do sell out in certain sizes, of course, but there’s still a chance you might find said piece online somewhere – even if it’s a return that’s recently made a size available again. I guess what I’m saying is that retail is still very much a tough old game, and the weather – be it too mild in autumn/winter or, these days, too hot in summer – is still the most talked-about thing (apart from business rates!) when it comes to what impacts trade the most. Tom Bottomley, Contributing Editor.

article_title: Mary Portas and Superdry's Julian Dunkerton join TheIndustry.fashion Fashion [Un]Bound Summit line-up
sub_title: The retail leaders will join senior executives from H&M, Topshop, Aligne and Toast at the one-day event in London this October.
article_content: Globally renowned retail expert Mary Portas and Superdry founder and CEO Julian Dunkerton have joined the speaker line-up for TheIndustry.fashion Fashion [Un]Bound Summit on 15 October 2026. The one-day event at The Forum, Leadenhall, will bring together about 200 fashion-industry leaders for interviews, presentations and panel discussions focused on changes in retail. Portas, the author, activist and founder of Portas Consultancy, will take part in a keynote interview with TheIndustry.fashion Co-founder Lauretta Roberts. The session will examine her approach to turning physical stores into places for human connection and building loyalty beyond individual transactions. She will also discuss how large and small brands can create consistent experiences across retail channels and develop a clear voice grounded in purpose. Portas has worked with British retailers including Harvey Nichols, John Lewis and Topshop during a career spanning more than 40 years. She is also known for presenting the BBC series Mary Queen of Shops and for her long-running advocacy for the British high street. Her consultancy works with businesses across fashion, beauty and lifestyle, with a focus on translating brand strategy into customer experience and company behaviour. Portas’s work on physical retail includes the government-commissioned Portas Review, published in December 2011. The review proposed measures covering town-centre management, business rates, vacant properties and local markets, while arguing that high streets should function as social and commercial centres. Julian Dunkerton CEO and Founder of Superdry Dunkerton’s appearance comes as Superdry continues its restructuring and repositioning. For the year ended 26 April 2025, the business posted a statutory profit after tax of £50.5 million, reversing a £67.7 million loss in the previous year. In November 2025, Dunkerton presented the Superdry & Co strategy at its Oxford Street flagship. The approach combines a revised mainline identity with the return of Bench and an offer spanning vintage and upcycled clothing. The Forum, Leadenhall: a brand new, state of the art event venue Additional confirmed speakers include some Of H&M UK and Ireland Managing Director Karen O’Rourke, Topshop and Topman Global Chief Marketing Officer Moses Rashid, Aligne CEO Ginny Seymour, Albaray CEO Paula Stewart and Toast CEO Suzie de Rohan Willner. See the full speaker line-up here . The summit programme will cover AI and new retail technologies, connected stores, circular business models, workforce development and creativity as a driver of demand. Tickets are on sale now, priced at £225 plus VAT, and are open to senior executives from fashion brands and retailers. Lunch, refreshments and a drinks reception are all included in the cost of each ticket. The event is staged at The Forum, Leadenhall, a brand new state-of-the-art event venue in the City of London, which will allow for an elevated and engaging experience for speakers and delegates alike. Industry suppliers can take part in the event through our flexible sponsorship packages. For more information, please contact partnerships@theindustry.fashion . TheIndustry.fashion Fashion [Un]Bound Summit is staged in proud partnership with global logistics expert Bleckmann, with StoryStream AI and Aptos sponsoring the programme.

article_title: Capri Holdings lowers outlook as Michael Kors weighs on growth
sub_title: Capri Holdings reported a 3.5% decline in first quarter revenue to $769 million for the period ended 27 June 2026, with weaker performance from Michael Kors offsetting growth at Jimmy Choo.
article_content: Capri Holdings reported a 3.5% decline in first quarter revenue to $769 million for the period ended 27 June 2026, with weaker performance from Michael Kors offsetting growth at Jimmy Choo. Michael Kors revenue fell 7.1% year-on-year to $590 million. On a constant currency basis, revenue declined 7.6%. The company noted that approximately $10 million of revenue was attributable to wholesale shipments occurring earlier than anticipated. Jimmy Choo delivered stronger results, with revenue rising 10.5% year over year to $179 million. On a constant currency basis, Jimmy Choo revenue increased 9.3%. Capri Holdings reported gross profit of $500 million, with a gross margin of 65.0%, compared with gross profit of $502 million and a gross margin of 63.0% in the prior-year period. The 200 basis point improvement in gross margin was primarily attributed to higher full-price sell-throughs and lower tariff rates compared with the first quarter of fiscal 2026. Looking ahead, Capri Holdings cautioned that results could vary materially from current expectations due to external factors, including changes in global economic conditions, additional tariff increases, inflationary pressures, shifts in consumer confidence and foreign currency fluctuations. The company now expects FY27 revenue of approximately $3.4 billion. The revised outlook reflects an estimated $50 million impact from lower-than-expected second-quarter revenue at Michael Kors due to inventory delays, a $50 million impact from softer EMEA trends related to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, and a $35 million impact from foreign currency headwinds compared with previous expectations. Chairman and CEO John D. Idol said: "Looking beyond fiscal 2027 the opportunity for Michael Kors and Jimmy Choo remains significant. "As our strategic initiatives continue to gain momentum, Capri Holdings is well positioned to drive sustainable growth, enhance profitability and create meaningful long-term value for our shareholders."

article_title: Oxfam branches into fashion rental with 14-day online pilot
sub_title: The charity is testing whether distinctive donated garments can generate income through repeated hires, supported by rental and fulfilment specialist ACS.
article_content: Oxfam has launched an online clothing rental pilot, offering distinctive donated garments to rent from £22 for 14 days. The charity describes the initiative as the first rental service launched by a national UK charity. It began the pilot on 3 August, ahead of its annual Second-Hand September campaign. The Oxfam Rental platform offers hundreds of garments selected from donated stock, including vintage finds and directional designer pieces considered less suited to its standard shop rails. The womenswear launch range features a Balenciaga dress with blue-and-white spots, a tailored yellow jacket by Stella McCartney and a strapless black Dolce & Gabbana dress. Oxfam will use the pilot to test demand for hiring second-hand fashion, focusing on customers seeking event clothing without committing to a purchase. Each item is cleaned, pressed and prepared before dispatch, then returned for another customer to hire. Oxfam said the model could extend garments’ useful lives while generating income for its humanitarian and charitable work. Julie Tyrell, Head of E-Commerce & Retail Sustainability at Oxfam, said: “We see pieces come through our shops that you simply won't find anywhere else - and until now, the only way to own one was to buy it outright. Rental means people can access that wardrobe for the moment they actually need it and then not let it just sit in a cupboard afterwards "This is another interesting option which gives people access to pieces that are genuinely different, without adding to that wear-once cycle. If our pilot shows people want to rent rather than buy for a single occasion, that's a real shift in how clothes get used, not just where they come from." Customers can choose their rental dates online, with delivery and prepaid return shipping included in the price. Oxfam says orders need to be submitted at least 48 hours before the hire period begins, although it recommends arranging delivery four days before an event. The service currently covers UK Mainland addresses, excluding Northern Ireland and the Channel Islands. Garments cannot be collected from or returned to Oxfam shops because the online operation is managed separately. Fashion rental and fulfilment company ACS is supplying the operational infrastructure, including garment preparation, dispatch and returns. According to Oxfam’s service information, womenswear items are hand-checked and ozone-cleaned ahead of each rental. Menswear is supplied through a partnership with ACS and includes suits, tuxedos and other occasionwear. Measurements are provided online, while product pages for vintage womenswear without standard labels include garment dimensions. Customers do not need to dry-clean items before returning them. Late returns carry a £10 daily charge, while optional insurance covers accidental damage beyond expected wear. The platform does not currently allow renters to buy hired garments. Anthony Burns, Chief Operating Officer at ACS, said the partnership would help extend the life of clothing while supporting Oxfam’s fundraising. "We are incredibly proud to partner with Oxfam on an initiative that demonstrates the power of circular innovation to deliver both environmental and social value. ACS and Oxfam share a commitment to creating a more sustainable future for fashion, while ensuring positive outcomes for communities. “By providing the operational infrastructure behind Oxfam's online rental proposition, we are helping to extend the life of garments, increase access to more sustainable fashion choices, and support the generation of vital funding for Oxfam's important work around the world. This partnership is a strong example of what can be achieved when organisations come together with a shared purpose and a commitment to driving meaningful change," Burns said, The pilot adds rental to the charity’s existing shop (the charity operates 500 stores nationwide) and e-commerce operations as it prepares for Second-Hand September, its campaign encouraging consumers to choose pre-owned fashion.

article_title: Backlash’s Katie Peake on why experiential retail matters to fashion now more than ever
sub_title: In an increasingly digital-first world, physical activations remain one of the most engaging ways for fashion brands to emotionally connect with customers, says Katie Peake, Co-Founder of brand experience agency Backlash.
article_content: In an increasingly digital-first world, physical activations remain one of the most engaging ways for fashion brands to emotionally connect with customers, says Katie Peake, Co-Founder of brand experience agency Backlash. Having worked in experiential advertising for the last 15 years, she has seen first-hand how the popularity of pop-ups has exploded. As customer expectations keep rising, Peake says the real challenge today is pushing the creative boundaries of what a pop-up can look like, and finding the many different ways it can deliver value for the brand. In this interview with TheIndustry.fashion, she reflects on why physical activations continue to be the most powerful form of capturing consumers’ hearts and minds, how Backlash’s creative-first approach sets the agency apart from competitors, and how experiential retail can solve real business problems while also sparking entirely new ways of connecting with customers. Since Peake launched Backlash in 2017, pop-ups have become such a fixture of fashion and beauty marketing that consumers now almost expect them. And there are good reasons for this. “Experiential is one of the only forms of marketing that actually can speak to people one-to-one,” explains Peake. For her, the format’s value lies in its ability to strengthen customer community and loyalty. Unlike a digital ad, which a consumer might engage with for a second or two, visiting an in-person destination demands dedicated attention from its audience and allows for a much more memorable interaction. Especially as, on average, a customer spends between five and 45 minutes inside a pop-up. “That's a really long time to have your target audience inside a physical advert, and I think that's what makes pop-ups so successful,” Peake adds. Backlash x Sunglass Hut's Covent Garden pop-up Personalisation and community building can be particularly impactful ways of ensuring a successful pop-up, since consumers are looking for experiences that are otherwise unavailable in a brand's existing physical retail or e-commerce spaces. In Peake’s experience, personalisation opportunities that work particularly well are product customisation services, or offering limited-edition merchandise that's not available anywhere else. Digital media, meanwhile, remains key to community building. It doesn't just help followers find the pop-up – it lets visitors share their experiences, strengthening community bonds both online and in-store. But experiential retail can go far beyond simply selling products. It can also help change the perception of a brand. One of Backlash's earlier projects, for example, saw it launch a denim laundrette pop-up with retailer NEXT. This addressed a difficult challenge: attracting younger shoppers to the retailer's jeans offering. By creating a pop-up space that was clearly meant to engage a younger audience, NEXT finally attracted its target customer. Visitors received one-to-one jeans consultations and could even exchange an old pair of jeans for a new one, with the activation exceeding its target-audience KPIs and follow-up survey benchmarks. Years of delivering brand activations have given Backlash a clear understanding of how the right combination of creative, design and execution drives impact. The agency has managed activations where visitors arrived at sunrise and queued for hours just to get a glimpse of the space. Today, the challenge isn't getting people through the door, Peake explains. It's making sure their experience stands out in an increasingly crowded market. For Backlash, that differentiation comes down to one thing: consistently creating a sense of wonder. Peake has worked in experiential marketing for more than 15 years, having started in traditional advertising across television, print and campaign production. Her move into physical experiences began when advertising agencies received briefs that did not fit their existing media departments. “I found this way more interesting than TV and print because I actually found thinking in a 3D world easier,” she shared. “It’s not an advert that you see on TV. It’s an advert that’s there for a few days, and people get to walk through.” Peake later became a Creative Director at 26, working on experiential projects for Coca-Cola and Nestlé. Together with her colleague Aarron Taylor, she built an experiential creative department from the ground up, later using this experience to launch Backlash in 2017. Following the launch, the pair quickly built strong relationships with both fashion and beauty brands, expanding its client base through word of mouth. Debenhams was among its first clients, with the retailer commissioning Backlash to deliver an entire wedding show. Despite a tight budget, Backlash delivered – and the project set the foundations for how the company still approaches work today. Central to Backlash’s value proposition is its identity as a creative-owned agency, with its co-founders infusing every project with a shared commitment to original thinking, innovation and thoughtful design. “We’re focused on creativity and we’re focused on the product that we create being high quality, standing out and being something we’re proud of,” Peake shares. This is also where the agency gets its name from: Backlash reflects the team's drive to do things differently from how other agencies might approach a project. Backlash x Marc Jacob's ' The Big Silver Box ' pop-up The creative-first ethos runs through every step of a Backlash project, starting with a thorough examination of the brief, intended audience and business problem before a visual concept is proposed. “We really pull apart briefs, and we really try and understand the brand before we come up with ideas,” Peake explains. “So we take quite a bit of time on that creative part, which sets us apart.” The creative team may spend around a week developing the initial direction, working closely with the client to ensure the concept is fully formed before the implementation begins. “A pop-up is really exciting because you can make it whatever shape, structure or materials you want,” shares Peake. “So the rulebook can almost go out of the window, as long as you're making sure it’s still got the look and feel of your brand.” By spending more time on the creative ideation, Backlash ensures that the activation not only brings a fresh perspective but also helps the brand stay ahead of the competition by creating a genuinely unique experience. With so many possibilities and unbridled creative freedom, it becomes even more important for the brief to be clearly defined. Peake’s top tip for any fashion brand eager to explore launching an activation would be to focus on just one objective – be that changing brand perception or driving awareness, and work from there. “It’s about focusing on the number one thing that you want to achieve as a brand, not the eight things,” Peake said. “Don’t overthink it. Speak to people who are experts in that field, and we can overthink it for you.” That philosophy shapes every aspect of how Backlash approaches the work. Rather than asking brands to juggle multiple suppliers and moving parts, the agency simplifies the process by bringing creative, design and project management together under one roof. Specialist construction partners are managed on clients' behalf, while Backlash oversees every stage of delivery. Its full-service offering spans location sourcing, staffing, health and safety, visual merchandising, retail systems and installation, giving brands a single point of contact and a seamless route from concept to completion. By accommodating both regional and global approvals, concepts can be adapted quickly, ensuring the final experience reflects the brand intentions in the best possible way. That’s once again where Backlash’s agile, collaborative approach with clients stands out. The agency’s track record speaks for itself. It has already produced a number of standout case studies, one of the most successful being the Marc Jacobs activation, "The Big Silver Box". What defined this activation was that “it was completely different to anything that they had in their UK stores,” according to Peake. “It was specifically launching a collaboration with Kim Kardashian and in that pop-up were items that you couldn't get anywhere else. “So it was not only visually really different to what the brand was doing in its flagship, but it also gave shoppers a reason to go there because it was the only place that you can get a very limited edition item.” The month-long installation was not only successful in achieving Marc Jacobs’ objectives, and it also won Best UK Pop-Up at the VM & Display Awards, with parts of its internal fit-out later reused in a flagship store. Backlash x Marc Jacob's 'The Big Silver Box' pop-up Of course, success can be measured in different ways. As budgets grow, brands are understandably looking for ways to measure marketing impact more comprehensively. As Peake outlines, success metrics need to correspond to the brand's key objectives — and that means looking beyond hard numbers alone. That's not to say numbers don't matter: data points like footfall, sales, social reach and customer feedback can all be collected and tracked. But they only tell part of the larger success story. The harder thing to capture is the long-term impression a campaign leaves on a customer's mind. Take one of Backlash's more recent pop-ups, with global retail chain Sunglass Hut. Visitors could browse a small selection of best-selling sunglasses in person, then scan a QR code to access the brand's full range via its e-commerce store. Each visitor also received a small gift — a very useful lens wipe that I still carry around in my purse — that doubled as a voucher for future use. It's a great example of how a pop-up can pique someone's interest and create a memorable experience while also building in long-term value. A visitor might not buy a new pair of sunglasses that day, but they walk away inspired, carrying a call to action they can act on later. While it is hard to quantify the exact impact of the pop-up on future sales, it is undeniable that an impression has been made that will influence consumers’ future decisions. Consumers will continue to expect more from the pop-ups they visit, which makes it ever-more important for brands to push the creative envelope. For Peake, fashion shows demonstrate how visually stunning sets and storytelling can generate impact far beyond immediately measurable data points. The same principle can be adapted to physical spaces, as they can become a brand’s creative microcosm, instead of another retail outlet. In other words, experiential retail's best days are still ahead — there's no shortage of creative, disruptive ways for brands to bring their customer proposition to life. In partnership with

article_title: In Conversation: Harvey Nichols, Nadine Merabi, FitFlop and more...
sub_title: Last month, we spoke to founders and business leaders from across the fashion industry about their product strategies, international expansion plans and
article_content: Last month, we spoke to founders and business leaders from across the fashion industry about their product strategies, international expansion plans and how they are differentiating their brands in an increasingly competitive market. “Product is king. Everything we do is tested in a human performance lab. It's clinically engineered, and unlike some others where it's cosmetic, everything for us has a purpose and a reason for being. We try to fuse comfort and aesthetics, because one without the other does not work long term.” -  Gianni Georgiades, CEO of FitFlop Five years after joining FitFlop, CEO Gianni Georgiades has repositioned the independent footwear business from a broad comfort proposition to a science-backed global brand with recognisable design codes. In this interview with TheIndustry.fashion, he discusses the brands transition from a legacy double-density constructions to lighter single-density engineered midsoles, and how this has supported FitFlop’s expansion across sneakers and clogs, while retaining its focus on comfort and performance. "We are doing a series of eight projects this year that we would class as really pushing the boundaries of clothing. I think it's massively important to do projects that are pure moonshot ideas, it's very important to test the limits of what we are capable of." - Nick Tidball, co-founder of Vollebak Product innovation is something that the two brothers and co-founders of experimental clothing company Vollebak know well. The brand is working on eight experimental projects during 2026, with three focused on wearable technology. Its first release this year, the Sonic Jacket, features a prototype design engineered to shift the wearer's cognitive and physiological state through sound. In this interview with TheIndustry.fashion co-founder Nick Tidball discusses Vollebak’s technology projects and distribution plans , including an appearance at Paris Fashion Week to assess wholesale demand. CQP founder Adam Lewenhaupt on trading finance for footwear and following his design dream "We have stayed very true to ourselves and we’ve been very authentic, which clearly shows in our products. I’d like to think we are leaders when it comes to creating products at the intersection of elegance and casual, and that our customers feel that we offer something different in terms of quality and fit." - Adam Lewenhaupt, founder of CQP We also sat down with another footwear pioneer this month, Adam Lewenhaupt, the Founder of Stockholm-based premium footwear brand CQP . Known for its understated, unique and carefully constructed sneakers, the brand has grown slowly and without external financing since Lewenhaupt founded it in 2014. The former investment banker told us all about CQP’s “handmade sneakers without compromise” and his journey so far. "What makes the resale space so rewarding is this constant evolution; heritage and archival pieces are regularly rediscovered, finding passionate new audiences as modern tastes circle back." - Dominic Durante, CEO of Designer Exchange The journey of building and growing businesses was also a theme that we followed in this interview with D esigner Exchange CEO Dominic Durante, who discussed how the pre-loved luxury retailer has been expanding without changing the simple model it established in 2013. All of Designer Exchange's stock comes directly from its customers, and the stores' 'buy, sell and exchange' model remains a strategy that is clearly working. Durante tells us all about it. "Looking back, it was both exciting and incredibly challenging. Those early years taught me resilience, adaptability and the importance of believing in your vision, even before anyone else does." - Nadine Merabi, founder and Creative Director of MERABI Lewenhaupt isn't the only founder who started his career outside of the fashion industry. Merabi founder and Creative Director Nadine Merabi began her fashion business in 2015 with a £250 sewing machine after a career as a competitive hockey player. Selfridges subsequently asked her to develop a full range, helping move the label beyond its early one-off designs. In her interview about starting and scaling MERABI , the designer describes learning every part of the operation herself, from sourcing fabrics to packing orders. The Manchester-headquartered brand is now expanding its offering even more, from its signature occassionwear range now to more every-day styles including denim. With a recently appointed new CEO , the brand is looking ahead towards its next phase of international growth. "Like many people in the fashion industry, my career began at 16 in a shop. It taught me that if you show drive and ambition, you can get noticed and supported into new and exciting roles. I moved from the shop floor into Head Office as an Assistant Buyer and my career developed from there." - Kate Benson, Chief Merchant at Harvey Nichols Another standout interview with a female fashion executive saw TheIndustry.fashion sit down with Harvey Nichols' Chief Merchant Kate Benson , where she traced back how her early retail experience established a customer-led approach that still informs her decisions today. While she started on the shop floor at 16, she now works across more than 300 brands and is overseeing changes to Harvey Nichols’ product strategy and branded spaces. In this interview she reflects on her journey through fashion, the lessons she has learned along the way, the leaders who have inspired her, and her ambitions for the next chapter of her career.

article_title: Puma turnaround continues as Q2 losses narrow despite falling sales
sub_title: Puma reported a 9.4% organic fall in second-quarter revenue to €1.69 billion, a steeper decline than its 1% currency-adjusted fall in Q1, as its distribution clean-up and move away from heavy promotions continued to weigh on sales. Yet the brand also showed progress on controlling costs and margins, with its EBIT loss narrowing.
article_content: Puma reported a 9.4% organic fall in second-quarter revenue to €1.69 billion (£1.45 billion), a steeper decline than its 1% currency-adjusted fall in Q1, as its distribution clean-up and move away from heavy promotions continued to weigh on sales. Yet the brand also showed progress on controlling costs and margins, with its EBIT loss narrowing. The results reflect Puma's ongoing strategic transformation plan under CEO Arthur Hoeld. The company had previously described 2026 as a transition year as it works to restore growth through cost efficiencies, inventory reductions and improvements to its distribution model, while investing in its digital infrastructure and direct-to-consumer channels. Puma said it now expects sales to improve sequentially during the second half while it reduces discounting, clears inventory and tightens distribution. Its aim remains a return to growth in 2027 through its reset plan. Revenue for the first half of 2026 declined by 5.2% on a currency-adjusted basis to €3.55 billion (£3.04 billion). The result follows Puma's 1% currency-adjusted sales decline in the first quarter , when revenue reached €1.86 billion (£1.59 billion) and inventory clearance ran slightly ahead of plan. Puma maintained its full-year guidance for a low- to mid-single-digit currency-adjusted sales decline. It also continues to expect an EBIT loss of between €50 million (£42.9 million) and €150 million (£128.6 million), including one-off costs associated with its efficiency programme. Hoeld said that in the second quarter Puma continued to rebuild itself as a brand-led organisation, and that operationally the brand took " significant steps towards a structurally healthier business model" by "reducing inefficiencies, optimising our cost base and improving our organisational setup". “After a solid first quarter and a softer second quarter in line with expectations, we expect sales to improve sequentially in the second half of 2026. This supports our confidence in the full-year trajectory, and we confirm our outlook for the full year," he added. Puma's EBIT loss narrowed to €53.1 million (£45.5 million) in Q2, compared with a loss of €109.1 million (£93.5 million) in the corresponding period of 2025. The improvement came despite weaker revenue and reflected measures intended to reduce costs and improve margins. Performance varied across markets. Sales in Europe, the Middle East and Africa fell 12.9% to €674.1 million (£577.7 million), affected by weak European demand and disruption in the Middle East. North American sales dropped 16.7%, while Latin America declined 13.8%. Asia-Pacific revenue grew 8.6%, supported by demand for low-profile footwear, including the Speedcat family. Footwear, Puma's largest product category, declined 11.7% to €935.6 million (£801.7 million). Growth in running, HYROX training products and low-profile trainers was insufficient to offset wider weakness. Apparel revenue fell 4.3% to €552.1 million (£473.2 million), while accessories declined 12%. The results follow a series of senior appointments under Hoeld, with talent coming from some of the brand's biggest competitors including Adidas, Nike and ASICS. Puma recently named Dusan Hamlin as Vice President of E-Commerce and Dennis Schröder as Managing Director for Europe , alongside Mark Langer as Chief Financial Officer , Laurent Fricker as Head of Sportstyle , James Carnes as Creative Director and Bertrand Blanc as Vice President of Global Wholesale . During the turnaround, Frasers Group took a 5.77% minority stake in Puma in March , building its position largely through derivatives. Puma is a major supplier to Frasers-owned Sports Direct.

article_title: In Review, July 2026: Headline highlights from SKIMS, M&S, Sports Direct and more...
sub_title: Store expansion continued across the UK and Europe, while warm weather shifted spending online, promotions held down prices and major fashion events brought buyers and new collections to London and Paris.
article_content: As July draws to a close, TheIndustry.fashion reflects on a month marked by sustained store investment and exciting new openings, as well as inflation and stronger online demand. The British high street has seen some great additions this month, from SKIMS opening its first standalone UK flagship, to Frasers Group introducing its combined Sports Direct and Everlast Gyms+ format outside the UK for the first time. Retailers have also invested in refurbishments with Marks & Spencer unveiling its Oxford Street Pantheon transformation. Across the sector, warm weather produced mixed results. While retail sales and clothing spending improved, supported by summer promotions, record temperatures reduced store visits and pushed a greater share of non-food purchases online. We have also seen a lot of interesting data stories this month, from the World Cup and summer racing calendar generating increased demand for football products and occasionwear. Meanwhile a host of events, from the Scoop fashion show trade show to Paris Haute Couture Week gave us the best of fashion this month. We also heard from top industry voices including FitFlop CEO Gianni Georgiades, and Harvey Nichols' Chief Merchant Kate Benson. British spectacle maker Cubitts has opened its first Manchester store , marking the brand's long-awaited arrival in the city after almost a decade of searching for the right location. Oliver Bonas is set to open stores in retail parks for the first time , with new locations at Glasgow Fort in September and Teesside Park later this year. Tod's launches Harrods pop-up for Red Dot sneakers Tod's, the Italian luxury footwear brand, has opened a dedicated pop-up at Harrods centred on its Red Dot men's sneaker collection. The temporary retail space features a selection of Red Dot sneaker styles for men, combining the brand's traditional hand craftsmanship with its focus on product innovation. Meadowhall strengthens fashion line-up with Mint Velvet, Belstaff and Michael Kors deals Meadowhall has added new stores from Mint Velvet and Belstaff , as well as a major refurbishment of Michael Kors' existing flagship. The three deals are part of the shopping centre's push to grow The Avenue with aspirational fashion brands and upgraded retail concepts. Frasers Group opens ‘landmark’ Sports Direct and Everlast Gyms+ flagship in Dublin Frasers Group opened an 85,000 sq ft Sports Direct and Everlast Gyms+ flagship at the former Debenhams site on Dublin's Henry Street. The four-storey location represents an €80 million city-centre investment, created 75 roles and introduced HOKA to Sports Direct stores. SKIMS opens first UK flagship on London’s Regent Street SKIMS has launched its first standalone UK flagship at 245-247 Regent Street, as the shapewear and lifestyle brand expands internationally. The 12,000 sq ft store is based in the former Ted Baker site and follows the 10-year lease agreed with The Crown Estate. Zara’s sister brand Lefties confirms late August opening for first UK store Inditex's budget fashion and lifestyle label Lefties has confirmed that its first UK store will open in Liverpool ONE in late August. The rollout will then move on to Lakeside in early October and Gateshead's Metrocentre in November. Nobody’s Child continues UK retail expansion with new store in Cambridge Nobody's Child prepared to open a 1,000 sq ft store at 3 Grand Arcade in Cambridge, taking its standalone UK estate to 10 boutiques. The Cambridge opening is its third of 2026, following launches at Bluewater Shopping Centre and in Harrogate. M&S relocates Weymouth store with fashion at the fore Marks & Spencer relocated its Weymouth store to Gateway Retail Park , creating more than 70 jobs and giving fashion a prominent role. The new location carries Per Una, Goodmove and Rosie Lingerie, alongside expanded denim and specialist bra selections. Sprayground lands in London with 10-day pop-up New York bag and luggage label Sprayground has opened a 10-day pop-up at the Future Stores space at 95 Oxford Street. Called Sprayground's Soho Playground, the residency ran until 26 July and featured an appearance from founder David Ben-David. Lululemon brings padel pop-up to Manchester’s Trafford Centre As part of the expanded store opening, Lululemon put on a two-week padel pop-up at Manchester's Trafford Centre . The bookable court was open until 23 July and reflected the sport's rising popularity. Wax London expands Fenwick partnership with new Kingston concession Wax London expanded its Fenwick partnership with a 500 sq ft concession in the department store's Kingston upon Thames branch. The new space followed its Newcastle concession and features custom rails, tinted acrylic surfaces and a vintage oak haberdashery counter. Marks & Spencer completes Pantheon flagship transformation and begins format test Marks & Spencer completed the renewal of its nearly 100,000 sq ft Pantheon flagship at 173 Oxford Street . The four-floor store brings Food, Fashion, Home and Beauty together and will test merchandising and customer-service approaches before successful features are rolled out elsewhere. Belstaff gears to open store at Caledonia Park British heritage brand Belstaff has signed for a 2,500 sq ft store at Caledonia Park Designer Outlet in Gretna, Scotland. The planned location will sit beside Crew Clothing and Moss and stock menswear and womenswear spanning outerwear, essentials and accessories. NEXT's 132,000 sq ft Bluewater anchor store to open this month NEXT is due to open a 132,000 sq ft anchor at Bluewater on 30 July, tripling its presence at the Kent shopping centre. The former House of Fraser unit will give Bluewater its first new anchor store since the destination launched in 1999. Damson Madder opens first permanent retail space at Selfridges London fashion label Damson Madder has opened its first permanent retail space at Selfridges' Oxford Street flagship on 6 July. Set within the Contemporary Studio on the third floor, it is the brand's largest physical presence and follows its Selfridges launch in 2024. New Look’s largest concept store to open at Metrocentre New Look has opened its largest concept store at Metrocentre on 9 July, taking 11,000 sq ft in the destination's Red Mall. The digitally enhanced format brings Click & Collect, self-service returns, digital browsing, refreshed fitting rooms and expanded product ranges. ’47 heads back to London’s Soho for new pop-up US cap brand ’47 opened a three-month pop-up at 13 Newburgh Street , returning to physical retail in London's Soho. The temporary store followed its 2023 Air Street unit and coincided with the launch of dedicated UK and EU e-commerce platforms. Garage continues UK retail expansion with new store at Lakeside Canadian activewear, athleisure and denim brand Garage has signed for a 4,221 sq ft store at Lakeside Shopping Centre in Essex. The latest UK location comes after openings on London's Oxford Street and at Bluewater, extending a business with 231 North American stores. Brook Taverner’s retail expansion gathers pace with new Guildford store British menswear retailer Brook Taverner opened its 17th UK store at 76 High Street in Guildford, Surrey. The retail expansion will continue with Ambleside and St Andrews locations, as the company targets an estate of up to 30 stores within five years. Clarks plans up to 20 new European stores as expansion gathers pace Clarks has opened at Santangelo Outlet Village in Italy as it plans between 15 and 20 new European stores this year. The continental expansion follows recent openings across Italy and Spain, with further locations planned in France, Belgium and the UK. Byan set to open first flagship store in London Spanish womenswear brand Byan prepared to open its first London flagship on Chelsea's King's Road in October. The permanent store follows the brand's three-month Covent Garden pop-up, which opened in November 2025 and was its first physical presence in the capital. In Pictures: Selfridges unveils FIFA 1904 World Cup pop-up featuring first-ever licensed fashion collection Selfridges opened a pop-up presenting the first official FIFA-licensed fashion collection, designed by Maison Kitsuné Creative Director Marcus Clayton. The FIFA 1904 collection was developed with VFILES and takes its name from the year in which football's international governing body was established. July's indicators pointed to softer price growth and improved spending, although physical footfall remained under pressure as hot weather moved more purchases online. UK retailers keep prices low as shop price inflation eases According to the British Retail Consortium, UK shop price inflation eased to 0.9% in July from 1.2% in June. The Shop Price Monitor found non-food inflation slipping to 0.2% as retailers stepped up promotional activity across clothing, footwear and food. Clothing prices fall 0.5% in June as retail competition holds down prices The Office for National Statistics said clothing and footwear prices dropped 0.5% in June after rising 0.2% in May . The latest inflation figures showed the Consumer Prices Index at 2.6%, while retailers still faced employment, packaging and energy costs. Heatwave and online shopping rebound delivers boost to June retail spending UK retail sales rose in June as hot weather supported demand for clothing and air-conditioning products, while summer discounting encouraged spending. Office for National Statistics figures also showed online shopping rebounding to its highest level in five years. This was reinforced by Barclays' Consumer Spend report which saw UK consumer card spending rose 1.9% year on year in June , improving on May's 0.8% growth but still below CPIH inflation. UK retail footfall falls 3.4% in June as heatwave keeps shoppers inside According to BRC and Sensormatic data, UK retail footfall dropped 3.4% year on year in June as record temperatures kept shoppers away from stores. The five-week figures put high streets down 6.2%, shopping centres down 2.5% and retail parks down 0.3%. Holiday demand set to drive summer retail spending KPMG UK found that 63% of consumers had booked or intended to book a summer holiday , with 75% of travellers planning purchases before departure. The Consumer Pulse survey showed 42% expected to buy clothing and 25% planned to purchase footwear. Consumer confidence sees six-point ‘Burnham bounce’ Consumer confidence increased by six points in July , its largest monthly improvement since November 2023, according to GfK. The headline confidence measure nevertheless remained negative at minus 17, despite heatwaves, football success and a change of Prime Minister supporting sentiment. Price beats ethics at the checkout for majority of Brits Although 68% of British consumers said ethical production mattered, the most common behaviour during their latest purchase was choosing according to price or quality alone. Research from Zero100 tested willingness to pay more for ethical options across clothing and other consumer categories. Summer racing events drive occasionwear demand, new data shows Data from Debenhams Group shows Britain's summer racing calendar boosted searches and sales in race-day fashion categories. The occasionwear findings covered Debenhams, Karen Millen and PrettyLittleThing, with demand spanning dresses, fascinators and statement accessories around major racing events. TikTok drives £10 billion boost to UK economy as fashion brands benefit TikTok-driven economic activity generated at least £10 billion in gross value added for the UK economy in 2025 and supported an estimated 153,000 jobs. The TikTok-commissioned research looked at the platform's influence on consumer spending, employment and business growth, including fashion brands. Debenhams Group sees demand in ‘football fashion’ surge as World Cup fever strikes Boohoo saw football-related product sales jump 1,827% between May and June , while searches rose 600% during the World Cup. The Debenhams Group data also recorded a 481% increase in official football shirt sales at Debenhams over the same period. Premier League shirt prices soar as fans hit by fresh cost hikes Eight Premier League clubs increased replica shirt prices , leaving supporters facing adult prices of up to £90. The club pricing review found Tottenham's adult first-team shirt had risen by £5 to £90, while a shirt for a young child cost £70. The Interview: Designer Exchange CEO on keeping the ‘buy, sell and exchange’ strategy simple and opening more stores
sub_title: Last month saw Designer Exchange open its latest store at 141 Grainger Street in Newcastle. The store features a curated selection of handbags, accessories and ready-to-wear from brands including Prada, Gucci, Louis Vuitton and Miu Miu.
article_content: Last month, Designer Exchange opened its latest store at 141 Grainger Street in Newcastle. The store features a curated selection of handbags, accessories and ready-to-wear from brands including Prada, Gucci, Louis Vuitton and Miu Miu. The new store forms part of the company's ongoing expansion strategy, joining existing Designer Exchange locations in London's Knightsbridge, Manchester, Birmingham, Cheshire Oaks and Madrid. Another store is set to open in Barcelona on 31 July. All of Designer Exchange's stock comes directly from its customers, and CEO Dominic Durante prefers to keep the company's 'buy, sell and exchange' model simple. It is a strategy that is clearly working. He tells us all about it. Designer Exchange is a business built around buying, selling and exchanging pre-loved luxury. From Hermès handbags and Louis Vuitton trainers to Cartier Love bangles and ready-to-wear, we offer a broad range of authenticated luxury products across different brands, styles and price points. Our headquarters are based at 191 Brompton Road in Knightsbridge, London, which is also home to our flagship store. What really sets us apart is our physical retail presence. We currently operate stores across the UK and Spain, which allows customers to see, touch and try on products before they buy. In a category such as pre-loved luxury, that level of trust and reassurance is incredibly important. We've also always believed in offering customers instant payment. Rather than operating on a consignment model, we buy items outright, taking on the risk ourselves and providing sellers with immediate cash or a higher value exchange voucher. Designer Exchange was established in 2013, with our first store opening in Knightsbridge, just around the corner from where our flagship store is today. As the business has evolved, we've opened stores in a number of locations across the UK, with some coming and going as we've refined our strategy. Previous locations have included Leeds, Kensington, Chelsea and Ashford. Today, we operate stores in Knightsbridge, Birmingham, Manchester, Cheshire Oaks, Newcastle and Madrid. We're also excited to be opening our second Spanish store in Barcelona this month, with further expansion plans in the pipeline. All of our stock comes directly from our customers. We purchase items outright from individuals within our community who are looking to sell their luxury pieces. That means our inventory is constantly evolving and gives us the opportunity to offer customers a broad mix of brands, styles and price points. Our model is simple: buy, sell and exchange. Customers can either visit one of our stores or sell to us online. Once we receive an item, our team carries out quality checks and authentication before making an offer. Once purchased, items are photographed, listed online and distributed across our stores ready for resale. The business has changed considerably since we launched in 2013. We've expanded into new cities, entered international markets and undergone two rebrands as the business has matured. Stores have come and gone over the years as we've adapted our approach, but some things have remained constant such as the buy, sell and exchange model and always offering instant payment. We’ve also always believed in the importance of physical retail. Looking back, those principles have served us well and continue to underpin the way we approach growth today. We're excited about the opportunities ahead. Our focus remains on continuing to expand the business while staying true to the model that has helped us grow over the last 13 years. We're encouraged by the response we've seen in Spain and continue to see opportunities, both within our existing markets and further afield as we bring the Designer Exchange proposition to new customers. There are a number of independent omnichannel retailers operating within our space and the big marketplaces like Vinted and eBay compete in terms of the sheer volume of luxury products available. In contrast to traditional models, we acquire inventory directly to provide sellers with immediate liquidity. For consumers, we offer a seamless bricks-and-mortar shopping experience heavily anchored by our 'Double Lock Guarantee', a strict authentication process that ensures absolute product integrity. We've always tried to maintain the luxury experience without creating an environment that feels intimidating or exclusive. Equally, we don't just focus on the biggest brands or the highest value products. Whether someone is looking for an item at £50 or £50,000, we want them to feel welcome and to have confidence that they'll find something that suits both their style and budget. Yes, although our physical stores remain central to the business and are what really differentiates us. In pre-loved luxury, customers often want to inspect an item and understand its condition before making a purchase. Having stores gives people that confidence and helps build trust in the buying experience. Absolutely. While we don't rely solely on social media, it has played an important role in driving awareness, building trust and showcasing the breadth of our offering. Instagram remains our strongest platform and aligns closely with our audience, while TikTok allows us to showcase more of our culture and the people behind the business. Employee generated content and store-led content continue to perform particularly well for us, as customers increasingly want to engage with the people and personalities behind the brand. Yes, Cheshire Oaks is currently our only outlet location. It was a natural fit for us as it's the largest designer outlet in the UK, with over 140 stores and a strong mix of luxury and premium brands. Importantly, it offers customers a full-day destination rather than simply a shopping trip, which helps drive significant footfall and attracts visitors from across the country. Opening in Madrid wasn’t initially our preferred option. We originally felt that cities such as Paris or Milan might be stronger choices given their global reputation in luxury fashion. However, our sister company, CeX, already had a significant presence in Spain, which gave us access to established infrastructure, local market knowledge and operational support. That made Madrid a very attractive opportunity and reduced many of the challenges associated with entering a new market. Looking back, it has proven to be an excellent decision. The Madrid store has been a real success for us, validating both the market opportunity and our approach. As a result, we’re excited to continue our expansion in Spain with the opening of our second store in Barcelona this month. Spain has become an important growth market for Designer Exchange and we’re very encouraged by the response we’ve seen from customers there. Beyond Spain, further expansion into other European countries is something we’re excited about in the not-too-distant future as we continue to grow the brand and bring our offering to new markets. It might sound like a cliché, but we genuinely believe luxury should be accessible to everyone. One of our key brand messages is making luxury accessible to all, so we aim to offer something for every style and every budget. That's something that's been important to us since the beginning and continues to shape the way we approach the business. Yes, both buyers and sellers benefit from the model. For buyers, we use our internal data and market insights to price competitively and ensure products are positioned to sell within a reasonable timeframe. For sellers, immediate payment removes much of the hassle and uncertainty associated with selling luxury goods privately. Those choosing an exchange voucher receive even greater value, allowing them to trade into something else within our inventory. We don't want to say too much at this stage, but we can confirm that, as well as Barcelona, we plan to open a store in Glasgow this year. Beyond that, watch this space. Louis Vuitton consistently stands out as our ultimate powerhouse brand, dominating both total sales value and overall volume. While it leads the charge, our broader top tier for handbags remains a star-studded lineup of legacy houses, rounded out by Gucci, Chanel, Mulberry and Christian Dior. In terms of shifting trends, we are seeing immense demand for vintage Louis Vuitton ‘Monogram’ pieces. We’ve also witnessed a fascinating spike in the secondary market value of Chloé ‘Paddington’ bags, sparked by Chloé reintroducing the iconic style on their recent runways. It’s a perfect example of how quickly first-hand retail shifts inject new energy and value into the resale market. What makes the resale space so rewarding is this constant evolution; heritage and archival pieces are regularly rediscovered, finding passionate new audiences as modern tastes circle back. Newcastle was a natural choice for us. It’s a city with an incredible energy, a rich cultural identity, and a community that genuinely loves and understands style. North East shoppers have a fantastic eye for fashion, but they are also incredibly smart consumers and, let’s be honest, Geordies love a bargain! We wanted to bring the physical experience of Designer Exchange right into the centre of the ‘Toon’, introducing brands to the city that can be hard to find physically, from Chanel and Hermès to Louis Vuitton, Prada and Miu Miu. But we aren't stuffy or exclusive. We are warm, welcoming, and open to everyone, offering authentic, high quality luxury goods at affordable prices. It’s about making premium fashion accessible, letting people touch and feel the pieces, and giving such unique items a ‘well deserved’ second home. An elevated yet completely down to earth experience. We want to demystify luxury. Whether you have £70 to spend on a sleek pair of sunglasses or a fun accessory, or you’ve saved up £15,000 for a ‘holygrail’ Hermès piece, there is absolutely something here for you. We cater to every single taste, style and budget. Whether you are a seasoned collector looking to sell a piece to fund your next purchase, or someone buying their very first designer handbag to celebrate a milestone, our team is there to guide you. When you walk through our doors, expect a welcoming space with an ever-changing inventory, and a passionate team that loves fashion just as much as our customers do. Pre-loved luxury is no longer an alternative, it's the first choice. Shopping secondhand is now a badge of honour that proves you’re a smart, stylish and a sustainable consumer. However, with the market booming online, buyers are constantly dodging counterfeits and scammers. That’s where we come in. Our bricks-and-mortar stores are built on absolute trust. Our expert authenticators meticulously vet every single piece before it hits the floor, so you get the thrill of finding a unique gem with none of the anxiety. We’re proving that you can offer affordable, circular fashion without ever sacrificing the premium boutique experience.
