How I started in fashion: Nadine Merabi, founder of MERABI
sub_title: Nadine Merabi is a competitive hockey player turned fashion creative director. Her early career as a sportsperson may not have been the obvious place for a fashion founder to start out, but Merabi had always been surrounded by creativity and had always appreciated the impact of colour, design and style.
article_content: Nadine Merabi is a competitive hockey player turned fashion creative director. Her early career as a sportsperson may not have been the obvious place for a fashion founder to start out, but Merabi had always been surrounded by creativity and had always appreciated the impact of colour, design and style. Her inspiration came from her stylish Lebanese father and, from him, she learned about the power of a good outfit. So, in 2015, she set to work on her £250 sewing machine to create clothing that made women feel their absolute best. Merabi began producing carefully crafted, one-off pieces of occasionwear for women, and it wasn't long before she caught the attention of Selfridges, who asked her to create a full range. The brand took off from there and has gone on to dress some of the most high-profile women in the fields of entertainment, fashion and, of course, sport. But the brand isn't just about dressing celebrities. Merabi has always been committed to creating the best quality clothing she can at an accessible price point. Today, the brand's range takes in occasion dresses, bridal wear, jumpsuits and new line of denim . While Merabi herself no longer makes the clothes, she does design them and is heavily involved in production. While the business is headquartered in Manchester, the brand has a store on London's South Molton Street and is available globally via its website . She talks us through her unexpected career path and the lessons she has learned along the way. Have you always had an interest in fashion? Why does it appeal to you and why did you want to work within it? I've always been drawn to fashion because of how it makes people feel. For me, clothing has never just been about what you wear, it's about confidence, self-expression and celebrating life's moments. Growing up, I was surrounded by creativity. My father had a great eye for style, and watching him sparked my own love of colour, texture and design from a young age. That curiosity eventually became a passion, and I realised I wanted to create pieces that made women feel their absolute best. Fashion gave me the opportunity to combine creativity with purpose. Every MERABI piece is designed to empower women to celebrate themselves, whether that's for a wedding, a milestone or simply a moment where they want to feel incredible. Tell us about your first job in fashion. What drew you to the role? What this experience was like? My first job in fashion was starting NADINE MERABI. Before that, I was a competitive hockey player, so fashion wasn't the obvious career path for me. But I'd always had a creative side and a fascination with how clothing could transform the way women felt. I recognised a gap in the market for modern, statement occasionwear that combined glamour with confidence, and I decided to take the leap and create it myself. In the early days, I was doing everything, from sketching designs and sourcing fabrics to packing orders and speaking directly to customers. There wasn't a roadmap; I learned every aspect of the business by doing it. Looking back, it was both exciting and incredibly challenging. Those early years taught me resilience, adaptability and the importance of believing in your vision, even before anyone else does. What were the most valuable skills or lessons you gained from that first experience? One of the biggest lessons I learned was that success comes from understanding every part of the business, not just the creative side. I also realised the importance of listening. Whether that's listening to your customers, your team or your suppliers, some of the best decisions come from staying curious and being open to learning. I've carried that mindset throughout my career. Even today, we're constantly speaking to our community and evolving the brand based on their feedback. Tell us about your current role. How did you get here and what do you most enjoy about it? As the Founder and Creative Director of NADINE MERABI, my role is incredibly varied, and that's one of the things I love most. Creatively, I work closely with our design team to shape every collection, ensuring each piece reflects the confidence, craftsmanship and timeless glamour that define MERABI. Alongside the creative direction, I'm also deeply involved in the wider business, from long-term strategy and product development to mentoring our team and staying closely connected to our community. Over the past decade, the brand has evolved significantly, but our purpose has remained the same: to create beautiful pieces that empower women to feel their most confident. The most rewarding part of my role is seeing women wearing MERABI during some of the biggest moments of their lives. Whether it's a wedding, a milestone celebration or simply a day where they want to feel their absolute best, knowing we've played a small part in those memories is incredibly special. If you could go back and give your younger self one piece of advice at the very start of your career, what would it be - and why? Trust yourself sooner. When you're starting out, it's easy to compare yourself to others or feel like you need all the answers before taking the next step. The reality is that building a business is a constant learning process. Some of our biggest lessons have come from the moments that didn't go to plan. Every challenge has helped shape the business we are today. You don't need perfect timing or permission. You just need the courage to start. What does the next chapter of your own career look like and how are you hoping to grow from here? The next chapter is about continuing to evolve MERABI while staying true to the values we've built the brand on. We're expanding into more versatile day-to-night dressing, growing internationally and continuing to invest in our community by listening even more closely to what women want from us. Personally, I want to keep growing as a leader. Building a business teaches you something new every day, and I'm passionate about creating a culture where creativity, collaboration and ambition can thrive. Has there been a person in fashion that you have always admired and why? I've always been inspired by people who have the courage to create something from nothing and stay true to their vision. Closer to home, one of my biggest inspirations has always been my father. He had an incredible sense of style and an appreciation for quality and craftsmanship, and I think that's where my love of fashion first began. Watching how he expressed himself through what he wore taught me that clothing can be a form of confidence and individuality, and that has stayed with me ever since. Beyond that, I'm inspired by entrepreneurs and founders who lead with authenticity, resilience and purpose. Building a business is never a straight line, and I have huge respect for people who continue to evolve while staying true to who they are. That's something I've always tried to bring to MERABI as we've grown.

article_title: Editors' Top Reads: News from Primark, Nadine Merabi, Designer Exchange and more...
sub_title: Here are some of this week’s news and features highlights handpicked by TheIndustry.fashion team.
article_content: Here are some of this week’s news and features highlights handpicked by TheIndustry.fashion team. This week I wrote about one of the cheekiest marketing stunts I have seen in quite a long time. Just as SKIMS opened its Regent Street flagship store, Primark placed a mobile billboard just in front to promote its £9 shaping bodysuit as a lower-priced alternative to Kim Kardashian’s widely popular shapewear offering. The slogan on the van showed models wearing the brand's own version of the bodysuit, with the slogan reading: "These Kim's prefer Primark £9 shaping bodysuit". In direct comparison, SKIMS Seamless Sculpt Thong Bodysuit, available in the Regent Street store, currently retails at £84. The move follows Primark's announcement last week that it had lowered prices across hundreds of products as part of a new “Iconic Value” initiative aimed at reinforcing its position as a destination for affordable fashion. While the move strengthens the retailer's value credentials, the reset also put it into closer price competition with online giant Shein , whose cost advantage is coming under regulatory pressure, argued our Editor-in-Chief Lauretta Roberts this week. Camilla Rydzek, Senior News and Features Writer. Congratulations to Fashion Roundtable for reading the mood music of the new Andy Burnham regime and trying to push this to the top of the agenda. The tireless fashion think tank and lobby group, led by Tamara Cincik, has issued an open letter to the Government urging them to implement a British-made-first policy, when it comes to the public procurement of uniforms, beginning with medical and military personnel. The group, which has the backing of business support platform Make it British and a number of other fashion industry signatories, argues that such a policy would support what is left of the UK fashion and textiles manufacturing base, and, hopefully, serve to grow it. The signatories have been at pains to point out, though, that handing over lucrative contracts to companies that are merely registered in the UK is not an acceptable solution. The uniforms must be made in factories here, many of which are in the North, which supports the aims of Burnham's Number 10 initiative. Burnham himself appears to appreciate British-made clothing and is often seen wearing made-in-Manchester Private White VC. The tabloid press jumped on this, criticising a so-called man of the people for wearing £80 t-shirts. But that approach seems to have backfired as the counter-argument that he's wearing durable clothing that supports British industry and jobs and industry is a far stronger one. Better that than he wears something cheap that is made in China. And better still would be his backing of this fine initiative to make uniforms here too. Lauretta Roberts, Co-founder, CEO and Editor-in-Chief. Nadine Merabi's journey from competitive hockey player to fashion founder wasn't conventional, but creativity had always been part of her life. Inspired by her stylish Lebanese father, she developed an early appreciation for the confidence that great design and dressing can inspire. In 2015, she launched her brand with a £250 sewing machine, creating beautifully crafted occasionwear designed to make women feel their best. Her designs quickly caught the attention of Selfridges, leading to a full collection and the rapid growth of the business. Today, the Manchester-based brand offers occasionwear, bridal, jumpsuits and denim, with a flagship store on London's South Molton Street and customers around the world. While Merabi no longer makes each piece by hand, she remains closely involved in every collection as the brand's Creative Director, overseeing both design and production. She shares the story behind her unexpected career path and the insights that have shaped her success . Sophie Smith, News Editor & Senior Writer. Knightsbridge-based ‘buy, sell and exchange’ business Designer Exchange has opened its sixth store today, and its second in Spain, adding a 1,720 sq ft store in Barcelona to its one in Madrid. It comes hot on the heels of its fourth UK store, which opened in Newcastle last month, with the company’s CEO, Dominic Durante, very much a believer in the bricks-and-mortar retail model. Our interview with him makes for an interesting read , as the business, which sells a constantly evolving selection of pre-owned handbags, accessories and ready-to-wear from some of the world's most sought-after fashion houses, including Hermès, Chanel, Louis Vuitton, Prada, Gucci and Miu Miu, pretty much sticks to the same simple strategy as it did when it was established in 2013. It was then that Designer Exchange’s first store opened in Knightsbridge, just around the corner from where its flagship store is today. Unlike traditional consignment platforms, Designer Exchange purchases luxury items directly from customers, offering immediate payment or an enhanced exchange voucher. Every item undergoes a rigorous authentication process before reaching the shop floor, providing confidence for buyers and a simple, transparent experience for sellers. While Designer Exchange does also have a strong online presence, it’s the physical stores that “remain central to the business”. Durante says that’s what differentiates it. What is also interesting is that Designer Exchange is part of CeX (Complete Entertainment Exchange), a global leader in second-hand retail and where many a decent mobile phone gets bought and sold. Durante explains that CeX already had a significant presence in Spain, which gave them access to an “established infrastructure, local market knowledge and operational support”. That made Madrid a very attractive opportunity and reduced many of the challenges associated with entering a new market. Hence, Barcelona was the next “natural step”, with expansion into further European countries now very much the plan. Another one to watch how it grows. Tom Bottomley, Contributor. I found this report particularly interesting because it challenges what luxury has traditionally been associated with. For years, fur and exotic skins have been seen as symbols of exclusivity, but the research suggests that many luxury consumers now place greater value on innovation, sustainability and ethical production. What stood out to me most was that 95% of those surveyed believed the use of fur and wild animal skins made luxury brands appear less prestigious. It highlights how consumer expectations are evolving, particularly as younger generations become more conscious of the environmental and ethical impact of their purchases. As luxury continues to redefine itself, it will be interesting to see whether more brands invest in next-generation materials that balance craftsmanship with sustainability. Catherine Rowe-Kosary, Junior Writer. When it emerged that Harvey Nichols owner – Hong Kong-based billionaire Sir Dickson Poon – was considering offloading the business after 35 years of ownership, I immediately assumed it would end up in either Asian or Middle Eastern hands. Especially given the likely sale price, the geographic spread of its stores and the investment needed to revive its fortunes. However, while there is interest from Asia and the Middle East (from Reliance Retail and Chalhoub Group respectively), we have ended up with a somewhat unexpected list of suitors. High street giant NEXT is acquisitive but it wouldn't have been first on my list of potentially interested parties. However a move for Harvey Nichols would, in one fell swoop, give it a huge foothold in luxury, which is a space it has been circling over the years with limited success. So there's that. Then we have Frasers Group, owner of Frasers, Flannels, Sports Direct and more, which was initially said to have been interested in the regional stores only, but is now talking of a tilt at the entire group. Frasers is ambitous; it's currently piling pressure on the board at Hugo Boss as it seeks to wrest control of the German fashion giant, and this week it was revealed that it has bought a small stake in Burberry. Given past experience, we shouldn't expect that stake to stay small for long. Now, Gordon Brothers, the US-based turnaround specialist, is reported to have thrown its hat its the ring . Gordon Brothers typically buys distressed retail brands with distinct design identities that it can parlay into its asset-light licensing model, which it has successfully done with Laura Ashley and soon will do with Radley. Harvey Nichols doesn't quite fall into that box but the precedent of buying the IP of a beloved department store has been set by fellow American group Authentic Brands, which acquired Barneys New York in 2019. The idea was to use the Barneys name on a range of products, which it does, but we are expecting to see some stores return with reports suggesting a new, smaller format store is set to open in Florida soon, with others in the pipeline. Could Gordon Brothers be thinking of a similar move? Seems likely. I'd be devastated if, like Barneys, the flagship store was closed though. However each potential bidder is being asked to commit £60m investment in the future development of the business, so maybe Sir Dickson won't let that happen. Lauretta Roberts, Co-founder, CEO & Editor-in-Chief.

article_title: Tommy Hilfiger launches ‘Always Denim’ campaign starring Romeo Beckham
sub_title: Tommy Hilfiger has today launched a new autumn 2026 campaign under the title ‘Always Denim’, starring Romeo Beckham alongside Dutch fashion model Yasmin Wijnaldum and a “next generation cast of tastemakers”.
article_content: Tommy Hilfiger has today launched a new autumn 2026 campaign under the title ‘Always Denim’, starring Romeo Beckham alongside Dutch fashion model Yasmin Wijnaldum and a “next generation cast of tastemakers”. Shot at The Mark Hotel in New York, including on the rooftop, the mood is one of “downtown escapes and time spent with friends”, with everyone wearing the latest Tommy Hilfiger denim collection featuring a wide range of washes, fits and silhouettes. Romeo Beckham wears the relaxed, 90s-inspired ‘Theo’ baggy jean with a cable-knit sweater before changing into the classic straight-leg ‘Dover’ jean, paired with a tucked-in denim shirt. He also wears a denim jacket with a Tommy Hilfiger flag on the back and a logo T-shirt. Yasmin Wijnaldum highlights the women’s offering in the high-rise ‘Sarah’ jean, known for its clean, flattering shape, alongside the low-rise ‘Daisy’ silhouette with its relaxed proportions. She also sports a burgundy varsity jacket with leather sleeves and ‘Tommy Hilfiger 1985’ on the back. Tommy Hilfiger said: “Denim has always represented the pinnacle of self-expression to me. When I was a teenager growing up in Elmira, I’d drive to New York City to buy jeans, customise them and sell them out of the trunk of my car. “Through every decade, it’s evolved with music, youth culture and changing attitudes, yet never lost that timeless appeal. This campaign celebrates that legacy through a new generation, showing how the classics continue to be reimagined in personal ways.” Romeo Beckham added: “There’s no right or wrong way to wear denim - that’s the whole point. One day I’ll wear it with a leather jacket, the next with a classic white T-shirt. You can take inspiration from rock, prep or vintage, any kind of style. “Tommy’s iconic denim has been around for my entire life, but it always feels current because everyone makes it work in a way that feels natural to them.” Last month saw Romeo Beckham capitalise on his growing exposure, as well as the fame of his parents, David and Victoria, with the launch of his own football-inspired label called Intra . Partnering with Justin Saul, who had previously revived the dormant skateboard clothing brand Elwood Clothing in 2020 by refocusing it on vintage-inspired essentials and streetwear, Intra is a sportswear label built around the intersection of football culture and fashion. The first Intra release, timed with the start of the World Cup, was called ‘The Nations Collection’. It featured three retro-inspired, limited-edition football jackets representing the USA, England and Brazil. The co-founders described this debut collection as “a love letter to a footballing culture that shaped us, cut and finished in the spirit of the eras we grew up worshipping”.

article_title: People Moves, July 2026: George at Asda, Gymshark, Temperley London and more...
sub_title: As July draws to a close, TheIndustry.fashion reflects on possibly the busiest month of appoints yet, marked by senior leadership shake-ups across luxury, retail, sportswear and fashion technology.
article_content: As July draws to a close, TheIndustry.fashion reflects on possibly the busiest month of appoints yet, marked by senior leadership shake-ups across the luxury, retail, sportswear and fashion technology sectors. The luxury fashion sector has been particularly active, with Bottega Veneta and Nadine Merabi appointing new CEOs, Chanel naming a new CFO, Manolo Blahnik hiring a new MD of the Americas, Rabanne welcoming a new Creative Director and Tory Burch appointing its first-ever Chief Brand Officer. Across sportswear we have seen new appointments at Gymshark, TALA and Puma, while retail businesses have welcomed both new faces and familiar ones, including Helen Connolly, who returned to George at Asda as CEO. TheIndustry.fashion highlights the most notable appointments, spanning roles from CEOs and commercial leadership to creative directors and finance positions. Luxury womenswear brand Nadine Merabi has appointed former Karen Millen Managing Director Briony Garbett as CEO. Nick Beighton joined as Non-Executive Chair and Hash Ladha became a Non-Executive Director. Adidas' new Chief Financial Officer Birgit Kretschmer joins the brand from fashion retailer C&A, where she also held the role of CFO. Kretschmer brings more than 30 years of experience to the new role, 25 years of which she has spent at Adidas in roles including CFO of adidas International BV and Western Europe. Gymshark promoted Global Supply Chain Director Matt Rogers to Chief Supply Chain Officer after he led sourcing and supply chain operations on an interim basis. Luxury styling entertainment platform DREST has appointed Julien Dulioust as General Manager of Game , where he will oversee product development, drive commercial performance and handle user acquisition. Schuh has appointed Tomas Petersson as its new President , succeeding Colin Temple, who is retiring after 38 years with the footwear retailer. Petersson will join the business at the end of July and work alongside Temple over the coming months to ensure a smooth leadership transition. British knitwear brand John Smedley has hired Stuart Pannell as CFO , Brian Lancaster as COO and Nick Watt as People Director. Bryan Jackson CBE also returned as Senior Independent Director. Luxury footwear brand Manolo Blahnik appointed Kimberly Mimnaugh as Managing Director of the Americas, overseeing regional retail, wholesale, ecommerce and operations from New York. Frasers Group was reportedly considering Michael Murray to lead Hugo Boss if its proposed takeover of the German fashion company succeeded. No appointment had been confirmed. Chanel appointed Hélène de Tissot as CFO , succeeding Philippe Blondiaux. She will join from Pernod Ricard in October, while Blondiaux will remain until year-end to support the transition. Puma named Dusan Hamlin as its new Vice President of E-Commerce, putting him in charge of its global digital commerce strategy. Kate Spade New York appointed Jonathan Saunders as Executive Creative Director , effective 26 August. He will oversee product design and visual identity from the brand’s New York headquarters. London activewear brand TALA confirmed Sally Hughes as permanent CEO after five months in the interim position and appointed former Pai Skincare executive Verity Linnell as CFO. British luxury house Temperley London appointed Morgaine McGee as CEO and Jack Isenberg as Design Director following founder Alice Temperley’s departure. Isenberg’s first collection will be presented in September. JD Sports Fashion appointed Independent Non-Executive Director Darren Shapland as Interim Chair following its annual general meeting. He will serve until a permanent successor to Andrew Higginson is found. The Very Group appointed former Bank of Ireland Chief Marketing Officer Henry Dummer as CEO of Very.ie, the Irish online retail business and flexible payments provider. Marks and Spencer appointed Jane Robson as Fashion, Home & Beauty Director of Sourcing, Quality and Sustainability, effective in August. She will succeed Monique Leeuwenburgh, who retires in October. Kering appointed Romain Spitzer as CEO of Bottega Veneta , effective 1 September. The former LVMH executive will report to Kering CEO Luca de Meo and join its Executive Committee. Designer label Roksanda appointed former Stella McCartney Head of Flou Simon Valer Dacsef as Head of Design, reporting to CEO Patricia Sancho. Calvin Klein and Tommy Hilfiger owner PVH appointed former Sephora Global COO Alexis Rollier as CFO. He will join in September and succeed Interim CFO Melissa Stone. Direct-to-consumer womenswear brand Beyond Nine appointed former AllSaints Global Ecommerce Director Liam Price as its first CEO. Rabanne appointed Olivier Rousteing as Creative Director after his 14-year tenure at Balmain. The house also announced the appointment on Instagram , with his runway debut scheduled for March 2027. American luxury brand Tory Burch appointed Klitos Teklos as its first Chief Brand Officer, tasking him with global marketing, social media and visual merchandising. Gymshark appointed former Boden executive Shaun Perkinson as Chief Technology Officer. He replaced John Douglas, who retired after five years with the activewear company. Liberty promoted Laura Simpson to Chief Marketing Officer alongside her existing position as Managing Director of LBTY, expanding her remit across group brand, marketing and customer strategy. Former Primark CEO Paul Marchant joined George at Asda as an advisor on the fashion and homeware business’s long-term strategy. UK discount retailer Poundland appointed former Superdry and M&S finance executive Shaun Wills as Chief Finance Officer while continuing its post-restructuring turnaround. Asda appointed Helen Connolly as CEO of George . The New Look CEO previously spent more than 15 years with George and will succeed Liz Evans. NEXT appointed former ASOS Head of ESG Jodie Leek to lead brand sales and marketing. Leek brings over 25 years of experience in global sourcing, supply chain management, and environmental, social and governance (ESG), to her new role. Dr. Martens appointed Melanie Richards as an Independent Non-Executive Director from 15 July. She also became Senior Independent Director and Chair of the Nomination Committee.

article_title: Poundland owner Gordon Brothers joins Harvey Nichols auction
sub_title: Gordon Brothers, the retail investment firm that owns Poundland and has previously owned Laura Ashley, has submitted an offer to acquire luxury department store Harvey Nichols.
article_content: Gordon Brothers, the retail investment firm that owns Poundland and has previously owned Laura Ashley, has submitted an offer to acquire luxury department store Harvey Nichols. The company lodged its bid ahead of a deadline this week, according to Sky News. Advisers to Harvey Nichols owner Sir Dickson Poon have set a further deadline next week as the 35-year ownership period moves towards a possible sale. Frasers Group and NEXT are viewed as the leading contenders , while Gordon Brothers and several international parties remain involved. Dubai-based Chalhoub Group and India’s Reliance Retail have also examined potential offers. Sir Dickson’s family has appointed FTI Consulting to oversee the process, alongside regional advisers tasked with attracting interest from Gulf investors. Prospective buyers must consider more than the acquisition price. Harvey Nichols has told bidders they must commit up to £60 million to support its continuing transformation programme. The funding would be used for the Edinburgh store refurbishment, as well as international expansion, digital development and management’s wider business plan. Chief Executive Julia Goddard, who joined Harvey Nichols in June 2024, has overseen investment at its Knightsbridge flagship. Recent work has included a wellness destination on the fourth floor and a redesigned ground floor with jewellery, lifestyle products and flexible spaces for brands. The flagship investment is understood to have improved performance, but the group has now endured five straight years of losses. Revenue fell 5% to £204.8 million in the year to 31 March 2024, while pre-tax losses widened to £34 million. Meanwhile, the retailer recently strengthened its senior leadership team with the appointment of Shaun Donnelly to Buying Director for Non Apparel & Menswear . Harvey Nichols employs about 1,200 people in the UK and runs seven stores in the UK and Ireland. Its large-format locations include London, Edinburgh, Birmingham, Leeds and Manchester, while its international network reaches markets such as Hong Kong, Dubai and Riyadh. Frasers, which owns Sports Direct, Flannels and House of Fraser, entered the Harvey Nichols sale process earlier in July despite concerns among some luxury suppliers about its potential ownership. A Harvey Nichols executive told suppliers in a memo that the retailer had been "obliged" to allow Frasers Group to participate in the process, while the company said Frasers’ admission would help ensure a competitive process. NEXT has also assessed the business, although it remains unclear whether it would retain the regional store estate or focus on the Harvey Nichols brand and intellectual property. Both retailers faced an initial 28 July offer deadline, with Frasers expected to advance its bid . Sir Dickson Poon's Dickson Concepts International bought Harvey Nichols from Burton Group in 1991 for £53 million. The company listed on the London Stock Exchange in 1996 before being taken private again six years later. Sir Dickson is no longer actively involved in running the group, having stepped down from the Harvey Nichols board and his other European directorships. In June last year, TheIndustry.fashion took an in-depth look at Harvey Nichols' transformation plans , featuring exclusive commentary on the challenges it faces and expert insights into how it might successfully navigate its transformation.

article_title: Adidas raises outlook and appoints new CFO after World Cup drives record Q2
sub_title: Adidas has raised its full-year sales forecast after posting record second-quarter revenue, supported by World Cup demand and continued growth in running.
article_content: Adidas has raised its full-year sales forecast and appointed a new CFO after posting record second-quarter revenue, supported by World Cup demand and continued growth in running. Summary of results: Direct-to-consumer sales increased 25% for the brand, including a 27% rise in e-commerce, while the German sportswear group maintained its operating profit outlook as it invested more heavily in marketing and distribution to support global demand. The company now expects currency-neutral sales to increase between 9% and 10% in 2026, compared with its previous guidance for high-single-digit growth. Adidas reported net sales of €6.7 billion (£5.74 billion) for the three months to 30 June, its highest quarterly total. Currency-neutral revenue rose 14%, extending the same growth rate recorded in the first quarter. Adidas CEO Bjørn Gulden, commented on the results: “Being the CEO of adidas is a privilege. Being the CEO of adidas during a World Cup is even better. This World Cup was like a fairy tale for me! I am so proud of what our teams around the world achieved. I do not think we could have scripted it better." Direct-to-consumer revenue increased 25% on a currency-neutral basis, with double-digit growth across every market. Ecommerce advanced 27%, while revenue from Adidas-owned stores rose 23%. Wholesale revenue increased 6%. Adidas said it had deliberately cut back supply to European retail partners as heavy discounting continued in parts of the lifestyle footwear market. The strategy was intended to protect full-price sales and limit further discounting. Gulden also noted that consumer sell-through had exceeded the volume supplied to retailers. “It is always great if your sell-out is stronger than your sell-in. I am sure many retailers wished they had more of our products,” he said. European sales increased 6%, while North America, Greater China, Latin America, emerging markets and Japan and South Korea delivered double-digit growth. Performance revenue rose 39%, driven by football, running and motorsport products. Adidas supplied kits to 14 federations at the 2026 FIFA World Cup, alongside the Trionda official match ball, pre-match teamwear and retro-inspired collections. Running sales grew around 30%, supported by demand for the Adizero range. Apparel revenue increased 35%, helped by World Cup collections and new Originals ranges designed for local markets. Footwear revenue grew 1% as performance footwear offset weaker lifestyle footwear sales. Gulden noted that this had long been the ambition of the brand and that the results showed its innovation in the performance footwear category was paying off. Lifestyle revenue increased 2% during the quarter, with Gulden commenting noting that the apparel business was "clearly 'on fire'." Second-quarter operating profit climbed 5% to €574 million (£492 million), even after an extra €212 million (£182 million) was spent on marketing and World Cup activations. Gross margin rose 0.8 percentage points to 52.5%, helped by full-price sales and a more favourable channel mix. In the first half, net sales came to €13.3 billion (£11.40 billion), while operating profit was up 11% to €1.28 billion (£1.10 billion). Adidas kept its full-year operating profit target at around €2.3 billion (£1.97 billion). The guidance excludes potential future refunds of between $250 million (£188 million) and $300 million (£225 million) relating to US tariffs. Adidas recognised only a small benefit from initial refunds during the second quarter. Adidas' new Chief Financial Officer Birgit Kretschmer joins the brand from fashion retailer C&A, where she also held the role of CFO. Kretschmer brings more than 30 years of experience to the new role, 25 years of which she has spent at Adidas in roles including CFO of adidas International BV and Western Europe. Gulden commented on the appointment that he is "extremely happy" to welcome back Birgit and that he believes her experience makes her the "perfect CFO for the future". "She knows the industry, she knows adidas and she has added the knowledge of cost discipline working as the CFO of a vertical retailer like C&A," he added.

article_title: Reformation’s raises $210.9 million in IPO
sub_title: Sustainable womenswear brand Reformation has raised $210.9 million (£159 million) after pricing its initial public offering (IPO) at $15 per share, the bottom of its marketed range.
article_content: Sustainable womenswear brand Reformation has raised $210.9 million (£159 million) after pricing its initial public offering (IPO) at $15 per share, the bottom of its marketed range. The California-based retailer sold 14.06 million shares, including 9.48 million issued by the company and 4.58 million sold by existing shareholders. Shares are expected to begin trading today on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker symbol REF. The IPO gives Reformation a market valuation of approximately $886 million, below the $1 billion valuation the company had targeted when it launched its roadshow earlier this month . Private equity firm Permira, which acquired a controlling stake in Reformation in 2019, is expected to retain approximately 49% ownership following the listing, down from 64.4% before the IPO. Founder Yael Aflalo's family trust will retain around 20% of the company's shares. Reformation said it intends to use approximately $125.1 million of the net proceeds to partially repay outstanding debt. As of 27 June 2026, the company had total outstanding debt of $250.3 million. Founded in Los Angeles in 2009 as a vintage clothing boutique, Reformation has grown into a global direct-to-consumer fashion business operating more than 70 stores across the US, UK, Canada and France, while serving customers in more than 150 countries through its e-commerce platform. The company reported revenue of $533.3 million (£401 million) for the 12 months ended 31 March 2026, alongside a net loss of $5.1 million (£3.8 million). It has also reported 20 consecutive quarters of double-digit net revenue growth through the first quarter of 2026, with around 90% of sales generated through its direct-to-consumer business. The IPO follows Reformation's announcement last week that it was seeking a valuation of up to $1 billion as it prepared to list on the New York Stock Exchange, marking one of the most closely watched fashion market debuts of the year.

article_title: Frasers lifts Hugo Boss stake to 37.58%
sub_title: Frasers Group has increased its holding in Hugo Boss to 37.58% after its €38-a-share takeover offer was cleared by regulators in Germany, making the offer "unconditional".
article_content: Frasers Group has increased its holding in Hugo Boss to 37.58% after its €38-a-share takeover offer was cleared by regulators in Germany, making the offer "unconditional". The Sports Direct and Flannels owner now holds or has received acceptances for 25,933,012 Hugo Boss shares. Ahead of the closing of the initial acceptance period for the Frasers offer, on 27 July, Hugo Boss shareholders tendered 5,035,651 shares, representing around 7.30% of the German luxury brand's share capital and voting rights. These shares were added to Frasers’ direct holding of 20,897,361 shares, or 30.28%. Frasers has since extended the acceptance period from midnight 31 July to midnight 13 August, Frankfurt time, which is equivalent to 11pm BST. The offer remains unchanged at €38 for each Hugo Boss share. Frasers launched its voluntary public takeover offer on 10 June for all Hugo Boss shares it did not already own. At launch, the bid valued the outstanding shares at approximately €1.98 billion and Hugo Boss as a whole at around €2.7 billion. The European Commission granted merger-control clearance on 27 July, satisfying the offer’s only completion condition. The bid therefore became legally unconditional on 28 July . Frasers had already crossed Germany’s 30% mandatory-offer threshold after buying a further 2,549,900 shares. Its holding stood at 30.28% before shares tendered during the initial acceptance period were included. The group has declared the €38 offer price final. Its enlarged position does not by itself give Frasers majority ownership of Hugo Boss. Hugo Boss’s Managing Board and Supervisory Board unanimously recommended that shareholders reject the bid in a reasoned statement issued on 25 June. The board described the €38 consideration as financially "inadequate" , arguing that it did not reflect the company’s standalone value or medium-to-long-term potential. Bank of America and Goldman Sachs provided external opinions supporting that assessment. The price represents a 4.8% premium to Hugo Boss’s closing price of €36.26 on 9 June, the final trading day before Frasers announced its offer. It is also 4.3% above the company’s three-month volume-weighted average price before the announcement. Hugo Boss CEO Daniel Grieder commented at the time: “Against this backdrop, we firmly believe that the offer price fails to capture the company’s intrinsic value and long-term potential.” Frasers CEO Michael Murray, who joined the Hugo Boss Supervisory Board in May 2025, was excluded from the committee assessing the offer. Frasers is, however, reportedly considering Murray as a future Hugo Boss CEO if its takeover succeeds.

article_title: Harry Styles’ stylist Harry Lambert awarded honorary degree from UCA
sub_title: Harry Lambert, who has styled Harry Styles since 2014, has been awarded an Honorary Master of Arts by the University for the Creative Arts (UCA) in recognition of his contribution to the fashion industry.
article_content: Harry Lambert, who has styled Harry Styles since 2014, has been awarded an Honorary Master of Arts by the University for the Creative Arts (UCA) in recognition of his contribution to the fashion industry. The British stylist graduated from UCA with a first-class degree in photography in 2008 and was presented with the award during the university’s graduation ceremony at London’s Royal Festival Hall on Thursday Best known for shaping Harry Styles’ fashion identity, Lambert has helped redefine contemporary menswear through gender-fluid tailoring, bold silhouettes and collaborations with emerging designers including Harris Reed and Steven Stokey-Daley. Harry Lambert Beyond his work with Styles, Lambert has styled a number of high-profile names including Emma Corrin and Alexander Skarsgård, creating some of recent years’ most talked-about red carpet looks. He has also collaborated with brands including Pandora, Zara and eBay. The honorary award recognised Lambert’s contribution to the fashion and creative industries, with actor Emma Corrin surprising him during the ceremony via a video message. “I don’t know anyone who works as hard and who brings more creativity, joy and inventiveness to their work,” Corrin said. Accepting the award, Lambert reflected on the role UCA played in his career. “UCA completely changed my life,” he said. “I realise now that inspiration doesn’t come from a postcode or a city, it comes from the people who challenge you, encourage you and help you see the world differently.” “And I still use the skills I learnt there every day. Thank you UCA, not only for this extraordinary honour, but for seeing something in me before I could fully see it in myself.” Lambert has become one of Britain’s most influential fashion stylists since meeting Styles in 2014, with the pair helping to challenge traditional menswear conventions through looks featuring pearls, feather boas, floral tailoring and flared silhouettes.

article_title: Fashion and textiles industry urges PM Burnham to back British-made uniforms through public contracts
sub_title: Fashion Roundtable and UK fashion industry signatories have called on Andy Burnham to introduce onshoring requirements for public-sector textiles.Fashion Roundtable wants NHS and defence uniform contracts tied to domestic production, arguing that dependable public orders could protect manufacturing skills and strengthen regional economies.
article_content: Fashion Roundtable and UK fashion industry signatories have called on Prime Minister Andy Burnham to introduce onshoring requirements for public-sector textiles, beginning with NHS and defence uniforms. The open letter, published on this week, asks for a meeting before the government finalises its Number 10 North initiative. Signatories include presenter and Buffalo Systems co-owner Ben Fogle, alongside representatives from the fashion and textiles sector. Tamara Cincik of Fashion Roundtable Fashion Roundtable, the fashion industry think tank and lobbying group, said procurement could connect Burnham’s commitments on decentralisation, reindustrialisation, regional growth and stronger local decision-making with existing UK manufacturing capacity. The wider UK fashion and textiles industry contributes £62 billion to GDP and supports 1.3 million jobs, according to figures cited in the letter. These totals cover the broader sector rather than domestic garment manufacturing alone. The open letter makes two principal requests: The manufacturing condition should cover where goods are produced, rather than where the successful bidder is registered, the group said. This would prevent UK-based intermediaries from winning contracts while continuing to source finished goods overseas. Kate Hills, founder and CEO of business support platform Make it British, said: “The single biggest ask is a British-made requirement in public contracts for textile goods, starting with defence and NHS uniforms, and crucially it must specify where products are manufactured, not just where the winning company is registered.” A February parliamentary debate put the British Army clothing budget at almost £80 million annually and NHS uniform frameworks at £125 million over five years. MPs were also told that 6% of UK military uniforms were made domestically, based on figures from a 2013 inquiry. Fashion Roundtable based its proposals on an April 2026 report produced with the University of Birmingham’s Local Policy Innovation Partnership Hub. The research identified dependable public orders as a way to retain skills and strengthen regional manufacturing. Its recommended procurement changes included longer contracts, clearer demand forecasts, contract sizes accessible to smaller manufacturers and improved payment terms. Fashion Roundtable said the sector’s main constraint was fragmented policy rather than an absence of skills or production capability. The organisation also cited the pandemic procurement process as evidence that a change in policy is needed. The UK Covid-19 Inquiry found that £9.9 billion of PPE was written off because it was unused or out of date, and called for a domestic strategy covering essential healthcare equipment. Fashion Roundtable CEO Tamara Cincik said: “During the pandemic I saw a total fiasco in the procurement of vitally needed PPE. Kate Hills and I were asked by the then government to attend regular calls on public procurement and it was clear to both of us that the right hand did not know what the left hand was doing, and this is all avoidable if public procurement is brought back onshore. Not only for the jobs and income it brings back to Britain, but also to ensure greater transparency, reduce waste and stabilise British manufacturing.” The Private White VC factory The intervention follows mainstream media criticism of Burnham for wearing clothing, including an £80 T-shirt and £700 jacket, from British company Private White VC, with suggestions that the cost of his fashion choices demonstrate he is out of touch with ordinary working people. However many have come out in support of Burnham's move. Private White VC produces clothing at a 173-year-old Greater Manchester factory and is one of the UK's last remaining British-made brands. The company has defended its pricing as a reflection of skilled local labour and garments designed for long-term use. Its CEO James Eden has appeared in media interviews defending Burnham's choice and said it was a show of support for British industry and jobs, as well as showing a commitment to sustainable and ethical practice. The episode placed the PM's individual purchasing choices under scrutiny, while Fashion Roundtable’s letter shifts the focus to government buying power. The organisation is seeking talks with Burnham before the structure and priorities of Number 10 North are settled. Anyone wishing to add their names to the letter are invited to email meg.pirie@fashionroundtable.co.uk

BFC launches 'Fashion Britain' to champion regional talent across the UK
sub_title: The British Fashion Council is extending its industry programme beyond London through Fashion Britain, as regional jobs and high-street investment gain prominence in government and industry discussions.
article_content: The British Fashion Council's new national initiative Fashion Britain looks to move the focus away from London and champion local talent and creativity, as regional jobs and high-street investment gain prominence in government and industry discussions. Launching this September, Fashion Britain will operate across six leading cities including London, Liverpool, Manchester, Newcastle, Bristol and Edinburgh. Each city will host public events, designer conversations, cultural collaborations and retail experiences, with further partners and schedules due to be announced. One of the first programme announcements is the BFC's partnership with ELLE UK to launch the National Designer Panel Series, which will see live conversations with designers, industry voices and emerging talent taking place across participating cities. The initiative forms part of BFC 2030: Access, Creativity, Growth , which repositioned the organisation as a business accelerator and set out a move from London-centred access towards UK-wide participation. "British fashion is one of our greatest cultural exports, yet for too long participation has been concentrated in too few places, " BFC Chief Executive Laura Weir. "Fashion Britain is about decentralising fashion, not by diminishing London’s global importance, but by recognising that the future of British creativity depends on strengthening the connections between every part of the UK." Weir further highlighted that the new programme "represents a fundamental shift" in the role of the of the BFC, and that it sees its responsibility "to champion creativity wherever it exists". The programme builds on the BFC’s City Wide Celebration format , which previously brought designer talks, cultural activity and retail activations to cities including Liverpool, Manchester and Newcastle. It also follows the pilot launch of Fashion Assembly, which takes fashion education into schools. The BFC is also expanding its designer support. Its reworked NEWGEN programme now offers longer-term funding , infrastructure, mentorship and industry access, while the BFC/GQ Designer Fashion Fund provides its winner with £100,000 and year-long mentoring. Fashion Britain arrives nine days after Andy Burnham became Prime Minister, bringing his focus on spreading employment across the country into government. Burnham has called for “good growth in every postcode” and pledged to reform business rates, support high streets and distribute jobs more widely. The implications extend beyond fashion’s creative workforce. Across the UK, retail provides jobs for 2.8 million people, and according to the British Retail Consortium (BRC), businesses in the sector have taken on £6.5 billion in extra employment costs since 2024. The BRC’s Buy into Retail Manifesto has called for lower employment costs for young workers, business rates reform, competitive electricity prices and greater investment in retail locations. The Council's announcement coincides with Fashion Roundtable and other UK fashion industry signatories calling on Andy Burnham to introduce onshoring requirements for public-sector textiles , beginning with NHS and defence uniforms. The open letter, published on this week, asks for a meeting before the government finalises its Number 10 North initiative. Signatories include presenter and Buffalo Systems co-owner Ben Fogle, alongside representatives from the fashion and textiles sector. The wider UK fashion and textiles industry contributes £62 billion to GDP and supports 1.3 million jobs, according to figures cited in the letter. These totals cover the broader sector rather than domestic garment manufacturing alone. Burberry has also pressed Burnham to consider fashion’s economic contribution outside London. Chief Executive Joshua Schulman recently highlighted the British luxury house’s manufacturing operations in Yorkshire and back-office facility in Leeds while calling for tax-free shopping to be restored . Schulman said Burberry’s tourist business had fallen by about 50% since 2019, largely because the VAT Retail Export Scheme was abolished in 2020. He linked international retail competitiveness to the regional jobs supported by Burberry. Fashion Britain’s first test will be whether September’s public programme develops into lasting commercial routes for regional designers. The BFC said participating partners and the full schedule will be disclosed in the coming weeks.
