ASOS introduces ARRANGE Bespoke to spotlight emerging fashion talent
sub_title: ASOS has launched ARRANGE Bespoke, a new collaboration series designed to spotlight emerging designers, with Central Saint Martins student Johannes Warnke selected as its first creative partner.
article_content: ASOS has launched ARRANGE Bespoke, a new collaboration series designed to spotlight emerging designers, with Central Saint Martins student Johannes Warnke selected as its first creative partner. Launching during Paris Couture Week, ARRANGE Bespoke debuts with a hand-crafted dress created by Warnke in collaboration with the ARRANGE design team. The piece combines repurposed off-cuts and surplus materials with ARRANGE’s signature naturally dyed peace silk, reflecting a shared focus on craftsmanship, construction and detail. Warnke, who is known for his distinctive draping style and experimental approach to design, reimagined ARRANGE’s signature sequins through movement and texture. The dress was created by collaging repurposed materials, combining different sequin sizes and shapes with layers of hand-dyed peace silk to create a softer, fluid silhouette. Johannes Warnke said: “I was interested in reimagining the ARRANGE signature sequins through movement, inspired by the streets of Paris and the way summer light filters through windows and curtains before falling onto the street.” The collaboration marks the first in an ongoing ARRANGE Bespoke series, which will invite emerging designers to reinterpret the label’s approach to occasionwear while showcasing the creative process behind each collection. ARRANGE is ASOS’ elevated fashion label, focused on premium occasionwear and statement designs. Through ARRANGE Bespoke, the retailer aims to highlight emerging creative talent and explore new perspectives on occasion dressing. Vanessa Spence, EVP Brand and Creative at ASOS, said: "ARRANGE Bespoke gives us an opportunity to celebrate fashion in its most expressive form while offering a glimpse into the creative thinking behind ARRANGE.” “By collaborating with emerging creative talent, we're able to spotlight the next generation of designers, bring fresh perspectives to each collection, and showcase the craftsmanship, creativity and storytelling that sits behind the product,” she added. The launch reflects how fashion brands are increasingly using designer collaborations to celebrate craftsmanship, creativity and emerging talent. The first ARRANGE Bespoke dress was photographed in Paris during Couture Week and will now be held in the ASOS archive as the first piece in the series. Further collaborations are planned as ARRANGE Bespoke continues to develop.

article_title: Adidas Originals and ASOS unveil fourth collection as partnership expands into menswear
sub_title: Adidas Originals and ASOS have launched the fourth instalment of their exclusive womenswear partnership, following the sell-out success of the previous three collections.
article_content: Adidas Originals and ASOS have launched the fourth instalment of their exclusive collaboration, introducing a new womenswear range and the partnership’s first-ever menswear collection following three sell-out drops. Available from 29 July for ASOS.WORLD loyalty members before launching globally on 30 July, the latest drop is fronted by professional boxer and model Ramla Ali for womenswear, while British footballer Noni Madueke leads the campaign for the debut menswear collection. Inspired by the freedom and spontaneity of late summer, the womenswear collection combines Adidas Originals' sporting heritage with ASOS' British fashion aesthetic, reimagining classic sportswear silhouettes through a more fashion-led lens. The range includes updated takes on Adidas Originals staples such as tracksuits, funnel-neck jackets, windbreakers and sleeveless 3-Stripes track tops, alongside statement jumpsuits inspired by the brand's recognisable Firebird design. Towelling, satin nylon, sateen finishes and sheer fabrics feature throughout, while sculptural proportions, dropped waists and signature ASOS embroidery bring a contemporary edge to familiar styles. Alongside the womenswear launch, ASOS has also expanded the partnership into menswear for the first time. Designed exclusively for the retailer's menswear customer, the collection reworks classic sportswear pieces with tailored influences, heritage-inspired fabrics and preppy silhouettes, reflecting the retailer's continued investment in menswear. Vanessa Spence, Executive Vice President of Brand & Creative at ASOS, said: "The success of the previous collections gave us the confidence to push the partnership further.” "By reinterpreting iconic Adidas Originals silhouettes through our British fashion lens, we've created a collection that feels confident, versatile and distinctly ASOS." The launch also introduces AI-powered virtual try-on for selected looks through the ASOS iOS app, which allows customers to view outfits on themselves or a virtual model. The latest drop comes as Adidas continues to strengthen its apparel business. In the first quarter of 2026, the sportswear giant reported a 14% increase in currency-neutral revenues to €6.6 billion (£5.7 billion) , with e-commerce sales rising 25% and direct-to-consumer sales delivering double-digit growth across all markets. The Adidas Originals x ASOS collections will be available exclusively on ASOS, with the womenswear range priced from £35 to £120 and the menswear collection ranging from £65 to £300.

article_title: Harry Styles’ stylist Harry Lambert awarded honorary degree from UCA
sub_title: Harry Lambert, who has styled Harry Styles since 2014, has been awarded an Honorary Master of Arts by the University for the Creative Arts (UCA) in recognition of his contribution to the fashion industry.
article_content: Harry Lambert, who has styled Harry Styles since 2014, has been awarded an Honorary Master of Arts by the University for the Creative Arts (UCA) in recognition of his contribution to the fashion industry. The British stylist graduated from UCA with a first-class degree in photography in 2008 and was presented with the award during the university’s graduation ceremony at London’s Royal Festival Hall on Thursday Best known for shaping Harry Styles’ fashion identity, Lambert has helped redefine contemporary menswear through gender-fluid tailoring, bold silhouettes and collaborations with emerging designers including Harris Reed and Steven Stokey-Daley. Harry Lambert Beyond his work with Styles, Lambert has styled a number of high-profile names including Emma Corrin and Alexander Skarsgård, creating some of recent years’ most talked-about red carpet looks. He has also collaborated with brands including Pandora, Zara and eBay. The honorary award recognised Lambert’s contribution to the fashion and creative industries, with actor Emma Corrin surprising him during the ceremony via a video message. “I don’t know anyone who works as hard and who brings more creativity, joy and inventiveness to their work,” Corrin said. Accepting the award, Lambert reflected on the role UCA played in his career. “UCA completely changed my life,” he said. “I realise now that inspiration doesn’t come from a postcode or a city, it comes from the people who challenge you, encourage you and help you see the world differently.” “And I still use the skills I learnt there every day. Thank you UCA, not only for this extraordinary honour, but for seeing something in me before I could fully see it in myself.” Lambert has become one of Britain’s most influential fashion stylists since meeting Styles in 2014, with the pair helping to challenge traditional menswear conventions through looks featuring pearls, feather boas, floral tailoring and flared silhouettes.

article_title: Editors' Top Reads: News from M&S, Vollebak, CQP and more...
sub_title: Here are some of this week’s news and features highlights handpicked by TheIndustry.fashion team.
article_content: Here are some of this week’s news and features highlights handpicked by TheIndustry.fashion team. The Interview: Vollebak co-founder on wearable tech, wholesale ambitions and building clothes for the next century Vollebak, the experimental clothing company founded by twin brothers Steve and Nick Tidball, has built a global following through products made from space-grade materials, fireproof fabrics and biologically engineered textiles. The brand currently sells exclusively online, operates on a 12-18-month development cycle for most products, and counts customers working in robotics, AI, physics, engineering and finance among its customer base. We gained an in-depth insight into the business from Nick, who spoke to TheIndustry.fashion about the brand's origins, its wholesale ambitions, how it continues to push the boundaries of what the future of clothing could look like and where it is heading next. Read the full interview here. Camilla Rydzek, Senior News & Features Writer. Marks & Spencer is making its London Fashion Week runway debut this autumn , unveiling a shoppable womenswear and menswear collection that customers can buy immediately online, in flagship UK stores and across key international markets. This move, which follows on from pitlane fashion show at Silverstone earlier this month, further underscores just how far M&S fashion has come in recent years. Which is to say, a very long way. Fashionability, value for money, construction, fabric and fit have all been pored over and improved. Now the retailer feels confident to show at LFW and will be live-streaming the event to include its customers in the excitement. Not only is this a great move for Marks & Spencer but it's a great thing for London Fashion Week, which had lost some of its sparkle (understandably in some respect given the fall out from Covid). It is most encouraging to see home grown brands support the event and I feel optimistic LFW could be on an upward trajectory again. Both Mulberry and Alexander McQueen are returning too. I hope to see more. I've said it before but a healthy London Fashion Week benefits us all, and it's certainly going to benefit Marks & Spencer. Lauretta Roberts, Co-founder, CEO and Editor-in-Chief. UK retail footfall falls 3.4% in June as heatwave keeps shoppers indoors The Interview: CQP founder Adam Lewenhaupt on trading finance for footwear and following his design dream It was interesting to hear CQP founder Adam Lewenhaupt’s take on design this week , with a focus on being ‘product first’ and preferring to build a few strong and long-term retail partnerships over quantity. It was also almost refreshing to hear how the Stockholm-based premium footwear brand, which was founded in 2014, doesn’t chase influencers or brand ambassadors like so many brands do now. Lewenhaupt says that is partly because of the “sometimes questionable cost/benefit ratio”, but also because he doesn’t really think CQP’s products are well suited for it. He believes their best ambassadors are their customers. With that in mind, they do their best to take “extremely good care of them”. That way they will keep coming back for more. Last month gave them a fresh reason to take another look at CQP, which takes its time to release what it believes to be standout products rather trying to create volume through far too many styles. To coincide with the start of the World Cup, CPQ launched its new ‘Stillo’ sneaker, though Lewenhaupt admits that was more coincidental timing than planned! It’s an ultra sleek trainer inspired by the first pair of football boots he got in the late 1980s, before synthetic materials took over and when stitching and other details contributed to the actual performance of a shoe. So far, he says that those customers who have bought the Stillo “absolutely love it”. Handmade in Portugal from Italian leathers and suedes, it’s easy to see why it could prove to be much more than a World Cup winner. I look forward to seeing more from CQP. Tom Bottomley, Contributor.

article_title: Wax London expands Fenwick partnership with new Kingston concession
sub_title: Following the success of its concession at Fenwick in Newcastle, Wax London is expanding the partnership with a new 500 sq ft space in the retailer’s department store in Kingston upon Thames.
article_content: Following the success of its concession at Fenwick in Newcastle, Wax London is expanding the partnership with a new 500 sq ft space in the retailer’s department store in Kingston upon Thames. The space has been designed with the same attention to detail Wax London is known for, including custom rails, dark tinted acrylic tops and a vintage 16-drawer oak glazed haberdashery counter giving the concession “a warm, considered feel”, while a wall mounted lightbox adds a clean, modern contrast. Roger Wightman, Managing Director of Wax London, said: “After our success in Newcastle, opening in Kingston was a simple decision. We've found a new customer at Fenwick with a real appetite for what Wax London stands for, and that connection to the brand feels genuinely exciting. “To see the concession model growing with such strong presence across the country is something we're incredibly proud of – and a big thank you to everyone who has made it possible.” Stephen Ayres, Concessions Director at Fenwick, added: “At Fenwick, we are focused on curating a compelling and differentiated brand mix for our customers, and Wax London is a fantastic example of this. “Since launching in Newcastle, the brand has demonstrated a strong affinity with our customer base, making Kingston a natural next step in the partnership. Wax London's commitment to quality, craftsmanship and contemporary British design aligns perfectly with the modern menswear offer we continue to build across our stores. “We are delighted to welcome the brand to Kingston and look forward to seeing it become part of the store's fashion destination.” At the heart of the floor plan of the new concession sits a central styling area, framed by side-hang wall rails and freestanding floor units. The existing balustrade glass panels have been treated with an orange-tint film, “a quiet nod to the brand’s earthy, sun-warmed palette”. Founded in 2015, Wax London unveiled its first ever in-store pop-up in Harrods, Knightsbridge, in May, described as “an exciting next step in its continued growth”, with further pop-up opportunities also now being considered to drive further brand awareness. Wax London currently operates five standalone UK stores, four of which are in London - on Soho’s Berwick Street, which was the first to open in 2023, Covent Garden’s Neal Street (2024), Spitalfields (2024), Canary Wharf (2025), as well as its first store outside of the capital in Victoria Leeds, which opened in October 2025.

article_title: Puma appoints new Vice President of E-Commerce
sub_title: PUMA has appointed digital commerce specialist Dusan Hamlin to the newly created role of Vice President of E-Commerce, as the sportswear giant continues to strengthen its direct-to-consumer business.
article_content: Puma has appointed digital commerce specialist Dusan Hamlin to the newly created role of Vice President of E-Commerce, as the sportswear giant continues to strengthen its direct-to-consumer business. Hamlin joins with more than 25 years of experience in digital transformation and e-commerce, having previously led digital initiatives at Adidas and Reebok. More recently, he co-founded global performance marketing company M&C Saatchi Performance and digital innovation consultancy This Place, while also serving on the board of Tokyo-listed software company Asteria Corporation. Reporting to Chief Commercial Officer Matthias Bäumer, Hamlin will oversee the global strategy and commercial direction of Puma's digital and e-commerce operations. The appointment follows Puma's decision in late 2025 to split its direct-to-consumer division into dedicated Global Retail and Global E-Commerce functions, reflecting the growing importance of online sales and digital consumer engagement to the business. Matthias Bäumer, Chief Commercial Officer at Puma, said: “With Dusan, we have found a proven digital transformation expert to take Puma's E-Commerce to the next level.” “Our digital channels have become increasingly important for our business in recent years. Considering this, it was crucial to establish dedicated e-commerce leadership to further develop our strategy and enhance the consumer experience across our website, apps and marketplaces.” Hamlin added: “We have a massive opportunity at Puma. We continue to significantly improve our platform capabilities, and we are now putting in place a world-class operating model and extended digital team to support our goals. Globally emerging technologies such as social commerce and AI-driven commerce at scale will be a key focus to meet our customers’ needs.” The appointment comes as Puma continues its strategic transformation under CEO Arthur Hoeld. The company has described 2026 as a transition year as it works to restore growth through cost efficiencies, inventory reductions and improvements to its distribution model, while investing in its digital infrastructure and direct-to-consumer channels. In its most recent quarterly results , Puma reported a 3.8% increase in direct-to-consumer sales despite an overall decline in revenue, highlighting the growing importance of its owned retail and digital operations as it lays the foundations for a return to growth from 2027. Since the beginning of the year Puma has been in a recruitment drive, with Hamlin becoming the sixth hire for the company over the last few months. Notably the majority of the new hires have backgrounds with the sportswear brand's biggest rivals, mainly Adidas and Nike, highlighting Puma's ambitions to establish itself as a top-three global sportswear brand. In May the sportswear brand appointed a new Managing Director for Europe , a new Chief Financial Officer, a new lead for its Sportstyle business unit. It also hired a new Senior Vice President of Creative Direction and a new Vice President of Global Wholesale .

article_title: Sosandar revenue rises 14% as EBITDA doubles and stores weigh on profit
sub_title: Sosandar grew FY26 revenue to £42.3m, with EBITDA reaching £2.1m, as its own website returned to growth and gross margin improved.
article_content: Sosandar grew FY26 revenue to £42.3 million, with EBITDA reaching £2.1 million, as its own website returned to growth and gross margin improved. Reducing frequent discounting helped the AIM-listed UK women’s fashion brand to increase sales and improve margins during the year ended 31 March 2026. Website growth and stronger marketing returns supported the result, while disruption at Marks & Spencer – which suffered a cyber attack last year that took its website offline for six weeks in sprint 2025 – constrained third-party revenue and the store estate continued to absorb earnings. Gross profit increased 17% to £27 million, ahead of the 14% rise in revenue. Gross margin has now improved by more than 600 basis points in two years, from 57.6% in FY24 to 64% in FY26. The retailer attributed the improvement mainly to lower promotional activity on its website. Better intake margins also contributed, supported by sterling’s strength against the US dollar and improved prices from suppliers. Adjusted profit before tax increased from £156,000 to £377,000. This excludes a £346,000 non-cash impairment charge relating to store assets. Statutory profit before tax was £31,000, compared with a £67,000 loss in FY25. Administrative expenses rose 16% to £26.6 million, reflecting higher growth investment and a full year of costs across the store estate. Marketing expenditure more than doubled from £1.1 million to £2.4 million, with spending directed towards Meta and Google alongside the return of printed consumer brochures. Co-CEOs Ali Hall and Julie Lavington said: “We set out at the start of the year to demonstrate that we could return to strong revenue growth while maintaining margins and improving profitability, and we have delivered on all three.” Revenue from Sosandar’s own website increased 24%, while total revenue from the website and stores rose 31% to £21.5 million. Website sessions grew 11% to 15.1 million and conversion improved from 2.42% to 2.68%. Orders increased by 23% to 404,614, with active customers up 15% to 204,492. Average order frequency rose 7% to 1.98, although average order value declined 4% to £109. Third-party revenue was broadly unchanged at £20.8 million after the M&S cyber incident meant there was no revenue from that partner for 11 weeks. When trading restarted, stock intake stayed constrained before getting back to normal levels in February 2026. Sosandar said it continued to be among the top-selling brands across its partners, including NEXT. Sosandar’s stores traded more strongly as they entered their second year, but the estate reduced adjusted profit before tax by £0.9 million. Store costs, including fit-out depreciation, doubled to £2.4 million. Market-town locations outperformed shopping-centre stores, which are taking longer to mature. Sosandar does not expect to open further stores in FY27 and will focus on making its existing locations profitable. Its current stores are located in Chelmsford, Marlow, Gateshead, Cardiff and Harrogate. The retailer assigned the lease for its loss-making Bath store to another retailer on 29 June, allowing it to close the location after the reporting period. Net revenue rose 22% to £11.6 million in the first quarter of FY27, against a comparative period affected by minimal M&S sales. Gross margin reached 65.2%, while own-website revenue increased 7%. Net cash stood at £8.9 million on 30 June, after a further £0.5 million of share buybacks. All third-party partners were trading ahead of the previous year, and Sosandar said it remained on track to meet full-year market expectations.

article_title: One Teaspoon to relaunch in the UK through Just Now Distribution
sub_title: Cult Australian denim brand One Teaspoon is set to return to the UK market for SS27 via Just Now Distribution, which in turn has appointed Janice Tassell of JT Brand Studio to handle wholesale sales for the UK & Ireland.
article_content: Cult Australian denim brand One Teaspoon is set to return to the UK market for SS27 via Just Now Distribution, which in turn has appointed Janice Tassell of JT Brand Studio to handle wholesale sales for the UK & Ireland. Founded in Sydney in 2000, One Teaspoon was previously stocked by Harvey Nichols, Selfridges, Harrods, Topshop, ASOS and Urban Outfitters and is a favourite of celebrities and style icons including Beyoncé, Rihanna, Zendaya, Kendall Jenner, Hailey Bieber, Gigi Hadid and Bella Hadid. The ‘No Plans’ SS27 collection offers premium denim alongside elevated ready-to-wear pieces, combining signature washes and modern silhouettes, with T-shirts retailing at £55-£90, denim shorts at £130-£150, jeans at £160-£260 and jackets at £200-£460. Juls Dawson, founder of Just Now Distribution, said: “One Teaspoon built a strong following in the UK throughout the 2010s, particularly during the premium denim boom. While the brand has continued to be available internationally through selected global online retailers, it has not had a dedicated UK distribution partner or consistent wholesale presence for several years, leaving a gap in the market. “We're seeing renewed consumer demand for authentic brands with genuine heritage and recognisable DNA. Fashion continues to cycle back towards premium denim, relaxed silhouettes and early-2000s influences - all areas where One Teaspoon has genuine credibility rather than simply following a trend. “At the same time, UK retailers are looking for brands with a clear identity and proven international recognition. One Teaspoon arrives with over 25 years of history, global distribution and strong cultural relevance, making now the ideal moment to reintroduce it to British consumers.” Janice Tassell added: “I am very excited to be working with the One Teaspoon and Just Now Distribution teams as this is a great opportunity to relaunch the collection in the UK and Ireland.” The SS27 collection will be showcased at The Fashion Huddle at 26-28 Hammersmith Grove in London from 13-22 July, before moving to the JT Brand Studio showroom at Fashion House in Islington from 23 July. Earlier this week Just Now Distribution announced it has been appointed, along with Luke Distribution, as commercial partners of US heritage workwear brand Dickies for the UK and Ireland. The joint venture will see Just Now Distribution lead all sales, wholesale development and market expansion activity for Dickies, supported operationally by Luke Distribution, led by Simon Poole, whose business brings significant expertise in logistics, finance, warehousing and systems integration.

article_title: H&M celebrates designer collab with WARDROBE.NYC at Paris Haute Couture Week
sub_title: H&M has celebrated the launch of its latest designer collaboration with New-York based luxury label the WARDROBE.NYC with an exclusive party during Haute Couture fashion week in Paris.
article_content: H&M has celebrated the launch of its latest designer collaboration with New-York based luxury label the WARDROBE.NYC with an exclusive party during Haute Couture Week in Paris. The cocktail party took place at Le Grand Café within the historic Grand Palais. The brand welcomed friends and fans of the brand to the party, including British model and digital creator Mia Regan and Northern Irish YouTuber, TikTok creator and influencer Olivia Neill, as well as singers Teyana Taylor, Audrey Nuna, Absolutely and Adéla. WARDROBE.NYC was founded by editor and stylist Christine Centenera and designer Josh Goot, with the new collaboration translating the duo's minimalist vision into a "definitive wardrobe - directional and effortlessly wearable in equal measure". Ann-Sofie Johansson, Teyana Taylor, Christine Centenera, Josh Goot The label was founded in 2017 and focuses on "practical urban minimalism", with pieces designed to be timeless yet wearable and created using high-quality materials. Prices at WARDROBE.NYC range from £255 for a classic T-shirt to £2,500 for a Crepe Safari Jacket. The new collaborative collection with H&M draws on the label's archives to present a "tight edit of archetypal urban style". Defined by its sharp tailoring and timeless colour palette, the collection is anchored by core pieces including wool coats, blazers and tailored skirts, complemented by more casual pieces including washed denim, padded bombers and hoodies. "This collection distills our signatures, and expresses our philosophy of modern urban dress. Paris felt like the right place to share this moment with many of the people who have been part of our journey since the beginning," said Goot and Centenera. Ann-Sofie Johansson, Creative Advisor and Head of Design Womenswear H&M, added: "What makes this collaboration unique in our history is that essentials are usually one element of a collection - here, they are the proposition. "Every piece is built around versatility and timelessness, and that level of singular focus felt genuinely new for us. Sharp considered basics as a complete wardrobe: that's not something we've explored before." The collection will launch across the UK in selected stores and online on 6 August 2026.

article_title: NEXT to open 132,000 sq ft anchor store at Bluewater this month
sub_title: NEXT is set to launch a new 132,000 sq ft anchor store at Bluewater in Greenhithe, Kent, on 30 July 2026, tripling the size of its current presence at the shopping centre and taking over the former House of Fraser unit, which has sat empty since the end of 2024.
article_content: NEXT is set to launch a new 132,000 sq ft anchor store at Bluewater in Greenhithe, Kent, on 30 July 2026, tripling the size of its current presence at the shopping centre and taking over the former House of Fraser unit, which has sat empty since the end of 2024. The opening gives Bluewater its first new anchor store since the centre launched in 1999. Across the launch weekend, Bluewater will put on live music and family entertainment, including face painting and an appearance from NEXT mascot Hamish the Highland Cow. Inside the expanded site, shoppers will find wider men's, women's and childrenswear ranges, plus a bigger homeware department and an in-store Costa café. NEXT is moving from its current 44,600 sq ft unit at the centre. NEXT store manager Terry Wetherell said: "We're incredibly excited to be opening the largest store across the NEXT portfolio at Bluewater Shopping Centre. We can't wait to showcase a broader range of our products and introduce new brands to the centre and our customers." Bath & Body Works will also relocate to a neighbouring 2,000 sq ft unit as part of the opening. TheIndustry.fashion first reported on the store opening in November 2024. At the time, Pablo Sueiras, Head of Brand Account Management at Landsec, said: "The best brands are investing in bigger, better stores in prime locations. NEXT is at the forefront of retail innovation, which has made it one of the most in-demand brands among consumers." The deal converts a vacated department store unit into a mono-brand anchor, a pattern that has become common across prime UK shopping centres as retailers seek larger-format spaces in high-footfall destinations. Bluewater encompasses more than 250 shops and is one of the largest retail destinations in the south-east of England. NEXT, which reportedly has a market capitalisation of more than £17.5 billion, currently operates more than 400 stores across the UK and has been busily expanding its brand portfolio over the last few years. Just last week NEXT was reportedly considering a bid for Harvey Nichols, the luxury department store chain put up for sale by its Hong Kong billionaire owner, Sir Dickson Poon. Previously, it has taken over a series of well-known retail names, among them FatFace, Joules and Reiss. It has also built UK distribution deals with Gap and Victoria's Secret. In January, NEXT also acquired footwear brand Russell & Bromley in a pre-pack insolvency rescue deal that focused on its brand and assets. The retailer initially kept the leases of three of the brand's key stores – in Chelsea, Mayfair and Bluewater, but later also re-opened its Richmond location . All remaining Russell & Bromley stores are now shut. Harvey Nichols would bring this acquisition-led approach into premium department store retail for the first time. Sky News reported that it is still not clear whether NEXT would carry on operating the network of regional stores after any takeover, or whether it would instead concentrate on the brand and other intellectual property assets, as it did with its Russell & Bromley deal.

article_title: Marks & Spencer to make London Fashion Week runway debut with 'see now, buy now' collection
sub_title: Marks & Spencer will join the official LFW schedule for the first time this autumn, marking 100 years in fashion with a "see now, buy now" womenswear and menswear range available online and in stores.
article_content: British high street retailer Marks & Spencer is making its London Fashion Week runway debut this autumn, unveiling a shoppable womenswear and menswear collection that customers can buy immediately online, in flagship UK stores and across key international markets. The debut, which M&S said coincides with its 100th year in the fashion industry, positions the retailer on the same runway calendar as luxury and designer brands. The collection will follow a "see now, buy now" model, with the show streamed live to bring the event directly to consumers. Stuart Machin, Chief Executive of Marks & Spencer, said: "For 100 years M&S fashion has been part of everyday life and now we will showcase our designs on fashion's global stage. "At M&S we focus on designing clothes with style, quality and value, and making fashion accessible to all. That's why we will stream our show, bringing one of the world's leading fashion weeks and the magic of M&S to everybody." The live stream and immediate retail availability distinguish Marks & Spencer's approach from the traditional fashion week model, where collections typically reach stores months after a runway presentation. Instead, M&S is using the platform as a combined marketing and sales event, linking content directly to conversion through its own channels. It follows a series of high-visibility fashion activations from the retailer. In May, M&S staged a summer show in Ibiza, and last week it held what it described as the first pit lane fashion show at Silverstone ahead of the Formula 1 British Grand Prix , where 50 models walked through the circuit's working garages. Machin framed the London Fashion Week debut as building on those events, suggesting the retailer views spectacle-led fashion moments as a core part of its brand strategy. It follows the retailer's first connection with London Fashion Week in 2014 , when it hosted an event showcasing its "Best of British" Autumn 2014 collection. Laura Weir, Chief Executive of the British Fashion Council, said: "As one of the great icons of the British high street, and a valued patron of the British Fashion Council, M&S has played an important role in the nation's retail and cultural story for generations. "Its debut shoppable collection at London Fashion Week is a significant moment, demonstrating how heritage, innovation and accessibility can come together to connect exceptional British design with consumers in new and relevant ways." M&S joins a September schedule that is gaining momentum with the return of prominent British names. Mulberry will stage its first runway show in six years under Creative Director Christopher Kane on 20 September, while Alexander McQueen is also set to present in London after years on the Paris calendar. It also follows Topshop's runway return earlier this year , when the retailer staged what it described as the world's first AI-powered shoppable catwalk in Manchester, allowing guests to shop the collection in real time.

Armani Prive’s couture show gave a masterclass in red-carpet dressing
sub_title: Armani Prive’s latest couture collection embraced a dark fantasy.
article_content: Armani Prive’s latest couture collection embraced a dark fantasy. It marked the second haute couture show designed solely by Creative Director Silvana Armani, who took the reins of the womenswear arm of the brand after the death of her uncle Giorgio Armani last September. She’s designed at Armani since the Eighties, and has made a name for herself by continuing the luxury label’s DNA with a contemporary update. Tailored trousers and structured jackets were a major part of the collection (Emma Da Silva/AP) The latest couture collection, for autumn/winter 2026-27, was a confident second showing from Armani. She opened the show with one of her signature looks: impeccably tailored cigarette trousers, paired with a rich blue beaded jacket. Deep, dark colours were represented throughout the whole collection. Intense burgundies made way into vivid navy blues, with blacks permeating the collection. Almost everything was iridescent, whether it was models draped in strings of glittering beads, wearing sequin-studded blazers, or with skirts made from a shimmering, almost liquid-like materials. Fabrics almost looked like liquid on the runway (Emma Da Silva/AP) This was firmly a collection for the red carpet, with a mixture of sharply tailored trousers and full-length gowns. Tassels trailing from bags, strings of beading, fluffy feathers and tulle overlays gave the outfits plenty of movement and interest. The silhouettes played off against each other perfectly: much of the suiting had structured, Eighties-style statement shoulders, while many of the gowns were strapless, leaving shoulders completely bare. There was a sculptural element to the clothes, too – such as a one-armed gown with a swooping, circular neckline, bringing a bit of geometry into the fashion. Meanwhile, sheer bodices on the occasional dress gave the collection more of a daring edge. Plenty of the outfits had sculptural elements (Emma Da Silva/AP) The beauty looks were kept simple but bold: models wore their hair back, with a slight bouffant, paired with a smokey eye to really give that red carpet feel. Not every detail landed – some of the models wore bow ties on bare necks, which might feel like a bit of an on-the-nose interpretation of eveningwear – but it was, on the whole, a confident and assured collection. While this was by no means an experimental collection – instead, it focused on red carpet wearability – there were hints of innovation, such as a strong-shouldered structure jacket with a deep-V at the back and a button fastening, almost looking like it was worn backwards. Silvana Armani presented plenty of red carpet-worthy gowns (Emma Da Silva/AP) The colour palette started experimenting with touches of gold as the show progressed, with a series of standout gowns closing the collection. The final look was a form-fitting, glittering black gown with a boat neckline, deep-V and long sleeves, accessorised with an oversized fan to add a dramatic flair. We might not see these outfits lighting up Instagram as the next viral collection, but we’ll certainly see the designs taking over the red carpet next season. Rosamund Pike was front row for the Armani Privé show (Emma Da Silva/AP) The front row was suitably star-studded, with the likes of actor Rosamund Pike – wearing a smart tuxedo – watching the show. Pike was joined by long-time Armani fan Cate Blanchett, who posed for photographers alongside her son, Ignatius Martin Upton. For the occasion, Tár star Blanchett chose an Armani Privé look she previously wore to the 2025 Emmy Awards. Cate Blanchett posed with her son Ignatius Martin Upton (Emma Da Silva/AP) The black jumpsuit – from the autumn/winter 2025 couture collection – had a plunging deep-V neckline, sheer cut-out panels at the side and crystal embellishments. Last September, Blanchett wore it with nothing underneath, but for the Paris fashion show, she paired it with what looks to be a white silk scarf around the neckline.

Temperley London founder Alice Temperley steps away from brand
sub_title: Temperley London, the independent British fashion brand founded in 2000, has confirmed that its Founder and Creative Director Alice Temperley is stepping away from the company.
article_content: Temperley London, the independent British fashion brand founded in 2000, has confirmed that its Founder and Creative Director Alice Temperley is stepping away from the company. The brand said that Temperley leaves "with the backing of the team and house she has helped build," and that details on a new leadership team and a new Design Director will follow. No successor has yet been confirmed, although further details on the appointment of the new leadership team and a new Design Director are to be announced "in due course," the company said. Alice Temperley MBE commented on her departure: “I am enormously proud of everything I have built at Temperley London. It has been the creative home of my life for over two decades. "The time is right for me to pursue a new direction, one that allows me to follow long-held passions, with the people I love, on things that feel completely true to who I am as a designer." She added that after departing her namesake brand she will be focusing her attention on a "new creative practice, an independent venture that will collaborate closely with her creative network, her family and 22 muses who have shaped her vision over the years." Details on her new venture are to be announced in due course. Alice Temperley, Founder of Temperley London The departure comes roughly two and a half years after Times Square Group LLC and its investment arm, Luxutte Capital, took a majority stake in the business in November 2023. At the time of that acquisition, the company said Alice Temperley and then-CEO Luca Donnini would remain in place as Creative Director and Chief Executive respectively. "This alliance opens a door to new horizons, allowing the Temperley London collection to extend its reach into bags, shoes, ready-to-wear, accessories, and swimwear. I am incredibly excited about this new journey with Times Square Group and looking forward to spending even more time in UAE engaging with our loyal clients in the GCC and the wider region," Temperley commented on the partnership at the time. Since March 2025 Sarita Jha, has taken over as Interim CEO for Temperley. However, the brand confirmed that her tenure in the role has now ended, with an announcement as to her replacement to be announced soon. In 2000, Alice Temperley MBE launched the label, one year after graduating from the Royal College of Art. She received an MBE in 2011 for services to the fashion industry. According to the brand's own website, she still heads up Temperley London’s creative direction, with the company operating from locations including Sloane Street in London, Ilminster in Somerset and Phoenix Studios. The brand, which has been operating for over 25 years, describes itself as one of Britain’s most recognisable fashion houses, which has been defining an aesthetic of intricate craft, embellishment and bohemian elegance.

Nobody's Child strengthens leadership as growth continues
sub_title: Nobody's Child has strengthened its senior team with two new appointments spanning merchandising and retail, as the brand continues to grow.
article_content: Nobody's Child has strengthened its senior team with two new appointments spanning merchandising and retail, as the brand continues to grow. The fashion brand, led by CEO Jody Plows, has appointed Jennie Clarke as Head of Merchandising and Amy Boswell as Head of Retail on an interim basis. Clarke spent the last 13 years at Phase Eight, most recently in the role of Head of Merchandising. Prior to this, she had stints at both Reiss and Hobbs. In a post on LinkedIn, Clarke commented that she was "looking forward" to her role and that she was "joining a business that is continuing to grow and make a real impact within the industry". Boswell has been appointed as the interim Head of Retail after spending five years as the Executive Assistant to Nobody's Child CEO Jody Plows. She previously held the same role for the Ann Summers CEO as well as the Founder of New Look. Nobody's Child also shared that its Digital Director, Kate Murray, who has been with the brand since December 2025, is also supporting the next phase of growth for the brand. Murray brings 14 years of experience to the role. Issy Campbell, People & Culture Lead at Nobody's Child, said: "Every senior leadership appointment is the result of a rigorous and considered recruitment process at Nobody's Child, ensuring we find people whose experience, values and ambitions align with our long-term vision. "These hires will play an important role in strengthening our leadership team as we continue to grow, innovate and deliver for our customers." The appointments arrive as Nobody's Child continues to grow its work around sustainability, circularity and traceability. In an interview with TheIndustry.fashion published in August 2025, Plows described the brand's DPP initiative as "the biggest and most complex sustainability project we've worked on" and said the company had launched the pilot years before anticipated government legislation. The brand won Best Use of Technology in the Planet category at TheIndustry.fashion Awards 2025 for that work, which was developed in partnership with tech firm Fabacus and traceability specialist Fairly Made.

article_title: M&S signals higher shareholder returns
sub_title: Marks & Spencer has told shareholders at its annual general meeting on 7 July, that it expects to increase capital returns in the coming years, even as it commits to higher investment spending on its food-led growth strategy.
article_content: Marks & Spencer has told shareholders at its annual general meeting on 7 July that it expects to increase capital returns in the coming years, even as it commits to higher investment spending on its food-led growth strategy. Chief Financial Officer Alison Dolan made the commitment, citing a robust balance sheet, a net funds position - meaning the company holds more cash than it has debt - and an investment-grade credit rating, which means that lenders deem the company to be a reliable borrower. "What that will mean is that over the coming years we will be in the position both to invest and to increase what we return to shareholders," Dolan said. She added that M&S expected to set out more detail on its shareholder-return policy, as well as the timing of future returns, over the course of the current 2026/27 financial year. M&S finished its 2025/26 financial year with net funds excluding lease liabilities of £338.2 million. The board is proposing a full-year dividend of 4.2p per share, a 16.7% increase on the prior year, following a final dividend of 3.0p. Planned capital expenditure for 2026/27 sits at £650 million to £750 million, with roughly two-thirds directed towards Food, which M&S describes as its fastest-growing and highest-returning division. The AGM also sought authority for a share buyback of up to 10% of issued share capital, though M&S said it had no present intention of using it. Archie Norman, Chairman of M&S, added that technology represents a key opportunity for the retailer and is an area in which the company is looking to invest further capital. "Getting the right product from the manufacturers, forecasting the right way, flowing it through our supply chain into the stores at the right time can deliver great benefits in terms of sales but also in terms of reducing clearance and wastage," Norman said. "In fashion, home and beauty, we have the chance to rebuild a supply chain based on automation and to flow product from our factories through the stores much, much more efficiently. "That does require some chunky investment, so it is a big commitment from shareholders, but it will deliver great returns for us," he added. Cyberattack weighs on profit The shareholder-return message comes after a year disrupted by a cyberattack that weighed on trading. Adjusted pre-tax profit fell 23.8% to £671.4 million, while statutory profit before tax dropped 28.8% to £364.6 million. In its annual report, the company said it had the capacity to deliver "attractive compound growth in earnings per share and free cash flow", describing its current dividend stance as conservative because of the investment phase. Norman told investors the business had begun the new financial year in "fighting fit form". "We'd like to be a business that delivers consistently high single-digit revenue growth and double-digit profit growth," he said. M&S shares have risen 16% so far this year. The next catalyst for investors will be the fuller capital-return policy Dolan said the company expects to set out before March 2027.

article_title: The Interview: Vollebak co-founder on wearable tech, wholesale ambitions and building clothes for the next century
sub_title: Vollebak, the experimental clothing company founded by twin brothers Steve and Nick Tidball, has built a global following through products made from space-grade materials, fireproof fabrics and biologically engineered textiles.
article_content: Vollebak, the experimental clothing company founded by twin brothers Steve and Nick Tidball, has built a global following through products made from space-grade materials, fireproof fabrics and biologically engineered textiles. The brand currently sells exclusively online, operates on a 12-18-month development cycle for most products, and counts customers working in robotics, AI, physics, engineering and finance among its customer base. The London-based label held its first pop-up shop in May, will show at Paris Fashion Week this year to assess whether wholesale is a viable route, and is developing eight experimental projects for 2026, three of which involve wearable technology. The first of these, the Sonic Jacket, is already in development. The twin brothers make a strong team, with their responsibilities having always been clearly divided across the business. Steve leads strategy, while Nick oversees the creative direction - a dynamic that mirrors the roles they held throughout their respective advertising careers. We gained an in-depth insight into the business from Nick, who spoke to TheIndustry.fashion about the brand's origins, its wholesale ambitions, how it continues to push the boundaries of what the future of clothing could look like and where it is heading next. It was probably a few things to be honest: A love of Ferran Adrià who ran El Bulli at the time, the wildly future facing restaurant, and our basic first principles idea was ‘why is no one doing utterly future facing ideas in clothing?’ Around the same time we were running ultra marathons in our early thirties – we realised that we could do fairly tough things and the tougher it got the more we enjoyed it. Thirdly, was reading the Steve Jobs book by Walter Isaacson – which was a revelation in how to redefine an entire industry. Then finally my background in architecture, where I was utterly obsessed with materials and the built form. I think it taught us that if you do exactly the same as everyone else it won’t work. Probably our biggest lesson in advertising was watching Lee Clow at work in Chiat/Day in LA, who had written all the greatest Apple ads ever, including the ad “Think different” that really stuck with us. I don’t massively see it as fashion – I see it as clothing. In the same way the human needs shelter and so the by-product is houses. The human needs protection from the elements and other things, so for that you have clothing. We simply try to clothe people for stuff that's happening now and in the future, with some materials that man has invented in the last few years – as opposed to materials that were invented 3000 to 100 years ago. Mostly word of mouth to be honest. We think people are always on the look out for utterly unique things – especially when they push forward what people believe to be possible in an industry. I think also having me and my twin brother as the people who run the company is a thing that people like and understand. We run a very transparent company – which our community likes because it's not some polished faceless brand. We then also do some fairly maverick things – like building a Spaceshop that we are taking around the world, or hiding a wardrobe full of free clothes in the New Mexico desert, or running a huge billboard outside of SpaceX telling Elon our jacket was ready for space travel. Most stuff I test on myself, and some we test before they are products. If we get access to fireproof materials, for instance, the first thing we will do is take a lighter to it in our office. And then some of our stuff has already been tested for us – our Mars parachute was tested by NASA landing the rover on Mars. So as far as tests go, we’d say that fabric is pretty good at the job it was built for! The Sonic Jacket will have a longer lead time than your typical products that’s for sure! It's a wild series of challenges that's more like building a car than a piece of clothing. But we knew this would be the nature of it when we went into the challenge. Nearly all of our products are on a 12-18 month cycle from ideation to being commercially available. We haven’t tried to reinvent that process. The Sonic Jacket It's a tricky balance to be honest! We see experimentation as the fundamental building block of progress, so we will always push to experiment as much as possible – otherwise we are not moving forward. I’m not sure where I’d position us. I think of ourselves as a clothing company very simply – kind of like the maverick outsiders in the industry. A company who try to take on a myriad of clothing challenges within the industry. Here are a number of the challenges we are taking on: Currently we sell only online. We had our first pop up shop in London this May and it was a super successful 3 days. I’m very interested in having a super brutalist futuristic shop permanently. And we are showing at Paris Fashion Week this year to see if wholesale is a route we want to pursue. Typically we have customers all around the world that are united by one thing – and that’s intellect. We have an extremely smart customer base that work in a huge number of industries from robotics, AI, physics, design, engineering, the arts, and the financial world. And when we meet our customers they are super smart, super aware of how the world operates, and hyper aware of their choices and the lives they lead and why. Yes, very early on a very clever guy told us to make clothes that are very wearable – so we stick to that – as a couple of our early pieces weren’t easy to wear. I think it would be a simple piece of psychology along the lines of 'there should be zero expectation that everything should go right and that the journey will be smooth'. This is an impossibility! It would have been good to know that from day 1. The same can be said of life. It's a wild journey – but it very rarely works out in the ways you think it will. We are doing a series of eight projects this year that we would class as really pushing the boundaries of clothing. I think it's massively important to do projects that are pure moonshot ideas, it's very important to test the limits of what we are capable of. Three of these projects this year are to do with wearable tech. The Sonic Jacket is the first idea of those. The other two are still in the R&D phase – so I can't talk about what they are yet! But one is to do with light. Purely from a personal level – the one product I want to make is a chess board from utterly wild materials. I believe chess is the most beautiful metaphor for life.

article_title: Liberty promotes former Coty CMO to head up marketing
sub_title: Laura Simpson has been promoted to Chief Marketing Officer at Liberty, a position she will be executing alongside her existing role as Managing Director of LBTY, the retailer's beauty proposition launched in October 2023.
article_content: Laura Simpson has been promoted to Chief Marketing Officer at Liberty, a position she will hold alongside her existing role as Managing Director of LBTY, the retailer's beauty proposition. In her new and expanded role, Simpson will lead Liberty's overarching brand, marketing and customer strategy across the Group, while continuing to drive the growth and development of LBTY. Under her leadership, the retailer's dedicated beauty destination has already delivered significant growth, expanded its brand portfolio and strengthened Liberty's position as a destination for beauty discovery, expertise and innovation, according to the luxury department store. Simpson initially joined Liberty to launch and lead LBTY in 2022, following stints as CMO at both haircare company Wella and Coty. Prior to this, she spent more than 18 years in senior leadership positions at consumer goods giant Procter & Gamble. Laura Simpson, CMO of Liberty The appointment reflects Liberty's continued investment in brand building, customer experience and long-term growth, as the business looks to strengthen its position across retail, beauty and luxury lifestyle, Liberty said. Simpson said: "Liberty has always stood for creativity, discovery and individuality, and I am incredibly proud to take on this expanded role. Having launched LBTY and seen the strong response from customers, I am excited to help shape the next chapter of growth for both the beauty business and the wider Liberty brand. There is a tremendous opportunity to continue building meaningful connections with our customers while celebrating everything that makes Liberty such a unique destination." Adil Mehboob-Khan, Chief Executive Officer at Liberty, added: "Laura has been instrumental in the successful launch and growth of LBTY, demonstrating an exceptional ability to combine commercial performance with brand-building and customer engagement. As we look to the future, her expanded role will be critical in ensuring we continue to strengthen Liberty's position as one of the world's most distinctive retail destinations. I am delighted to welcome Laura to her broader role and look forward to seeing her continue to drive the business forward." This marks the third senior leadership change at Liberty since the beginning of the year. In January, the luxury department store appointed Lydia King as Managing Director of Retail, succeeding Sarah Coonan . In the role, she is responsible for Liberty’s buying and merchandising functions, as well as oversight of the Liberty flagship store. The same month, Liberty also appointed Alex Pregnolato as its new Chief Financial Officer . Pregnolato previously held the position of CFO at both De Beers and Versace Americas. Both appointments reflect Liberty's ongoing ambitions to expand its international reach while remaining rooted in its heritage of creativity, curation and cultural relevance.

article_title: Net-A-Porter warehouse workers resume strike action after rejecting latest pay offer
sub_title: GMB members at Net-A-Porter's Charlton warehouse in South London have begun two days of strike action after rejecting the company's latest pay offer, with the union arguing the proposal relies on performance targets workers called "unrealistic".
article_content: GMB members at Net-A-Porter's Charlton warehouse in South London have begun two days of strike action after rejecting the company's latest pay offer, with the union arguing the new proposal relies on performance targets workers deem "unrealistic". The strike, taking place from 7-8 July, follows a ballot that saw 69.7% of members vote to reject the revised pay package. (Of the nearly 100 GMB members, a total of 73.3% of members voted on the latest action). Industrial action had previously been scheduled by GMB for June, but was postponed to allow for negotiations brokered by independent public body, ACAS, to go ahead. Those negotiations produced a revised proposal that combined salary increases with a performance-related bonus, which workers have now rejected. Warehouse workers first raised the dispute over the London Living Wage in March. The rate stands at £14.80 per hour in 2026. According to earlier GMB figures, the company's previous proposal would have put the lowest-paid workers on £14.41 per hour, £761 below the annual equivalent of the London Living Wage for a 37.5-hour week. "Industrial action is always a last resort, but our members have spoken clearly and deserve a fair pay increase and to be treated with the respect their hard work deserves," said Craig Prickett, GMB Regional Organiser. "GMB postponed strike action in good faith to allow negotiations under the auspices of ACAS. Our members wanted to reach an agreement and gave the company every opportunity to improve its offer. He added that members specifically raised concerns that a "significant part" of the proposed pay package relied on performance targets that they believed to be "unrealistic, unachievable and, in many cases, outside of employees' control". "Many workers felt some of the targets would be difficult to achieve consistently and could be affected by factors outside of their direct control. Members also questioned why they should have to rely on a bonus mechanism to reach pay levels they believe should be reflected in their basic rate of pay." Prickett added that fresh redundancies added to workers' discontent, which is leaving "many employees facing uncertainty over their jobs". The redundancies sit within the broader transformation plan of LuxExperience, Net-A-Porter's parent company, which the group confirmed in May included partial workforce reductions across several sites. The Charlton warehouse has seen industrial action before. Workers first walked out on 20 May this year, and in 2023, 91% of GMB members voted for strike action ahead of Christmas before a last-minute agreement brought pay up to the then London Living Wage of £13.15 per hour. Prickett said GMB remained ready to engage if the company returned with an improved offer. LuxExperience had previously commented that it "fully respects our employees' right to take industrial action" and remained "open to engaging in constructive dialogue with union representatives" while protecting the long-term sustainability of the business. In May, LuxExperience, which also owns Mr Porter, Yoox and Mytheresa, reported stable sales and continued profitability for the third quarter ended 31 March 2026 and confirmed its full FY26 guidance. Yet, Net-A-Porter reported a decrease in net sales of 5.1% to €231.6 million in the third quarter, on a constant currency basis. Its adjusted EBITDA also saw a slight decrease of €1.1 million in Q3. Michael Kliger, Chief Executive Officer of LuxExperience commented on the results saying: "Net-A-Porter and Mr Porter as well as Yoox showed further sequential improvements, fully in line with our ongoing transformation plan for both segments." TheIndustry.fashion has reached out to LuxExperience for comment.

article_title: John Lewis explores closure of in-store services, putting 200 jobs at risk
sub_title: John Lewis is consulting on proposals to close its foreign exchange bureaux across 30 stores and remove dedicated gift-wrapping areas in 25 stores, putting around 200 jobs at risk across the 36-shop estate.
article_content: John Lewis is consulting on proposals to close its foreign exchange bureaux across 30 stores and remove dedicated gift-wrapping areas in 25 stores, putting around 200 jobs at risk across the 36-shop estate. The changes have not been finalised yet, but if approved, they would reportedly take effect in autumn. The move would see the bureau de change service removed entirely from affected branches, while gift wrapping would be absorbed into general store operations, with dedicated areas and staff removed from the store layout. The proposed changes across these two service areas would put around 200 roles at risk. John Lewis said affected staff would be supported through formal consultation and that redeployment into other roles within the partnership would be explored where possible. The service closures are part of a wider reshaping of the John Lewis store offer. In June, the retailer said it would put £50 million into five stores this year, including more than £20 million at its Glasgow branch in Buchanan Galleries, as part of an £800m multi-year transformation programme spanning stores, technology, services and hospitality. That programme has put the focus on expert advice, personal styling appointments, nursery consultations, and food and drink. Hospitality now makes up more than one in five store transactions, and John Lewis reported 10% sales growth across its 62 cafés and restaurants over the past year. The retailer is also planning to expand its Platter John Lewis concept to 32 locations by the end of 2027. The retailer has also put an emphasis on expanding its My John Lewis loyalty programme , forming part of a broader strategy to expand its beauty category as it seeks to respond to rising consumer demand. John Lewis Managing Director Peter Ruis said in June: "We're continuing to invest across our estate so our shops reflect the things customers value most about John Lewis, expert guidance, inspiring products and the confidence to make the right choice." John Lewis employees also received an annual bonus for the first time in four years in March, on the back of stronger profitability as the high street firm progressed further with its turnaround.

article_title: NEXT considers bid for Harvey Nichols
sub_title: British retailer NEXT is considering a bid for Harvey Nichols, the luxury department store chain put up for sale by its Hong Kong billionaire owner Sir Dickson Poon just last week, according to Sky News.
article_content: British retailer NEXT is considering a bid for Harvey Nichols , the luxury department store chain put up for sale by its Hong Kong billionaire owner, Sir Dickson Poon, just last week. Sources have told Sky News that the auction is still in its very early stages, but that NEXT plans to take a "serious look" at the business. The sale follows a long stretch of weakening performance. In its latest financial accounts, Harvey Nichols reported revenue of £204.8 million for the 12 months to 31 March 2024, down 5% from a year earlier. Pre-tax losses climbed to £34 million, making it a fifth straight year of losses. The business has about 1,200 employees in the UK and runs seven stores in the UK and Ireland, with large-format sites in London, Edinburgh, Birmingham, Leeds and Manchester, plus smaller-format branches in Bristol and Dublin. Internationally, it operates six large-format stores in Riyadh, Doha, Dubai, Hong Kong and Kuwait. The softer luxury-goods market, together with the ending of VAT-free shopping for tourists after Brexit, has been pointed to as a major reason for the prolonged losses. In recent years, NEXT, which reportedly has a market capitalisation of more than £17.5 billion, has taken over a series of well-known retail names, among them FatFace, Joules and Reiss. It has also built UK distribution deals with Gap and Victoria's Secret. In January, NEXT also acquired footwear brand Russell & Bromley in a pre-pack insolvency rescue deal that focused on its brand and assets. The retailer initially kept the leases of three of the brand's key stores – in Chelsea, Mayfair and Bluewater, but later also re-opened its Richmond location . All remaining Russell & Bromley stores are now shut. Harvey Nichols would bring this acquisition-led approach into premium department store retail for the first time. Sky News reported that it is still not clear whether NEXT would carry on operating the network of regional stores after any takeover, or whether it would instead concentrate on the brand and other intellectual property assets, as it did with its Russel & Bromley deal. Harvey Nichols has continued turnaround work during the ownership review. CEO Julia Goddard, who was appointed two years ago, has overseen a multimillion-pound refurbishment of the Knightsbridge flagship, including the installation of a new wellness destination on the fourth floor that combines fitness, beauty treatments, nutrition and athleisure retail in May. At the time of opening, in May, Lucy McPhail, Beauty Director at Harvey Nichols, said: "The launch of the new fourth floor marks an important step in the continued evolution of our Knightsbridge flagship." Goddard has also led investment into the retailer's digital operations, with internal key performance indicators said to be "moving in the right direction" following the initiatives. Meanwhile, the retailer recently strengthened its senior leadership team with the appointment of Shaun Donnelly to Buying Director for Non Apparel & Menswear. Investment has also gone into digital operations, with internal KPIs said to be "moving in the right direction," according to Sky News. Sir Dickson Poon's Dickson Concepts International bought Harvey Nichols from Burton Group in 1991 for £53 million. The company listed on the London Stock Exchange in 1996 before being taken private again six years later. Sir Dickson is no longer actively involved in running the group, having stepped down from the Harvey Nichols board and his other European directorships. In June last year, TheIndustry.fashion took an in-depth look at Harvey Nichols' transformation plans, featuring exclusive commentary on the challenges it faces and expert insights into how it might successfully navigate its transformation. In addition to NEXT, likely buyers are expected to include wealthy individuals from Asia and the Middle East, sources told Sky News. It has also been reported that Frasers Group had been in discussions to buy Harvey Nichols' regional stores but is not currently thought to be part of the corporate sale process. The business is expected to change hands in the coming months.

article_title: Dior closes couture show with a bridal gown days after Taylor Swift’s wedding dress
sub_title: Days after Taylor Swift married Travis Kelce in a bespoke Dior haute couture wedding gown by Jonathan Anderson, the designer closed his latest couture show with an ethereal bridal look.
article_content: Days after Taylor Swift married Travis Kelce in a bespoke Dior haute couture wedding gown by Jonathan Anderson, the designer closed his latest couture show with an ethereal bridal look. Swift and her husband both wore Dior for their wedding ceremony at New York’s Madison Square Garden on Friday, with the French fashion house confirming Anderson designed both looks “in close collaboration” with the newlyweds. Created in Dior’s ateliers at 30 Avenue Montaigne in Paris, the commission marked Anderson’s first haute couture bridal gown for a major celebrity. Swift completed the look with bespoke Christian Louboutin shoes and Cartier jewellery. The strapless Dior haute couture bridal gown from the back (Emma Da Silva/PA) While the wedding gown itself has yet to be publicly revealed, Anderson ended Dior’s autumn/winter 2026/27 haute couture show with a romantic bridal finale – a strapless ivory gown embroidered with delicate floral textures, softly frayed detailing and a sweeping train – which was perhaps a nod to the design Swift wore on her big day. Northern Irish designer Anderson entered a new era at Dior in 2025 when he became the first creative director since Christian Dior himself to oversee the label’s menswear, womenswear and haute couture collections. For his second couture outing, Anderson looked to American sculptor Lynda Benglis, whose expressive, free-flowing works informed a collection centred on movement rather than rigid structure. Free-flowing forms with muscular structure permeated the collection through pleating (Emma Da Silva/AP) “What I love about Lynda is that there is something which has got this spontaneous joy, but at the same time it is muscular,” Anderson said before the show. “She is not scared of an idea. “I find her deeply inspiring and someone who challenges my viewpoint on how I see the form in my own work.” Metallics and pleats with slouchy forms dominated the runway (Emma Da Silva/AP) That philosophy translated into clothes that appeared to shift and transform with every step. Dior even streamed the runway in slow motion, allowing viewers to fully appreciate the way fabrics rippled, folded and caught the light. Pleating came to the surface as a defining trend. Long V-neck gowns in liquid silks skimmed the body in slinky, relaxed ease, while accordion pleats, concertina folds and tucks created silhouettes that seemed to expand and contract in motion. Metallic fabrics shimmered throughout the collection in bronze, silver and rose gold, their iridescent finishes amplifying every fold. Anderson also revisited one of his favourite colours, frog green, using the vivid yellow-toned shade across sculptural dresses, jackets and accessories. Frog green appeared once again at this Dior collection (Emma Da Silva/AP) The collection balanced these modern techniques with unmistakable Dior signatures. Peplums and cascading ruffles nodded to Christian Dior’s revolutionary 1947 New Look, while the house’s iconic bow appeared oversized across shoulders, cinching waists or decorating the front of plunging gowns. Dior’s signature peplums and bows flooded the runway (Emma Da Silva/AP) Fans became wearable sculptures, attached across bodices before opening dramatically across the torso, while feather trims followed the sweeping lines of bias-cut dresses. Applique fans were incorporated to dresses (Emma Da Silva/AP) Classic tweeds and checks grounded the collection, from oversized fringed capes to richly textured tailoring, contrasting with the softer fluidity elsewhere. Flowers remained central to Anderson’s vision for the house. Waterlilies appeared as embroidered embellishments on dresses, jewelled handbags and even shoes, while colourful floral appliques bloomed across powder blue skirt suits and textured jackets. Tasselled necklaces, bracelets and oversized earrings brought bursts of colour to otherwise restrained palettes. Florals adorned shoes, dresses, bags and more (Emma Da Silva/AP) Some garments deliberately retained loose threads and raw-edged finishes, lending couture an unexpected sense of spontaneity and craft, while emerald, royal purple and gold pieces hinted at Eighties opulence, without slipping too far into nostalgia. At times, an Eighties colour palette was employed (AP Photo/Emma Da Silva) Among those watching from the front row was singer Sabrina Carpenter, wearing a sheer white draped midi dress adorned with floral applique. Actor Priyanka Chopra attended in a vibrant turmeric-yellow petal gown alongside husband Nick Jonas, while Dior ambassador Josh O’Connor paused photographers’ calls to find his parents in the crowd before posing with them. The actor wore a checked sheer shirt and matching trousers from Dior’s 2027 menswear collection, finished with a loosely tied sequinned black-and-white cravat. Even without any published photos, Taylor Swift's wedding to Travis Kelce generated an estimated $26.7 million (~ £20 million) in media impact value in the 48 hours following the wedding night, according to a new report from Launchmetrics. Launchmetrics asses the MIV, a monetary value calculated from social media, online posts, interactions and articles. The biggest winner of the night was Dior, whose MIV was calculated at $15 million (~ £11 million), while Cartier generated an estimated $5.9 million (~ £4 million), and Christian Louboutin an estimated $5.8 million (~ £4 million). Launchmetrics estimates that the value will increase again once photos of the actual garments, jewellery and shoes are published.

Chanel goes all-in on florals for its latest couture show
sub_title: Florals for spring might not be groundbreaking, but what about florals for autumn?
article_content: Florals for spring might not be groundbreaking, but what about florals for autumn? That’s exactly what Chanel channelled for its autumn/winter 2026-27 haute couture show in Paris. The setting was a fairytale brought to life (Emma Da Silva/AP) It marked creative director Matthieu Blazy’s second couture collection with the storied French label, and he put the natural world front and centre – a stark contrast to Schiaparelli’s futuristic fashion show the day before. Back in January, the setting of Blazy’s first couture outing was a woodland fantasy, complete with giant pink toadstools and matching trees. He continued the theme for his second collection, leaning more into florals and a fairytale vibe. A post shared by CHANEL (@chanelofficial) A promotional clip posted on Instagram showed a cartoon girl in a classic French townhouse, surrounded by vines, leaves and flowers growing around her – eventually forming Chanel’s iconic interlocking ‘C’ logo in front of the Eiffel Tower. Chanel brought this vision to life for the show, with models walking amongst large scale twisting vines studded with giant flowers and even chairs, with whimsical clothes to match. The front row was typically star-studded, with the likes of actors Tilda Swinton and Elizabeth Debicki watching the reveal of the new collection. The show’s magical vine and flower-decorated theme (Emma Da Silva/AP) While there was plenty of the heritage brand’s DNA on the runway – such as tweed two-pieces with skirts and boxy jackets, and two-tone slingback heels – Blazy continues to inject his own aesthetic into the clothes. The floral setting was reflected in the clothes, but often in unexpected ways. A model wore a silvery beaded jacket with purple, yellow and red embroidered flowers, and blue flower-shaped buttons that continued around the neckline. This colour scheme was continued into an unusual spiky feathered headpiece that gave the traditional jacket a modern edge. Spiky feathered accents permeated the collection (Emma Da Silva/AP) These pointy feathered details continued throughout the collection, and have become a signature of Blazy’s time at Chanel. One model had two multi-coloured feathered pieces attached to the back of her red dress at the top and bottom, while another wore a gold version as a hat. Elsewhere, Blazy made a case for slouchy midi dresses often with a dropped waist, giving a modern spin to flapper-inspired designs. Flapper-inspired designs and floaty fabrics added to the collection’s whimsy (Emma Da Silva/AP) Colour choices were somewhat muted – there were a lot of pastels in floaty fabrics – but still unexpected, such as a lilac shift dress detailed with 3D red, white and black florals. It wasn’t all about feminine designs on the Chanel catwalk, with some models showcasing more of an edge. Blazy continues to experiment with masculine tailoring – for example, one model wearing a dark grey coat with black fern-like detailing and structured shoulders, paired with matching slouchy trousers. Blazy also experimented with more masculine tailoring (Emma Da Silva/AP) There were some red carpet-worthy dresses in there, too – like a bedazzled midi dress with an asymmetric neckline, covered in gold and silver beading and buttons. Gold and silver tones were an unexpected element on the runway (Emma Da Silva/AP) While this haute couture week looks ahead to the upcoming autumn/winter season, celebrities don’t necessarily have to wait to get their hands on the clothes. Hours after Schiaparelli’s couture show on Monday, actor Zendaya wore one of the brand’s sculpted bodice gowns to attend The Odyssey premiere in London. So who knows, maybe we’ll see stars wearing Blazy’s latest creations sooner than you might think. Zendaya wore a Schiaparelli haute couture creation straight from the runway on Monday night (Ian West/PA) While Dior has been in headlines this week for designing singer Taylor Swift’s wedding dress, Chanel has already made waves for creating fellow popstar Dua Lipa’s bridal gown for her June wedding. Lipa’s gown was a halterneck style with intricate beading and a feather-studded train, marking the first haute couture wedding dress designed by Blazy for a friend of the house. Chanel typically finishes its couture collection with a bridal look (Emma Da Silva/AP) As always, Chanel ended its haute couture show with a bridal look – but it was a much more traditional lace creation compared to Lipa’s outfit. The bride wore a full layered lace skirt that grazed her ankles, paired with a sheer jacket that revealed a bra underneath, topped off with a veil.
