Off-White launches L/AB diffusion line with more accessible price points
sub_title: Off-White has launched a new lower-priced diffusion line with prices running from about $45 to $220 (£34 - £166), called L/AB c/o Off-White.
article_content: Off-White has launched a new lower-priced diffusion line called L/AB c/o Off-White, aimed at younger consumers, with prices ranging from about $45 to $220 (£34-£166). In comparison, the core Off-White range runs from $175 to $4,000 (£132-£3,025). The line will be sold globally online, through select streetwear specialty stores, and through mainstream wholesale accounts, with Off-White planning two seasonal collections per year, in spring and fall, plus additional drops targeted at specific markets. The assortment is built around sportswear staples, including fleece, T-shirts, hoodies, tracksuits, sneakers, underwear and some outerwear. On its website, Off-White says: "Through customisable everyday essentials, collaborative experiences, and ongoing creative exchange, it empowers a new generation to participate in culture, rather than simply consume it. "Conceived as a purposeful work in progress, L/AB c/o Off-White encourages experimentation, collective creativity, and the continual recoding of culture." Cristiano Fagnani, Off-White's CEO, told WWD that the line's target audience are Gen Z and that it is designed as "a toolkit" and "a wardrobe you can build on and keep mixing and matching over time." "Off-White has always been built as an open platform that aims to make itself available in terms of product to the widest possible range of consumers and communities," he added. While North America will be the primary market, distribution will also span Europe, Asia and other markets. L/AB, which Off-White says stands for "Laboratory of Fun", is positioned around sport, music and fashion, with a focus on community sports, open street tournaments and campus collection drops. Off-White's own site frames the project as a brand "for the next generation of creatives, cultural catalysts and emerging talent". The diffusion line follows an earlier lower-priced Off-White project. I n 2018, the brand introduced Off-White For All, which offered accessibly priced unisex hoodies and graphic T-shirts aimed at Millennials. That project has since been retired. Fagnani framed L/AB as a more developed effort. "In a way, we've been warming up for this for the past 10 years by doing a lot of smaller things, but now we're conveying this through a more robust expression of the brand," he said. The CEO of Off-White's owner, Bluestar Alliance, Joey Gabbay, commented that L/AB "represents an important evolution within the Off-White universe, expanding how new generations can engage with the brand through product, experiences, and creative participation."

article_title: Christopher Kane to lead Mulberry's London Fashion Week comeback
sub_title: The British luxury brand will show its first ready-to-wear collection under creative director Christopher Kane on Sept. 20, with product due in stores in January 2027.
article_content: Mulberry’s six-year runway absence will come to an end in September, when it stages its first womenswear collection by Christopher Kane on the London Fashion Week schedule, marking a strategic push back into ready-to-wear under CEO Andrea Baldo. Scheduled for 20 September, the show will be titled "Mulberry by Christopher Kane", with the collection set to arrive in stores and online in January 2027. Kane was appointed Creative Director of women's ready-to-wear in March , with the runway debut now giving the appointment its first public outing on the fashion calendar. Kane, a Central Saint Martins graduate, brings four British Fashion Awards to the role, including Womenswear Designer of the Year. His eponymous label held a regular London Fashion Week slot before closing in 2023. His brand sat within Kering between 2013 and 2018. "It is an honour to return to London Fashion Week with Mulberry, I am so grateful to the BFC and fashion community for their support since the announcement. It’s an exciting time and I look forward to sharing SS27 with everyone," said Kane. The show sits within Baldo's "Back to the Mulberry Spirit" strategy, which focuses on rebuilding momentum in categories beyond Mulberry's accessories core. The brand ended its clothing and footwear licence with Onward Luxury Group in 2020 during pandemic-era cost-cutting. The last ready-to-wear range, created by former creative director Johnny Coca, was for autumn/winter 2020. "London has long been a global platform for creativity and culture, making it the ideal stage to debut the Mulberry by Christopher Kane collection," Baldo said. He added that the show underlines Mulberry's "absolute commitment in supporting and championing British talents, creativity and craftsmanship". Baldo, who came from Ganni in 2024, already has early commercial results to point to behind the creative reset. Under his leadership, Mulberry recorded a 5.7% increase in total sales in the 52 weeks to 28 March 2026. In the second half, the brand recorded growth in all of its markets, with the UK seeing a 13.7% boost in like-for-Like sales. BFC boss Laura Weir has framed Mulberry's return as part of a broader effort to bring established houses back to the London schedule. "One of my earliest ambitions as CEO of the British Fashion Council has been to have iconic British brands return to the London Fashion Week schedule, so it is a real pleasure to welcome Mulberry back," she said. "As one of Britain's most iconic luxury houses, its return strengthens London Fashion Week creatively, culturally and commercially. This marks an exciting new chapter for the brand under Christopher Kane's creative leadership and an important moment for British fashion." Mulberry follows Alexander McQueen , which is also set to show in London for spring 2027 after years on the Paris calendar. Both returns point to renewed confidence in the city's position within the global fashion week circuit.

article_title: JD Sports pulls Hip off high street as brand moves online only
sub_title: JD Sports Fashion is removing its Hip brand from the high street after closing the last two physical stores this week, although the retailer will continue to trade the label exclusively online.
article_content: JD Sports Fashion is removing its Hip brand from the high street after closing the last two physical stores this week, although the retailer will continue to trade the label exclusively online. The Manchester branch of The Hip store has already shut, while the Leeds store is reportedly due to close before the end of the month. The Leeds site is said to be taken over by Size?, another retailer within the JD Sports group. JD Sports took over Hip in 2014 after the brand had spent a year seeking investment, though the value of the deal was never disclosed. Hip had first started in Leeds in 1987 as an independent menswear store, broadening into womenswear in 2022, and now sells premium streetwear and sportswear labels including Carhartt, Salomon and Stone Island. For Hip, moving to online-only brings nearly four decades of physical retail to a close. The closures are part of a reduction in JD Sports' UK physical retail footprint. The group reduced its UK store estate by 24 locations (on a net basis) earlier in 2026 as it set out a strategy centred on "fewer, bigger and better" shops, with investment focused on higher-productivity locations. As part of this strategy, JD Sports opened its Trafford Centre flagship in Manchester, which is now the retailer's largest store globally and showcases its investment in a "small number of destination stores to anchor regional presence and elevate brand expression". In its latest financial filings, JD Sports reported a 2.5% increase in organic sales at constant currency rates to £12.66 billion , driven by growth in all regions except for the UK, where organic sales declined by 2.5%. The retailer's profit before tax and adjusting items (PBTAI) was down 7.7% to £852 million, compared to £923 million in 2025. Unlike EBITDA, the PBTAI measurement disregards items such as acquisition-related charges, restructuring costs and integration expenses to reflect a more organic view of earnings. JD Sports commented on the results saying that geopolitical tensions, including in the Middle East, had created "heightened uncertainty" that could feed through to higher energy and fuel costs across its store and logistics networks, as well as indirect pressure on pricing and consumer demand. Commenting on the financial results, CEO Régis Schultz noted that he remained confident in the group's medium ‑ term trajectory. He further highlighted the retailer's focus on "further enhancing and optimising our product offer, customer experience and store footprint, and delivering strong cost and cash discipline - in essence, 'controlling the controllables'."

article_title: Harvey Nichols owner explores sale after 35 years
sub_title: Harvey Nichols is reportedly up for sale after 35 years under the ownership of Hong Kong billionaire Sir Dickson Poon.
article_content: Harvey Nichols is reportedly up for sale after 35 years under the ownership of Hong Kong billionaire Sir Dickson Poon. Sky News reported that the London-headquartered luxury department store group has appointed financial advisers, including FTI Consulting, to evaluate strategic options for the loss-making business. Options under review are said to include bringing in investment partners, as well as an outright sale. Talks are already underway with prospective buyers and investors from around the world, according to sources cited in the report. Prospective buyers are likely to include wealthy individuals from Asia and the Middle East, according to Sky News, with Harvey Nichols expected to change hands in the coming months. In its most recent financial accounts, Harvey Nichols posted revenue of £204.8 million in the 12 months to 31 March 2024, a 5% decline year-on-year. Pre-tax losses rose to £34 million, marking a fifth consecutive year of losses. The business employs about 1,200 people in the UK, operating seven stores across the UK and Ireland, including five large-format locations in London, Edinburgh, Birmingham, Leeds and Manchester, alongside two smaller-format stores in Bristol and Dublin. Internationally, it has six large-format stores situated in Riyadh, Doha, Dubai, Hong Kong (two stores) and Kuwait. Harvey Nichols' London flagship, based in Knightsbridge, has been undergoing a multimillion-pound refurbishment under the oversight of CEO Julia Goddard, who was appointed two years ago. This includes the recent unveiling of a new wellness destination, which brings together fitness, beauty treatments, nutrition and athleisure retail in a single space. Located on the fourth floor, the new space features a Pilates studio, overlooking the rooftops of Knightsbridge. At the time of opening, in May, Lucy McPhail, Beauty Director at Harvey Nichols, said: "The launch of the new fourth floor marks an important step in the continued evolution of our Knightsbridge flagship." Goddard has also led investment into the retailer's digital operations, with internal key performance indicators said to be "moving in the right direction" following the initiatives, according to Sky News. Meanwhile, the retailer recently strengthened its senior leadership team with the appointment of Shaun Donnelly to Buying Director for Non Apparel & Menswear. Sir Dickson's Dickson Concepts International acquired Harvey Nichols from Burton Group in 1991 in a £53 million deal. The company floated on the London Stock Exchange in 1996 but was taken private again by Sir Dickson just six years later. The business traces its roots to 1831, when Anne Harvey went into partnership with Ben Nichols. Sir Dickson is no longer actively involved in running the group, having stepped down from the Harvey Nichols board and his other European directorships. In June last year, TheIndustry.fashion took an in-depth look at Harvey Nichols' transformation plans, featuring exclusive commentary on the challenges it faces and expert insights into how it might successfully navigate its transformation.

article_title: Accent Group rejects Frasers Group's 'opportunistic and inadequate' takeover bid
sub_title: Accent Group, the Australian footwear and lifestyle retail group, has shared in an initial response that it rejects Frasers Group's "unsolicited, highly opportunistic" takeover bid from 15 June.
article_content: Accent Group, the Australian footwear and lifestyle retail group, in an initial response, has rejected Frasers Group's "unsolicited, highly opportunistic" takeover bid from 15 June. Following Frasers' initial bid of A$0.65 cash per share for stock that the company does not already own, Accent Group formed an Independent Board Committee, which unanimously recommended that shareholders take no action and not sell into the bid. The bid values the target shares at A$390.8 million (around £206 million). Accent's committee excluded Frasers nominee director Dave Forsey due to a conflict of interest. This follows an initial announcement form 15 June, in which the Victoria-based Accent Group said its board was weighing up the offer. The committee cited several reasons for rejecting Frasers Group's offer, starting with the argument that the offer price was  "materially inadequate". At A$0.65, the bid matched Accent's last closing price before it was announced on 15 June. However, by 26 June, the last practicable date before the target's statement, Accent shares had traded up to a close of A$0.71. Accent also highlighted Frasers' earlier purchases. Via a subscription agreement in May 2025, Frasers paid A$1.718 per share. Its on-market buying in February 2026 averaged more than A$0.92 per share. The committee said Frasers was now asking other shareholders to sell at a price well below what it had itself paid. The committee also said Frasers was trying to gain more influence over Accent without paying a control premium. In its bidder's statement, Frasers said it "does not expect to achieve more than 90% and in such a case is comfortable with a shareholding of less than 90% if it achieves representation on the Accent Board proportionate to its ownership and is able to effect the changes it considers necessary". Accent said Frasers' immediate goal was to increase its voting power to at least 26%, a level that would, under the subscription agreement, allow it to ask for an additional nominee director. The committee argued that Frasers, already the largest shareholder with a stake of nearly 23%, was seeking to boost its exposure to Accent's Sports Direct ANZ business, which the committee described as a key strategic asset and core value driver. Accent said that, as the global operator of the Sports Direct brand, Frasers is uniquely placed to understand the medium-term earnings potential of the Australian operation. Accent said the bid was "highly opportunistic" and came at a time of cyclical weakness in discretionary retail that had pushed share prices lower across the sector over the past 12 months. The offer, the committee said, overlooked the upside from initiatives in its 2030 Strategic Growth Plan, announced on 13 May 2026, which targets at least A$1.9 billion in sales, a 9% EBIT margin and approximately 950 stores by 2030. The company has identified roughly A$40 million of gross cost savings through FY28 and plans up to 20 new store openings a year. The offer period is scheduled to run from 30 June to 30 July unless extended or withdrawn. For now, it is unclear if Frasers Group will follow-up with a new offer. Frasers Group's takeover offer for Accent Group followed shortly after its bid for a majority stake in German luxury fashion brand Hugo Boss , valued at €1,925.4 million (£1,683.0 million). Last week, Frasers confirmed in an official statement that its €38-per-share offer for the Hugo Boss shares it does not yet own was final , highlighting that it would "not increase the Offer Price" during the acceptance period.

article_title: Zalando accounts come under German watchdog review over About You deal
sub_title: Germany's financial watchdog BaFin has opened a review of Zalando's 2025 consolidated financial statements and management report, citing "concrete indications" that the online fashion retailer may have breached accounting rules connected to its acquisition of About You.
article_content: Germany's financial watchdog BaFin has opened a review of Zalando's 2025 consolidated financial statements and management report, citing "concrete indications" that the online fashion retailer may have breached accounting rules connected to its acquisition of About You. BaFin said it would publish the outcome regardless of whether it identifies an accounting error. The review is focused on whether Zalando gave proper disclosure in the notes to its annual accounts for a deal involving a related party, while the underlying transaction is not in question. According to Reuters, the issue concerns the omission of the fact that Danish billionaire Anders Holch Povlsen, Zalando's biggest shareholder, also held a stake in About You at the time of the acquisition. Zalando said it had received notice of the review and was in "close and constructive dialogue" with BaFin, adding that the review had no impact on its financial KPIs or performance. In an official statement, the company described the matter as a "formal and materially insignificant aspect of the notes to the financial statements". It added: "All relevant information regarding the acquisition of the About You shares, including the companies involved, the transaction structure, and the purchase price, was already publicly accessible as part of the public tender offer." Zalando shares fell about 7% on 26 June after the review became public, erasing most of the stock's gains for the year. In its first-quarter results published in May, Zalando noted that its integration of About You had already contributed positively to the group's revenue and profit. Group revenue grew by 23.8% on a reported basis, reaching €3 billion, while adjusted EBIT rose 38.7% to €65 million. The company noted that its adjusted EBIT margin had improved from 1.9% to 2.2%, supported in part by €10 million in synergies from the About You acquisition, before integration costs. Within the B2C segment, Zalando further highlighted that the About You consumer-facing app had delivered double-digit growth. Robert Gentz, Co-CEO of Zalando, commented on the results, saying that he was "very satisfied with the progress in ... integrating About You." Zalando and About You first announced their intention to combine in December 2024. In July 2025, Zalando acquired about 91% of About You's share capital through a voluntary takeover offer and additional share purchases in a deal valued at about €1.13 billion. The final legal step was completed in November 2025, with the remaining minority shareholders' stakes in About You transferred to a Zalando subsidiary at €6.50 per share.

article_title: Editors' Top Reads: News from Derek Rose, Uniqlo and more...
sub_title: Here are some of this week’s news and features highlights handpicked by TheIndustry.fashion team.
article_content: Here are some of this week’s news and features highlights handpicked by TheIndustry.fashion team. British sleep and leisurewear brand Derek Rose celebrates a centenary in the fashion business this year and this deserves due recognition. So few brands make it beyond a decade, let alone a century. And not many remain in private ownership either. Derek Rose, now run by CEO Sacha Rose, offers many lessons in longevity for us all in this in-depth interview with our esteemed contributor Eric Musgrave . A deep understanding of your customer and what they do in your clothes is vital. Often brands focus on quality, which is clearly no bad thing, but the team at Derek Rose always consider what a wearer might be doing while wearing their clothes, and how they would want them to feel while doing it. This mindset informs all the details in the garments and it's smart. It started with Sacha's father, the late Derek Rose, recognising that having horizontal button holes on pyjamas allows the garment a bit of movement while wearers wriggle around in their sleep, and now extends to Sacha Rose adding pockets on trousers for AirPods, as he was always losing his. Also of huge importance is considered expansion. Just because your brand doesn't have a certain category in its line-up, doesn't mean that it should. That said, Derek Rose has just ventured into denim, but in a very limited way. Derek Rose denim is the jeans equivalent of a soft white t-shirt. Nothing in the wardrobe is cheap, but it's likely to become a firm favourite with the wearer and that's the aim. Another key takeaway is that sometimes you have to scale something back to grow it again. Sacha Rose took the tough decision to cut back its manufacturing base in Congleton a few years ago; it was a move that was necessary to save the brand as a whole. Now it has built it back up again to 50 people who work on sampling, product development, personalisation, and the manufacturing of silk and woven cashmere garments. Had it persisted with full garment manufacturing in the UK, the brand may not be here now. And we're very glad it is. Lauretta Roberts, Co-founder, CEO and Editor-in-Chief. Uniqlo's new scalable upcycling initiative is truly exciting . The key here is that the new collection is not a one-off trial or pilot programme. It was designed with scalability in mind, while retaining creativity and the central ethos of the Uniqlo brand - quality and accessibility. Called Everyday Re.Imagined, the new collection was created in collaboration with graduates from the BA Fashion course at Central Saint Martins, who created the blueprint designs for each of the upcycled design pieces. The core idea is to take the most returned types of items, including some that may be damaged, and give them to expert seamstresses working across the brand's 15 Re.Uniqlo Studios in the UK and Europe to re-imagine them. While each piece will retain its unique character - no two designs will be exactly the same - the general pattern of the garment will be the same. Most importantly, each item is designed to be crafted in-store in less than an hour. For me this is one of the first, and really exciting, milestones that shows how circular design can be applied in real-life. Price points remain accessible (prices range from £29.90 to £89.90), because Uniqlo is building and optimising on its existing infrastructure. While for now limited pieces will be available in 15 locations, technically the initiative could be expanded into the 70 stores that already have a Re.Uniqlo Studio - in 23 markets. Speaking at an event on Tuesday, Uniqlo Europe's Head of Sustainability, Maria Samoto le Dous, noted that the upcycled collection forms part of Uniqlo's long-term sustainability strategy and that the brand has plans to scale the project, potentially evolving designs seasonally. I am really, really excited about this project and can't wait to see how it will develop and what kind of impact it will have. Camilla Rydzek, Senior News & Features Writer. I love a good data story, so this new research from American Express caught my attention this week . The study finds that social media is driving an estimated 1.7 billion visits to UK high streets every year - the equivalent of ov 30 million visits a week. In fact, 63% of UK adults have visited a shop, restaurant or other hospitality venue in the past year after being influenced by content they saw on social media. Among Gen Z consumers aged 18-8, that figure rises to 88%! As someone within this group, I can definitely relate - I’m constantly saving social media recommendations and building a list of cute high streets and hidden gems to check out. The positive news for retailers is that this influence doesn’t stop at a single visit. More than four in five people (82%) return to a business after a socially influenced first experience, rising to an impressive 96% among Gen Z. Even more importantly, these visitors often become advocates. Nearly four-fifths (79%) say they go on to share their experience - whether by recommending the business to friends, posting on social media or leaving an online review. As American Express puts it: "For merchants, particularly those looking to attract younger consumers, the ability to turn online hype into memorable in-person experiences has never been more important." Sophie Smith, News Editor & Senior Writer.

article_title: Paul Costelloe branches out into socks and bed linen with new license partners
sub_title: Paul Costelloe has expanded its product offer with licensing partners for socks and bed linen, marking the evolution of the brand under the direction of William Costelloe, son of the brand’s late eponymous founder.
article_content: Paul Costelloe has expanded its product offer with licensing partners for socks and bed linen, marking the evolution of the brand under the direction of William Costelloe, son of the brand’s late eponymous founder. The new bedding collection, in partnership with Ferguson’s Irish Linen, has just launched, while the luxury socks collection for men and women, in partnership with Bullit Design UK, is launching for AW26. The socks launch builds on a long-standing relationship, as Bullit Design UK has worked closely with the brand for many seasons, developing hosiery and socks for the Paul Costelloe couture collections showcased at London Fashion Week each season. The new standalone collection is a natural extension of that successful partnership, bringing Paul Costelloe's signature blend of quality, craftsmanship, and timeless style to a dedicated retail offering across two distinct ranges: ‘City’ and ‘Weekend’. Every sock features hand-linked toe seams for a smoother finish and enhanced comfort. Commenting on the launch, William Costelloe said: “By combining premium yarns, thoughtful design, and exceptional comfort, we've created a collection that offers strong appeal across both gifting and core retail categories. “We look forward to introducing the range to customers and retail partners at Harrogate (the trade fair at Harrogate Convention Centre from 19-22 July 2026) this summer.” Ferguson’s Irish Linen was established in 1854 and is widely recognised as being among the finest Irish weavers, making it the perfect fit for the new Paul Costelloe linen collection of bedding, which is entirely woven to order. The late designer, who founded his eponymous label in Dublin in 1979 with luxury womenswear, was a lifelong champion of Irish linen on the international stage, utilising the natural fabric in his fashion collections throughout his entire career. William Costelloe commented: “This collection is incredibly personal to us. Linen was always something my father felt deeply passionate about from the very beginning of his career. He understood its beauty, its integrity, and its connection to Irish craftsmanship long before sustainability became part of the wider conversation.” Paul Costelloe sadly passed away at the age of 80 in November 2025, with his son William then tasked with taking the leadership reins, signalling a fresh chapter in the brand’s storied legacy. William Costelloe added: “Though my father is greatly missed, his creative spirit and love for timeless design continue to inspire everything we do.” Read TheIndustry.fashion's interview with William Costelloe ahead of his London Fashion Week debut here: William Costelloe on honouring his father’s legacy and shaping the future of Paul Costelloe.

article_title: Nadine Merabi launches first denim capsule as daywear push continues
sub_title: Nadine Merabi, which has built its reputation in occasionwear and partywear since launching in 2015, has released its first denim collection.
article_content: Luxury ready-to-wear brand Nadine Merabi, which has built its reputation in occasionwear and partywear since launching in 2015, has released its first denim capsule collection. The four-piece range, priced from £245, follows the brand's first move into daywear earlier this year and extends its push beyond event dressing into everyday wear. The capsule is made from dark indigo stretch denim and comprises the Jordan Denim Top, Kendra Dark Denim Trousers, Harley Denim Jumpsuit and Jenna Denim Midi Dress. Each piece carries design codes from the brand's core line, including sculpted fits, flared-leg silhouettes, gold hardware buttons and contrast stitch detailing. The jumpsuit features a corset-style bodice engineered to cinch the waist, while the midi dress includes structured padded cups and a thigh-high split. The brand said the range was designed around its signature silhouettes, reimagined in denim for day-to-night versatility. Nadine Merabi, founder and creative director, said: "We wanted to bring the confidence and glamour of MERABI into a fabrication that women can wear every day. By reimagining some of our most iconic silhouettes in dark indigo denim, we've created pieces that feel elevated, versatile and effortlessly chic from day to night." The denim launch lands a few months after the brand made two senior advisory appointments to support its next stage of growth. In March 2026, Nadine Merabi appointed former ASOS and Matches CEO Nick Beighton and former Jigsaw, Oasis & Warehouse CEO Hash Ladha as strategic advisers , with a remit to support growth in the UK, US and European markets. Those appointments coincided with the brand's 10th anniversary. The company has also been building out its physical retail presence. It trialled pop-ups in London, New York and Manchester before opening its first permanent site on South Molton Street in London in 2024. Denim represents a category shift for a label that made its name with embellished, occasion-focused pieces. By translating its fitted silhouettes and finishing details into a fabric associated with casual wear, the brand is positioning itself for more frequent purchase occasions and a wider share of its customer's wardrobe. The move from occasionwear specialist to a broader ready-to-wear proposition aligns with the international growth agenda set out by its new advisory team earlier this year.

article_title: Lacoste celebrates tennis star Novak Djokovic's GOAT status with new collection
sub_title: Lacoste has launched its second GOAT capsule collection in tribute to ambassador and tennis player Novak Djokovic, swapping its iconic crocodile logo for a goat.
article_content: Lacoste has launched its second GOAT capsule collection in tribute to ambassador and tennis player Novak Djokovic, swapping its iconic crocodile logo for a goat. With the collaboration, the French sportswear brand celebrates Djokovic's status as a GOAT - 'Greatest Of All Time' - a title worthy of the tennis stars' talents. In a career spanning close to two decades, he has won 101 Association of Tennis Professionals -sanctioned titles, including 24 Grand Slam wins and 40 Masters 1000 crowns. "Few athletes leave a lasting mark on the history of their sport. Novak is one of them," said Éric Vallat, CEO of Lacoste. The new capsule features 11 pieces including polo shirts, T-shirts, a tracksuit jacket, trousers, a sweater, a cap, wristbands and socks - all carrying the exclusive GOAT logo in place of Lacoste's crocodile. The hero product is a polo shirt featuring a gold GOAT emblem, restricted to 100 units and sold exclusively at the brand's Regent Street store. A second version in Lacoste's signature green will be offered more broadly worldwide. Djokovic will unveil the collection at the Regent Street flagship, as London is significant in Djokovic's career, just in time for the city's tennis season starting. Vallat added: "With this GOAT collection, we wanted to celebrate an extraordinary champion whose excellence, longevity and determination have shaped the history of tennis. By exceptionally transforming our iconic crocodile into a goat, we pay tribute to the GOAT with creativity and a touch of humour." The accompanying campaign was directed and photographed by director Max Siedentopf, who has worked with the likes of Gucci, Adidas, Nike and Balenciaga, with a series of humorous short films showing Djokovic appear alongside a group of goats. The GOAT capsule is the second of its kind for Lacoste, following the first edition, which launched in August last year and also featured Djokovic. The capsule lands during a busy period of tennis-led activity for the brand. Earlier this week, Lacoste unveiled Club Lacoste at Selfridges London , a pop-up tennis clubhouse open until 12 July that has already toured New York, Melbourne, Miami and Roland-Garros. The new campaign also follows Lacoste's refreshed visual identity, which it unveiled in April, and made its crocodile more prominent and brought back serif characters drawn from its archives. The updated visual identity was first showcased in the second edition of the brand's 'Life is a Beautiful Sport' campaign , which also featured Djokovic in a short film.

article_title: TOAST reveals 99% of clothing range now made from natural fibres
sub_title: TOAST, the British fashion and lifestyle brand founded in Wales in 1997, has released its 2025 Social Conscience Report, showing that 99% of its clothing products now come from natural fibres, while over 7,500 garments were given a second life.
article_content: TOAST, the British fashion and lifestyle brand founded in Wales in 1997, has released its 2025 Social Conscience Report, showing that 99% of its clothing products now come from natural fibres, while over 7,500 garments were given a second life. The annual report, structured around three pillars: Cherish Materials & Make, Minimise Waste, and Enrich & Educate, sets out the brand's progress on sourcing, circularity, supply chain visibility and community programming. Suzie de Rohan Willner, CEO at TOAST, commented that the brand's accomplishments were the result of "years of investment, collaboration and the dedication of exceptional teams across our business, all working towards meaningful progress". Suzie de Rohan Willner will be speaking at TheIndustry.fashion's annual Fashion Summit on 15 October 2026 . In the report, the brand highlighted that it now uses 99% natural and cellulosic fibres, up from 92% the previous year. It has also increased its use of certified organic cotton from 39% to 52%, with plans to further increase this number over the coming years. TOAST also completed a two-year direct-to-farm cotton pilot, which focused on sourcing cotton through direct relationships with farmers rather than relying on third-party certifications. The pilot was looking to trial a new approach to transparency; however, the supply chain, which spanned multiple regions, proved too complex, with the relatively small production volumes per fabric making the process inefficient and hard to scale. TOAST said, however, that the project was a learning experience. The brand also established new sourcing partnerships across the UK and Europe, with 51% of its annual production spend now supporting European manufacturers. The brand's circular programme, TOAST Circle, has also seen success, giving 7,559 garments a second life through its repair, exchange, renew and reworn initiatives. Using WRAP's displacement methodology, the brand calculated that its repair service and reworn collection prevented 4,849 new purchases in 2025. Donations from customers rose 29% year-on-year, with 67% of donated items graded, sorted and sold via Reworn, and the remainder donated to charity partner Traid. For the first time, TOAST also completed a full Scope 1, 2 and 3 greenhouse gas emissions assessment, measuring its direct, indirect and value-chain greenhouse gas emissions. The brand noted that it expected its Scope 3 emissions to account for the largest share of its overall carbon footprint, and that in 2026 it would begin to explore how to reduce its Scope 3 emissions and build a future roadmap to meet reduction targets. "Looking ahead, we remain committed to learning, improving, and sharing openly. By continuing to educate ourselves, collaborate with our community and industry, and plan for future generations, we hope to contribute to positive change that reaches beyond our own business," de Rohan Willner commented in the report. Suzie de Rohan Willner, CEO of TOAST, will be speaking at TheIndustry.fashion's annual Fashion Summit on 15 October 2026 .

article_title: Burberry partners with Leeds Beckett University to foster fashion talent
sub_title: Burberry has announced a formal partnership with Leeds Beckett University (LBU) and its BA (Hons) Fashion Design course as the brand builds on its commitment to support emerging fashion talent.
article_content: Burberry has announced a formal partnership with Leeds Beckett University (LBU) and its BA (Hons) Fashion Design course as the brand builds on its commitment to support emerging fashion talent. The partnership is meant to create new opportunities for students to gain industry insight and develop skills that will help their careers in the creative sector. Rooted in a shared connection to Yorkshire, the British luxury fashion brand first partnered with the University for a pilot programme in 2024 and is now formalising the relationship. Burberry has had presence in the region for a long time, with an office in Leeds and manufacturing sites in Castleford and Keighley. The partnership has seen second-year students at LBU working on a live industry brief, where they were tasked with redesigning and constructing a Burberry trench coat using surplus gabardine fabric, famously used for weather-resistant outerwear and first invented by Thomas Burberry in 1879. These trench coat designs were then presented by students in February at Burberry’s Castleford manufacturing site. The designs were judged by Burberry colleagues, with two students awarded work experience in Castleford, where they will gain hands-on insight into the design and production process behind the classic trench coat. For final year students, the partnership will see students receive professional guidance and mentorship on their graduate collections, across both their creative and professional practices. In May, students’ final garments and portfolios were judged Burberry manufacturing teams, with exceptional students receiving an award, which includes a paid internship also at Burberry’s Castleford manufacturing site. Alexandra McCauley, Chief People Officer at Burberry, said: "Yorkshire has long been an important part of Burberry’s story, and we are proud to support the next generation of creative talent in the region. "Through our partnership with Leeds Beckett University, we are creating opportunities for emerging designers to develop their skills, gain industry experience and build meaningful connections with the luxury fashion industry. "By investing in local talent today, we are helping to strengthen the future of British craftsmanship, manufacturing and creativity for years to come." Sam Hudson-Miles, Course Director for BA (Hons) Fashion Design at LBU, added: "This partnership gives our students a unique opportunity to engage directly with one of Britain's most iconic luxury brands, combining creative exploration with valuable industry experience. "By responding to a live brief inspired by the Burberry trench coat, students are challenged to develop their own design voice while gaining insight into the craftsmanship, heritage and innovation that underpin the fashion industry. "Experiences like this play an important role in preparing the next generation of creative talent for their future careers." Last month, Burberry reported that it had swung back to profit after its bet on Gen Z shoppers and move to revive its British heritage paid off, but it flagged worries over the possible impact of an Iran war on consumer spending. Its “Burberry Forward” strategy has also involved reviving the brand’s heritage and focusing on bestselling items, such as its trench coats, scarves and distinctive check pattern, after efforts to modernise failed to deliver a boost. Founded in England in 1856, Burberry has come under pressure in recent years from weaker spending across the luxury sector and its key Chinese market being hit particularly hard.

Cubitts opens 13,000 sq ft King's Cross headquarters and optical manufactory
sub_title: British spectacle maker Cubitts today unveils its 13,000 sq ft headquarters and optical manufactory in King's Cross, consolidating design, production, glazing, repair, bespoke consultation and training in a single central London site.
article_content: British spectacle maker Cubitts today unveils its 13,000 sq ft headquarters and optical manufactory in King’s Cross, consolidating design, production, glazing, repair, bespoke consultation and training in a single central London site. Cubitts has described the new space, called The Yard, as the only spectacle-making workshop in central London. The site occupies former Victorian stables once linked to the nearby Crosse & Blackwell vinegar brewery at 6 Blundell Street, just off Caledonian Road, and was designed by 51 Architecture. The move formalises an integrated operating model that Cubitts has built around repairability, craft and owned physical space. After years working from offices, railway arches, and improvised workshops, the brand now houses its full team, manufacturing operations and client-facing services in one permanent location. The Yard's working optical workshop uses five-axis CNC machines for frame production, with finishing and assembly carried out by hand. An on-site optical laboratory features next-generation glazing and milling equipment that, according to Cubitts, is designed to reduce water and energy consumption. A bespoke consultation room allows clients to commission custom frames. Master spectacle maker Lawrence Jenkin, who originally taught Cubitts founder Tom Broughton the craft of frame making, will also have his workshop at the site. Jenkin will work alongside Cubitts' makers, supporting skills training in a trade that has largely disappeared from central London. Tom Broughton said the site reflects the brand's roots in the area. “Cubitts has always been rooted in King’s Cross. We began on my kitchen table in Cubitt Street and have moved through a series of increasingly unlikely spaces - offices, arches, borrowed corners - but never quite found our home,” he said. “The Yard at Blundell Street is that home. Just off the Cally, in the shadow of Pentonville Prison, it feels very King’s Cross: a working building for a working part of London.” The building has retained its original London stock brick, cobbled floors, pine boards and Victorian stable fabric. “We’ve stripped away the paint and the lipstick, and let the building speak for itself,” Broughton said. The headquarters also houses a training academy for the company’s opticians and makers, along with Cubitts’ growing archive of historically significant spectacles spanning more than two centuries. A commercial kitchen and communal dining space will host talks, suppers, exhibitions and industry events. A newly commissioned exterior mural by artist David Shrigley accompanies the opening, giving the building a public-facing identity and extending Cubitts’ relationship with artists and makers. The streets around Clerkenwell and King’s Cross were once home to many of Britain’s spectacle makers, according to Cubitts. The Yard positions itself as a return of that craft to the area, now built around contemporary manufacturing and an in-house service model that runs from design through to fitting and repair.

The Eric Musgrave Interview: Derek Rose CEO Sacha Rose 'I think of end users, not customers'
sub_title: This year’s centenary celebrations for premium British brand Derek Rose are being guided by Sacha Rose, the third generation to run the family-owned
article_content: This year’s centenary celebrations for premium British brand Derek Rose are being guided by Sacha Rose, the third generation to run the family-owned business. Putting people before profit and product before price, he has transformed the fortunes of the company once known only for its pyjamas. Seven years working as a lawyer in corporate finance and in a hedge fund satisfied Sacha Rose’s need for intellectual challenges but provided little stimulus for his creative tendencies. In October 2003, at the age of 30, he joined the family business, Derek Rose Ltd, which had a worldwide reputation for fine pyjamas and dressing gowns. It was, he recalls, “not in a good state” and radical restructuring was needed before he could indulge his interest in creating a wider selection of high-quality, functional products. Initially he worked with his father, Derek, and his sister Nancy (“she is older in age but younger in spirit than me”, he says), but by 2005-06 he was in sole charge of the business that traced its heritage back to his grandfather Lou Rose, who had started making shirts in 1926, later specialising in nightwear. Derek joined Lou in 1953. By the early 1970s the company had been restructured and the immaculately-dressed and always charming Derek took over to create the global reputation of Derek Rose nightwear as a classic British brand of quality and taste. Derek died on August 29, 2025, aged 92. The many obituaries for him included ones in The Daily Telegraph and The New York Times. Sacha, who has two sons aged 17 and 20 with his Swiss-born wife Claudine, has been much less high-profile than his legendary father but his achievements have been equally impressive. He has taken the sales of the company from £3m 20 years ago to £14m today, expanding its product range and introducing direct-to-the-consumer sales while retaining a significant wholesale business. With micromodal T-shirts retailing at £105 and brushed cotton PJs selling for £260, Derek Rose is unashamedly premium. Sacha Rose likes to think of the products as “good value”. Sales are split 80:20 men's to women's, 70:30 retail versus wholesale, and about 35:65 UK against international. Back around 2005, sleepwear accounted for around 97% of sales; today it’s around 30% but the CEO admits categorising Derek Rose’s products across sleepwear, loungewear, leisurewear, resortwear and underwear is difficult. Crucially, all are designed, as the company says, “with the goal of enriching a customer’s enjoyment of their free time”. The important point, says Rose, is always to consider what is the desired end use. Congratulations on the centenary of your family’s involvement in the industry. How does it feel? It's quite exciting and special to be the third generation of a family enterprise and to be able to celebrate a landmark like this with so many people who have been with us in the business for such a long time. At Christmas we’ll be releasing a special centenary capsule collection. My grandfather was Jack Lewis Rose, but everyone called him Lou. He was born in the East End of London in 1900, so he was quite young when he started his shirt-making business in 1926. We think he always made the shirts in the north-west of England, close to the mills weaving cotton fabrics in those days. Lou jumped on the idea of pyjamas after seeing the higher echelons of the British Army bringing the garments back to England after serving in India. He was a smart man and one of his innovations was to have the buttonholes horizontal, not vertical, to allow a little more movement and so comfort when the wearer was in bed. I spoke to my father about this last year when he was on his deathbed, which was so typical of him – always talking shop. Derek joined Lou in 1953 and after splitting from some partners they set up Derek Rose Ltd in the early 1970s and concentrated on nightwear. Dad was fantastic designing the prints and handling the worldwide sales. He was so happy just meeting and talking to people. He would absolutely remember what a buyer had selected from him in 1977 or whenever! Why did you take so long to join him? It was never my intention to be in the business. I studied French at university and then studied law. I wanted to be a lawyer and, more importantly, I wanted the training and the qualification. I qualified as a corporate finance solicitor and the work was fascinating. I learned a huge amount. It was a very privileged way to start my working education. Then I did something called structured finance in a hedge fund, which again was really interesting work as hedge funds were just taking off. It was a great learning curve. All of us have this creative element within us. The one thing I didn't have from law and finance was any sort of creative output. I knew as soon as I got involved in the business that it was a really important thing to have. I joined the business in October 2003, when it was not in a good state. Talking to my dad beforehand I had wondered, Can I do something? Can I help fix it? Can I move it forward? Going through historical board meeting minutes, I saw the decision had been taken to shut our UK production, which was based in Congleton, Cheshire. But no one had the heart to execute what was the correct decision. I presented a slightly different argument, which was, if we don't do this, instead of losing some jobs, we will lose all the jobs. These were people's livelihoods and the episode shaped my thinking around what the priorities of any business should be. It's why I feel so strongly about people being at the heart of a business. Back then we had about 120 people in Congleton. I knew we couldn’t keep production here, but we could retain sampling and development. I said if we get it right, if we do the right products, we may be able to build that team again. That section, which we call The Silk Studio, was initially just five people: now it’s 18. We now employ about 50 people in Congleton, including warehousing and office staff. We make all our silk products and our woven cashmere garments, and it’s where we do the fun stuff – our three types of personalisation on garments. Of things that have made me happy over the years, the revival of Congleton production is possibly close to being number one on the list. Maybe it's the emotions around having to close our UK production in the first place. The Derek Rose Centenary Campaign When did you take full control? With my legal background, I said I can only join the business on the basis that I have control from day one. By 2006 my sister Nancy left to do what she’s very good at, helping cancer patients with palliative care. Dad stepped down around the same time but of course I’d have been mad not to massively rely on and leverage the experience of my father and my sister. But my position meant if we ever had a disagreement, I could push ahead with something and I had the bandwidth to make mistakes. Seeing the difference of how things are done in this industry and how it is in a big corporate environment was interesting. It’s part of the charm of the fashion industry and a challenge at the same time. It was fun to be able to marry the best bits of both. How did you go about changing the company? I went around the business and asked, What are we doing? Everybody said, Oh, we make the best pyjamas and dressing gowns in the world. No one was thinking, We help people enjoy their free time. Everything was product-centric, not end-user focused or use-focused. My business plan from 2003 said, We want people to be comfortable and enjoy their free time more. Business is really simple and can be summed up in three questions: What am I selling? Who am I selling it to? How am I selling it? When you are a business that is nearly 99% sleepwear your channels are limited because your sales are so biased towards Q4 and the winter months. If you had your own shops, you’d run out of cash during the rest of the year. I wanted to do more channels than wholesale, but I had to walk before I could run. We needed a viable product strategy, but before product comes people. So I had to make a few adjustments in terms of personnel within the business, filling gaps and so on. How did we get sales from £3m to £14m? It had to be a mixture of what products am I selling, and through what channels? The hardest bit was getting from £3m to £4m because at the early stage you don't have the product mix and the product pipeline. On top of that we were losing money and we didn’t have the cash. When I joined the business, one guy said to me, Good luck, you’re working with vapour. On your website there is a lot about putting people before profit. Is that the modern Derek Rose ethos? It's a really good question: what is the purpose of the business? Internally and externally, we serve two masters. Internally – and I don't care if people disagree – my thinking is we're here to protect and create jobs. With that as our focus, I need to have a decent balance sheet, I need to have cash in the business. That's part of the mindset of the small management team of six that runs the business with me. That's really important. Of course, we could make more money, but that's not our priority. When we're looking at our decision making, it's not profit first. Profits are a byproduct of our decision making. We have this team-centric thinking, which slightly changes the way you approach things. We have the luxury of being a privately-held business and having a group of people around the table who feel the same way – if we go down this path, we're looking after people better. A great example is us making our cashmere and silk garments in Congleton. Of course, we could make them for less and make more profit by manufacturing abroad. But how nice to grow that business in the UK, how nice to grow that team in the UK… Our external mindset reflects the fact I'm a bit of a nerd. People talk to me about the customer or the consumer; I'll talk about the end user. I'm very, very functional in my thinking and my design. Great design is huge amounts of function combined with the very important skill of wrapping the form around it. You could add function as an afterthought. We want to be looking after people and treating people as best as we possibly can. And, as a company, we make garments so people can make the most of their free time, or the time that they value. We're designing for people to enjoy what we do. If someone wears our PJs and sleeps 1% better because of them, we've done our job. Derek Rose Knightsbridge Are you profitable? Our profits go up and down. It depends on what we want to invest in. We've been investing well over the years, but I've made loads of mistakes that have cost us money. The buck stops with me. We've also been able to invest in people and product and that doesn't always pay off straight away. We've got a new cutting table in Congleton, which is a fantastic piece of technology, but these things cost tens of thousands of pounds. We employ a little over 90 people in total and we have a fantastic team. We have just recruited so we can start to do marketing and launch our first-ever marketing campaign. Historically, we've been quite comfortable with people finding us through word of mouth. I've always loathed the idea of marketing and I haven't been the greatest fan of social media and its impact on the world, but the reality is, it's part of business and we want to do it well. We see an opportunity to do marketing well with taste and class. Our first person joined us a few months ago and our second is joining in a couple of months. We're going to build up that team and that function, which is really exciting and again a big investment. How have you managed to keep wholesale as about 30% of your turnover? Wholesale is a really important channel because you've got relationships. We enjoy working with people we've known for donkey’s years, such as the Harry Rosen team in Canada, or Harrods and Selfridges, or Toby (Bateman) and Jeremy (Langmead) at Mr Porter. We work with a lot of really nice, decent people who are passionate about the industry. Wholesale is also a window into the world. If you're working with the right people, and they're kind enough to put your brand in front of their customers, it's bit of a privilege. It's a good thing. Certainly retailing is hard for multi-brand stores. It's a challenging environment and rents are always going up. In the UK, we also have the problem of the removal of the VAT refund scheme for international shoppers. We have singularly shot ourselves in the foot there. How easy was it to extend the product range from PJs and dressing gowns? You can't fix a business and you can't develop product well until you've got all the infrastructure, people and processes in place. So in the first few years everything was foundational. It’s particularly important to get in place the mentality that you are in a period of change or development. That took until 2007. I was adamant any product we wanted to develop and launch could only exist if it's brilliant in its own right. I never wanted anybody to buy anything because it's got our name in it. I always said, if you took the rest of the business away and just had that product, can it justify its existence? Over the years, we have spent huge amounts of time and energy researching and developing products, and a lot of them never see the light of day. We were a woven fabrics business and I wanted to expand into loungewear and jersey. The challenge was, why would someone buy a white T-shirt from me, one of the world's most commoditised products? We worked with different mills, then focused in on one and developed a quality that we felt was both unique and worthy of answering that question. It was about a year developing that one fabric. Similarly, in 2013 we launched underwear after just over two years of research and development. We put together a specialist team of three garment techs who collectively had 122 years of experience in underwear. It's just not in our nature to rush out a product. You have to benchmark existing products in their space, but by what criteria? Then you must work out how you can do better. Then you have to execute the plans. That's our approach. I can think of many products we could launch tomorrow, but I can't execute all of them at a level better than what's out there. Overall, we knew we wanted products for the enjoyment of free time, whether you're relaxing on a sofa at home, or taking the dog for a walk, or having dinner by the pool on holiday. We wanted to see if we could design a product that would be brilliant in that moment. I used to travel by air a lot and I always want to be as practically comfortable as possible. Whether I am on a zero to two-hour flight, a two to five-hour flight, or five hour-plus flight, we have designed different products for them. I’m always paranoid about losing my passport, so all of the products in that category have passport-size pockets using pin lock zippers, which are specialised fasteners where the slider locks in place when the puller is pressed down to prevent accidental opening. That's the kind of thinking behind our products, to make sure they're great in their own right and they fit into the Derek Rose lifestyle. A post shared by Derek Rose (@derekroselondon) How easy has it been to extend into womenswear? It’s growing but it’s only 20% of sales. I don't think I'm saying anything radical to state women shop differently from men. They are more fashion-led, they have less brand loyalty and they are prepared to wear things, comparatively speaking, of lower quality, in synthetic fabrics. It’s a more competitive marketplace with more price pressure. Our challenge is to bring across our standards from the men's side, the passion for natural fibres and the emphasis on quality and longevity. We won't compromise on quality or price. We serve a more discerning female customer. Alongside this, we have only a tiny business in kidswear, but our family pyjama sets are fun to do, so once again not being solely profit-driven, we get the enjoyment of offering these. Beyond pyjamas and dressing gowns, your product range is tricky to categorise… It's actually a bit of a nightmare. Currently we have our T-shirts in our loungewear category. We sell huge quantities of T-shirts, but people are not buying them just for loungewear or sleepwear. They're buying them as part of their daywear, they wear them with jeans, some do sport in them. We really struggle with categorisation and how to present it online. There's a project ongoing to effectively redefine all that stuff. Defining our customer base is the same. In the space of 15 minutes at a trunk show I’ve sold the same navy jersey T shirt to a 16-year-old and a 76-year-old. How do you narrow that down? The nice thing about our customers is that they wear it how they want to wear it. I met a 30-year-old man in a Swiss mountain village who was wearing our Derek Rose lounge trousers with a leather jacket, sunglasses, cool necklace and trainers. It turned out he was a mega-fan of the brand who wore them every day because they are so comfortable. Internally we've adopted the phrase "Live as you please" to describe how people buy and wear our products. Why have you recently added men’s denim jeans at £270? Over the years, we've been very slowly and very conservatively expanding our product mix. It's always been, what would I like to wear in my free time? I'm not a suit and tie person. I’m a T-shirt and jeans or hoodie and jeans person. Our mindset has always been, I want a really comfortable pair of jeans. I just want it to be function-led and comfort first as an end user experience. How nice to wear the jeans that are the denim equivalent of our beautifully soft T-shirt. I wanted each of our products to be the customer’s favourite, the one they reach for first when fishing clothes out of the cupboard. The jeans are not about attracting new or existing customers. It's just about being able to dress people, head to toe, in products that are each designed and directionally more focused on the end user experience than the average that's out there. I must mention our AirPod pockets! All of our trousers have a special elasticated mini pocket for your AirPods to sit in because I'm always paranoid about losing mine. Okay, I admit I need to get out more... Outside the UK, where do you manufacture? Mainly the Czech Republic and Portugal. We have been in what was Czechoslovakia since the 1970s. We like to find a good partner and then work with them for as long as humanly possible. My dad, or maybe it was my grandfather, always said you make money on your input costs, so we control everything from the ground up. We specify the very core elements of everything we work with. We don't buy a fabric, we will have a fabric made to our specification. We control that all the way through the production. We're hugely obsessed with efficiency and reliability of delivery. If you're not building from the ground up, how do you make it special? A post shared by Derek Rose (@derekroselondon) With your T-shirts at £105 and brushed cotton PJs at £260, do you regard Derek Rose as a luxury or a premium brand? Luxury is a word that has been abused so horrendously. I'm not interested in whether we are premium or luxury. I am interested in the concept of value, which is the result of price and quality. If I pay £105 for a T-shirt, what am I getting for that versus one that costs, say, £20. Is it just more expensive or is it a different experience? Will it last longer? Will it keep its shape better? Will it keep its colour better? Will it pill less? Will I be wearing that T-shirt in 10 years’ time? People are so fashionably interested in sustainability, but if you're interested in sustainability, buy quality, make clothing an investment, and make it last. Is £105 good value? If you knew how much that fabric costs per metre, you'd actually find out that this is quite significantly underpriced. It’s phenomenal value! Your four stores are in prosperous London locations – Hampstead, Knightsbridge, Notting Hill and Marylebone. Are more planned? There's an opportunity for us to grow retail, which is another way to create more jobs, which is really exciting. When we opened the first store in Ledbury Road, Notting Hill, in 2016 I didn’t even want to make a profit – sorry to sound like a broken record. The idea was, if we achieved break even, then we’d have created a couple of jobs and have given ourselves some brand marketing in a nice area. The way we look at stores hasn’t really changed much. Obviously we are also trying to give customers a positive experience. Funnily enough, we've gone full circle and have just finished a redesign for the Notting Hill store that hopefully will be implemented in the next six months. It is a radical redesign of that space, a more experiential approach to retail with less emphasis on volume of product and selling. We might struggle to do even one or two other locations in London, but higher on the list would be a store in LA, New York or San Francisco. We have never looked outside London because with our prices and product mix we’d struggle elsewhere in the UK. Tell us about your new part-time role at premium British menswear brand Drake’s. You are now COO, having been appointed soon after the company was acquired privately by Anders Holch Povlsen, billionaire owner of the Danish Bestseller fashion group. I have a brilliant team here at Derek Rose and I am not 100% occupied. I’ve known and admired Drake’s since the days of founder Michael Drake and I’m friendly with the current CEO Michael Hill, who worked with Michael. They've got a phenomenal brand, brand identity and a product marketing engine. They've got a lot of really exciting and talented people across all the disciplines. Sometimes it's just helpful to have someone in the room who's made all the mistakes and done a lot of the stuff before. That's what I'm contributing. What your personal strengths and weaknesses as the person running Derek Rose? I have a relatively simple job in many regards, which is to build a great team around me and then to enable them to do their jobs. We have a management team of six and my job is to support, empower and challenge. I need to know enough about what people are doing and what the team are doing in order to be able to challenge people, to properly support them and empower them. The key is, they know they have to come to me and say, This is what I need. Or can you support me on this? It's a collaborative way of working. We're all wired differently. I'm very functional, but also creative. I think I have a decent balance, so I'm good on the ideation side and moving things forward. One of my favourite things is to question everything, but I'm very comfortable delegating and empowering people. What am I not good at? I don't suffer fools. I need people to know their business. I've learned over the years that if you're going to fail, fail fast. Inside Derek Rose Knightsbridge What have been the significant high points and low points of your time as CEO? In the company we say we like to whisper about the wins and shout about the losses. The positives are made up of lots of little wins, while the negatives tend to be bigger impact events. Going back to around 2004, sterling was devalued against other currencies, including the Czech crown. We make a lot in the Czech Republic and suddenly the exchange rate moved something like 40% overnight. Then the credit crunch of 2008-09 was pretty brutal. Next came Brexit and Covid. I've learned not to stress about such external challenges because they are beyond my control but you still need to find a way to deal with them. On the plus side, I am really proud to have kept The Silk Studio and have built that up. It was great for us as a group of people, as a business, and for communicating the message of the importance of people. I'm also really proud of never laying people off, even during the credit crunch of 08-09. I apologised to one of our invoicing staff in Congleton for imposing a wage freeze and she berated me, saying everyone was just pleased to still have a job in a world where friends in other businesses were being laid off. What has been the biggest mistake? Hiring is probably one of the hardest things in business. A general mistake is hiring incorrectly. My biggest mistake has been not moving people out quickly enough who weren't up to the job. You like them, you want them to do well, you support them, but deep down you know it’s not working and they’d probably be happier elsewhere. In your centenary year, what’s the biggest challenge for Derek Rose? It’s brand awareness. When you've not done marketing for 20 years, that's probably not a surprise. In that 20-year period, the whole media landscape has changed with digital, social media and influencers. It's not enough just to be in the best stores around the world and have people telling their friends, I've got a lovely pair of jeans from Derek Rose. We are aware we are arriving late at the party, but maybe we are, fittingly, fashionably late!
