Australian menswear brand M.J. Bale makes London debut with Duke Street store
sub_title: Australian menswear brand M.J. Bale has chosen 30 Duke Street for its London debut, taking a lease on a 2,636 sq ft space.
article_content: Australian menswear brand M.J. Bale has chosen 30 Duke Street for its London debut, taking a lease on a 2,636 sq ft space. The new store, which has a frontage on Jermyn Street, marks the brand's first step into the UK market, expanding on its network of more than 80 stores in its native Australia. M.J. Bale was founded in 2009 by Matt Jensen and offers tailored men's suits, tuxedos, jackets and shirts. The brand describes itself as creating "rugged elegance for the guy who loves life and knows how to live it". It is also the Official Tailor to the Australian Test Cricket team, as well as a host of other sporting teams. The menswear brand has likely chosen the location because it is closely associated with premium menswear. Jermyn Street has long served as a hub for tailoring and formalwear in London, and the brand's decision to open there positions it alongside established names in the category, including Hawes & Curtis, Hackett and Sunspel. The store has not yet opened. Property developer Great Portland Estates (GPE), which owns the space, described the deal as a pre-let, meaning the lease was signed ahead of the building's practical completion.

article_title: Alexander McQueen returns to London Fashion Week for SS27
sub_title: British luxury fashion house Alexander McQueen will return to the official London Fashion Week schedule this September, presenting its Spring 2027 collection in the British capital.
article_content: British luxury fashion house Alexander McQueen will return to the official London Fashion Week schedule this September, presenting its s pring 2027 collection in the British capital. The brand, which typically shows in Paris, is scheduled to stage a runway show on 20 September. The presentation will mark Creative Director Seán McGirr's first Alexander McQueen show in London and will feature both womenswear and menswear collections. Laura Weir, CEO of the British Fashion Council (BFC), welcomed the move, saying McQueen's return was "a statement of confidence in British creativity at its most fearless and distinctive". Founded in London in 1992 by Lee Alexander McQueen, the label held its early runway shows in the city before relocating to Paris, where many of the industry's leading luxury houses present their collections. Irish designer Seán McGirr was appointed Creative Director of Alexander McQueen in October 2023, succeeding Burton, who departed after 27 years with the house. Prior to joining McQueen, McGirr served as Head of Ready-to-Wear at JW Anderson. McGirr said: "London has always been at the heart of McQueen; there's a uniquely visceral energy to the city that runs throughout the house's history and continues to inspire everything we do today." Newly appointed CEO Gianfranco D'Attis added: "London is where our story began and remains central to our identity. We are proud to reaffirm our commitment to the British Fashion Council and to the city's extraordinary creative ecosystem." McQueen's return comes as the British Fashion Council continues efforts to strengthen London Fashion Week's position within the global fashion calendar. Since becoming CEO in 2025, Weir has introduced measures aimed at broadening participation and increasing the event's reach, including changes to entry requirements and fee structures.

article_title: Valentino shareholders pledge 2026 support as sales fall and debt rises
sub_title: According to a filing seen by Reuters, Valentino’s shareholders have agreed to provide more financial backing for 2026 after the Italian luxury house saw sales fall sharply, moved to an operating loss and added to net debt in 2025.
article_content: Valentino shareholders have agreed to provide more financial backing for 2026 after the Italian luxury house saw sales fall sharply, moved to an operating loss and added to net debt in 2025. Rome-based Valentino, which is controlled by Qatar-backed Mayhoola with a 70% stake and counts Kering as a 30% shareholder, said it received €100 million of capital injections last year and has locked in further commitments for 2026. “In 2025, capital injections totalling €100 million were made and further financial commitments for 2026 were formalised,” the group said in the filing cited by Reuters. The support comes after a year in which Valentino’s revenue fell 15% to €1.12 billion and EBITDA fell 41% to €174 million, reflecting softer luxury demand and weakness across regions, according to the company’s financial statements. Valentino’s operating result moved from a €31 million profit in 2024, the same year it named Alessandro Michele as its Creative Director, to a €103 million loss in 2025. Under IFRS 16 reporting measures, the house saw net debt climb to €1.13 billion at the end of 2025 from €1.08 billion a year earlier. When lease liabilities are excluded, it rose to €472 million from €377 million. By category, the filing showed fashion jewellery and fragrances were more resilient than other lines, while leather goods and footwear declined overall. Women’s ready-to-wear represented 24% of total revenue in 2025, down from 25% a year earlier, reflecting weaker performance in directly operated stores. In the filing, the luxury house said it will keep controlling costs, improve process efficiency and safeguard brand value as it works through the softer luxury cycle.

article_title: British Fashion Council launches bold blueprint for circular fashion economy
sub_title: The British Fashion Council’s (BFC) Institute of Positive Fashion (IPF) has launched the Circular Fashion Ecosystem Report, presenting a blueprint for a
article_content: The British Fashion Council’s (BFC) Institute of Positive Fashion (IPF) has launched the Circular Fashion Ecosystem Report, presenting a blueprint for a circular fashion economy in the UK. It seeks to address the fashion industry’s impact on the planet through linear production models, and the report defines the roles that all stakeholders, from academia to consumers, must play, with three main targets to allow for a “viable, resilient and prosperous ecosystem”. The first target is to reduce the volume of new clothing, the second is to maximise utilisation and revaluation through product circularity, and the third is to optimise sorting methods and materials recovery. The targets are underpinned by 10 priority actions, including circular design, the use of sustainable fibres and recycling. The UK fashion market represents one of the largest globally, with revenues of £118 billion, 890,000 workers and contributes £35billion to the UK’s pre-pandemic GDP. Systemic change is needed to address waste across the supply chain, the high volume of clothes bought annually in the UK (a staggering four billion pieces of apparel in 2019) and the percentage that currently is destined for landfill. The report shows that the UK fashion ecosystem is actually well positioned to move the industry forward to be fully circular. Caroline Rush, CEO of BFC, said: “The UK has all the ingredients needed to create a blueprint for a circular fashion economy that will deliver significant environmental, commercial and societal benefits.  The mammoth job at hand to put this into action can be supercharged through a Sustainable Fashion Programme that sees, industry, the government and stakeholders all come to the table to play their part beyond their focus of each individual business. “We are already seeing this with our emerging designers, however with large commercial businesses, re-commerce businesses, academia, innovators, funders, logistics providers, waste management and recycling providers and the broader ecosystem coming together with the government, we have an opportunity to create this target state quicker, and in doing so creating jobs and skills benefiting the UK as a whole.”

article_title: Browns partners with Thrift+ to offer donation service with credit rewards
sub_title: Browns is launching a partnership with on-demand donation service and second- hand retail platform Thrift+, with a “clear out your wardrobe in exchange
article_content: Browns is launching a partnership with on-demand donation service and second- hand retail platform Thrift+, with a “clear out your wardrobe in exchange for giving back and getting Browns credit” message to its customers. It will give customers the ability to easily donate unwanted clothing and accessories, giving them a new life elsewhere, all while making a pledge to their chosen charity and in turn earning Browns shopping credits. The launch is an extension of Browns’ offering of “conscious services”, which includes the retailer’s partnership with repairs service The Restory, as well as initiatives including "Made to Order"’ and "Made to Measure", which aim to reduce waste. Ida Petersson, Buying Director at Browns, said: “Thrift+ are making such monumental and ever important waves in the conscious space. Not only are we now looking to give our clothes a second life, but through doing so, we’re also offering a helping hand to our communities - all through their ingenious platform. “ We’ve seen a shift in customers pivoting to being more environmentally conscious , in the way they shop and resell, and Thrift+ are engaging that one step further, by then helping through charitable means.” Joe Metcalfe, Thrift+ Co-Founder and CEO, added: “Teaming up with a brand as iconic as Browns is really exciting for us at Thrift+. Their conscious initiatives are making big strides in reducing the environmental impact of fashion, and we're delighted to partner with them on the next step - providing customers with an on-demand takeback service.” Listen to our recent podcast with Ida Petersson of Browns here .

article_title: Vestiaire Collective now valued at $1.7bn following latest investment
sub_title: Vestiaire Collective, the luxury fashion resale platform, is now valued at $1.7bn (£1.25bn) following a fresh fundraise which led to a $209m (£153m)
article_content: Vestiaire Collective, the luxury fashion resale platform, is now valued at $1.7bn (£1.25bn) following a fresh fundraise which led to a $209m (£153m) investment headed by SoftBank Vision Fund 2 . Joining Softbank Vision Fund 2, a private-equity vehicle of the Japanese tech giant, in this latest funding round were Generation Investment Management, as well as existing shareholders such as Conde Nast and Eurazeo, as well as some funds managed by Fidelity International and Koreyla Capital. The French-based business raised a similar sum of money in March of this year (circa £153m) securing the backing of luxury conglomerate Kering, which took a 5% stake in the business, and Tiger Global Management, underscoring the potential the fashion market and investors see in the luxury resale space, which Vestiaire Collective pioneered. Vestiaire Collective said it would use the latest funds to invest in its technology and to enter new markets and it would be seeking to reduce its environmental impact, in particular around deliveries. CEO Maximilian Bittner said of the latest deal: “We are honoured and delighted that SoftBank Vision Fund 2 and Generation Investment Management have decided to partner with Vestiaire Collective. It is a recognition of our achievements, and also confirms the attractiveness of our positioning embracing luxury, technology, sustainability and community. Their respective experiences as preeminent global investors supporting high-growth business models will be highly valuable to us in our next phase of development.” Vestiaire Collective, which was launched in 2009, has been evolving its business model of late to include direct deals with luxury brands and retailers. It began life as a peer-to-peer sales service but earlier this year announced a deal with Kering-owned Alexander McQueen to power its resale service and has also partnered with luxury multi brand retailer Mytheresa. These deals form part of its "brand approved" strategy.

article_title: IKEA takes on eBay and Vinted with new UK second-hand marketplace
sub_title: Ikea is looking to take on the likes of eBay and Vinted with plans to launch a new marketplace platform for its second-hand furniture and homewares.
article_content: IKEA is looking to take on the likes of eBay and Vinted with plans to launch a new marketplace platform for its second-hand furniture and homewares. The Swedish retail giant hopes the platform will make it “as seamless as possible” for consumers to buy and sell their pre-owned IKEA products. It has not confirmed a launch date but said it would provide more details “in the coming months”. Members of the firm’s membership scheme, IKEA Family, will be able to connect with other customers through the platform. The furniture giant has already launched trials of second-hand marketplace services in other countries, including Spain and Norway. An IKEA spokeswoman said: “At IKEA, we are always looking for new ways to make life at home even better and help our customers discover products they love. “With the launch of IKEA second-hand marketplace in the UK, we’re taking a meaningful step toward creating a destination that simplifies access to pre-owned IKEA furniture. “We’re creating a trusted and vibrant space to make it quick and easy for our IKEA Family members to trade directly with one another.” The move represents a push by IKEA into the second-hand market amid the growing use of eBay, Vinted and Facebook Marketplace by consumers. Other retailers such as John Lewis and Currys also sell pre-loved and refurbished products through their platforms. Vinted, especially, recently reported a jump in annual revenues of 38% to €1.1 billion (£957 million) for 2025, particularly highlighting its "strong" performance in women's and children's clothing. The platform said that beyond its core fashion category it had also expanded into more consumer goods categories, including sports, homeware, electronics and collectibles, welcoming more members as a result. This increase in members has also translated into a 47% increase in gross merchandise value traded on the platform to €10.8 billion (£9.4 billion) over the year. With competition in the resale market intensifying, eBay only last month completed its $1.2 billion (£890 million) acquisition of fashion resale platform Depop, following clearance from the UK Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) earlier this month. The deal, first announced in February, strengthens eBay's position in the fast-growing fashion resale market and expands its reach among Gen Z and Millennial consumers through Depop's community-led marketplace. Resale in fashion and beyond is only gaining more traction with consumers, Vinted's 2025 Impact report revealed. It showed that nine in ten of surveyed UK buyers check the resale platform before buying new items, with 35% saying that they think about the resale value of an item before purchasing something new. Vinted has coined the term "Vinted Math" to describe this shift towards more value-conscious consumer behaviour, with CEO Adam Jay commenting that the findings show that "people are changing not just where they shop, but how they value what they own".

article_title: Editors' Top Reads: News from Karen Millen, The Materialist, Odd Muse and more...
sub_title: Here are some of this week’s news and features highlights handpicked by TheIndustry.fashion team.
article_content: Here are some of this week’s news and features highlights handpicked by TheIndustry.fashion team. At just 22, Aimee Smale launched her clothing brand, Odd Muse, from her bedroom during the Covid-19 pandemic. What began as a personal project has since evolved into a $30 million fashion business, with a one-million-strong Instagram following and retail spaces in both London and New York. As a young woman myself, I’m naturally drawn to success stories that champion women and showcase what can be achieved at such a young age. As someone who also spends a lot of time on social media, I’ve frequently come across Aimee and Odd Muse online, which made me particularly keen to learn more about the founder behind the business. In this conversation , Smale shares the story behind Odd Muse, the inspiration that shaped the brand, and why community has been central to its growth. She also reflects on her approach to building a lasting business and the lessons she has learnt along the way. Sophie Smith, News Editor & Senior Writer. It's great to see a British brand make a high street return . So many went online only during the tricky pre- and post-pandemic era, in part because many of them got snapped up by online retail group Debenhams (formerly Boohoo Group). Karen Millen was one such case, having been acquired by Debenhams, along with Coast, in 2019. Its stores were not part of the deal. Debenhams wanted the IP of Karen Millen and you can understand why as it has always had a distinct handwriting (it's perfect for the modern working woman) and a defined customer base. I've always felt Debenhams did a good job of honouring the Karen Millen brand in the designs it has produced since the acquisition and now it's great to see it available on the high street once more. A deal has been signed with The Foschini Group (TFG) to make Karen Millen available in its stores. which includes Hobbs and Whistles. So far only three locations have been revealed ( read about them here ) and the businesses have been tight lipped about how many locations will follow. Obviously, it is to be hoped many more locations will follow as Karen Millen will sit nicely next to those two brands, where its past fans will be pleased to see it again, and new ones will no doubt be created too. Lauretta Roberts, Co-founder, CEO and Editor-in-Chief. I had the great pleasure of speaking to Liv Khan, the co-founder of The Materialist , a business that is turning a structural problem across fashion manufacturing – surplus fabric – into a scalable sourcing channel for brands at every level of the market. Khan co-founded The Materialist together with Lavinia Santovetti in 2024, and says the platform now holds over 10,000 fabric varieties in its showroom, with fabric rolls available at various quantities, from 30 to 3,000 metre lengths. In this interview, Khan addresses misconceptions around deadstock quality and scale, explains why fashion has historically handled surplus differently from other industries, and sets out what it takes for brands to move deadstock from capsule experiment to embedded sourcing strategy. Camilla Rydzek, Senior News Writer.

article_title: Frugi partners with thelitteloop on rental scheme for childrenswear
sub_title: Frugi, the British ethical childrenswear brand, has partnered with the shared wardrobe for kids, thelittleloop, to offer a rental service for kids
article_content: Frugi, the British ethical childrenswear brand, has partnered with the shared wardrobe for kids, thelittleloop, to offer a rental service for kids clothing. Parents can sign up for a subscription service to rent a bundle of clothes with the ability to swap out style later. Some 122 Frugi styles, known for their vibrant colours and reversible appliqués, will be available via the service. Based in Cornwall and backed by specialist retail investor True, Frugi already builds sustainability and longevity into its clothes with details such as extendable cuffs, waistbands and straps so the clothes can grow with the children. It also uses 100% GOTS certified organic cotton for 85% of its clothing. The remaining 15% are made from old polyethylene (PET) plastic bottles that have been spun into yarn to make a durable, water-proof fabric for outerwear, accessories, and swimwear. Joining the rental revolution which is sweeping through fashion at the moment takes the Frugi brand another step forward on its sustainability journey. “We’re thrilled to collaborate with thelittleloop, who share in our ethical and environmental values to help reduce both our customers’ and our own impact on the environment,” said Frugi CEO Sarah Clark. “Using organic cotton, which is more durable, means our clothes are made to last, and thelittleloop is helping us to further extend the lifespan of these clothes, that have been and will continue to be loved for more generations,” “We don't just want to make it easy for parents to dress their kids in style without the guilt of fast fashion,” said thelittleloop founder Charlotte Morley. “We also want to support brands like Frugi who are going above and beyond to make clothes in the best possible way. Their clothes are such incredible quality that they work perfectly for rental. "Plus, we hope we can help even more people than before access these ethically produced garments for their children instead of resorting to the high street. Working with Frugi has been a dream come true and I’ve been blown away by how open they’ve been to adopt such a revolutionary new way of doing things.” While adult fashion, and in particular womenswear, has become the focus of resale and rental services to date, kidswear offers a growing opportunity. Recently upscale department store Harvey Nichols partnered with Kids O'Clock to offer a childrenswear resale drop-off destination within the department store.

article_title: The Interview: The Materialist's co-founder Liv Khan on why deadstock fabric is a sourcing opportunity, not a compromise
sub_title: The Materialist is building a business around turning a structural problem across fashion manufacturing – surplus fabric – into a scalable sourcing channel for brands at every level of the market.
article_content: The Materialist is building a business around turning a structural problem across fashion manufacturing – surplus fabric – into a scalable sourcing channel for brands at every level of the market. Liv Khan, who co-founded The Materialist together with Lavinia Santovetti in 2024, says the platform now holds over 10,000 fabric varieties in its showroom, with fabric rolls available at various quantities, from 30 to 3,000 metre lengths. The Materialist's business proposition is simple, yet pioneering. The platform connects fashion houses, designers, students and "other visionaries" with high-quality fabrics that have gone un-used in a manufacturing process. A staggering 25% of fabrics that are produced end up being unused, so there is no shortage of stock. Most importantly, the platform isn't just inspiring a more circular textiles ecosystem – it's scaling it. The commercial model of the business is built around repeat supply rather than one-off collaborations, with core fabrics, such as plain black wools and white cotton poplin, forming a core part of the offer alongside seasonal and luxury pieces. Recent pop-ups with LVMH-backed Nona Source and Vivienne Westwood have raised its profile, but the brand has its sights set on far more. In this interview, Liv addresses misconceptions around deadstock quality and scale, explains why fashion has historically handled surplus differently from other industries, and sets out what it takes for brands to move deadstock from capsule experiment to embedded sourcing strategy. Surplus fabric, new and unused material the industry calls deadstock, is a problem baked into the way fashion manufacturing works, with at least 25% of all fabric produced ending up unused. The causes are largely structural. Mills and brands routinely overestimate what they need, and minor but unavoidable production variations, such asa shade inconsistencies, slight weaving or dyeing defects, mean large volumes are rejected before a single garment is cut. Minimum order quantities compound the issue further: brands are locked into buying more than they require, and when external shocks like Brexit or Covid cause cancelled or reduced orders, that excess only grows. It varies. More brands are making genuine efforts to work through their own inventory, but doing so properly requires resources – stock needs to be catalogued, stored, and managed, which many brands don't have the capacity for. Beyond that, the most common routes are selling to jobbers at a low per–metre price, donating to students or educational institutions, or simply doing nothing – leaving stock to sit in warehouses for seasons, sometimes years. It's a problem that touches every level of the industry, from small independent labels to large high street retailers. What's been missing is a reliable, efficient way for brands to actually unlock the value sitting in their inventory – and to ensure it doesn't ultimately end up as waste. That's exactly what we provide. The biggest misconception is around quantity. Many designers and buyers assume deadstock means offcuts and end–of–roll remnants –a few metres of this, a few metres of that. In reality, we hold over 10,000 varieties in our showroom alone, many with more than 300 metres available and some with quantities as high as 3,000 metres - it's a genuine, scalable resource. The other persistent myth is around quality. Deadstock carries an unwarranted reputation for being defective or second–rate. Our fabrics are premium, luxury, and brand new – they simply weren't used by the original buyer. That's it. There's no hidden reason they're available. Both of these perceptions have begun to shift over the last couple of years as deadstock has moved further into the mainstream conversation around sustainable sourcing, but they still come up regularly – which is why education remains such an important part of what we do. The fundamental difference is how other industries treat surplus materials as an asset to be recovered, whereas fashion has historically treated it as a problem to be hidden or disposed of. In automotive, surplus components are rigorously tracked, returned to suppliers, repurposed across model lines, or fed back into manufacturing. Waste has a clear cost attached to it, and there are established systems for managing it. Interior design works similarly – surplus fabric and materials are catalogued, held as samples, or sold on through well–established trade channels. There's no stigma attached to it; it's just inventory management. Fashion, by contrast, has long had a cultural resistance to transparency around surplus. Admitting to excess stock – particularly in luxury – has been seen as a brand risk, which is partly why so much has historically been destroyed rather than redistributed. The supply chain is also far more fragmented, with fabric often held at both mill and brand level, with little visibility across either. What's changing is that sustainability pressure and cost pressure are converging. Brands that once wouldn't acknowledge their deadstock publicly are now actively looking for solutions, which is exactly where we operate. The infrastructure for managing surplus fabric properly is finally starting to catch up with the scale of the problem. Our range is broad enough that we're not really beholden to trends in the way a conventional fabric supplier might be. We carry everything from tailoring wools, cotton shirting, silks, lace and organza through to jerseys, technical fabrics, tulles, satins and faux furs: there's genuine depth across categories. What we do see is a natural seasonality in how clients come to us. Designers tend to arrive with a specific collection in mind, and we work with them across multiple departments within a brand – womenswear, menswear, kidswear, accessories – which means we need to hold a wide and varied inventory at any given time. A core part of our offer is continuity fabrics: plain black wools, white cotton poplin, and other wardrobe staples that never really go out of demand and can be worked into collections season after season. Alongside those, we regularly receive more special or seasonal pieces – bridal satins, for instance – and when something exceptional comes in, we make sure our network knows about it. There's always something new arriving, which keeps the offer fresh without it ever being trend–dependent. Supply is strong and constantly moving. We're receiving new stock all the time, which is necessary because good deadstock sells quickly – clients who know the market move fast when they see something they want. Quantities vary enormously, which is part of what makes us different from the offcuts–and–remants perception we touched on earlier. We hold anywhere from 30 metres up to 3,000 metres on a single article, which means we can genuinely service brands at scale, not just independent designers looking for a few metres to sample with. It really depends on the client and where they are in their process. Some arrive with a very specific brief – a swatch they need to match, a particular weight or composition – and we work to find the closest possible option from what we hold. But the most exciting and, we'd argue, most impactful way of working is when a whole design team comes in at the very beginning of the design process and uses our inventory as a starting point for their collection. Rather than deadstock being a last–minute substitute or a sustainability add–on, it becomes the foundation – collections are built around what's available, which is how it should work. When clients engage with us that way, there's far more scope to embed deadstock meaningfully into the core of the brand's sourcing strategy. It also tells us something about their intentions – these are the brands making a genuine, considered commitment to more sustainable sourcing, rather than ticking a box. That's the kind of relationship we find most rewarding, and frankly, it produces better results for everyone. It was a brilliant collaboration and Nona Source are a fantastic partner – they're doing important work in proving that deadstock and luxury are not mutually exclusive, which is a message the industry still needs to hear. Our approaches are closely aligned in many ways, but where we differ is in the breadth of what we offer. We work with brands holistically – clients can come to us to source deadstock fabric, but they can also use us to sell their own excess inventory, or participate in our donation programmes supporting emerging designers and students. It's a full circle solution rather than purely a sourcing platform, which means brands can address both sides of the problem: what they need to buy and what they need to clear. The Vivienne Westwood pop–up was a real highlight for us, and there's plenty more in the pipeline. We have a whole wishlist of brands we're hoping to work with over the next year – household names that we believe will genuinely help bring deadstock into the mainstream conversation. Beyond fashion, we're also increasingly working with theatre, film and TV, which is a really exciting space for us, as well as expanding into the interiors world. Both industries have a huge appetite for quality fabric and a real appreciation for what deadstock can offer. We don't want to give too much away just yet, but watch this space! Experimentation is easy; integration is the hard part. A brand can dip into deadstock for a capsule collection, generate some great press around it, and then quietly go back to their usual supply chain. Scaling it requires a genuine shift in how a brand approaches the design and sourcing process. The brands that make it work at scale are the ones that stop treating deadstock as a constraint and start treating it as a creative starting point – which brings us back to how we prefer to work with clients. When design teams come to us at the beginning of the process rather than the end, deadstock stops being a compromise and becomes a genuine foundation. There are also practical requirements: you need a reliable supply partner who can offer consistency and volume, not just one–off pieces. That's a big part of what we've built – continuity fabrics that can be reordered, and enough depth of stock across categories that brands can plan around us with confidence rather than treating us as a back up option. Ultimately, it comes down to intention. The brands that scale deadstock successfully are the ones where sustainability is embedded in the business, not bolted on for marketing purposes. You can usually tell the difference quite quickly. It varies by brand, and often comes down to individuals rather than departments. That said, design teams tend to be the earliest adopters – there's a natural creative excitement around working with something exclusive and designers really appreciate our quality. Interestingly though, once finance, production and buying teams understand what we offer, they're often just as enthusiastic – sometimes more so. Our fabric is competitively priced and available immediately, which solves real problems for those teams around budget, lead times and speed to market. The biggest shift is moving deadstock from an afterthought to a starting point. For too long it's been treated as a compromise – something you turn to when a preferred fabric isn't available, or when a brand needs a sustainability marketing story. That thinking has to change. The industry also needs to let go of the idea that working with what already exists is a creative limitation. The most exciting work we see comes from designers who treat constraint as a creative tool, not an obstacle. And practically, brands need to build sourcing timelines that allow deadstock to be genuinely considered from the beginning – not approached at the last minute when decisions have already been made. Treat fabric that already exists as the first option, not the last resort. The last few years have been about foundations – getting a real understanding of the industry and how it works; building our product, and establishing strong supplier relationships and partnerships. We feel confident those foundations are solid, and now we're ready to scale. The ambition is to become the number one destination for sustainable fabric sourcing – not just within fashion, but across industries. We're growing our supplier base, expanding our network, and building out some genuinely exciting new features on our platform that will make it far simpler for brands to find exactly what they need without having to manually browse thousands of products. A lot of what we're developing uses AI to automate processes that have remained stubbornly analogue for decades – sourcing fabric is still an incredibly time–consuming, human–intensive process, and we want to change that. There's a lot coming!

article_title: Mary Portas and Superdry's Julian Dunkerton join TheIndustry.fashion Fashion [Un]Bound Summit line-up
sub_title: The retail leaders will join senior executives from H&M, Topshop, Aligne and Toast at the one-day event in London this October.
article_content: Globally renowned retail expert Mary Portas and Superdry founder and CEO Julian Dunkerton have joined the speaker line-up for TheIndustry.fashion Fashion [Un]Bound Summit on 15 October 2026. The one-day event at The Forum, Leadenhall, will bring together about 200 fashion-industry leaders for interviews, presentations and panel discussions focused on changes in retail. Portas, the author, activist and founder of Portas Consultancy, will take part in a keynote interview with TheIndustry.fashion Co-founder Lauretta Roberts. The session will examine her approach to turning physical stores into places for human connection and building loyalty beyond individual transactions. She will also discuss how large and small brands can create consistent experiences across retail channels and develop a clear voice grounded in purpose. Portas has worked with British retailers including Harvey Nichols, John Lewis and Topshop during a career spanning more than 40 years. She is also known for presenting the BBC series Mary Queen of Shops and for her long-running advocacy for the British high street. Her consultancy works with businesses across fashion, beauty and lifestyle, with a focus on translating brand strategy into customer experience and company behaviour. Portas’s work on physical retail includes the government-commissioned Portas Review, published in December 2011. The review proposed measures covering town-centre management, business rates, vacant properties and local markets, while arguing that high streets should function as social and commercial centres. Julian Dunkerton CEO and Founder of Superdry Dunkerton’s appearance comes as Superdry continues its restructuring and repositioning. For the year ended 26 April 2025, the business posted a statutory profit after tax of £50.5 million, reversing a £67.7 million loss in the previous year. In November 2025, Dunkerton presented the Superdry & Co strategy at its Oxford Street flagship. The approach combines a revised mainline identity with the return of Bench and an offer spanning vintage and upcycled clothing. The Forum, Leadenhall: a brand new, state of the art event venue Additional confirmed speakers include some Of H&M UK and Ireland Managing Director Karen O’Rourke, Topshop and Topman Global Chief Marketing Officer Moses Rashid, Aligne CEO Ginny Seymour, Albaray CEO Paula Stewart and Toast CEO Suzie de Rohan Willner. See the full speaker line-up here . The summit programme will cover AI and new retail technologies, connected stores, circular business models, workforce development and creativity as a driver of demand. Tickets are on sale now, priced at £225 plus VAT, and are open to senior executives from fashion brands and retailers. Lunch, refreshments and a drinks reception are all included in the cost of each ticket. The event is staged at The Forum, Leadenhall, a brand new state-of-the-art event venue in the City of London, which will allow for an elevated and engaging experience for speakers and delegates alike. Industry suppliers can take part in the event through our flexible sponsorship packages. For more information, please contact partnerships@theindustry.fashion . TheIndustry.fashion Fashion [Un]Bound Summit is staged in proud partnership with global logistics expert Bleckmann, with StoryStream AI and Aptos sponsoring the programme.

article_title: Oxfam branches into fashion rental with 14-day online pilot
sub_title: The charity is testing whether distinctive donated garments can generate income through repeated hires, supported by rental and fulfilment specialist ACS.
article_content: Oxfam has launched an online clothing rental pilot, offering distinctive donated garments to rent from £22 for 14 days. The charity describes the initiative as the first rental service launched by a national UK charity. It began the pilot on 3 August, ahead of its annual Second-Hand September campaign. The Oxfam Rental platform offers hundreds of garments selected from donated stock, including vintage finds and directional designer pieces considered less suited to its standard shop rails. The womenswear launch range features a Balenciaga dress with blue-and-white spots, a tailored yellow jacket by Stella McCartney and a strapless black Dolce & Gabbana dress. Oxfam will use the pilot to test demand for hiring second-hand fashion, focusing on customers seeking event clothing without committing to a purchase. Each item is cleaned, pressed and prepared before dispatch, then returned for another customer to hire. Oxfam said the model could extend garments’ useful lives while generating income for its humanitarian and charitable work. Julie Tyrell, Head of E-Commerce & Retail Sustainability at Oxfam, said: “We see pieces come through our shops that you simply won't find anywhere else - and until now, the only way to own one was to buy it outright. Rental means people can access that wardrobe for the moment they actually need it and then not let it just sit in a cupboard afterwards "This is another interesting option which gives people access to pieces that are genuinely different, without adding to that wear-once cycle. If our pilot shows people want to rent rather than buy for a single occasion, that's a real shift in how clothes get used, not just where they come from." Customers can choose their rental dates online, with delivery and prepaid return shipping included in the price. Oxfam says orders need to be submitted at least 48 hours before the hire period begins, although it recommends arranging delivery four days before an event. The service currently covers UK Mainland addresses, excluding Northern Ireland and the Channel Islands. Garments cannot be collected from or returned to Oxfam shops because the online operation is managed separately. Fashion rental and fulfilment company ACS is supplying the operational infrastructure, including garment preparation, dispatch and returns. According to Oxfam’s service information, womenswear items are hand-checked and ozone-cleaned ahead of each rental. Menswear is supplied through a partnership with ACS and includes suits, tuxedos and other occasionwear. Measurements are provided online, while product pages for vintage womenswear without standard labels include garment dimensions. Customers do not need to dry-clean items before returning them. Late returns carry a £10 daily charge, while optional insurance covers accidental damage beyond expected wear. The platform does not currently allow renters to buy hired garments. Anthony Burns, Chief Operating Officer at ACS, said the partnership would help extend the life of clothing while supporting Oxfam’s fundraising. "We are incredibly proud to partner with Oxfam on an initiative that demonstrates the power of circular innovation to deliver both environmental and social value. ACS and Oxfam share a commitment to creating a more sustainable future for fashion, while ensuring positive outcomes for communities. “By providing the operational infrastructure behind Oxfam's online rental proposition, we are helping to extend the life of garments, increase access to more sustainable fashion choices, and support the generation of vital funding for Oxfam's important work around the world. This partnership is a strong example of what can be achieved when organisations come together with a shared purpose and a commitment to driving meaningful change," Burns said, The pilot adds rental to the charity’s existing shop (the charity operates 500 stores nationwide) and e-commerce operations as it prepares for Second-Hand September, its campaign encouraging consumers to choose pre-owned fashion.

article_title: The Interview: Founder Aimee Smale on building Odd Muse, one timeless piece at a time
sub_title: At just 22, Aimee Smale launched her clothing brand, Odd Muse, from her bedroom during the Covid-19 pandemic. What began as a personal project has since
article_content: At just 22, Aimee Smale launched her clothing brand, Odd Muse, from her bedroom during the Covid-19 pandemic. What began as a personal project has since grown into a significant fashion business, becoming a $30 million brand with a one-million-strong Instagram following and retail spaces in London and New York. Smale’s rapid rise as a young founder saw her named under the Forbes 30 Under 30 list in 2023, but she says the origins of Odd Muse can be traced back to a simple frustration with the fashion industry. Speaking to TheIndustry.beauty, Smale explains that she felt there was a gap between trend-led fashion and true investment dressing. "Everything was either disposable or completely inaccessible. I felt all that was being offered to younger women was the throw away fashion culture, we were being spoken to like we just needed an outfit for the weekend, no one was designing capsule pieces at a mid luxury price point," she says. This gap became the foundation for Odd Muse: creating elevated, timeless pieces at a more accessible price point. Smale believes the brand’s early growth came from addressing that genuine need in the market. "I wanted to create a brand that felt elevated, intentional and timeless, but still wearable and relevant to everyday life," she adds. With limited resources at launch, Smale says her own belief in the idea and her story as a founder became a big part of Odd Muse’s identity. "From the very beginning, I knew I had no marketing budget or real experience, but I had my story. I was a 22-year-old who genuinely believed I was onto something. I was willing to leave my job and invest everything I had into building it. That level of conviction naturally became part of the brand’s voice," she reveals. Since launch, Odd Muse has focused on creating wardrobe staples intended to last beyond a single season, from structured tailoring to versatile everyday pieces. "It’s a more considered way of dressing and buying. Also, from a brand perspective, it builds trust. When customers invest in Odd Muse, they know it won’t feel irrelevant in three months and that’s incredibly powerful," notes Smale. Maintaining relevance while staying true to the brand’s core identity remains a key consideration. Rather than constantly reinventing, Smale says the business has focused on carefully expanding into new categories. "One thing about Odd Muse is, we’re still so new to this! For example, we only just launched Knitwear in year four. I think bringing what our customers love about the brand into new categories and really taking our time category by category is one strategy," she says. This measured approach has allowed the brand to evolve while maintaining consistency. "Our customer is slowly on this journey as we evolve into a legacy brand, I think that’s how we continue to keep it fresh and exciting. We take our time with everything we do, we don’t try and do it all at once and our customer comes with us," shares Smale. "Meanwhile, our core silhouettes stay consistent. Some styles that we have been running for the last three to four years continue to be 50% of our whole business. That’s what we’re trying to achieve when we’re designing, something that can be relevant and continue to sell. It just proves our mission." Beyond product, Smale credits community-building and strong storytelling as key parts of Odd Muse’s development. Remaining self-funded has also influenced how the company operates. "We treat our audience like a community, not just customers. That means consistency, transparency, and bringing them into the journey - whether that’s product development, behind-the-scenes or brand decisions. It’s not just about selling; it’s about building a world people want to be part of," she explains. "I think the founder strategy I fell into helps. For years, not a lot of customers have been able to put a name to a face when it comes to established fashion brands. I’ll always proudly be 'that odd muse girl'." From its beginnings online, Odd Muse has expanded into physical retail, with stores designed to strengthen the connection between customers and the brand. While digital remains a key driver of global growth, Smale says stores provide an opportunity for customers to experience the product in person. "Our physical spaces allow customers to fully understand the product: fit, fabric, quality and that deepens trust. But also, an invite to experience the Odd Muse universe IRL," she highlights. "The two channels really complement each other: digital drives discovery and retail builds connection." The brand opened its Covent Garden store in 2023 following a successful pop-up, before expanding with a New Bond Street location in London. Smale says the two spaces serve different purposes: Covent Garden is more high-energy and community-focused, while New Bond Street reflects the brand’s ambitions in the luxury market. "New Bond Street is a three-storey townhouse on London’s most prestigious shopping street, inviting our community off Oxford Street and onto a luxurious street they may not have previously been able to shop on regularly," adds Smale. The brand has also expanded internationally with its Mercer Street store in Soho, New York, which Smale describes as an important milestone for Odd Muse’s US growth. "This was a huge step change for the brand, it heightened our credibility, and was huge for US growth. I’ve never seen a UK self-funded brand take a step like that before. I still pinch myself!," Smale reveals. Looking ahead, she says future retail expansion will be approached carefully, with a focus on locations where there is already a strong customer base. "For us, retail isn’t about opening as many stores as possible, it’s about opening the right spaces that genuinely add to the brand," she says. Reflecting on her journey as a young female entrepreneur, Smale says some of her biggest lessons have centred around trusting her instincts, developing strong leadership skills and building resilience. "My biggest learnings are probably to trust your instinct early and not wait for permission. Also, building the right team is everything. As you scale, your role changes completely - it becomes less about doing and more about leading," she notes. "And resilience. There’s always another challenge, but that’s part of building something meaningful. I always credit myself for how many times over the years where I have just got back up again. My failures have been my biggest lessons." For aspiring founders, Smale’s advice is to begin before everything feels perfect. "Start before you feel ready. You don’t need everything figured out - you just need a clear idea and the willingness to learn quickly," she suggests. "Also, focus on building something with depth. It’s easy to start a brand, but much harder to build one that lasts." As Odd Muse continues to grow, Smale’s ambition remains focused on creating a globally recognised fashion brand built around longevity. "We want to continue expanding internationally, strengthen our core collections, and deepen the brand experience across every touchpoint - online, offline, and community," she concludes. "Ultimately, it’s about longevity. I want Odd Muse to be a brand that people come back to for years."

article_title: Peter Ackroyd MBE, champion of the wool industry, dies aged 76
sub_title: Peter Ackroyd MBE, Chairman of the Campaign for Wool and a leading international advocate for the natural fibre, has died aged 76.
article_content: Peter Ackroyd MBE, who was Chairman of the Campaign for Wool and a leading international advocate for the natural fibre, has died aged 76. Ackroyd was a leading figure in the wool and textile industry, with a career spanning more than five decades. Tributes have poured in from across the sector following Ackroyd's passing, with colleagues and others throughout the global supply chain remembering him as a warm and well-respected leader. In January 2025 Ackroyd became Chairman of the non-profit Campaign for Wool, succeeding Sir Nicholas Coleridge CBE, after serving as the organisation’s Chief Operating Officer from 2009. The not-for-profit international organisation aims to raise awareness amongst consumers about the unique and sustainable properties of wool as a natural fibre and to promote the many ways it can be used and the products in which it can be used. In a tribute to Ackroyd the organisation noted his five decades of "distinguished service to the international wool and textile industry, as well as his unswerving devotion to championing wool as one of the world's most remarkable natural fibres." "Those who worked alongside Peter will remember not only his remarkable knowledge of the global wool industry, but his humour and ability to lighten any room with one of his speeches and fluency in many languages, along with his generosity, kindness and steady determination." "His counsel, integrity and lifelong devotion to the industry leave a permanent legacy that will continue to shape the future of wool for years to come." Coleridge described him as "a lifelong Wool Man of the highest calibre, who knew every mill, every player and wool champion in the UK and beyond." "He was a Great Man, a gentleman and a friend to so many of us. He will be profoundly missed by the entire wool community,” he added. Ackroyd worked across business development, research projects and international promotion during a career that began in the 1970s. He served as President of the International Wool Textile Organisation and was both Global Strategic Advisor to Australian Wool Innovation and Woolmark. He was formerly Vice President of the Strategy Committee for Première Vision and President of the Bradford Textile Society. He received an MBE in 2006 for services to the textile industry. Under the patronage of His Majesty King Charles III, who first conceived the initiative in 2008, Ackroyd used his Campaign for Wool roles to promote wool’s environmental and technical properties, while connecting farming, manufacturing, fashion and retail businesses. When his appointment as Chairman was announced in late 2024, Ackroyd called for wool-producing countries to work together more closely. He argued that the sector needed to challenge the growth of synthetic materials, disinformation and greenwashing by fast-fashion retailers. A host of tributes gathered by online news platform SheepCentral, which reports on the Australian sheep and wool industries, recognised Ackroyd’s humour, multilingual skills and willingness to mentor colleagues. Australian Wool Innovation said Ackroyd had represented Australian wool growers across the international supply chain for decades. Scott Carmody, its Head of Domestic Operations, described him as generous with his knowledge and unwavering in his support for the industry. Michael Jackson, Managing Director of AWTA (Australian Wool Testing Authority), recalled Ackroyd’s hospitality during visits to Yorkshire mills and his extensive relationships across Europe and Asia. David Michell, Chairman of Wool Industries Australia, highlighted his dependable knowledge and ability to put complex industry issues into perspective. The Campaign for Wool extended its sympathies to Ackroyd’s family, friends and colleagues. It further shared that funeral arrangements and details about the organisation’s future governance will be announced in due course.

article_title: Fashion and textiles industry urges PM Burnham to back British-made uniforms through public contracts
sub_title: Fashion Roundtable and UK fashion industry signatories have called on Andy Burnham to introduce onshoring requirements for public-sector textiles.Fashion Roundtable wants NHS and defence uniform contracts tied to domestic production, arguing that dependable public orders could protect manufacturing skills and strengthen regional economies.
article_content: Fashion Roundtable and UK fashion industry signatories have called on Prime Minister Andy Burnham to introduce onshoring requirements for public-sector textiles, beginning with NHS and defence uniforms. The open letter, published on this week, asks for a meeting before the government finalises its Number 10 North initiative. Signatories include presenter and Buffalo Systems co-owner Ben Fogle, alongside representatives from the fashion and textiles sector. Tamara Cincik of Fashion Roundtable Fashion Roundtable, the fashion industry think tank and lobbying group, said procurement could connect Burnham’s commitments on decentralisation, reindustrialisation, regional growth and stronger local decision-making with existing UK manufacturing capacity. The wider UK fashion and textiles industry contributes £62 billion to GDP and supports 1.3 million jobs, according to figures cited in the letter. These totals cover the broader sector rather than domestic garment manufacturing alone. The open letter makes two principal requests: The manufacturing condition should cover where goods are produced, rather than where the successful bidder is registered, the group said. This would prevent UK-based intermediaries from winning contracts while continuing to source finished goods overseas. Kate Hills, founder and CEO of business support platform Make it British, said: “The single biggest ask is a British-made requirement in public contracts for textile goods, starting with defence and NHS uniforms, and crucially it must specify where products are manufactured, not just where the winning company is registered.” A February parliamentary debate put the British Army clothing budget at almost £80 million annually and NHS uniform frameworks at £125 million over five years. MPs were also told that 6% of UK military uniforms were made domestically, based on figures from a 2013 inquiry. Fashion Roundtable based its proposals on an April 2026 report produced with the University of Birmingham’s Local Policy Innovation Partnership Hub. The research identified dependable public orders as a way to retain skills and strengthen regional manufacturing. Its recommended procurement changes included longer contracts, clearer demand forecasts, contract sizes accessible to smaller manufacturers and improved payment terms. Fashion Roundtable said the sector’s main constraint was fragmented policy rather than an absence of skills or production capability. The organisation also cited the pandemic procurement process as evidence that a change in policy is needed. The UK Covid-19 Inquiry found that £9.9 billion of PPE was written off because it was unused or out of date, and called for a domestic strategy covering essential healthcare equipment. Fashion Roundtable CEO Tamara Cincik said: “During the pandemic I saw a total fiasco in the procurement of vitally needed PPE. Kate Hills and I were asked by the then government to attend regular calls on public procurement and it was clear to both of us that the right hand did not know what the left hand was doing, and this is all avoidable if public procurement is brought back onshore. Not only for the jobs and income it brings back to Britain, but also to ensure greater transparency, reduce waste and stabilise British manufacturing.” The Private White VC factory The intervention follows mainstream media criticism of Burnham for wearing clothing, including an £80 T-shirt and £700 jacket, from British company Private White VC, with suggestions that the cost of his fashion choices demonstrate he is out of touch with ordinary working people. However many have come out in support of Burnham's move. Private White VC produces clothing at a 173-year-old Greater Manchester factory and is one of the UK's last remaining British-made brands. The company has defended its pricing as a reflection of skilled local labour and garments designed for long-term use. Its CEO James Eden has appeared in media interviews defending Burnham's choice and said it was a show of support for British industry and jobs, as well as showing a commitment to sustainable and ethical practice. The episode placed the PM's individual purchasing choices under scrutiny, while Fashion Roundtable’s letter shifts the focus to government buying power. The organisation is seeking talks with Burnham before the structure and priorities of Number 10 North are settled. Anyone wishing to add their names to the letter are invited to email meg.pirie@fashionroundtable.co.uk

article_title: Chanel ends shredding of unsold goods ahead of EU ban
sub_title: The luxury house said products that cannot be sold now pass through L’Atelier des Matières, following court disclosures about its historical destruction practices in Hong Kong.
article_content: Chanel has stopped shredding products that cannot be sold and now directs them to L’Atelier des Matières, its recycling business for luxury and premium goods. The French luxury house confirmed the shift on this week, just ahead of a European Union prohibition on the destruction of unsold apparel, clothing accessories and footwear coming into force for for large companies. Chanel’s confirmation came after evidence was heard in a Hong Kong criminal trial over 724 handbags and wallets earmarked for destruction in 2017. Prosecutors said that, back then, Chanel Hong Kong was disposing of 10,000 to 20,000 discontinued products every six months. However Chanel disputed this. “The figure mentioned during the trial does not reflect Chanel’s current global practices, which have evolved in line with its sustainability commitments,” the company said in a statement provided to WWD . Chanel said all products worldwide that cannot be commercialised, from deadstock to defective goods, are now managed through L’Atelier des Matières. An initiative created by Chanel in 2019, the business processes products for reuse within circular material supply chains. L’Atelier des Matières is part of Nevold, Chanel’s independent business-to-business hub for circular materials, which was formally launched in 2025. The luxury house put between €50 million and €80 million into its development Nevold also incorporates wool-spinning mill Filatures du Parc and upcycled natural-materials specialist Authentic Material. It was established separately from Chanel to supply recycled materials to other fashion companies and industrial sectors. Its products include thread combining virgin and end-of-life fibres, as well as recycled leather used for internal reinforcements in handbags and shoes. Around 30% of Chanel handbags and 50% of its shoes are said to contain these recycled components. Chanel’s current setup aligns with the EU’s Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation. Under the rules, large companies are barred from destroying unsold apparel, clothing accessories and footwear starting 19 July 2026, subject to specified exemptions. Companies must also disclose information about unsold consumer products discarded as waste. A standardised reporting format will apply from February 2027, while disclosure duties already cover large businesses. The European Commission estimates that between 4% and 9% of unsold textiles in Europe are destroyed before they are ever worn, creating about 5.6 million tonnes of CO₂ emissions. Medium-sized companies are due to come under the destruction ban in 2030. National authorities will oversee compliance, with exemptions covering circumstances such as safety concerns and product damage.

article_title: In Pictures: CDLP expands Essentials collection with Grey Melange launch
sub_title: Swedish menswear brand CDLP has introduced Grey Melange to its Essentials collection following years of material development to recreate the classic colourway in premium TENCEL™ Lyocell fabric.
article_content: Swedish menswear brand CDLP has introduced Grey Melange to its Essentials collection following years of material development to recreate the classic colourway in premium TENCEL™ Lyocell fabric. The new Grey Melange range marks the first time the brand has offered the shade across its signature TENCEL™ Lyocell essentials, including underwear, tank tops, T-shirts and socks. Long associated with athletic-inspired basics and everyday essentials, Grey Melange has traditionally been difficult to produce in premium TENCEL™ Lyocell due to technical limitations in the dyeing process. CDLP said it spent several years refining the material before successfully introducing the colourway to its core collection. To coincide with the launch, the brand has unveiled a new campaign starring British dancer, performer and model Sam Salter. Shot in a South London laundromat, the campaign celebrates the simplicity and versatility of wardrobe staples while highlighting the new addition to the Essentials range. Sam Salter said: “I have always been a fan of CDLP. They prove simplicity is the key and you don’t always have to do the most to have great style. The quality, detail, cut and fit make the brand a personal stand-out for me.” Christian Larson, co-founder and creative director of CDLP, sa id: “Sam is the perfect person to introduce it - confident, charismatic, and full of joy. His effortless authenticity aligns perfectly with the spirit of CDLP.” Founded in Stockholm in 2016, CDLP specialises in elevated everyday essentials made using responsibly sourced materials, with TENCEL™ Lyocell remaining a core component of its product offering. The latest launch expands the brand’s permanent Essentials collection with one of the most recognisable colourways in underwear. The launch reflects continued investment in product innovation as premium apparel brands look to differentiate core essentials through fabric development and material performance, while responding to consumer demand for elevated everyday basics.

Stella McCartney and pushchair brand Bugaboo unveil multi-year partnership
sub_title: British fashion house Stella McCartney has partnered with premium pushchair brand Bugaboo on a special-edition collection launching globally in September 2026.
article_content: British fashion house Stella McCartney has partnered with premium pushchair brand Bugaboo on a special-edition collection launching globally in September 2026. The agreement marks the start of a multi-year partnership focused on parenting products that combine fashion, functionality and lower-impact materials. It is Bugaboo’s first major collaboration in more than 10 years, following previous projects with fashion brands including Missoni and Kith. The Amsterdam-founded company expects the partnership to strengthen its position among design-conscious parents while extending its reach within fashion and culture. Stella McCartney said: “As a mother, I want the things I design to reflect the world I want to build. Working with Bugaboo felt completely natural, as it’s a brand that shares our commitment to innovation and responsibility. “This collection is for every mum who wants to bring her own individuality and playfulness into parenthood.” The companies said the collection will use recycled polyester fabrics made from plastic bottles, water-free dye technology, recycled aluminium and bio-based materials. The materials are intended to reduce environmental impact while maintaining product quality and performance. Responsible materials have long been central to Stella McCartney’s brand positioning. In May, the latest H&M collaboration included recycled content , organic cotton and wool that was certified to the Responsible Wool Standard, plus coated materials made using industrial corn and recycled vegetable oil. The fashion house also recently announced a new licensing partnership for the development, production and distribution of Stella McCartney Kids with Altana, which also develops kidswear for Moschino, CP Company and Paul & Shark. That licensing partnership covers the childrenswear line’s production chain while keeping design under Stella McCartney’s in-house team. Founded in Amsterdam, Bugaboo built its premium position around engineering-led pushchairs and design. The Stella McCartney deal forms part of a wider strategy to develop collaborations and link parenting products more closely with personal style. Adriaan Thierry, CEO of Bugaboo, said modern parents expect their purchases to reflect both their design preferences and values. “Stella has transformed expectations around luxury fashion and responsible design, while Bugaboo has spent more than two decades redefining mobility for parents through category-leading innovation,” he said. “By combining Stella McCartney’s distinctive creative perspective with Bugaboo’s heritage of purposeful design and engineering excellence, we’ve created a collection that speaks to a new generation of parents who refuse to choose between performance, style and values.” The collaboration gives Stella McCartney a route into the parenting category beyond childrenswear, while providing Bugaboo with access to the designer’s global fashion audience. The first products from the partnership will become available worldwide in September 2026.

article_title: Price beats ethics at the checkout for majority of Brits
sub_title: Over two-thirds (68%) of Brits say ethical production matters to them, but when it came to their last actual purchase, the single most common behaviour was ignoring ethics altogether and buying based on price or quality alone.
article_content: Over two-thirds (68%) of Brits say ethical production matters to them, but when it came to their last actual purchase, the single most common behaviour was ignoring ethics altogether and buying based on price or quality alone. That’s according to new research from supply chain intelligence firm Zero100, which tested the extent to which customers are willing to pay more for a more ethical option across clothing, toiletries, household goods, and food. The research found that shoppers are willing to stretch to around 8% more (80p on a £10 purchase) for an ethical or more sustainable product before defaulting to the cheaper option, while more than a quarter (28%) will not pay a penny extra. At around 8%, the premium ceiling is tight enough that any significant cost increase - whether caused by supply chain disruption, a change in sourcing or reformulation - can push a product out of reach for most shoppers. For clothing alone, just 12% of respondents in a survey of 2,000 UK adults (conducted in April 2026 by OnePoll on behalf of Zero100) chose the most ethical option regardless of cost. Choosing based on price or quality alone, with no ethical consideration, was the single most common behaviour across every category: 40% for clothing, 42% for toiletries, 42% for household goods, and 43% for food and drink. In each category, only between 7% and 10% of respondents said they actively considered the ethical option before choosing the cheaper alternative instead. Jenna Fink, VP of Research & Advisory at Zero100, said: “British consumers haven’t tuned out on sustainability; the data shows clearly that it matters to them. But caring about something and being willing to pay more are two different things. “The brands that understand this are shifting how they think about the problem entirely. Sustainability is a cost to engineer out, not a premium to charge for.” The strongest commercial argument for getting this right may lie in Zero100’s own company performance data. An analysis of 469 businesses found that those embedding sustainability into their core operations – meaning sustainability accountability sits within day-to-day business functions rather than in a separate team or initiative – generate roughly 23% higher operating profits and 20% higher net profits than those that do not. What keeps British shoppers loyal, even as prices rise, is quality, with 63% of respondents saying that product and service excellence would retain their custom even if a brand’s prices increased. This points to a consistent theme running through the data: what retains customers is not ethical positioning, but operational performance. Most UK shoppers are also more forgiving about price rises than brands might assume. Only 27% say that price increases directly linked to supply chain pressures are unfair, suggesting that when businesses are honest and specific about why costs are rising, most shoppers are more understanding than brands might expect. Transparency campaigns may also be delivering less than brands hope. While 36% of UK consumers say that knowing more about a brand’s supply chain would make them more likely to trust its ethical claims, nearly half (48%) have never actually checked for that information before making a purchase. The data also points to consumers being under genuine financial pressure rather than simply not caring. Fink added: “The data tells a more human story than the headline numbers suggest. Many British shoppers are actively choosing between their values and their budgets every time they shop, and the budget is winning, often because the gap between the ethical option and the affordable one remains too wide. “The brands that close that gap through smarter operational decisions are the ones that will win lasting loyalty, not just from shoppers who can afford to pay more, but from the much larger group who want to, but can't.”
